How a GPU Works, and How to Optimize Its Performance

Using one H200 as the example, we zoom from a whole large model down to a single instruction and bit: how the GPU works, where the time goes, and how to make it faster.

A draft GPU tutorial, under review round by round. Every figure is interactive: press the buttons, drag the timeline.

1What Questions Does This Book Answer, and With Which Example?

In this book, we follow one sentence through a 62-layer large language model, derive the three inference regimes, and then open up one layer to see how the hardware runs it and how to push it as fast as it can go.

That comes down to three questions. First, once a sentence enters the model, what steps turn it into the next token? Second, the model has only one set of fixed parameters (called weights), so why does running it to generate output (called inference) split into three regimes? Those regimes are prefill (processing the whole known input at once), decode (token-by-token decoding, generating 1 new token at a time), and verify (speculative decoding verification: guessing a few tokens first and checking them all in one pass). Primer 1, Sections 5 to 7 cover all three. Third, when we open up one layer, what does each step compute, what does it hand to the next step, and how do we push it, step by step, close to the shortest time the hardware allows?

The whole book uses only one example: the 62-layer Muse Spark Open. It is an open-weight Mixture of Experts (MoE) large language model with about 816 billion total parameters, where each layer picks only a few small expert networks out of many to run (see Primer 1, Section 2). Our task comes from a public GPU performance optimization competition. Muse Spark Open runs across 8 NVIDIA H200s (a data-center GPU), and we write the GPU program for one layer on a single card. For each layer type, the task gives the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow, called the lower bound. You can calculate the non-expert part of that bound directly from the full-layer rules in Primer 2, Section 4. The expert part is whatever is left after you subtract everything else from the given bound (see Primer 2, Section 1). We first take apart every step of that single layer on one H200. Then, at the end of Chapter 9, we add the 62 measured single-layer times back up into a full decode pass and state which parts are measured and which are not measured (for how the 8 GPUs split the work, see the opening of Primer 1).

We wrote this book for engineers and students who want to make large language model inference run fast or understand low-level GPU performance. By the end, you will be able to break down one layer's execution time across its stages and calculate whether each step is memory-bound or compute-bound, read GPU machine instructions to locate where time is going, and judge whether a code change pays off or is a net loss at the current token count.

2In What Order Does the Book Dissect the System?

We zoom in through the profiler's six levels, from coarse to fine. Each chapter opens up the part we saw in the previous chapter, and a single matrix-vector multiplication ties the evolution together from chapter to chapter.

The opening three chapters are Primers (Primer 1 to Primer 3), which look in turn at the full model, a single layer, and a minimal GPU program (kernel; see Primer 3). Then we enter Part I (Chapters 1–6), which maps to Level 1 through Level 6 of a profiler (a performance profiling tool that measures the latency and utilization of each hardware unit): Chapter 1 starts at the execution timeline, and each subsequent chapter zooms in one level deeper.

One worked example runs through all of Part I. It is the first matrix multiplication in a layer when the input has only 1 token, which makes it a matrix-vector multiplication, gemv (one matrix times one vector; see Primer 2, Section 2). Primer 3 writes its first version, and each of Chapters 1–6 uses that chapter's new mechanism to make it one step faster. Multi-token GEMM, at 8 to 256 tokens, needs mechanisms that are not all in place until Chapter 6, so we walk through its full evolution in one go in the final section of Chapter 6.

Part II (Chapters 7–9) returns to a layer's two main operators and the full-layer assembly. The two operators are attention, which looks across the context, and Mixture of Experts (MoE), which picks experts to compute for each token (see Primer 1, Section 2 for what they are). The two operators and the full-layer assembly each walk their own evolution chain from slow to fast, and the end of Chapter 9 adds the measured single-layer time back up into the full 62-layer decode pass. In Part III, Chapter 10 summarizes how to take a slow kernel and track down its bottleneck one level at a time. Finally, Appendix A explains what changes in hardware from H200 to the next-generation NVIDIA GPU (B200), Appendix B provides a quick-reference table of machine instructions (the low-level instructions the GPU actually executes), and Appendix C provides the glossary and term index.

4What Prerequisites Do You Need, and What Can You Skip on a First Read?

You only need to know how to read C/C++, multiply matrices, and understand CPU caches and multithreading; we build every GPU concept from scratch.

Before starting this book, you need only four things:

  • Reading C/C++: pointers, arrays, loops, and functions;
  • Multiplying matrices and computing vector dot products;
  • Knowing what a CPU cache is: a small, fast copy of memory sitting close to the compute core;
  • Knowing that multiple threads can read and write the same memory at the same time, and that doing so can cause errors.

You do not need any prior GPU background. Primer 3 writes our first CUDA GPU program from scratch, and Chapters 1–6 open up the GPU hardware one level at a time. Chapter 2, Section 6 explains when data written by one GPU thread becomes visible to other threads, and compares that behavior with common desktop and server CPUs (x86). And you do not need an H200 on hand to read this book.

On a first read, you can skip three parts and come back to them when you need them:

  • The one-line cost breakdown under each step caption in the interactive figures;
  • Multi-token GEMM in the final section of Chapter 6 (Section 8), which draws on all the mechanisms from Chapters 1–6;
  • Chapter 10 and the three appendices, which are meant for reference.

5How Do You Use the Figures and Charts in This Book?

Every figure draws the real hardware units and data paths, and you step through them using the buttons and sliders outside the figure. We plot every measured result as a chart and state how it was measured.

Each interactive figure in this book opens right in the middle of an active execution step. You can use the buttons outside the figure to switch modes, or drag the slider to walk through execution one step at a time; each step's caption card lists the formula, the inputs (tensor shape, data type, and where they live), the outputs (where they are written), what gets handed to the next step, and a single line for the cost of that step.

We plot latencies, speedups, and before-and-after comparisons as charts right under the paragraph they belong to, without separate figure numbers. The main text states only the conclusion and at most one key number. Primer 3, Section 5 and Chapter 10 explain how we measure latencies in this book. Each chart's note states in only one sentence how that chart was measured, and we do not mix results from different measurement setups in the same chart. Finally, the lower-bound line in a chart shows the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow; it is calculated, not measured (see Primer 2, Section 4).

This book works at two reading speeds: skim only the section headings, the bold sentences, and the figure readouts to catch the mechanism of each section, or read the full text to follow one causal chain through the entire derivation.

6How Are Units, Terms, and Formulas Written Throughout This Book?

  • Units: We use decimal units (MB, GB, TB/s) for device memory capacity, weight size, and bandwidth (bytes transferred per second), and binary units (KiB, MiB) for on-chip storage and tile sizes. Memory vendors quote bandwidth in decimal units, whereas on-chip storage is aligned to powers of 2.
  • Token: Throughout this book, we call the basic unit processed by the model a token, and do not shorten it to "word."
  • Operator and kernel: An "operator" is one computation step in the model (such as a single matrix multiplication); we call the function that implements it on the GPU a kernel throughout this book (not a "core"). One operator can be implemented by one or several kernels.
  • Single layer and full model: "single layer" means one decoder layer on a single GPU, with time measured in µs; "full model" means the complete 62-layer network, with time measured in ms.
  • Speedup notation: "~XXX× faster" and "a ~XXX× speedup" mean old time ÷\div÷ new time (the ratio, without subtracting 1). "X%X\%X% faster" means old time ÷\div÷ new time −1- 1−1, and a latency drop is written as "takes X%X\%X% less time."
  • Formulas and tensor shapes: We typeset formulas in math notation; a multidimensional array of numbers is called a tensor, and we write a tensor shape as W :  [rows,  columns]  BF16\shape{W}{\text{rows},\;\text{columns}}{BF16}W:[rows,columns]BF16—the tensor name, the length of each dimension in square brackets, and the element data type in the subscript (for example, BF16 stands for 16-bit floating point, and we explain each data type the first time it appears).
  • Chinese and English terms: We explain each English technical term the first time it appears, and Appendix C at the end of the book provides the glossary and term index.

Takeaway: This book follows a single model on a single H200 from start to finish: first we trace how one sentence passes through the entire model, and then we open up one layer level by level down to instructions and bits.

When you feed a sentence into the 62-layer Muse Spark Open, what steps turn it into the next token? And if the weights are the exact same, why do we split inference into three regimes: prefill, decode, and verify? Let's answer the second question first, because the reason is simple: on every forward pass (when running only a few tokens), a single GPU has to stream about 9.0 GB of fixed weights out of device memory. You pay that read cost per pass, not per token. How many known tokens you have in hand before the pass starts decides which regime you run.

The model runs across 8 H200 GPUs (an NVIDIA data-center GPU), and each GPU stores and computes only a slice of each layer's weights (Primer 2, Section 1 shows how we slice them). Throughout this book, we look at only one of those GPUs. The cross-GPU communication that sums or concatenates results across the 8 GPUs stays out of our single-GPU ledger, and we did not measure it either (Primer 2, Section 2 shows where each layer exchanges data). Figure P1-1 lays out the whole model from input to output. This chapter and Primer 2 will unpack every block in turn; for now, let's trace the order they run in.

1Inbound: How Does One Sentence Become the Two Inputs to Layer 0?

We first split a sentence into integer token IDs and look up their vectors; after RMSNorm, we get Layer 0's two inputs: 32-bit stream_0 and 16-bit x_0.

A GPU only crunches arrays of numbers. So in Step 1 of Figure P1-2, we first split the input sentence into tokens and map each one to its integer ID in the 202,048-entry vocabulary. We call the full trip from embedding lookup all the way to scoring every candidate in the vocabulary one forward pass (or one pass for short), and we write T for the number of tokens processed together in that pass (our running example in this chapter uses a 5-token prompt, so T = 5). Those T IDs form a 1D array ids of shape [T][T][T].

The model represents every token with 8,192 numbers. That width is the hidden size, and every 8192 you see in the tensor shapes below is that same dimension. In Step 2, we use ids to look up the embedding table Wembed :  [202048,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{embed}}{202048,\;8192}{BF16}Wembed​:[202048,8192]BF16, where BF16 is 16-bit floating point (2 bytes per number). Note that this lookup is not a matrix multiplication: it just grabs the T rows indexed by ids and writes them out as e :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{e}{T,\;8192}{BF16}e:[T,8192]BF16. Each GPU stores only about 1/8 of the embedding table's rows. Whenever an ID falls outside a GPU's local 1/8 slice, that GPU fills the row with zeros, and all 8 GPUs then sum their local eee tensors so every GPU has the complete eee. Because the lookup reads only these T rows, it does not count toward the fixed weights we have to read on every pass in Section 4.

Next, we turn eee into Layer 0's two inputs. RMSNorm (root mean square normalization) divides a vector vvv by the square root of the mean of its squared elements, RMSNorm(v)=v/1n∑ivi2+ϵ\mathrm{RMSNorm}(v) = v / \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i v_i^2 + \epsilon}RMSNorm(v)=v/n1​∑i​vi2​+ϵ​ (where ϵ\epsilonϵ is a tiny constant to avoid dividing by zero), keeping the numerical range stable. Weighted RMSNorm does that same division and then multiplies elementwise by a learned scale vector of the same length, with a separate scale vector learned at each site that uses one. The RMSNorm right after embedding lookup does not multiply by a scale vector: it divides and immediately casts to FP32 (32-bit floating point, 4 bytes per number) to produce stream0 :  [T,  8192]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{stream}_0}{T,\;8192}{FP32}stream0​:[T,8192]FP32. Later layers never overwrite this tensor—they add their outputs onto it (Primer 2, Section 2 shows how), which is why we call it the residual stream, written stream. In the source code, this post-embedding normalization is called embed_norm. It runs only once at the very start, leaving each token's vector with an RMS of about 1, and from that point on the residual stream itself is never normalized again.

Why keep two copies of the state at different precisions? Because all 62 layers add their outputs into the same stream, we store the residual stream in 32-bit FP32, which keeps more significant digits than 16-bit formats. Inside each layer, though, the matrix multiplications take 16-bit BF16 inputs so they read half as many bytes and run faster. That is why at the end of Step 2 we copy stream_0, run a weighted RMSNorm on the copy, and cast it to BF16 to get Layer 0's matrix-multiplication input x0 :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_0}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x0​:[T,8192]BF16 (input_layernorm in the source code). Every layer prepares its input the exact same way—copy the residual stream and normalize the copy, leaving the residual stream itself untouched. Starting from Layer 1, Layer l−1 computes this input for Layer l at the end of its own final stage, using Layer l's scale vector (Primer 2, Section 2). So the two normalizations at the start are not doing duplicate work: the first sets the starting scale of the residual stream, and the second prepares the input to Layer 0. Throughout the book, we write stream_l and x_l for these two inputs to Layer l.

Each layer merges results back into the residual stream twice (Primer 2, Section 2 gives the equation). At each merge, we normalize the new term to an RMS of about 1 and multiply it elementwise by β\betaβ, while multiplying the existing residual stream elementwise by α\alphaα. Both α\alphaα and β\betaβ are 8,192-element vectors derived from a learned vector at that merge site (this book leaves out the exact formula). At every coordinate iii, they satisfy αi2+βi2=1\alpha_i^2 + \beta_i^2 = 1αi2​+βi2​=1; only when βi\beta_iβi​ gets extremely close to 1 does αi\alpha_iαi​ hit a floor of about 0.03, nudging the identity slightly off. Because the first normalization already set Layer 0's residual stream to an RMS of about 1, as long as the two terms being combined are roughly uncorrelated and each has a similar magnitude across all 8,192 coordinates, their sum keeps an RMS of about 1 too. Every merge follows this rule, so the residual stream stays near the same scale all the way through 62 layers (we did not measure those two statistical conditions).

2Passing Through 62 Layers: What Goes to the Next Layer, and What Stays for Future Tokens?

Vertically, each layer hands the updated stream and x down to the next layer; horizontally, it writes each token's key and value into the layer's KV cache for future tokens to read.

Why does every layer stash its keys and values in memory? When a token enters Layer l, it first projects x_l into three vectors: a query Q, a key K, and a value V. It takes the dot product of its own Q against the K of itself and every earlier token to get a list of similarity scores sis_isi​, runs softmax (pi=esi/∑jesjp_i = e^{s_i} / \sum_j e^{s_j}pi​=esi​/∑j​esj​) to turn those scores into weights that sum to 1, and computes a weighted sum of those tokens' V vectors—that step is attention. Because each token looks only at itself and earlier tokens, we call it causal attention. Here is the key observation: once an earlier token's K and V are computed, they never change, yet every future token will need to read them again. Accordingly, each layer stores the computed K and V in its own region of device memory—the KV cache, written K_cache[l] and V_cache[l].

Click Step 3 in Figure P1-2 and you can see the handoff: each Layer l (l = 0..60) passes stream_{l+1} and x_{l+1} down to the next layer. Only the final layer (l = 61) is an exception—with no next layer after it, it outputs only stream_{62} and skips computing x.

K and V come from multiplying x by a narrower weight matrix, so they are much narrower than x. We slice them into chunks of 64 numbers, where each chunk is one key-value head (KV head). We slice Q into 64-wide query heads the same way, and several query heads share a single KV head as each one runs the attention step above (Primer 2, Section 1 shows how many query heads share each KV head and how they are grouped). Each layer has 16 KV heads in total, so across 8 GPUs each GPU handles 2 of them.

Every number in the KV cache is stored in FP8 (8-bit floating point, 1 byte per number). On a single GPU, the cache space that one token takes up in one layer is called one slot (KV cache slot), which comes to 2 (K, V)×2 (heads)×64×1 B=256 B2\ (K,\ V) \times 2\ (\text{heads}) \times 64 \times 1\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{B}2 (K, V)×2 (heads)×64×1 B=256 B.

The second half of every layer is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) block: each layer has 256 experts, and each GPU holds 32 of them (its local experts). Each expert is a feed-forward network (FFN) with 3 weight matrices: the first two each project the input into a vector, one passes through an elementwise nonlinearity to act as a gate that multiplies the other elementwise, and the third matrix projects that product back out. Before the experts run, a tiny scoring matrix scores all 256 experts; each token routes to only its top 8 experts and takes a score-weighted sum of their outputs (see Primer 2, Section 2). Framing the experts are two shared matrices that every token passes through: one squeezes the vector narrower before the experts, and the other widens it back to 8,192 dimensions afterward (Primer 2, Section 1 gives their shapes).

Across all 62 layers, two things change from layer to layer. First is how far back attention looks: 46 sliding-window layers look only at the most recent 2,048 positions, while 16 full-attention layers attend to the entire history from the very start. Second is how expert weights are stored: the middle 60 layers compress their experts to 4-bit precision at 28.3 MB per expert, while the first and last layers leave them uncompressed (Primer 2, Section 1 shows how 28.3 MB is calculated).

3Outbound and Loopback: How Do 8,192 Numbers Turn Back into a Token ID?

After the final RMSNorm, we pick out only the rows that need a prediction, score all 202,048 vocabulary candidates to get logits, and feed the chosen token ID back to Step 2 (embedding lookup).

In Step 4 of Figure P1-2, once all 62 layers finish, we cast all T rows of stream_{62} to BF16 and run them through a weighted final RMSNorm. Only then do we pick out the rows that actually need a next-token prediction; call that row count R (because RMSNorm works row by row, normalizing before or after picking rows gives the exact same result). During prefill, the prompt already tells us the next token for positions 1–4, so we take only the last row (R = 1); during decode, we only have 1 row to begin with (R = 1); and during verify, we check predictions across all 8 positions at once, so we keep all 8 rows (R = 8; see Section 7). Those R rows form hfinal :  [R,  8192]  BF16\shape{h_{final}}{R,\;8192}{BF16}hfinal​:[R,8192]BF16.

Step 5 runs lm_head (vocabulary projection, the matrix that scores every candidate token in the vocabulary). We split the vocabulary evenly by rows across the 8 GPUs, so each GPU holds about one eighth—Wlm :  [≈25k,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{lm}}{\approx 25\text{k},\;8192}{BF16}Wlm​:[≈25k,8192]BF16, or 0.414 GB. Each GPU multiplies h_final by its local shard to get its slice of logits z :  [R,  vocabulary/8]  FP32\shape{z}{R,\;\text{vocabulary}/8}{FP32}z:[R,vocabulary/8]FP32, and the 8 GPUs concatenate their slices into the full 202,048-candidate scores. Notice the contrast with Step 2: inbound embedding lookup fetches only T rows by index, whereas outbound scoring has to take the dot product of every candidate with h_final. Regardless of R, every forward pass has to stream the entire 0.414 GB local shard.

Step 6 applies the logit softcap: we multiply each score by a fixed scale factor sss and pass it through c⋅tanh⁡(⋅/c)c\cdot\tanh(\cdot / c)c⋅tanh(⋅/c) (where sss and ccc are model constants) to smoothly cap every score inside [−c, c][-c,\ c][−c, c] so no single score blows up. Once capped, these RRR rows of unnormalized candidate scores are called logits, with shape logits :  [R,  202048]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{logits}}{R,\;202048}{FP32}logits:[R,202048]FP32.

In Step 7, we select the new token ID next_id from logits (this book leaves out the sampling rules). Step 8 feeds next_id right back into Step 2 (embedding lookup) as the row index for the next pass, so from this point on we never run the tokenizer again.

We call the number of valid slots in the KV cache the committed sequence length, and the next pass writes its first new token at position (committed sequence length +1+ 1+1). Prefill advances the committed sequence length by T (5 in our example, so the next pass starts at position 6), decode advances it by 1, and verify advances it by however many tokens get accepted in that pass (Section 7).

4Forward-Pass Accounting: What Is the Minimum Number of Bytes One GPU Must Read per Pass, and How Long Does That Take?

When you run only a few tokens, every pass still streams ~9.0 GB of fixed weights plus 28.3 MB per active compressed expert, while the KV cache traffic for those few tokens is negligible.

A GPU's main device memory is HBM (High Bandwidth Memory); bandwidth is how many bytes it can move per second, and the H200 has a nominal peak HBM bandwidth of 4.8 TB/s. Because the weights on a single GPU add up to several gigabytes, they cannot fit on the chip itself—so every forward pass has to stream them fresh from HBM (Chapter 2, Section 2 covers how much fits on-chip).

Before we compare the three regimes, let's do the math on what a single forward pass has to read from HBM. The bill breaks into three parts, starting with the fixed weights you pay for on every pass. Matrices that every token passes through—without any token-dependent routing—are called dense matrices, and each layer has 5 of them: the projection matrix for Q, K, V, and gating values (a set of scaling coefficients; see Primer 2, Section 2), the attention output matrix, the router scoring matrix for the experts, and the two matrices that squeeze the vector narrower before the experts and widen it back up afterward.

Across the three regimes in this chapter, our GPU reads 138.4 MB of dense weights per layer (Primer 2, Section 1 breaks down each matrix), or 8.58 GB across all 62 layers; add the 0.414 GB local shard of lm_head from Section 3 and the total comes to 8.995 GB (about 9.0 GB). Here is the catch: whether you feed 1 token in a pass or batch 5 or 8 tokens side by side, you still read that exact same 9.0 GB.

Even if the GPU did nothing else at all, just streaming those fixed weights into the chip takes at least 8.995 GB÷4.8 TB/s≈1.87 ms8.995\ \mathrm{GB} \div 4.8\ \mathrm{TB/s} \approx 1.87\ \mathrm{ms}8.995 GB÷4.8 TB/s≈1.87 ms (before counting experts or cross-GPU communication).

The second part of the bill is the expert weights, which you pay for based on how many experts the pass actually touches. Across the middle 60 layers, each local expert you touch adds 28.3 MB of reads; touching 1 local expert per layer on average across those 60 layers adds 60×28.3 MB≈1.7 GB60 \times 28.3\ \mathrm{MB} \approx 1.7\ \mathrm{GB}60×28.3 MB≈1.7 GB, or about 0.354 ms at 4.8 TB/s. The experts in the first and last layers are uncompressed at about 100.7 MB each (Primer 2, Section 1); we set them aside for now, so 1.7 GB counts only the middle 60 layers rather than all expert reads. When a pass runs only 1 token, each GPU touches 1 local expert on average, but whichever GPU lands the most local experts in that layer touches more than 1. We call that GPU the busiest GPU, or straggler rank (when a pass runs multiple tokens, it is defined as the GPU receiving the most (token, expert) pairs). Primer 2, Section 1 shows how many local experts the busiest GPU touches per layer on average, and how the benchmark lower bound counts them. As a pass processes more tokens together, it touches more experts overall, though different tokens often land on the same expert and share a single read of its weights.

The third part is the KV cache, at 256 B per visible historical token in each layer (Section 2). Even the largest pass in this chapter (verify in Section 7) reads only a dozen or so slots per layer. That is well inside Section 2's 2,048-token sliding window, so sliding-window layers and full-attention layers read the exact same number of slots here: less than 0.21 MB across all 62 layers, which is a rounding error next to 9.0 GB. That holds only while the history is short, though; once the history reaches tens of thousands of tokens, the picture changes (Primer 2, Section 5).

Once we stream all those weights into the chip, how much math do we actually do on them? We write FLOP for floating-point operations, counting one multiply-add as 2 FLOPs. A single BF16 weight takes up 2 bytes, and each of the T tokens in the pass does one multiply-add with it for a total of 2T2T2T FLOPs—which works out to about T FLOPs for every 1 byte of BF16 weight read. Meanwhile, in the time it takes an H200 to read 1 byte from HBM, its compute units can execute hundreds of FLOPs (Primer 2, Section 4 gives the exact number). So when T is small, the compute units spend almost all their time sitting idle waiting on HBM; Primer 2, Section 5 shows how large T has to grow to flip that balance.

5Prefill: Why Can Known Tokens Run in Parallel in a Single Pass?

Under causal attention, each token uses only its own and earlier tokens' keys and values—all computed in the same pass—so we can stack all 5 tokens into a matrix and run them together.

When a user first submits a prompt, the pass that processes it is called prefill. Because all 5 tokens at positions 1–5 are already in hand before computation starts (T = 5), there is no need to feed them one by one: we stack all 5 rows directly into xl :  [5,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{5,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[5,8192]BF16 and push them through side by side, so each weight matrix multiplies a 5-row matrix at once instead of multiplying a single vector across 5 separate passes.

On this pass, each layer writes 5 slots (5×256 B5 \times 256\ \mathrm{B}5×256 B) into its KV cache, and because the cache starts out empty, it reads no prior history. Once all 5 rows finish Layer 61, we take only the last row (R = 1, Section 3) to predict token 6. Look at the bill for this pass: because all 5 tokens share the same fixed-weight read, each token pays an amortized cost of only about 1.80 GB, and we do about 5 FLOPs per byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). When a prompt is very long, we slice it into chunks and run them across several passes (Primer 2, Section 5).

6Decode: Why Can Each Pass Process Only 1 Token, and What Is Its Bottleneck?

Token 7 does not exist until token 6 is generated, so decode can feed only 1 token per pass while still re-reading all the fixed weights—doing only ~1 FLOP per byte read.

Once prefill produces token 6 and we move on to generating token 7 and token 8, the picture changes completely. A large language model generates text autoregressively: producing each new token requires computing over all preceding tokens. Until we finish computing token 7, token 8 does not exist yet. So from this step on, we enter decode (token-by-token decoding), where the input to each pass shrinks to just the single token we just generated, token 6 (T = 1). Each layer writes 1 new slot into the KV cache and reads 6 slots in total—that new slot plus the 5 slots left behind by prefill—before finishing Layer 61 with R = 1 to produce token 7. Put decode next to prefill and the bottleneck jumps right out: to generate that 1 token, the fixed-weight read per token shoots up 5× (9.0 GB vs. 1.80 GB). As noted at the start of the chapter, we count only the bytes that a single GPU reads from HBM here, leaving cross-GPU communication out of the ledger.

When many requests are active online at the same time, we can batch each request's 1 new token into a single pass so they all share that one read of the fixed weights. Up to 8 merged tokens, those fixed weights stay at about 9.0 GB; past 8 tokens, one dense matrix switches to having every GPU read a full copy, bumping the fixed weights to about 12.6 GB, after which they stop growing with the token count (Primer 2, Section 1). Because every request has its own history, each one still reads its own KV cache; once the fixed weights are paid for, each extra merged request adds only its own KV reads and any additional experts it touches. As long as the pass is still waiting on HBM, its runtime is governed mainly by how many bytes it reads. Sharing the fixed weights means pass latency grows much more slowly than the request count—though it does not stay flat, since the dense matrix that switches to a full read above 8 tokens, the extra experts touched, and each request's own KV cache all add bytes. Under the benchmark's single-layer lower bounds, batching 16 requests instead of 1 raises throughput by about 8× on sliding-window layers and about 5× on full-attention layers (Primer 2, Section 5 covers how multiple requests merge into one pass and how latency and bottlenecks shift).

7Verify: How Can One Request Yield More Than 1 Token in a Single Pass?

We first draft 7 candidate tokens, stack them with the known token 6 into an 8-row pass, and compare left to right up to the first mismatch—getting 1 to 8 tokens in a single pass.

If running 1 token for a single request streams 9.0 GB of fixed weights, and running 8 tokens side by side streams that exact same 9.0 GB, can we pack 8 tokens into a single pass for one request too? That is the idea behind verify (speculative decoding verification). It is not a step that runs after decode, but an alternative way to run decode: it starts from the exact same post-prefill state, with 5 slots in the KV cache and token 6 already known. A separate drafting mechanism (such as a small draft model, or drafter) first proposes 7 candidate tokens for positions 7 through 13, called draft tokens. Right or wrong, all 8 tokens are concrete numbers before the pass begins—so just like prefill (Section 5), we stack them into xl :  [8,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{8,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[8,8192]BF16 (T = 8) and push them through all 62 layers in a single pass. Each layer writes 8 slots into the KV cache and reads 13 slots in total (including the existing 5 slots), and at the end we send all 8 rows into lm_head (R = 8) so we can check the prediction at every row.

Why can a single pass verify all 7 guesses at once? Because under causal attention, row i looks only at the first i rows (Section 2). That means the output of row i (i = 1..8) is the large model's prediction for position 6 + i, assuming the draft tokens at positions 7 through 5 + i are all correct. In particular, row 1 depends only on the known tokens 1–6 and on no draft tokens at all, so its prediction for position 7 is guaranteed to be valid.

To keep the accounting concrete, let's assume greedy decoding where we always pick the highest-scoring token (if serving uses probabilistic sampling, acceptance switches to a probabilistic rule as well, which this book leaves out). Walking from left to right, we compare the large model's predictions against the draft tokens one by one: we accept every draft token before the first mismatch, and at the first mismatch we reject that draft token and directly adopt the large model's own prediction for that position. That way, even if all 7 draft tokens miss, the pass is still guaranteed to yield token 7; if the first k draft tokens match, the pass yields k + 1 tokens in one shot (up to 8).

What about the KV cache slots that the rejected draft tokens already wrote across all 62 layers? We just leave them where they are: the committed sequence length advances only by k + 1, and later passes read only up to the committed sequence length, so those rejected slots are never read and future passes simply overwrite them.

Look at the bill for this pass: we still stream the exact same 9.0 GB of fixed weights, doing about 8 FLOPs per byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). Spread across the k + 1 tokens produced by the pass, each token's share drops to 9.0 GB÷(k+1)9.0\ \mathrm{GB} \div (k + 1)9.0 GB÷(k+1)—falling from 9.0 GB when every draft token misses (k = 0) all the way down to 1.12 GB when all 7 hit (k = 7), as shown in the chart below.

Of course, verify comes with its own costs. Compared with decode, it pays three extra bills: the time to run the drafting mechanism itself, writing 7 extra KV slots and reading 7 extra KV slots per layer, and any extra local experts that 8 tokens may hit beyond a single token (adding 28.3 MB of reads per layer for each extra local expert hit). If the very first draft token misses, the pass yields only 1 token after paying all three extra bills, coming out slower than plain decode. Verify pays off only when the average number of tokens yielded per pass exceeds "(verify pass latency +++ drafting latency) ÷\div÷ decode pass latency"; we did not measure drafting latency or how many extra experts 8 tokens touch.

Once you see the full-model ledger across prefill, decode, and verify, it becomes clear why the next chapter can narrow its focus to just 1 layer. The three regimes differ only in how many tokens run side by side in a pass, and apart from the inbound embedding steps at the start and the outbound scoring steps at the end, the main body of every pass simply repeats the exact same single-layer structure 62 times: each layer takes (x_l, stream_l) from the layer before it, reads and writes its own KV cache, and hands the updated inputs to the next layer (Section 2). Once we open up 1 layer and understand what it computes and how many bytes it reads as T varies, we understand the main body of all 62 layers.

Takeaway: Every forward pass reads the fixed weights once, so how many tokens we can process in parallel in that pass defines the three regimes: prefill (batching known prompt tokens together), decode (generating 1 token at a time), and verify (drafting 7 candidate tokens and verifying them together).

Next chapter's question: If we open up any one of the 62 layers on a single H200, what steps does it break into, and what is the fastest that each step can run under decode and prefill?

In Primer 1, we treated every layer as a black box that takes in (xl, streaml)(x_l,\ \mathrm{stream}_l)(xl​, streaml​) and hands back (xl+1, streaml+1)(x_{l+1},\ \mathrm{stream}_{l+1})(xl+1​, streaml+1​). Now let's pry one of those boxes open: how fast can each stage inside a layer possibly run, and is it waiting on HBM bandwidth or on the Tensor Core (the dedicated on-chip unit for matrix multiply-accumulate)?

1Why Do the Matrices on a Single GPU Have These Shapes?

Eight GPUs split attention by head and experts by index, while keeping a full copy of three dense matrices on every GPU; for T≤8T \le 8T≤8, a single GPU reads 138.4 MB of dense weights per layer plus the weights of whichever local experts get routed.

Let's start with attention, which we slice across the 8 GPUs using TP8 (tensor parallelism: splitting the same matrix by head across 8 GPUs). Across the layer, Q has 128 query heads of width 64 (Primer 1, Section 2); divided across 8 GPUs, our GPU handles 16 query heads and 2 key-value heads. On our GPU, every 8 query heads share 1 key-value head—a layout called GQA (grouped-query attention; see Chapter 7, Section 2). Each query element also gets a gate value (a scaling factor that we will use in Section 2). Stack Q, K, V, and the gate together and our local projection matrix has 1,024+128+128+1,024=2,3041{,}024 + 128 + 128 + 1{,}024 = 2{,}3041,024+128+128+1,024=2,304 output rows: its shape is Wqkv :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{qkv}}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}Wqkv​:[2304,8192]BF16, taking 37.75 MB. Once attention finishes, the output matrix projects those 1,024 columns back to 8,192 dimensions with shape Wo :  [8192,  1024]  BF16\shape{W_o}{8192,\;1024}{BF16}Wo​:[8192,1024]BF16, taking another 16.8 MB.

Next, look at the experts, which we split across GPUs using EP8 (expert parallelism: assigning different experts to different GPUs). Splitting all 256 experts evenly across 8 GPUs puts 32 local experts on each GPU. Each expert takes a narrowed 4,096-dimensional vector as input (from the narrowing matrix pooler in the next paragraph). In Primer 1 we saw that each expert has 3 matrices; in code, we pack the first two side by side into a single matrix w13w_{13}w13​ that projects 4,096 dimensions to 8,192, with the first 4,096 columns holding the gate ggg and the last 4,096 columns holding uuu (Section 2, Stage 6 shows how they combine). The down projection w2w_2w2​ then maps 4,096 dimensions back to 4,096, so the two matrices together hold 3×409623 \times 4096^23×40962 weights. Across the middle 60 layers, expert weights are stored in NVFP4 (4-bit floating-point format): every 16 weights share a 1-byte scale factor while each weight's own 4 bits store its relative value, averaging 0.5625 B per weight (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout). That puts 1 compressed expert at 28.3 MB, whereas the first and last layers (layers 0 and 61) keep their experts in uncompressed 2-byte BF16 at 100.7 MB per expert.

Finally, three dense matrices are not partitioned across GPUs—every GPU stores a full copy of each. The small router matrix handles routing (picking experts for each token) by scoring all 256 experts; stored in 4-byte FP32 with shape Wrouter :  [256,  8192]  FP32\shape{W_{router}}{256,\;8192}{FP32}Wrouter​:[256,8192]FP32, it takes 8.4 MB. Before the experts, pooler (Wpool :  [4096,  8192]  BF16\shape{W_{pool}}{4096,\;8192}{BF16}Wpool​:[4096,8192]BF16) narrows 8,192 dimensions down to 4,096 and takes 67.1 MB. After the experts, unpooler (Wunpool :  [8192,  4096]  BF16\shape{W_{unpool}}{8192,\;4096}{BF16}Wunpool​:[8192,4096]BF16) widens 4,096 dimensions back up to 8,192, also at 67.1 MB.

There is a twist in how unpooler runs, though. When T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each GPU computes only 1/8 of the columns of output f (1,024 columns), reading only the corresponding 1,024 rows of WunpoolW_{unpool}Wunpool​ (8.4 MB) before an 8-GPU all-gather stitches the full T×8,192T \times 8{,}192T×8,192 result together. Once T>8T > 8T>8, each GPU simply reads the entire 67.1 MB matrix and computes all 8,192 columns locally, skipping that all-gather. Add up the exact byte counts of the five dense weight matrices a single GPU reads per layer at T≤8T \le 8T≤8 and you get 138.4 MB—the exact number we used in Primer 1. For T>8T > 8T>8, the dense weights read per layer jump to about 197.1 MB, or about 12.6 GB across all 62 layers plus lm_head.

Now let's work out how much expert weight data we read at T=1T = 1T=1. A single token picks 8 experts, so on average one GPU lands 8×32/256=1.08 \times 32 / 256 = 1.08×32/256=1.0 local expert. Because all 8 GPUs exchange expert results once per layer, though, any GPU that finishes early has to wait for the slowest one. What sets the layer's runtime is not the average GPU, but the busiest GPU—the GPU whose local experts receive the most (token, expert) hit pairs in that layer (at T=1T = 1T=1, that is simply the GPU that touches the most local experts). If a token picks its 8 experts uniformly at random, the busiest GPU out of the 8 touches about 2.56 local experts on average.

For a sliding-window layer at T=1T = 1T=1, the benchmark specification sets a lower bound (minimum execution time) of 40.0 µs (Section 4 defines the lower bound). Everything the layer reads outside the experts is easy to add up directly: 138.4 MB of dense weights, 2,048 sliding-window slots of historical KV cache (0.52 MB), and the layer's own inputs and outputs (reading and writing the FP32 stream and the BF16 x, about 0.1 MB). That comes to about 139 MB in total, or about 29 µs at 4.8 TB/s. Subtracting that leaves 11.03 µs (about 53 MB) in the lower bound for the experts, which works out to about 1.87 local experts. That 1.87 is not how many experts the busiest GPU actually touches. Because routing fluctuates around the mean from run to run, the benchmark's lower-bound formula counts only 75% of the mean number of distinct local experts touched on the busiest GPU so that the bound stays a lower bound. Divide 1.87 by 75% to work backward, and the busiest GPU actually touches about 2.5 local experts on average—right next to the 2.56 from uniform random selection. As for unpooler switching its read strategy at T=8T = 8T=8, the benchmark takes that threshold straight from the baseline inference code (the existing serving program for this model used as the timing baseline).

2What Does Each of the 8 Stages in a Layer Compute, and What Does It Pass to the Next Step?

Stages 1–3 compute attention and add the result back into the residual stream; Stages 4–8 split into two branches to select experts and project down the hidden dimension, merge at Stage 6, and add back into the residual stream.

Let's walk through the attention half of the layer first (you can click any stage in Figure P2-2 to see its full step card). Stage 1 (qkv_gate) multiplies qkv=xl Wqkv⊤\mathrm{qkv} = x_l\, W_{qkv}^{\top}qkv=xl​Wqkv⊤​: it takes xl :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x_l}{T,\;8192}{BF16}xl​:[T,8192]BF16 and produces qkv :  [T,  2304]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16}qkv:[T,2304]BF16, then slices that output by column into four pieces—q (1,024), k (128), v (128), and gate (1,024)—and hands them to Stage 2. When T=1T = 1T=1, this stage simplifies to a single matrix-vector multiplication y=Wxy = W xy=Wx (gemv), which we will use as our running example all the way through Part I.

Stage 2 (attention, gated attention; see Chapter 7, Section 1) starts by running per-head RMSNorm on q and k. In the 46 sliding-window layers, it then applies rotary position embedding (RoPE; the 16 full-attention layers skip RoPE): each pair of elements rotates by an angle set by the token position, so the position-dependent part of the q–k inner product depends only on how far apart the two tokens are. After that, it casts the freshly computed k and v down to 1-byte FP8 and writes them into the layer's KV cache.

Next, Stage 2 reads the visible historical KV cache—only the most recent 2,048 tokens in a sliding-window layer, or the entire history in a full-attention layer. Each query head takes its q, computes the inner product against every historical k in its shared key-value head, runs softmax (Primer 1, Section 2) to turn that row of scores into weights that sum to 1, and takes the weighted sum over the historical v vectors. One final per-head RMSNorm and an elementwise multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(\text{gate})σ(gate) (where σ\sigmaσ is the sigmoid function mapping values into 0..10..10..1) produces the attention output oattn :  [T,  1024]  BF16\shape{o_{attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16}oattn​:[T,1024]BF16 for Stage 3.

Stage 3 (o projection and first gated residual) multiplies the local GPU's 1,024-column attention output by WoW_oWo​ to get a=oattnWo⊤a = o_{attn} W_o^{\top}a=oattn​Wo⊤​, and all 8 GPUs sum their partial aaa tensors with an all-reduce to form the full a :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{a}{T,\;8192}{BF16}a:[T,8192]BF16. Next, we blend that summed aaa into the layer's incoming residual stream stream_in\mathrm{stream\_in}stream_in (that is, streaml\mathrm{stream}_lstreaml​): stream_mid=α1⊙stream_in+β1⊙RMSNorm(a)\mathrm{stream\_mid} = \alpha_1 \odot \mathrm{stream\_in} + \beta_1 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(a)stream_mid=α1​⊙stream_in+β1​⊙RMSNorm(a). Here α1\alpha_1α1​ and β1\beta_1β1​ are two length-8,192 FP32 coefficient vectors—one value per coordinate—derived from a length-8,192 vector learned for Stage 3 (satisfying α12+β12=1\alpha_1^2 + \beta_1^2 = 1α12​+β12​=1 elementwise; see Primer 1, Section 1). Because they do not depend on the token, we read them only once per layer. Finally, Stage 3 runs the pre-FFN normalization h=RMSNorm(stream_mid)⊙(1+wpre_ffn)h = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{stream\_mid}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}})h=RMSNorm(stream_mid)⊙(1+wpre_ffn​) and hands hhh to both Stage 4 and Stage 5: Stage 5 gets h :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{h}{T,\;8192}{BF16}h:[T,8192]BF16, whereas Stage 4 gets an FP32 copy of the same hhh when T≤8T \le 8T≤8 and shares the BF16 hhh when T>8T > 8T>8. Because the learned length-8,192 vector wpre_ffnw_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}}wpre_ffn​ stores an offset relative to 1, the formula multiplies by 1+wpre_ffn1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}}1+wpre_ffn​—the weighted RMSNorm from Primer 1.

At hhh, the dataflow forks into Stage 4 and Stage 5. Because neither branch depends on the other, they can run side by side (Chapter 9, Section 1 shows how we schedule them). One branch is Stage 4 (router), which scores all 256 experts as s=σ(cr⋅hWrouter⊤)s = \sigma(c_r \cdot h W_{router}^{\top})s=σ(cr​⋅hWrouter⊤​), where crc_rcr​ is a fixed scaling constant. For T≤8T \le 8T≤8, router runs in FP32 from start to finish; for T>8T > 8T>8 on H200, the baseline inference code splits the FP32 weights into high and low BF16 halves, runs two BF16 matrix multiplications, and accumulates the results in FP32. To pick the winning experts, we add a bias (router_bias, stored in the checkpoint) to each expert's score and take the top 8. That bias is used only to pick the winners; the final routing weights still come from the unbiased scores. Stage 4 hands two outputs to Stage 6: the chosen expert indices topk_ids :  [T,  8]  int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32}topk_ids:[T,8]int32 (int32 is a 32-bit integer, 4 bytes each) and the normalized routing weights topk_weights :  [T,  8]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32}topk_weights:[T,8]FP32 (the 8 selected unbiased scores divided by their sum).

The other branch is Stage 5 (pooler), which narrows the hidden state via p=RMSNorm(hWpool⊤)⊙(1+wpre_expert)p = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(h W_{pool}^{\top}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{pre\_expert}})p=RMSNorm(hWpool⊤​)⊙(1+wpre_expert​) and sends p :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16}p:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 6.

The two branches meet again at Stage 6 (expert stage; see Chapter 8, Section 1). Out of the 8 experts a token picks, we run only the ones that live on our GPU. For each local (token, expert eee) pair, we run four steps:

  1. Project gu=p W13,e⊤\mathrm{gu} = p\, W_{13,e}^{\top}gu=pW13,e⊤​ to get the first 4,096 columns ggg and the last 4,096 columns uuu.
  2. Apply SwiGLU: inter=silu(g)⊙u\mathrm{inter} = \mathrm{silu}(g) \odot uinter=silu(g)⊙u, where silu(z)=z⋅σ(z)\mathrm{silu}(z) = z \cdot \sigma(z)silu(z)=z⋅σ(z).
  3. Run the down projection y=inter W2,e⊤y = \mathrm{inter}\, W_{2,e}^{\top}y=interW2,e⊤​ back to 4,096 dimensions.
  4. Normalize each yyy and accumulate it weighted by its routing weight: mtok+=wtok,e⋅RMSNorm(y⊙(1+wpost_expert))m_{\mathrm{tok}} \mathrel{+}= w_{\mathrm{tok},e} \cdot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(y \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_expert}}))mtok​+=wtok,e​⋅RMSNorm(y⊙(1+wpost_expert​)) (note that multiplying by 1+wpost_expert1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_expert}}1+wpost_expert​ happens before the RMS division here—the opposite order from Stage 3), where wtok,ew_{\mathrm{tok},e}wtok,e​ is the token's topk_weights entry for expert eee. Once every local (token, expert) pair finishes, Stage 6 hands m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 7.

From there, Stage 7 (unpooler) computes f=m Wunpool⊤f = m\, W_{unpool}^{\top}f=mWunpool⊤​, widening the vector back up to f :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{f}{T,\;8192}{BF16}f:[T,8192]BF16 (for T≤8T \le 8T≤8, computing only our GPU's 1,024 columns; see Section 1) and passing it to Stage 8.

Finally, Stage 8 (second gated residual) blends the expert branch back into the residual stream: stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn))\mathrm{stream\_out} = \alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid} + \beta_2 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(f \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_ffn}}))stream_out=α2​⊙stream_mid+β2​⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn​)), which becomes the streaml+1\mathrm{stream}_{l+1}streaml+1​ handed to the next layer. Just like Stage 6, multiplication comes before division here, and α2,β2\alpha_2, \beta_2α2​,β2​ come from a vector learned for Stage 8 with α22+β22=1\alpha_2^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1α22​+β22​=1 elementwise. To wrap up the layer, Stage 8 also computes the next layer's input xl+1=RMSNorm(stream_out)⊙(1+wnext)x_{l+1} = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{stream\_out}) \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{next}})xl+1​=RMSNorm(stream_out)⊙(1+wnext​) (the final layer skips xl+1x_{l+1}xl+1​).

Because Stage 8 reads no weight matrices—only a few length-8,192 vectors—we only need to look at Stages 1–7 when we calculate minimum execution times below.

Beyond the all-reduce inside Stage 3, the 8 GPUs run a second all-reduce sum on mmm right after Stage 6; when T≤8T \le 8T≤8, they also run an all-gather after Stage 7 to stitch each GPU's 1,024 columns into 8,192 columns. All three cross-GPU collectives sit on the main chain, so all 8 GPUs must wait for each one to finish before moving on (their communication time stays outside our single-GPU ledger; see Primer 1).

3Which Memory Reads Must Wait for the Previous Step to Finish?

In single-request decode, inter-stage activations account for under 0.2% of total bytes read; the five dense weight matrices and historical KV cache can be read from the start, and expert weights can be prefetched as soon as Stage 4 selects the experts.

If we draw these 8 stages by "who has to wait for whose output," we get a directed acyclic graph (DAG, where each solid arrow means "must wait for this result"; see Figure P2-3). The whole layer forms a single serial main chain that forks only at hhh into Stage 4 and Stage 5 and merges back at Stage 6. Outside that main chain sit two extra edges: one sends stream_mid straight from Stage 3 to Stage 8, and the other keeps the KV cache written by this layer horizontally for future tokens.

Every byte a stage reads from memory falls into one of two buckets. The first bucket is activations: the intermediate results that the previous stage just produced in the current forward pass. Until that previous step finishes, they do not exist yet. As for size, the benchmark lower bound counts only the layer's own inputs and outputs—about 0.1 MB in single-request decode (Section 1)—and the intermediates passed between stages inside the layer add up to only a few tenths of a megabyte. The second bucket is weights and historical KV cache, which are already sitting in HBM before the current forward pass even begins.

Where do Stage 6's expert weights fit in? Those bytes are also sitting in HBM from the start, with one catch: Stage 6 has to wait for Stage 4 (router) to produce topk_ids before it knows which experts to read. Because Stage 4 runs in parallel with Stage 5 (pooler), the moment Stage 4 finishes we can start prefetching the selected expert weights from HBM while Stage 5 is still running. We will see how hardware exploits that overlap in Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 9, Sections 4–5.

4How Fast Can a Stage Possibly Run, and What Is It Waiting On?

Minimum execution time is the slower of byte transfer time and compute time; below 206 FLOP/B the stage is HBM-bound, and above 206 FLOP/B it is Tensor Core-bound.

A single H200 has two hard hardware ceilings: HBM read bandwidth tops out at 4.8 TB/s, and Tensor Core BF16 matrix-multiplication throughput tops out at 989 TFLOP/s (Chapter 5, Section 3 shows how a single matrix instruction works). Even if you overlap memory transfers and math perfectly, a stage can never finish faster than whichever of those two jobs takes longer:

tmin⁡=max⁡ ⁣(bytes transferred4.8 TB/s, FLOP989 TFLOP/s)t_{\min} = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{bytes transferred}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}},\ \frac{\text{FLOP}}{989\ \text{TFLOP/s}}\right)tmin​=max(4.8 TB/sbytes transferred​, 989 TFLOP/sFLOP​)

That minimum time is the stage's lower bound (floor). By the same token, the full-layer lower bound is whichever is longer: total bytes moved across the layer divided by 4.8 TB/s, or total operations across the layer divided by 989 TFLOP/s. Note the assumption baked into that full-layer formula: while one stage is still doing math, the weights for later stages are already streaming in (Section 3). Under this definition, the full-layer lower bound can never exceed the sum of the individual stage lower bounds.

Compare the two terms inside the maximum and you can tell right away which side is the bottleneck. We call the number of floating-point operations a stage performs per byte transferred its arithmetic intensity, written I=FLOP/byteI = \text{FLOP} / \text{byte}I=FLOP/byte (in FLOP/B). Divide the machine's peak compute throughput by its peak memory bandwidth and you get its ridge point—on an H200, 989/4.8≈206989 / 4.8 \approx 206989/4.8≈206 FLOP/B. Plot achievable compute throughput against arithmetic intensity and you get the roofline model in Figure P2-4.

Whenever I<206I < 206I<206, moving bytes takes longer than doing the math: the compute units sit waiting on memory, so the stage is memory-bound (HBM-bound). Whenever I>206I > 206I>206, the math takes longer than moving the bytes: data already on chip waits on the matrix units, so the stage is compute-bound (Tensor Core-bound).

Let's plug in the numbers for Stage 1's gemv at T=1T = 1T=1. In Primer 1, Section 4, we saw that at T=1T = 1T=1 we do only 1 operation per byte of BF16 weight read, putting the arithmetic intensity at I≈1I \approx 1I≈1 FLOP/B—just 1/2061 / 2061/206 of the ridge point. Even if we use the Tensor Core, we can tap at most 0.5% of its compute ceiling (Figure P2-4). So the lower bound for this step is set entirely by streaming the weights:

37.75 MB4.8 TB/s=7.86 µs\frac{37.75\ \text{MB}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}} = 7.86\ \text{µs}4.8 TB/s37.75 MB​=7.86 µs

That 7.86 µs lower bound is the finish line that every gemv version in Part I will try to close in on.

Of course, the theoretical lower bound assumes perfect overlap between memory transfers and math at 100% of rated bandwidth, which real hardware does not hand you for free. Each kernel launch (a function run in parallel by thousands of threads on the GPU; see Primer 3, Section 1) carries a fixed overhead that does not shrink when you read fewer bytes (Primer 3, Section 5 measures an empty kernel to size this up, and Chapter 10, Section 1 isolates the launch and event-recording portion). And to get anywhere near 4.8 TB/s, the chip has to keep enough unanswered read requests in the air at the same time (called in-flight reads; Chapter 2, Section 3 measures how much you need). As a result, measured runtime always sits above the lower bound—and squeezing out that gap is what the rest of this book is all about.

5As the Token Count T Grows, Which Stages Become Tensor Core-Bound First?

Dense weights are shared across all tokens in the forward pass, historical KV is shared only across new tokens of the same request, and expert weights are shared only across tokens routed to that expert; thus dense stages cross 206 FLOP/B first.

Let's write BBB for the number of concurrent requests batched into a single pass and LLL for the number of new tokens per request in that pass, so the total token count is T=B×LT = B \times LT=B×L. In online serving, the exact same layer runs across three typical regimes:

  • Regime 1 (decode, T=1T = 1T=1): A single request with 80,000 historical tokens generates tokens one by one, with B=1, L=1B = 1,\ L = 1B=1, L=1.
  • Regime 2 (verify, T=256T = 256T=256): 32 concurrent online requests with varying history lengths each verify 8 draft tokens at once, with B=32, L=8B = 32,\ L = 8B=32, L=8.
  • Regime 3 (chunked prefill, T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384): When a prompt is tens of thousands of tokens long, holding tens of thousands of activation rows in device memory all at once would use too much memory, so we break the prompt into 16,384-token chunks and run them one after another—a technique called chunked prefill. Here we look at chunk 5, where 65,536 tokens are already cached, with B=1, L=T=16,384B = 1,\ L = T = 16{,}384B=1, L=T=16,384.

As TTT grows, why don't all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B at the same time? It comes down to how many tokens get to share each byte you pull from HBM:

  • Dense weights (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7): We stream these in once and share them across all TTT tokens in the pass, so their arithmetic intensity III grows roughly in proportion to TTT. The four BF16 dense matrices cross 206 FLOP/B once TTT reaches two to three hundred (Chapter 5, Section 2 gives the exact crossover and measurements). Still, when a matrix is narrower—for instance, o has only 1,024 input columns—each token's own input and output activations make up a larger share of the byte traffic and pull the arithmetic intensity down slightly, which is why at T=256T = 256T=256 qkv_gate has already crossed 206 while o sits just below it. As for router, it has only 256 rows and its 4-byte FP32 weights do half as much math per weight byte as BF16, so it crosses 206 much later; its lower bound is still evaluated against 989 TFLOP/s.
  • Historical KV cache (Stage 2): Different concurrent requests have different conversation histories, so 1 byte of historical KV cache is shared only across the LLL new tokens of that same request. When L=1L = 1L=1, for each 256 B KV cache slot we read, our 16 query heads each run one 64-dimensional inner product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum (64 multiply-adds apiece, at 2 FLOPs per multiply-add), totaling 2×2×16×64=4,0962 \times 2 \times 16 \times 64 = 4{,}0962×2×16×64=4,096 FLOPs and giving an arithmetic intensity of I=4096/256=16I = 4096 / 256 = 16I=4096/256=16 FLOP/B. At L=8L = 8L=8 in verify, the arithmetic intensity climbs ~8× to 127.5 FLOP/B—still short of 206.
  • Expert weights (Stage 6): The weights of 1 local expert are shared only across the tokens that actually route to it in this pass. Because H200 Tensor Cores have no native 4-bit floating-point matrix multiply, we have to unpack expert weights to BF16 on chip before multiplying (Chapter 6, Section 3 shows how), keeping the compute ceiling at 989 TFLOP/s. Each routed token does 1 multiply-add (2 FLOPs) per weight (0.5625 B on average), giving a per-token arithmetic intensity of 2/0.5625≈3.562 / 0.5625 \approx 3.562/0.5625≈3.56 FLOP/B. Reaching the 206 FLOP/B ridge point takes roughly 206/3.56≈58206 / 3.56 \approx 58206/3.56≈58 tokens landing on the same expert in the same pass.

Start with Regime 1: decode (T=1T = 1T=1). With only 1 token in flight, no bytes are shared across tokens at all: all 7 stages sit between 0.5 and 16 FLOP/B (Figure P2-4), every one of them waiting on HBM. The 6 non-expert stages add up to about 29 µs, and the expert stage takes the 11.03 µs budget from Section 1. The chart below shows the stage-by-stage breakdown, where the 7.86 µs bar for qkv_gate is the gemv lower bound from Section 4.

Next, look at Regime 2: verify (T=256T = 256T=256, where B=32B = 32B=32 requests each verify L=8L = 8L=8 tokens). Here the three large dense matrices (qkv_gate, pooler, and the fully read unpooler) cross 206 FLOP/B first and become Tensor Core-bound. Meanwhile, o sits right below 206, router stays low because its weights take 4 bytes each, and attention shares historical KV reads only across the L=8L = 8L=8 tokens within each request, stopping at 127.5 FLOP/B.

What about the expert stage? Under uniform routing, the 256×8=2,048256 \times 8 = 2{,}048256×8=2,048 hit pairs spread evenly across all 256 experts: our GPU gets 256 hit pairs, touches nearly all 32 local experts, and feeds each expert only 8 tokens on average.

The benchmark specification instead defines its lower bound under skewed routing (where popular experts attract more tokens; see Chapter 8, Section 1). Subtract the non-expert memory reads from the full-layer lower bound, and the remaining expert budget comes to about 16.0 local experts. That number comes from the benchmark's lower-bound formula, which counts 75% of the mean number of distinct local experts touched on the busiest GPU (the GPU receiving the most hit pairs). Work backward, and the busiest GPU touches about 21 local experts on average—fewer than the ~32 under uniform routing. Why does skew lower the time bound? Because we read expert weights once per distinct active expert, not once per token: concentrating hits onto fewer popular experts leaves fewer distinct experts to read on the busiest GPU, pulling the full-layer lower bound down. Under that lower-bound formula, at least 256 hit pairs spread across 16.0 experts, so each expert gets at least about 16 tokens—still far short of the 58 tokens needed to become Tensor Core-bound. Counted at 256 hit pairs, the expert stage's arithmetic intensity is about 57 FLOP/B (Figure P2-4), well below 206, so it remains HBM-bound and leaves the full layer with 3 compute-bound stages and 4 memory-bound stages.

Even so, check the full-layer lower bound: dividing total arithmetic by 989 TFLOP/s already takes at least a bit over half of the byte-transfer time (about 54% at the minimum of 256 hit pairs). Because the benchmark does not state the actual number of hit pairs on the busiest GPU, we treat the full layer as still memory-bound here. Compared with T=1T = 1T=1, the lower bound of a sliding-window layer grows to only about 3.6× its T=1T = 1T=1 value, while processing 255 additional tokens in the same pass (see the chart below).

Finally, look at Regime 3: chunked prefill (T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, chunk 5 of a long prompt with 65,536 tokens already cached). Under uniform routing, each local expert now gets 16,384×8/256=51216{,}384 \times 8 / 256 = 51216,384×8/256=512 tokens—well past the 58-token threshold—and attention's LLL is 16,384 as well. At this point, all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B and become Tensor Core-bound. By the rule from Section 4, once every stage is Tensor Core-bound, the full-layer lower bound is simply the sum of the stage lower bounds; if we assume uniform routing and include causal attention within the current chunk, the stage bounds of a full-attention layer add up to about 9.87 ms, differing by only about 0.2% from the benchmark's 9.85 ms—the benchmark formula adds extra expert work for skewed routing but leaves out in-chunk attention, and the two effects largely offset each other.

One final note: every lower bound above counts only the memory traffic and arithmetic on a single GPU, excluding kernel launch overhead (Primer 3, Section 5) as well as cross-GPU communication time (Primer 1); likewise, the skewed routing distribution is the load assumption set by the benchmark.

Once you know what a stage is waiting on, you know how to make it faster: HBM-bound stages speed up when you read fewer bytes and pack the available memory bandwidth more tightly (Chapters 2, 3, and 6), whereas Tensor Core-bound stages speed up when you keep the matrix units fed (Chapter 5). Part I starts with the cleanest HBM-bound stage in the layer—gemv at T=1T = 1T=1—and pushes it step by step toward its 7.86 µs lower bound.

Takeaway: What a stage waits on comes down to how many tokens share each byte it reads. In single-request decode, no bytes are shared and all 7 stages are HBM-bound; as the token count and byte sharing grow, the stages become Tensor Core-bound one by one.

Next chapter's question: At T=1T = 1T=1, Stage 1 is a single matrix-vector multiplication y=Wxy = W xy=Wx, and reading WWW takes at least 7.86 µs. If we write that calculation as a minimal CUDA program, what does the code look like, and what does each keyword do?
