Primer 2 left off at a hard lower bound: at T=1T = 1T=1, Stage 1 needs at least 7.86 µs just to stream WWW out of HBM. Before we can try to approach that line, we need working code on the GPU. What does a minimal CUDA program look like, and how does it coordinate thousands of threads to compute y=Wxy = W xy=Wx together?

1How Does CUDA Turn the Row Loop of y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx into Parallelism?

The outer row loop disappears: each of the 2,304 rows goes to a thread block (CTA) scheduled onto the 132 SMs in batches, while the 128 threads inside each CTA split up the 8,192 columns and accumulate them in parallel.

Our job is to compute y=Wxy = W xy=Wx from Stage 1 of Primer 2, where W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 and x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16 both sit in HBM and each output row is yr=∑k=08191Wr,k xky_r = \sum_{k=0}^{8191} W_{r,k}\, x_kyr​=∑k=08191​Wr,k​xk​. Let's write M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304 for the number of rows and K=8,192K = 8{,}192K=8,192 for the number of columns. To keep the code short, the listing below writes the output yyy in FP32; the real Stage 1 writes BF16 and slices it into q, k, v, and gate for Stage 2. The arrows at the end of the lines point to the chapters that unpack the hardware mechanism behind each line.

// #include <cuda_bf16.h> and device memory allocation omitted; stream is a pre-created CUDA stream
__global__ void gemv_kernel(const __nv_bfloat16* W, const __nv_bfloat16* x,
                            float* y, int K) {
    __shared__ float smem[128];                                // → Chapter 3
    int row = blockIdx.x;                                      // → Chapter 2
    int tid = threadIdx.x;                                     // → Chapter 3
    float acc = 0.0f;                                          // → Chapter 3
    for (int k = tid; k < K; k += blockDim.x) {
        acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k])                // → Chapter 3 (load), Chapter 6 (conversion)
             * __bfloat162float(x[k]);                         // → Chapter 5 (multiply-add)
    }
    smem[tid] = acc;
    __syncthreads();                                           // → Chapter 4
    if (tid == 0) {                                            // → Chapter 4
        float sum = 0.0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < blockDim.x; ++i) sum += smem[i];
        y[row] = sum;
    }
}
gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);                // → Chapter 1, Chapter 2

Let's read through the code from top to bottom. At the top, __global__ marks the function as a kernel—a function launched once by the CPU and executed in parallel by thousands of threads on the GPU. CUDA calls a group of threads that team up on a piece of work a thread block (CTA) (short for cooperative thread array, and called block in code), and all the CTAs from a single launch make up a grid. The launch statement on the last line spins up M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304 CTAs at once, with 128 threads in each CTA running this function from start to finish. Inside the loop, __bfloat162float converts 2-byte BF16 values into 4-byte FP32 values before multiply-adding them into the thread's own acc (Chapter 6 covers what that conversion costs in hardware).

Notice what happened to the outer loop: on a CPU you would loop over the rows one after another in time, but in CUDA we flatten that outer loop into 2,304 CTAs—one per row—and let the GPU dispatch them across its SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) units. An SM is the hardware core that actually executes instructions; an H200 has 132 of them, and any given CTA stays on a single SM from start to finish. Each SM can hold only so many resident CTAs at once, so whichever CTAs do not fit in the first batch wait in line until slots free up (Chapter 2, Section 1 and Chapter 3, Section 1 explain how many fit and why).

2What Does the Launch Statement Do, and When Is yyy Ready?

A kernel launch statement just enqueues a command into a CUDA stream and returns right away before yyy is computed; by default, the next kernel in the same CUDA stream is guaranteed to see the data written by the previous one.

Look closely at the triple angle brackets on the last line: gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>. The first argument sets the number of CTAs for this launch (M=2,304M = 2{,}304M=2,304), and the second sets the number of threads per CTA (128). The third argument asks for extra dynamically allocated shared-memory bytes per CTA; we don't need any here, so we pass 0. The fourth argument picks the target CUDA stream—a queue of GPU commands that execute in the order you enqueue them, stored in the variable stream. When the CPU runs this launch line, it simply drops a command into the queue and immediately moves on without waiting for the GPU to finish—a mechanism called asynchronous launch.

By default, commands in the same CUDA stream run strictly in enqueue order, so an earlier kernel happens-before the next one: without a single line of extra synchronization, the next kernel is guaranteed to see everything the earlier kernel wrote to memory. You can also let a successor kernel start early to overlap with its predecessor; Chapter 1, Section 4 covers the rules for that. And when the CPU itself needs the result in hand, it calls cudaStreamSynchronize(stream) to block until the stream finishes.

3How Does Each Thread Know Which Segment to Compute?

Via built-in hardware thread coordinates: blockIdx.x identifies the CTA index, threadIdx.x identifies the thread index within the CTA, and blockDim.x gives the CTA size used as the loop stride.

If thousands of threads all run the exact same function, how does each thread know which numbers to read? Hardware gives every thread its own built-in coordinates. Start with row = blockIdx.x: the CTA index runs from 000 to 2,3032{,}3032,303, mapping straight to the row of WWW that this CTA claims. Next, tid = threadIdx.x (0..1270..1270..127) and blockDim.x (128) split the columns of that row across the 128 threads: on loop iteration rrr (r=1..64r = 1..64r=1..64), thread tid reads column k=tid+128 (r−1)k = \mathrm{tid} + 128\,(r - 1)k=tid+128(r−1).

With 8,192 columns per row split across 128 threads, each thread runs 8,192/128=648{,}192 / 128 = 648,192/128=64 iterations, and across all 64 iterations the 128 threads together read one full 16 KiB row of WWW and 16 KiB of xxx. Better yet, on any single iteration, adjacent threads read adjacent addresses in that row, covering a contiguous 256 B span across the CTA. Hardware groups every 32 adjacent threads into a warp; Chapter 3, Sections 1–2 show how a warp issues load instructions together and how hardware coalesces those adjacent addresses into fewer memory requests.

You can check this formula yourself in Figure P3-1 by dragging the sliders to row = 2, tid = 5, and iteration 24 (r=24r = 24r=24): on that step, the thread reads column k=5+128×23=2,949k = 5 + 128 \times 23 = 2{,}949k=5+128×23=2,949, fetching W[2 * 8192 + 2949] = W[19333] and x[2949].

4How Are 128 Partial Sums Safely Reduced into One Value?

Each thread writes its partial sum to CTA-shared smem, __syncthreads() waits until all 128 threads finish writing, and thread 0 sums the values and writes back yry_ryr​.

The three kinds of variables in this kernel live in three different storage tiers. First, row, tid, and acc reside in registers, with each thread holding its own private instance. Second, the array __shared__ float smem[128] (128×4 B=512 B128 \times 4\ \text{B} = 512\ \text{B}128×4 B=512 B) sits in on-chip shared memory, where all 128 threads in this CTA can read and write it, while by default other CTAs cannot see it (Chapter 3, Section 1 covers these two levels of on-chip storage, and Chapter 7, Section 12 shows how to group several CTAs so they can access one another's shared memory). Third, W, x, and y sit in global memory in HBM, where every CTA can read and write them.

Summing many partial results into one total is called a reduction. Since each thread holds acc in its own private register, this code gathers the 128 partial sums via shared memory smem, starting with every thread executing smem[tid] = acc.

Right after that store comes __syncthreads() (a CTA barrier). It holds all 128 threads in this CTA at that line until every last one of them has arrived; once past the barrier, every thread in the CTA is guaranteed to see the values that all 128 threads just wrote into smem. Keep in mind that this guarantee applies only inside a single CTA—exchanging data across different CTAs takes a different set of rules (Chapter 2, Section 6). If you omit __syncthreads(), thread 0 may read smem[i] before thread i has finished writing its partial sum into that slot.

Once past the barrier, thread 0 loops over the 128 values one by one and writes their sum to y[row]. The other 127 threads exit right away and do no more work, but the CTA still holds onto its SM slot until thread 0 finishes. That keeps the code dead simple and produces the right yry_ryr​, at the cost of 512 B of shared memory per CTA, 1 CTA barrier, and 128 dependent additions run serially by a single thread. Because the first batch of CTAs starts at nearly the same time and reaches the epilogue at roughly the same time, the SM may have no other in-flight memory reads left to hide that serial loop behind, so those 128 additions can add straight onto the runtime (we did not measure this epilogue cost separately). Chapter 4, Sections 5–6 show how to put all 128 threads to work on the reduction together.

5How Do We Measure Latency Here, and What Part Lies Outside the Kernel?

Each run flushes the on-chip cache first, brackets a single kernel launch with GPU events, and takes the median of 500 runs—including ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead incurred even by an empty kernel.

We time every gemv version in Part I with the exact same setup. Before each timed launch, we read a large block of unrelated data to flush the chip's fast small storage (the on-chip cache), forcing the GPU to stream WWW fresh from HBM. We then bracket a single launch with two GPU events—timestamps that the GPU records directly inside the CUDA stream—run 20 warmup iterations, and take the median across 500 timed runs. Flushing the cache before each run mirrors what happens in single-request decode from Primer 2 (Chapter 2, Section 2 explains why).

If we time an empty kernel that does nothing at all with the exact same method, it still measures ~4.6 µs—the baseline cost we call fixed overhead. Every measured latency we report in Part I includes that 4.6 µs without subtracting it out, whereas the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound from Primer 2 does not include it. Back-to-back kernels also pay handoff overhead between launches, which we will meet in Chapter 1, Section 1.

6Why Assign a Thread Block per Row Instead of a Single Thread? (gemv v0 → v1)

Assigning one row per thread launches only 18 CTAs, leaving most of the 132 SMs idle, and adjacent threads read addresses separated by an entire row; switching to one CTA per row speeds up execution by ~12.5×.

We number each gemv version in Part I starting from v0. If you bring your CPU loop habits straight to CUDA, the most obvious first try is v0, where each thread computes one entire row on its own: row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x, launched with <<<18, 128, 0, stream>>> (2,304/128=182{,}304 / 128 = 182,304/128=18 CTAs), so each thread loops across all 8,192 columns of its row from start to finish. v1 is the kernel from Section 1, launched with <<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>, which assigns a full 128-thread CTA to each row:

// v0: each thread computes 1 full row on its own(int row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x;)
for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);
// v1: the 128 adjacent threads of 1 CTA cooperate to read one row in segments (full code in Section 1)
for (int k = tid; k < K; k += 128) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);

Here is what happens when we time both versions on the H200 using the method from Section 5:

That 12.5× gap comes from two places. First, almost the entire chip is sitting idle: hardware dispatches work to SMs one CTA at a time (Chapter 2, Section 1), and 18 CTAs can occupy at most 18 of the 132 SMs while the other 114 SMs do nothing.

Second, look at the memory access stride. On a GPU, the 32 adjacent threads of a warp issue one load instruction together, and device memory transfers at least a 32-byte segment per transaction (Chapter 3, Section 2 covers coalesced access). In v0, those 32 threads ask for 32 addresses that sit a full row (16 KiB) apart from one another: a single load instruction is forced to haul back 32×32=1,02432 \times 32 = 1{,}02432×32=1,024 B even though the current iteration uses only 64 B of it. Each 32 B segment holds the next 16 BF16 elements of that row, and the current iteration uses just 1 of them; the other 15 sit untouched until the next 15 iterations, when they may still be in the on-chip cache (Chapter 3, Section 2).

In v1, those same 32 adjacent threads read a contiguous 64 B span on every iteration: memory transfers just two 32 B segments, and every byte gets used right away.

Moving from v0 to v1 buys us two things: 2,304 CTAs that fill all 132 SMs, and adjacent threads that read contiguous bytes. In exchange, we pay the three costs from Section 4: 512 B of shared memory, 1 CTA barrier, and 128 serial additions.

There is one more side effect: in v0, all 32 threads in a warp read the same x[k] on a given iteration, so 32 rows share one read; in v1, each CTA reads all 16 KiB of xxx on its own, so across 2,304 CTAs they read as many bytes of xxx in total as of WWW (Chapter 2, Section 2 shows how the on-chip cache absorbs those repeated reads).

What if a matrix has fewer than 132 rows to begin with? Then even 1 CTA per row cannot fill all 132 SMs, and we have to split each row across multiple CTAs (Chapter 2, Section 5).

Look back at the chart above, though: even after a 12.5× speedup, v1 still takes ~7× the 7.86 µs lower bound. Subtract out the 4.6 µs fixed overhead, and its effective bandwidth for reading WWW is still only about one-sixth of 4.8 TB/s. Why is a kernel that fills all 132 SMs still so far from the hardware ceiling? Answering that question is the job of Chapters 2–4.

Takeaway: CUDA flattens the outer loop into 2,304 CTAs that go onto the SMs in batches; having a group of adjacent threads work together on a single row is what fills all 132 SMs and lets them read contiguous bytes.

Next chapter's question: A single v1 launch takes tens of microseconds, and part of that is fixed overhead that does not depend on byte count—yet a single model layer has to launch a sequence of kernels in order. Where does the time between consecutive kernels go, and how do we squeeze it out?

Timeline — Where Does the Time Between Two Adjacent Kernels Go, and How Can We Eliminate It?

In Primer 3, every timing run of gemv_kernel (v1) carried ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead (see Primer 3, Section 5). When you actually run a single model layer, though, the GPU doesn't run just that one kernel—it launches a whole chain of kernels back to back along a CUDA stream. Where does the time between two adjacent kernels go, and how can we eliminate it?

Figure I-1 lays out the six zoom levels of Part I, going step by step from the outermost timeline all the way down to instructions and bits. In this chapter, we start at the outermost level—Level 1: Timeline.

To see what happens on the timeline, let's put gemv_kernel from Primer 3 back where it sits inside a single layer: right after a normalization kernel and right before a post-processing kernel, forming a three-kernel chain. We'll use this one example from start to finish in this chapter:

  1. Normalization kernel: reads x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16, writes xn :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x_n}{8192}{BF16}xn​:[8192]BF16, and computes xn=x⋅rx_n = x \cdot rxn​=x⋅r, where r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵr = 1/\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k x_k^2 + \epsilon}r=1/K1​∑k​xk2​+ϵ​ (see Primer 1, Section 1 for the RMSNorm definition; we skip multiplying a weight vector here). This step launches just 1 CTA of 1,024 threads.
  2. gemv_kernel (v1): multiplies weight W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 to compute y=Wxny = W x_ny=Wxn​ and writes y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32, launching 2,304 CTAs of 128 threads each.
  3. Post-processing kernel: runs elementwise operations on y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32 (standing in for the actual per-head normalization and rotary position embedding (RoPE); see Primer 2, Section 2), with 256 threads per CTA across ⌈2304/256⌉=9\lceil 2304/256 \rceil = 9⌈2304/256⌉=9 CTAs in total.

All three steps use only the four building blocks we met in Primer 3: thread blocks (CTAs), threads, a CUDA stream, and global memory.

1Why Does the GPU Stall Between Two Kernels?

The gaps between two kernels come from two places: first, when the CPU issues commands slower than the GPU runs them, the command queue runs dry and the GPU sits waiting on the CPU; second, even when commands are already waiting in the queue, the next kernel still cannot start until every CTA of the previous kernel has exited. We call the first one the CPU launch gap and the second one the hardware handoff gap.

Let's do the math for the first gap. A kernel launch statement just drops a command into the CUDA stream and returns right away (see Primer 3), so the CPU is the producer, the GPU is the consumer, and the CUDA stream is the queue between them. Suppose each kernel runs on the GPU for tgput_{gpu}tgpu​, while the CPU takes tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ to issue one launch command. Whenever tcpu>tgput_{cpu} > t_{gpu}tcpu​>tgpu​, the GPU finishes the current kernel before the next command even reaches the queue. The queue runs dry, the start-to-start spacing between back-to-back kernels stretches out to tcput_{cpu}tcpu​, and the GPU sits idle for ~tcpu−tgput_{cpu} - t_{gpu}tcpu​−tgpu​ every time. Flip that around to tcpu≤tgput_{cpu} \le t_{gpu}tcpu​≤tgpu​, and the CPU stays ahead of the GPU: the queue always has commands waiting, and that idle wait vanishes.

Small kernels are where this gap hurts most, because their tgput_{gpu}tgpu​ is only a few microseconds. In our three-kernel chain, both the 1-CTA normalization kernel and the 9-CTA post-processing kernel are that small. Our benchmark script fires off the three launches in sequence from Python, and the first two rows of Figure 1-1 compare two ways of running them: in Row 1 ("CPU one-by-one launch"), the stream queue is empty when timing starts, and Python issues the three launches one by one; in Row 2 ("Pre-filled command queue"), we first enqueue a kernel that keeps the GPU busy for a short window before timing starts, and the CPU uses that window to queue up all three launch commands ahead of time.

In our measurements, launching the kernels one by one from the CPU is ~41 µs slower than starting from a pre-filled command queue (see the chart in Section 5). By the queue rule we just walked through, those 41 µs land in two places: the first launch (when timing starts with an empty queue) and the ①→② boundary (because ① runs for only a few microseconds). While ② runs on the GPU for ~50 µs (its 54 µs standalone timing includes ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead), the CPU uses that time to queue up ③, so the ②→③ boundary no longer waits on the CPU. We did not separately measure how large tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ is on its own or how the 41 µs split between those two places.

Now look at the second row of Figure 1-1, "Pre-filled command queue". Even when all three commands are already waiting in the queue, a gap still separates adjacent bars. The CPU has nothing to do with this second gap: a single CUDA stream enforces its ordering guarantee (happens-before; see Primer 3, Section 2) by waiting until the previous kernel has completely finished and all of its writes are visible before starting the next one. So every time execution crosses a kernel boundary, the hardware has to step through the full handoff: the last CTA of the previous kernel exits, its writes become visible, and the CTAs of the next kernel are dispatched onto the 132 SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1 for dispatch). While the last few CTAs of the previous kernel are still wrapping up, the SMs that finished early are already sitting idle; once that last CTA exits, every SM on the GPU sits empty until the next kernel lands on them.

2Which Gap Does CUDA Graph Eliminate, and Which Does It Leave Behind?

A CUDA Graph pre-records the entire chain and submits it in a single call, wiping out the CPU launch gap while leaving the hardware handoff gaps between nodes.

A CUDA Graph records a sequence of GPU commands and their dependencies ahead of time, with each kernel in the graph represented as a graph node. Using one takes two steps. First comes recording and graph instantiation (cudaGraphInstantiate): during warm-up before formal timing, we record the three kernel launches in order into a single graph, and at instantiation time the driver (the CPU-side software that manages the GPU) validates the whole graph and does most of the launch setup up front. Second comes replay: at runtime, the CPU makes a single cudaGraphLaunch call (see the code in Section 5) to submit the whole graph at once, without redoing that setup on later runs. Because you pay the CPU launch time tcput_{cpu}tcpu​ only once for the entire chain instead of once per kernel, the first gap from Section 1 disappears (Row 3 of Figure 1-1).

Each graph node is still a separate kernel, though, and back-to-back nodes still obey the ordering rule of a single CUDA stream: the next node cannot start until every CTA of the previous node has exited and all of its writes are visible. So the second gap stays right inside the graph. On this three-kernel chain, we did not measure each handoff boundary on its own. To give you two reference points: in replays of a real inference computation graph, the calibrated launch overhead per node has a median of ~1.0 µs. In a separate test that only adds empty kernels to a graph, each extra empty kernel adds 0.37–1.19 µs to the full-graph time.

Compare that with "Pre-filled command queue" from Section 1: pre-filling the queue can hide CPU launch time too, but only as long as the CPU stays ahead of the GPU, whereas full-graph replay does not depend on the CPU keeping up at all. On our three-kernel chain, full-graph replay also runs slightly faster than a pre-filled command queue (see Section 5 for the measurements).

Here is how the CUDA Graph trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: you wipe out the CPU launch gap in one stroke (see Section 5 for the measured speedup on the three-kernel chain).
  • What it costs: you do an extra recording and instantiation pass during warm-up. Once the graph is instantiated, every kernel's arguments, launch configuration, and device memory addresses are locked into it. To change them, you have to call a graph update API (such as cudaGraphExecUpdate or cudaGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams) or record the graph again. When the input token count TTT varies, the common approach is to record a separate graph for each value of TTT (or pad the input up to a recorded TTT).
  • When it loses: on this three-kernel chain, full-graph replay beats both standard stream-launch modes; we did not measure the extra cost of recording multiple graphs or padding shapes, or whether it loses in other scenarios.

3What Do You Save and What Do You Pay When Fusing Two Kernels into One?

Fusing two kernels into one saves a boundary, a launch, and a global-memory round trip; you pay with one extra step in the main kernel, and it works only when the next step does not force all CTAs to stop and wait for each other.

Putting the work of two adjacent kernels into a single kernel—so the intermediate result stays in registers or on-chip memory instead of taking a round trip through global memory—is called kernel fusion. Every extra standalone kernel costs you more than a Section 2 hardware handoff: it also writes its intermediate result out to global memory, only for the next kernel to read it right back in. On the same H200, we timed each of the three kernels on its own and the full chain back to back, all using standard stream launches from a pre-filled command queue: the full chain (61.6 µs; see Section 5) runs only ~7.4 µs longer than gemv_kernel alone.

And that ~7.4 µs still includes the actual math inside normalization and post-processing. Fusing the kernels doesn't make that math disappear—you still have to run it—so ~7.4 µs is only an upper bound on what fusion can save.

So how do we actually fuse them? First, let's name one part of a kernel: the elementwise work that runs after the main loop finishes and right before the final result is written out is called the epilogue.

Folding post-processing into the epilogue is straightforward. In gemv_kernel, right after thread 0 of each CTA finishes the intra-CTA reduction for its row's dot product, that result is already sitting in its register. Because elementwise post-processing doesn't need results from any other CTA, thread 0 can just finish that math in place before writing out y[row].

Folding normalization in takes one more step of thought. In xn=x⋅rx_n = x \cdot rxn​=x⋅r, the scale factor r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵr = 1/\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k x_k^2 + \epsilon}r=1/K1​∑k​xk2​+ϵ​ depends on the sum of squares across the entire vector xxx. At first glance, it looks as if you have to finish reading all of xxx to get rrr before the matrix multiply can even start. But look back at the v1 loop in Primer 3: to compute its own row's dot product, every CTA already reads the entire vector xxx (8,192 elements) from start to finish. Since every CTA reads all of xxx anyway, it can accumulate the sum of squares ∑kxk2\sum_k x_k^2∑k​xk2​ right alongside the dot product in that same loop, compute rrr after the intra-CTA reduction in the epilogue, and multiply it into the dot product at the end to write out y[row]=r⋅∑kW[row,k] xky[\text{row}] = r \cdot \sum_k W[\text{row}, k]\,x_ky[row]=r⋅∑k​W[row,k]xk​. That works because:

y=W(x⋅r)=r (Wx)y = W(x \cdot r) = r\,(Wx)y=W(x⋅r)=r(Wx)

Without a normalization weight vector, those two expressions are algebraically identical; even with a weight vector, the expression just becomes r W(wnorm⊙x)r\,W(w_{\text{norm}} \odot x)rW(wnorm​⊙x), which still uses only the data read by the current CTA. Numerically, only two things change: you skip one BF16 rounding step from writing xnx_nxn​ out to global memory (rounding a 32-bit float to the nearest 16-bit value; see Chapter 6, Section 1), and you change the rounding order of the multiply-adds.

Keep in mind that fusion cuts out only the kernel boundaries and global-memory round trips; the computation you fold in still has to run. We measured this on a faster gemv kernel: folding the start of Stage 2 (per-head normalization and writing the FP8 Q and KV cache; see Primer 2, Section 2) into the epilogue of Stage 1 still adds ~1.1 µs inside the kernel itself (see the chart below). In that kernel, each CTA still computes 1 row. Each of the 64 CTAs in a Q or K head adds 1 to that head's counter after writing its row, and the last CTA to increment the counter runs per-head normalization and writes out FP8 while the rest exit right away (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for how the counter works). The V CTAs each write the FP8 V cache directly without a counter. How that extra 1.1 µs splits across those steps was not measured.

Whether two steps can be fused boils down to one question: can the second step get the data it needs without forcing every CTA across the GPU to stop and wait for one another? You can fuse in two cases: either the data is already inside the same CTA, or the results from multiple CTAs only need to come together in one place so the last CTA to finish writing can wrap them up (see Chapter 2, Section 6). Normalization fits the first case because every CTA already reads all of xxx (the vector is only 16 KiB, so by capacity it should stay in the on-chip cache; see Chapter 2, Section 2—we did not measure the hit rate). Here is how the fusion trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: you cut out 2 hardware handoffs and 2 launches, and the intermediate result xnx_nxn​ (16 KiB, which is small at T=1T = 1T=1) no longer goes out to global memory only to be read right back in.
  • What it costs: the main kernel takes on an extra step in its loop or epilogue, the code gets more complex, and all 2,304 CTAs redundantly compute the exact same rrr (each CTA does 8,192 extra multiply-adds and one extra intra-CTA reduction).
  • When it loses:
    • When every CTA of the second step needs results produced by many CTAs of the first step, forcing both steps into one kernel requires a device-wide barrier where all CTAs across the GPU stop mid-flight and wait for the slowest CTA to finish writing. Device-wide synchronization also requires every CTA to be co-resident on the chip at once, or else it will deadlock (see Chapter 2, Section 6). In that case, keeping two separate kernels is usually better—and the next section shows how to overlap them partially.
    • Even the second fusible pattern above (letting the last finishing CTA do the work) can lose: if the step you fold in is a small kernel that could otherwise enter early using the method in the next section, fusing forces it to wait behind the very last CTA of the preceding kernel, losing that overlap and running slower in measured runs (see Chapter 9, Section 6).

4Can the Next Kernel Start Before the Previous Kernel Finishes?

Yes. PDL lets the next kernel land on SMs early to start reading weights, and wait until the previous kernel's writes are all visible before reading its output.

As we saw in Primer 2, Section 3, static weights don't depend on the activations from the previous step, so nothing stops you from reading them early. And in our three-kernel chain, the normalization kernel has only 1 CTA—while it runs, it occupies just 1 SM and leaves the other 131 SMs sitting idle. In a standard CUDA stream, though, the hardware ties two things together: the next kernel (which we'll call the dependent kernel (successor)) can start dispatching only after the previous kernel (the primary kernel (predecessor)) has completely exited. Hopper (the H200 architecture) provides PDL (Programmatic Dependent Launch) to uncouple those two events in four steps (Figure 1-3):

  1. When launching the successor kernel, the CPU passes an extra launch attribute telling the GPU that the successor may dispatch before the predecessor finishes.
  2. Inside the predecessor, each CTA issues a trigger call after finishing its main loop and before writing back its output; once every predecessor CTA has triggered (or exited), the hardware may dispatch CTAs of the successor onto idle SMs (the specification permits early dispatch, though it does not guarantee it).
  3. Once a successor CTA lands on an SM, it starts with work that does not depend on the predecessor's output—at the "normalization → gemv" boundary, it fires off the first batch of weight reads for WWW from HBM. Any bytes read before the wait call returns must sit in on-chip storage until xnx_nxn​ is ready (see Chapter 9, Section 4 for how a single layer prefetches weights), so how much you can prefetch is bounded by on-chip capacity.
  4. Right before reading the predecessor's output, the successor issues a wait call; once that call returns, the entire predecessor grid has finished executing and all of its global-memory writes are visible to the successor.
// Predecessor: issue the trigger (placement: see below)
cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion();
// Successor: the CPU launches the successor through the launch API with the PDL launch attribute; the successor first issues reads that do not depend on the predecessor, then waits
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();   // read the predecessor's output only after this call returns

There is one hard rule here: in this chapter's pattern, code that reads the predecessor's output must be placed after the wait call—and until the wait call returns, the successor must not write into any buffer the predecessor might still be reading (our three-kernel chain does not run into this; Chapter 9, Section 5 shows a concrete case). Where you place the trigger call inside the predecessor only controls how early the successor can land on SMs; it does not change visibility.

Looking at the timeline, PDL can save at most two pieces of time: the overlap between the predecessor's epilogue and the successor's independent work (whichever is shorter), plus any reduction in the handoff gap itself. We timed that handoff in a small test program built to measure just this one step (which we'll call a microbenchmark): in a 1-CTA test setup, we link two kernels with PDL and have the successor call wait right at entry, measuring ~0.64 µs per handoff. Since this figure and the 1.0 µs in Section 2 come from separate tests, the two cannot be subtracted directly.

Where should you put the trigger call? That depends on how many SMs the predecessor occupies. When the predecessor uses only a few SMs (like the 1-CTA kernel in our example), triggering right at function entry has almost no effect on the predecessor (we did not benchmark early versus late triggering here). When the predecessor fills every SM on the GPU, though, triggering at function entry lets early-dispatched successor CTAs stall on the wait call while holding onto SM resources, slowing down the predecessor CTAs that are still running. In our measurements, doing that slowed the predecessor attention kernel by up to ~1.65 µs (see Chapter 7, Section 11).

Triggering early only slows you down, though—it can never deadlock. The hardware starts dispatching the successor only after every predecessor CTA has either triggered or exited. By that point, no predecessor CTA is still waiting in line for an SM: every one that has not yet exited is already on an SM running, so the successor cannot block it from finishing. Still, whenever the predecessor fills all SMs, you should place the trigger call after the predecessor's main loop finishes and right before its epilogue writeback.

Here is how the PDL trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: you overlap the successor's predecessor-independent reads (such as prefetching static weights) with the predecessor's epilogue (we did not measure the latency change from enabling PDL on this gemv chain).
  • What it costs: in this chapter's pattern, the successor has to insert a wait call before its first read of the predecessor's data; if you accidentally put a read before the wait call, it can intermittently read stale values left over from the previous replay without any runtime error (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for measured reproductions of this bug).
  • When it loses: when the predecessor fills all SMs on the GPU and triggers too early at function entry, early-dispatched successor CTAs hold onto SM resources and slow down the predecessor (see above and Chapter 7, Section 11 for the measured counterexample).

5gemv Evolution v1 → v2: Recording the Three-Kernel Chain into a Single CUDA Graph

Full-graph replay runs ~1.7× faster than CPU launch from an empty queue and ~1.6 µs faster than a pre-filled command queue, while each individual kernel's runtime stays the same.

In this step we change only how the chain is launched—the machine code of the three kernels running on the GPU is byte-for-byte identical to v1:

// v1: the CPU puts [normalization, gemv_kernel, post-processing] into the CUDA stream one by one
gemv_kernel<<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, xn, y, K);
// v2: during warm-up, record these three steps on stream and instantiate them into graph_exec; at runtime, submit once
cudaGraphLaunch(graph_exec, stream);

We use the same timing setup as in Primer 3, Section 5, except now the GPU events bracket the entire three-kernel chain (Row 3 of Figure 1-1 is v2). Look at the first chart below: stepping from the first bar ("CPU one-by-one launch") to the second bar ("Pre-filled command queue") shaves off ~41 µs—the CPU launch gap from Section 1. Stepping from the second bar to the third bar ("Full-graph replay (v2)") trims another ~1.6 µs (we did not break down where that 1.6 µs comes from). Section 2 covered what you pay to use CUDA Graph.

Now look at the second evolution-chain chart below: when we time gemv_kernel by itself, the difference between v2 and v1 sits well inside measurement noise—the single-kernel runtime hasn't budged at all. That is our starting point for the next chapter.

Takeaway: The dead time between adjacent kernels comes from two places—the CPU falling behind on launches, and the hardware waiting for every CTA of the previous kernel to exit; CUDA Graph wipes out the first, kernel fusion cuts down how often you pay the second, and PDL overlaps the second with useful weight reads.

Next chapter's question: Even after we strip away every gap between kernels, gemv_kernel by itself still takes 54.08 µs—nearly 7× slower than the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound. Its 2,304 CTAs already fill all 132 SMs, so where is all that time going?

The Full H200 Chip — 2,304 CTAs Fill All 132 SMs, So Where Does the Time Still Go?

In Chapter 1, we squeezed out the gaps between kernels, yet the runtime of a single gemv_kernel itself did not budge. Now let's open up that kernel and zoom in to Level 2: the full H200 chip.

The 2,304 CTAs of v1 already fill all 132 SMs, yet gemv takes 54.08 µs while the lower bound for reading WWW once is only 7.86 µs—looking at the full chip, where does all that extra time go?

Throughout this chapter, we'll trace gemv_kernel from v1 / v2: weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16, input x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16, output y :  [2304]  FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}y:[2304]FP32, launched with <<<2304, 128>>>.

1How Are CTAs Distributed Across 132 SMs, and Why Does the Final Batch Hold Back the Entire Kernel?

The whole GPU can hold at most 2,112 resident CTAs at once; the remaining 192 CTAs have to wait for slots to free up and then walk all 64 serial load iterations from scratch.

The GPU hardware dispatches work to the 132 SMs in units of CTAs (see Primer 3, Section 1). Each SM has a cap on how many CTAs it can keep resident at once, and for v1 that cap is 16 (we'll work out why in Chapter 3, Section 1). Across all 132 SMs, the whole GPU can hold at most 132×16=2,112132 \times 16 = 2{,}112132×16=2,112 resident CTAs at the same time.

We call that device-wide concurrent CTA capacity (wave size) 1 wave. Keep in mind that a wave is the on-chip capacity at any moment, not a batch that has to finish in lockstep before the next batch starts: as soon as one CTA finishes and exits, the next pending CTA immediately takes the slot it freed.

Now pack v1's 2,304 CTAs into a chip capacity of 2,112: 2,304=2,112+1922{,}304 = 2{,}112 + 1922,304=2,112+192. The first batch of 2,112 CTAs starts together, and because every CTA in v1 does the exact same amount of work, all 2,112 finish and exit at almost the same moment. Only then do the remaining 192 CTAs step into the freed slots and start computing. This final partial batch of less than 1 wave is the tail (tail wave), with remainder r=192r = 192r=192 (Figure 2-1).

Why do those mere 192 tail-wave CTAs nearly double the runtime of the whole kernel? Look inside a single CTA's loop: each of its 128 threads loads 1 element of WWW per iteration, so sweeping across one row of 8,192 columns takes 8,192/128=648{,}192 / 128 = 648,192/128=64 iterations. The catch is that every iteration has to wait for its loaded data to return before the next iteration can start, because a thread issues its instructions in order (in-order issue). In v1's compiled loop, the next iteration's load sits behind the current iteration's multiply-add, and that multiply-add stalls until the current iteration's data comes back from global memory. As a result, each thread has only 1 read of WWW in flight at any moment (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for how in-order issue works).

A CPU core hides that wait with out-of-order execution and hardware prefetching. On a GPU, each warp issues instructions strictly in order and never skips past a stalled instruction to fire off later reads; while one warp waits on data, the SM switches to issuing reads from other warps instead. We did not measure whether the H200 has hardware prefetching. To keep more reads in flight on each SM, we change the code directly: either keep more threads resident on the SM (see Chapter 3) or have each thread issue several reads at a time (see Chapter 4).

Step back to the full chip, and v1's total runtime looks like two 64-iteration serial load chains laid end to end: the 2,112 CTAs of wave 1 walk the first 64-iteration chain, and the 192 tail-wave CTAs immediately walk a second 64-iteration chain of the exact same length from scratch. Throughout the tail wave, only 192 of the 2,112 device-wide slots are active (~9%) while the other ~90% sit empty, yet the entire kernel cannot finish until those last 192 CTAs complete all 64 iterations.

Which 192 CTAs end up in the tail wave? The CUDA specification makes no guarantee about CTA dispatch order. On the H200, however, when we instrumented a 132-CTA PDL-chained kernel in Chapter 8 with the global nanosecond timer, the highest-numbered CTA (CTA 131) began ~2.0–3.2 µs after CTAs numbered below 100—consistent with ascending blockIdx.x dispatch. Extending that pattern to v1 places the 192 highest-numbered CTAs in the tail wave (though we did not measure this directly). Correctness never hinges on this ordering; v3 uses it purely for speed.

2How Long Does One Read Take to Return from HBM to an SM, and Why Does xxx Not Need to Be Read 2,304 Times from HBM?

An unloaded HBM read round trip takes ~0.33 µs, whereas hitting the device-wide L2 cache takes ~0.18–0.23 µs; WWW streams from HBM while xxx stays in cache for reuse.

Figure 2-2 traces the memory path from off-chip memory into the compute units. On the outside sits off-chip HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, rated bandwidth 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Section 4), one step onto the die sits the on-chip L2 cache (shared across all 132 SMs, 60 MiB total capacity), and inside each SM sit the L1 cache (each SM's private level-1 cache), shared memory, and registers (we'll unpack their capacities and details in Chapter 3, Section 1).

A default global memory read checks the local SM's L1 first; if the data isn't there, it checks the device-wide L2. If the data is sitting in L2 (a cache hit), L2 hands it straight back to the SM; if it isn't in L2 either (a cache miss), the request goes off-chip to HBM, pulls the data back through L2, and delivers it to the SM. In this section we focus on those outer two levels, L2 and HBM; keep in mind that L2 is the only cache level shared across all SMs, a fact we'll rely on again in Section 6 for cross-SM merging.

To measure the round-trip latency from issuing a read to getting the data back in a register, we first need a hardware time unit: the clock cycle, one tick of the SM clock. Unloaded, one round trip from HBM takes ~600 clock cycles. A round trip that hits in L2 takes ~328 clock cycles when the data sits in the half of L2 nearer to this SM, and ~414 clock cycles in the farther half. We convert clock cycles to time at ~1.8 GHz (~0.56 ns per cycle), which gives ~0.33 µs and ~0.18 µs (~0.23 µs for the far half of L2; see the chart below).

With those numbers in hand, we can answer both questions left open in Primer 3. First, during a single kernel execution, every element of the weight matrix WWW (37.75 MB) is read only once by one CTA, so it gets no L2 cache hits. In real inference, that same WWW is not read again until the next forward pass; between the two passes, about 9.0 GB of fixed weights (see Primer 1, Section 4) stream through the 60 MiB L2 and evict the previous pass's WWW well beforehand, which is why flushing the on-chip cache before timing matches real execution (see Primer 3, Section 5).

Second, the input vector xxx is only 16 KiB—a tiny fraction of the 60 MiB L2 cache. From capacity alone, we can infer that once the first batch of CTAs reads xxx for the first time and pulls it from HBM into L2, later reads of xxx by CTAs on the same SM mostly hit in that SM's L1, and the rest hit in L2 (we did not measure the L1 or L2 hit rate on v1).

Now plug those latencies back into the serial load chain from Section 1. In each loop iteration of v1, every thread issues one read of WWW (from HBM) and one read of xxx (hitting in L1 or L2) at the same time, so the wait per iteration is roughly one HBM round trip. Multiplying by the 0.33 µs unloaded round-trip latency puts a 64-iteration serial chain at roughly 64×0.33≈21 μs64 \times 0.33 \approx 21\ \mu\text{s}64×0.33≈21 μs, which Section 8 will use as the reference for estimating tail-wave duration. Two serial chains back to back come to ~42 µs, and adding 4.6 µs of fixed overhead gives ~47 µs, ~7 µs shy of v1's measured 54.08 µs. This rough model is only meant to capture the order of magnitude; we did not separately measure where the remaining difference comes from.

3How Many Bytes Must Each SM Keep in Flight Simultaneously to Saturate HBM?

When all SMs read concurrently, round-trip latency grows with bytes in flight; reaching the bandwidth plateau takes ~64 KiB in flight per SM, whereas v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight.

The bytes that an SM has requested from memory but has not yet received are called bytes in flight. Little's Law ties bytes in flight, bandwidth, and round-trip latency together:

bytes in flight=bandwidth×round-trip latency\text{bytes in flight} = \text{bandwidth} \times \text{round-trip latency}bytes in flight=bandwidth×round-trip latency

In plain terms, for an SM to claim its full share of memory bandwidth, the bytes it keeps in flight at once have to cover an entire round trip.

Let's work out how high that target is. When all 132 SMs stream continuously from HBM, they reach a measured bandwidth plateau (the flat region where adding more bytes in flight no longer raises bandwidth) of ~4.54 TB/s, or ~34 GB/s per SM. If we plugged the unloaded 0.33 µs round trip from Section 2 straight into Little's Law, it would look as if each SM needed only 34 GB/s×0.33 μs≈11 KiB34\ \text{GB/s} \times 0.33\ \mu\text{s} \approx 11\ \text{KiB}34 GB/s×0.33 μs≈11 KiB in flight.

When the whole chip reads together, though, the story changes. We ran a separate bandwidth-sweep microbenchmark (not gemv): all 132 SMs read HBM continuously, with 1–6 CTAs on each SM. Each CTA uses 16 B loads (see Chapter 3, Section 8) to keep 16 KiB in flight at all times—the exact byte size of 1 row of WWW—so each SM keeps 16–96 KiB in flight. With only 16 KiB in flight per SM, measured device-wide bandwidth falls far short of the plateau (see the chart below), and Little's Law puts the average round trip at ~0.94 µs—much longer than the unloaded 0.33 µs. Even with only 1 CTA reading across the GPU, the round trip is ~0.82 µs; we did not measure where that extra time goes.

Follow the chart to the right: only when each SM keeps 64 KiB in flight at once (4 CTAs, equal to the byte size of 4 rows of WWW) does device-wide bandwidth reach its knee point, flattening out on the ~4.54 TB/s plateau beyond that. 64 KiB is the measured knee point; once you are on the plateau, keeping even more bytes in flight buys no extra bandwidth, so the round trip from round-trip latency=bytes in flight÷bandwidth\text{round-trip latency} = \text{bytes in flight} \div \text{bandwidth}round-trip latency=bytes in flight÷bandwidth only stretches out longer. Right at the 64 KiB knee point, Little's Law puts the average round trip at ~1.9 µs, ~6× the unloaded latency. We did not measure which segment of the path takes that extra time; a common explanation is queueing.

Put that 64 KiB knee point next to v1 and the second reason v1 is slow jumps right out. In v1, each thread keeps only one 2 B read of WWW in flight per iteration, so 1 CTA (128 threads) has just 128×2 B=256 B128 \times 2\ \text{B} = 256\ \text{B}128×2 B=256 B in flight, and all 16 CTAs on 1 SM add up to only 4.0 KiB (Figure 2-3). That doesn't even reach the leftmost 16 KiB bar on the chart, and sits a full 16× below the 64 KiB knee point.

Put Section 1 and this section side by side: Section 1 counted how many steps are in the serial load chain, while this section measures how busy each step keeps HBM. Because v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM—nowhere near the bandwidth plateau—the device-wide read load is light, which is why the rough model in Section 2 could estimate using near-unloaded round-trip latency (we did not directly measure v1's per-iteration round-trip latency). Pushing bytes in flight per SM from 4.0 KiB up to 64 KiB is the job of Chapters 3 and 4; holding more bytes in flight takes more registers or on-chip memory, and Chapter 3 works out that budget.

4Can We Tell L2 Which Data to Keep?

Yes. Tagging streaming data as evict-first and reused data as evict-last preserves reused data when L2 thrashing would otherwise evict it, but only adds overhead when it would not be evicted anyway.

In Section 2, we inferred from capacity that the 16 KiB vector xxx stays inside the 60 MiB L2 cache. While gemv runs, though, 37.75 MB of single-use weights WWW also stream through L2—could that stream evict the data we want to reuse? Left to itself, the L2 hardware has no way of knowing which data will be read again shortly and which data is use-once-and-discard. When a large stream of single-use data pours through L2, it can evict data that later CTAs still need to re-read.

To override that default behavior, we can attach an L2 residency hint (cache policy) to each load (see Appendix B for the code syntax): tag single-use streaming data with evict_first (telling L2 to evict it first when space runs tight), and tag data re-read repeatedly across CTAs with evict_last (telling L2 to hold onto it until last if possible).

When does this actually pay off? Look at a standalone microbenchmark (Figure 2-4): first read in 8–32 MB of data to be reused (Figure 2-4 uses 32 MB as the example), then stream through 64 MB of single-use data—more than the 60 MiB L2 can hold—and finally re-read the reused data from the first step. When we tag the two reads evict_last and evict_first, the re-read runs at 5.70–7.33 TB/s, matching 98.8%–100% of the interference-free bandwidth (which implies, from the bandwidth ratio, that nearly all of the reused data remained in L2), or 1.7–1.9× cold HBM. Without those hints (leaving both reads at default eviction priority), re-read bandwidth falls to 3.36–4.19 TB/s—only 5%–7% above cold HBM (3.16–3.91 TB/s), indicating that most of the reused data was evicted from L2.

Here is how the L2 residency hint (cache policy) trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: keeps reused data in L2 when heavy streaming traffic would otherwise evict it (see the microbenchmark numbers above).
  • What it costs: you first construct two residency hints (done once), and every subsequent read has to carry one of them, making the code more verbose.
  • When it loses: when the reused data would not be evicted anyway, the extra hints only add overhead. On gemv, xxx is only 16 KiB and is not evicted in the first place. When we tried adding these two hints on top of v3 from Section 8 (call it v4; v4 also tags L1 as evict-first / evict-last, and a variant with only the L2 hints is slower too), it measured ~1 µs slower, so we do not count it as a step of its own. v5 in Chapter 3, Section 8 still carries these hints, and we did not measure their effect in v5 separately.

5When Only a Few CTAs Remain in the Tail Wave, How Can More SMs Compute the Same Row Together?

Partitioning a row along the reduction dimension KKK across multiple CTAs and merging is called Split-K; splitting only the tail-wave rows in half is called K-halves, where each half-row runs only 32 iterations.

Back in Section 1, we saw the bottleneck: the tail wave has only 192 CTAs, yet each one still has to grind through all 64 serial load iterations while ~90% of the chip's slots sit idle. Since one row's inner product is just a sum of 8,192 terms, we can slice it straight in half along KKK:

y[row]=∑k=04095W[row,k] xk⏟first half+∑k=40968191W[row,k] xk⏟second halfy[\text{row}] = \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{4095} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{first half}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=4096}^{8191} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{second half}}y[row]=first halfk=0∑4095​W[row,k]xk​​​+second halfk=4096∑8191​W[row,k]xk​​​

Those two halves don't depend on each other at all: we can hand them to two CTAs on two different SMs to compute in parallel, each producing one partial sum, and then add the two partial sums together.

When does splitting only the tail wave pay off best? The condition is simple: the tail-wave remainder rrr must be at most half of 1 wave capacity (r≤2,112/2=1,056r \le 2{,}112 / 2 = 1{,}056r≤2,112/2=1,056). As long as that holds, splitting rrr rows into 2r2r2r half-row CTAs packs all 2r2r2r CTAs right into the slots that were sitting empty during the tail wave, without spilling into an extra wave. We call splitting only the tail-wave rows in half K-halves (tail-wave half splitting). In v1, r=192r = 192r=192, so splitting in half gives 2r=384≤1,0562r = 384 \le 1{,}0562r=384≤1,056, right in the sweet spot. With that one cut, each half-row CTA's serial load chain drops from 64 iterations to 32 iterations, and device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave double at the same time (384 CTAs instead of 192; Mode 2 in Figure 2-5).

Generalize that idea to the whole grid and you get Split-K: whenever you have too few output rows or output tiles to fill even 1 wave capacity, slice the reduction dimension KKK into SSS pieces so SSS CTAs team up on the same output, multiplying the total CTA count by SSS (see Chapter 5, Sections 6–7 for Split-K on multi-token GEMM, and Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results along the evolution chain).

Here is how the Split-K and K-halves trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: K-halves cuts each tail-wave CTA's serial load chain in half (from 64 iterations to 32) and doubles device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave (see Section 8 for the measured speedup).
  • What it costs: each split row writes two 4 B partial sums (8 B total) and needs one extra cross-SM merge, and the grid's block-index mapping gets more complex. In the Section 6 microbenchmark, one cross-SM handoff takes ~0.67 µs; we did not measure the wait-free merge in v3 on its own.
  • When it loses: it loses when the remainder rrr exceeds half a wave, or when splitting too finely pushes the total CTA count past 1 wave capacity. We did not measure 4-way splitting on gemv; on an expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 3, splitting into 4 slices measured slower than splitting into 2.

6When Two SMs Each Compute Half a Row, How Do They Add Them Together Safely?

After writing its partial sum, each half-row CTA performs an atomic add on an L2 counter, and the last arriver (receiving old value 1) sums both halves; the two CTAs need not be co-resident on the chip.

First, why does the handoff have to go through L2? Because each SM's L1 cache is private to that SM, and the hardware does not automatically keep L1 caches coherent across different SMs. As we saw in Section 2, L2 is the only cache level shared by all SMs. With the global memory accesses we use in this chapter, cross-SM data exchange can only meet in the central L2 cache (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for another cross-SM path).

Second, how do the two CTAs decide who does the addition? That is the job of an atomic add: hardware fuses "read the old value, add the new value, and write back to memory" into a single indivisible operation so no other thread can slip in between, and hands back the old value from before the add. As soon as each half-row CTA finishes its partial sum, it does an atomic add of 1 on the same zero-initialized counter (int32, 4 B): the first one there (the first arriver) gets old value 0 and exits on the spot; the second one to reach the counter (the last arriver) receives old value 1, sees that its partner has already checked in, and adds the two halves together.

An atomic add by itself, though, is still not enough. Even though the first arriver writes its partial sum part before adding 1 to the counter in the source code, without memory-ordering constraints the CUDA memory model does not guarantee that another SM will see the new value of part before it sees the new value of the counter. On the hardware, the counter update can beat part to L2, or the last arriver can hit a stale line sitting in its own SM's L1 cache.

Before we look at the code, let's put the three memory orderings in plain language:

  • relaxed: guarantees only that the atomic operation itself is indivisible, without constraining the order of other reads and writes before or after it.
  • release: orders all prior reads and writes by this thread before this write; as long as the memory scope (see below) covers both threads, those prior writes become visible to any thread that observes this write via an acquire read.
  • acquire: keeps any subsequent reads and writes by this thread from being reordered ahead of this read.

Combining release and acquire gives acq_rel. Every synchronization on a GPU also carries a memory scope (scope)—such as within a CTA, across the whole GPU (device), or across the whole system. Smaller scopes are cheaper in hardware, so you normally specify the smallest scope that covers the communicating threads (if omitted, CUDA C++ atomic types default to system scope). Here the two half-row CTAs can be dispatched to any two SMs on the GPU, so the scope must be at least device (device-wide scope, written thread_scope_device in CUDA C++).

This is a spot where a GPU behaves very differently from a typical CPU. The x86 TSO memory model allows only one kind of reordering: store followed by load. When a core writes A and then reads B, the read can finish before the write to A becomes visible to other cores, acting as if the read moved ahead of the write; forbidding that on x86 takes an MFENCE, while per-core caches are kept coherent automatically by hardware protocols such as MESI.

The GPU memory model gives none of those automatic guarantees for unsynchronized normal (weak) reads and writes: all four orderings—read-read, read-write, write-write, and write-read—can be reordered. Note that normal weak reads and writes also differ from relaxed atomic operations, which still guarantee a single consistent modification order on the same address. To constrain ordering across different addresses on a GPU, you either use release / acquire or insert a standalone memory fence (an instruction dedicated to ordering reads and writes before and after it). An acq_rel fence (fence.acq_rel) guarantees that prior reads and writes are not reordered after subsequent writes, and subsequent reads and writes are not reordered before prior reads. It does not forbid store-load reordering, and the algorithms we use do not depend on forbidding it.

So the classic "write data first, then write flag" pattern that works out of the box on x86 has to be written on a GPU with scoped release / acquire operations.

#include <cuda/atomic>
// tail_store (last-arriver merge): thread 0 runs this after the intra-CTA reduction (a __syncthreads() precedes it)
// i = row index within the tail wave (0..191); half = 0 for the first half, 1 for the second half
part[2 * i + half] = sum;                                   // write this half-row's partial sum
cuda::atomic_ref<int, cuda::thread_scope_device> c(cnt[i]);
if (c.fetch_add(1, cuda::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) {      // got old value 1: I am the last arriver
    y[row] = part[2 * i] + part[2 * i + 1];
    c.store(0, cuda::memory_order_relaxed);                 // used again only by the next launch
}

Those few lines of code lock down the ordering through four connected steps:

  1. Cumulativity: When a thread executes a release, it publishes not only its own writes, but also any writes from other threads that it already observed before that release through an acquire or an intra-CTA barrier. That lets a synchronization chain pass the baton hop by hop, and each hop only needs a scope wide enough to cover the two threads at that hop. Say thread A writes data and hands it to thread B in the same CTA across an intra-CTA barrier; when B then does a device-scope release and thread C on another SM does a paired device-scope acquire, C is guaranteed to see A's write. If the B→C hop used only CTA scope, the chain would snap right at that hop.
  2. Intra-CTA merge to thread 0: In tail_store, only thread 0 writes the single scalar part and does the atomic add. Even when many threads in a CTA each write their own partial sums (as in Section 7), we still don't need every thread to do an atomic add: run one __syncthreads() first (see Primer 3, Section 4) and let thread 0 do a single release; by cumulativity from step 1, that publishes every prior write from the entire CTA at once.
  3. Cross-SM pairing: The first arriver's release and the last arriver's acquire act on the exact same counter cnt[i]. The atomic read-modify-write chain on that counter passes the first arriver's release straight to the last arriver's acquire, so the two take effect by paired synchronization and guarantee that the part written by the first arriver is visible to the last arriver. What we observe on the hardware (an empirical observation, not a specification guarantee) is that release pushes this SM's writes out to L2 first, while acquire invalidates this SM's L1 so subsequent reads fetch fresh data from L2. The last two bars in the first chart below measure that exact cost.
  4. Counter reset: Once the last arriver adds the two halves and writes y[row], resetting cnt[i] back to 0 only needs relaxed—the counter won't be touched again until the next kernel launch, and kernel completion in between already provides a stream-order boundary (see Chapter 1, Section 1).

Notice a crucial property of this "last arriver merges" pattern: it never requires the two CTAs to be co-resident on the chip. The first arriver exits right after its atomic add without waiting on anyone, and the last arriver simply reads and sums both halves when it gets there. No matter how far apart in time the two half-row CTAs are dispatched, they can never deadlock.

Compare that with the alternative where one CTA sits in a loop repeatedly polling a flag written by another CTA until a condition holds—a spin-wait. Unlike operating-system threads on a CPU, GPU hardware does not preempt a resident CTA off its SM to make room for an undispatched CTA from the same launch. Whenever you use spin-wait, you must guarantee that the waiting and signaling CTAs are on the chip at the same time: because the CUDA specification guarantees neither dispatch order nor co-residency for a standard launch, if spinning CTAs fill every on-chip slot without exiting, the CTA that is supposed to write the flag can never get an SM, and the GPU deadlocks.

If you genuinely need one CTA to wait on another, there are three specification-sanctioned ways to avoid deadlock. First, put the flag-writing producer in a separate preceding kernel. Second, use cooperative launch, where the driver guarantees that all CTAs of the entire grid are co-resident on the chip at once and refuses to launch if they do not fit (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how many CTAs fit per SM). Third, when only a few CTAs wait on each other, Hopper lets you declare those CTAs as a group, and the specification guarantees that all CTAs in the group are scheduled onto SMs simultaneously to run concurrently (see Chapter 7, Section 12). Under a standard launch, putting the producer at the lowest block indices by counting on the ascending dispatch order observed in Section 1 can also run to completion—but if the driver or hardware ever changes dispatch order, it can deadlock silently without reporting an error.

Finally, let's tally the hardware cost of device-wide synchronization. Why is device-wide release / acquire so much pricier than relaxed? It comes straight back to cache coherence: because per-SM L1 caches are not coherent with each other, a release has to wait until all prior writes from this thread have settled in the central L2 before other SMs can see them; and after an acquire, the SM can no longer trust stale lines sitting in its own L1 cache.

Timing a standalone device-wide acq_rel memory fence by itself (the second chart) makes the cost even clearer: when a prior write is still in flight, the fence waits ~200 extra clock cycles. From the memory model, we infer that this extra time goes to waiting until the write is visible across the GPU (reaching L2); this is not verified with hardware counters.

We also ran a separate cross-SM handoff microbenchmark: one CTA writes 256 values and hands them off via __syncthreads() and a release atomic add to a CTA on another SM that repeatedly polls with acquire loads (sleeping briefly between polls). The median time for one complete cross-SM handoff is ~0.67 µs.

Here is how the last-arriver merge via L2 works out:

  • What you gain: safely merges across SMs without launching a second reduction kernel and without requiring the two CTAs to be co-resident on the chip.
  • What it costs: each merge pays for one device-wide acq_rel atomic add (~1,078 clock cycles on a single thread) plus the last arriver's reads. We did not measure that cost separately in v3; for reference, the spinning cross-SM handoff microbenchmark above takes ~0.67 µs. Invalidating the local SM's L1 also slows down later re-reads, and you have to allocate an extra counter array and a partial-sum workspace buffer.
  • When it loses: when the partial sums to be merged are large or numerous, making that single last-arriver CTA serially read back and sum all of them by itself turns that CTA into a brand-new tail bottleneck.

7When There Are Many Partial Sums, How Do We Avoid Making the Last CTA Read Them All Alone?

Two alternatives: either have each of the SSS CTAs reduce 1/S1/S1/S of the rows, or have all CTAs issue non-fetching atomic adds directly into a pre-zeroed output buffer.

In Section 6, gemv only split each tail-wave row in half: one counter tracked 1 row, and the last arriver only had to read back two 4 B scalars. Now suppose we pack many output rows of gemv into a single tile, split that tile into SSS slices along KKK, and have a group of SSS CTAs share one counter—the partial sums that the last arriver has to read back on its own multiply right along with it. When we compute multiple tokens at once, that volume grows much larger still: for instance, when a tile of 64 tokens by 256 output columns is split along KKK across S=4S = 4S=4 CTAs (see Chapter 5, Sections 6–7 for tiled matrix multiplication), the 4 FP32 partial sums add up to 4×64×256×4 B=256 KiB4 \times 64 \times 256 \times 4\ \text{B} = 256\ \text{KiB}4×64×256×4 B=256 KiB. If we stuck with Section 6 and made that lone last-arriver CTA serially read back and sum the other 3 slices (192 KiB), its load chain would turn into a brand-new long tail (Figure 2-7, Mode 1).

The first fix is parallel slice reduction (Figure 2-7, Mode 2): instead of letting the first S−1S - 1S−1 arriving CTAs exit right away, keep all SSS CTAs around to split the merge work evenly across four steps:

  1. Each CTA writes its partial sums into the global workspace buffer and synchronizes within the CTA.
  2. Thread 0 of each CTA does an acq_rel atomic add on the counter to claim a ticket number ttt (the old value returned by the atomic add, counting up from 0; the paired synchronization rule is the same as in Section 6). Notice that this counter is never reset. The reason is simple: no CTA knows whether the other S−1S - 1S−1 CTAs have all seen the ticket count reach the target and exited their spin loops; if any CTA reset the counter to 0 right then, a CTA still spinning would never see the count reach the target. Instead, each subsequent call just keeps adding SSS more tickets on top.
  3. Once every ticket in this group has been claimed, the counter reaches (⌊t/S⌋+1)⋅S(\lfloor t / S \rfloor + 1) \cdot S(⌊t/S⌋+1)⋅S. Thread 0 repeatedly reads the counter with acquire until it is at least that target (the last ticket holder does not need to wait), confirming that all SSS partial sums are in place; once thread 0 finishes waiting, it runs another __syncthreads() before the rest of the threads in the CTA start reading (see Chapter 5, Section 7 for how counter wraparound is handled).
  4. Using its own slice index along KKK, each CTA reads back only its assigned 1/S1/S1/S row slice from all SSS partial sums (16 rows each when S=4S = 4S=4), sums them, and writes out the result.

Because earlier-arriving CTAs now spin-wait for later-arriving CTAs, the co-residency rule from Section 6 applies in full force: all SSS CTAs must be resident on the chip at the same time. Use cooperative launch from Section 6, or declare the SSS CTAs as a co-resident group (see Chapter 7, Section 12); relying on the observed ascending dispatch order also runs to completion, but the specification does not guarantee that. Here is how parallel slice reduction trades off:

  • What you gain: spreads the merge reads evenly across SSS CTAs, cutting off the long tail of a single CTA serially reading back all partial sums (see Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results).
  • What it costs: still needs a partial-sum workspace buffer, one ticket claim with spin-wait, extra merge code in every CTA, and co-residency across all SSS CTAs.
  • When it loses: when there are very few partial sums to merge (such as just 2 scalars in Section 6), the time saved by splitting the reads may not pay back the spin-wait overhead; we did not measure where that crossover point lies.

The second fix is even more direct—direct atomic add (Figure 2-7, Mode 3): as soon as each CTA finishes its slice of the inner product, all threads fire non-fetching atomic adds straight at the output array in global memory, adding without reading back the old value and without waiting for a return. That gets rid of the partial-sum workspace buffer, the ticket claim, and the counter all at once.

To use it safely, though, you have to satisfy three prerequisites:

  1. The output buffer must be zeroed before the first addition: the specification-safe way is to zero the output in a separate preceding kernel. If you use dedicated CTAs inside the same kernel to zero the output and publish a completion flag, you have to use the paired release / acquire synchronization from Section 6 and satisfy the co-residency requirement (see Section 6).
  2. The final result is visible only to the next kernel: inside the current kernel, no CTA has any way of knowing when the other CTAs have finished adding. The final sum across all partial sums becomes visible to the next kernel only after the current kernel finishes (or after the dependent kernel (successor) crosses the wait call in Chapter 1, Section 4).
  3. The output is no longer bitwise deterministic: because floating-point addition is not associative and the order in which CTAs reach L2 can shift from run to run, the accumulated floating-point values can differ in their last few bits.

Here is how the direct atomic add trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: eliminates both the partial-sum workspace buffer and the counter array.
  • What it costs: the output buffer must be zeroed ahead of time, the result is no longer bitwise deterministic, and when many CTAs atomically add to the same output address at once, requests queue up at L2 (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for measurements and analysis on single-request attention).
  • When it loses:
    • As the kernel in Chapter 6, Section 8 is written, the compiler compiles scalar BF16 atomic adds into a compare-and-swap retry loop: fetch the old value, compute the new value, and store it only if that memory location was not modified in the meantime—otherwise start over and retry, which runs slower in measurement (see Chapter 6, Section 8; Chapter 5, Section 7 covers paired BF16x2 atomic adds that pack two adjacent BF16 values together).
    • If output zeroing is folded into the same kernel and the compute CTA publishes its readiness flag immediately after writing zeros, measured runtime also regresses (Chapter 5, Section 7 explains the mechanism and measurements).

8gemv Evolution v2 → v3: Splitting the 192 Tail-Wave Rows in Half with K-halves

v3 splits the last 192 rows into 384 half-row CTAs, cutting the tail-wave load chain from 64 iterations to 32 and achieving a ~1.25× measured speedup.

In code, v3 is straightforward: the first 2,112 CTAs (indices 0..2111) still compute one full row each, just as before, while the next 384 CTAs (indices 2112..2495) pair up two to a row, each sweeping 4,096 columns and then running the counter-merge snippet from Section 6 (tail_store) to merge both halves through the central L2 and write y[row]. We place those half-row CTAs at the very end of the grid because, under the ascending dispatch order observed in Section 1, the highest-indexed batch lands squarely in the tail wave:

// v3: the first 2,112 rows use 1 CTA per row; the last 192 rows use 2 half-row CTAs per row (grid = 2,496)
gemv_v3<<<2112 + 2 * 192, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, M, K, part, cnt);

With that change in place, each SM still keeps 16 CTAs resident at once (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for why that limit doesn't change). By a rough estimate from the unloaded round-trip latency, shortening the tail-wave serial load chain by about half saves an estimated ~10 µs (see Figure 2-8's readout for the formula).

On the hardware, v3 runs ~1.25× faster than v2, saving slightly more time than our simple tail-wave model estimates; the reason is not determined. The trade-off is one cross-SM handoff on each of the 192 tail-wave rows, along with an additional workspace buffer for partial sums and a counter array (192×12 B≈2.3 KB192 \times 12\ \text{B} \approx 2.3\ \text{KB}192×12 B≈2.3 KB in all; Section 5 covers when this loses).

Even with v3 in place, 43.34 µs is still ~5.5× the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound (the lower bound accounts for only 18.1% of total time, including fixed overhead). The rest of that gap comes straight from the second bottleneck we uncovered in Section 3: v3 still keeps a mere 4.0 KiB in flight per SM at a time.

Takeaway: A kernel finishes only when its last CTA exits, and whether HBM reaches saturation depends on how many bytes each SM keeps in flight at once. Splitting the tail-wave rows in half and merging them through L2 brings gemv down from 54.19 µs (v2) to 43.34 µs (v3).

Next chapter's question: Saturating HBM takes ~64 KiB in flight per SM (Section 3), yet v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM. Now let's open up a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and once data enters the SM, how does it reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Single SM — Once Data Enters the SM, How Does It Reach Registers and Shared Memory Quickly and Safely?

  • Preface

  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
