In Chapter 2, Section 3, we measured that each SM has to keep about 64 KiB of normal loads in flight to saturate HBM, yet v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM. Now let's open up a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and once data enters the SM, how does it reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Once data enters an SM from L2, it takes one of two paths to the execution units. The first is the register path: at T=1T = 1T=1, a single thread uses each byte of WWW only once, so loading it straight into registers is enough, and we will keep pushing gemv along this path. The second is the shared memory (SMEM) path: when TTT tokens share the same block of WWW, many threads in a CTA read that block over and over, so we stage it in SMEM first. In this chapter, we will use a 16 KiB tile of WWW to unpack how these on-chip mechanisms work, and Chapters 5 and 6 will put them straight to work.

1How Many CTAs Can Reside on One SM Simultaneously?

Look at which of the SM's four fixed resource pools runs out first; gemv v1 fills all 64 warp slots first, so each SM holds 16 CTAs.

As long as the 32 threads in a warp (Primer 3, Section 3) do not branch apart, they issue the same instruction together (Chapter 4, Section 1 shows how the scheduler picks a warp each cycle, and Chapter 4, Section 4 covers branches). Each SM has four fixed-size resource pools, and whichever pool runs out first decides how many CTAs can reside on that SM at once:

  • warp slot: 64 slots per SM (2,048 threads).
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32 slots per SM.
  • SMEM (shared memory): Each SM has 256 KiB of on-chip storage. At most 228 KiB of that can go to SMEM, and the driver reserves an extra 1 KiB for each resident CTA. Whatever is left serves as that SM's L1 data cache (L1 caches are not coherent across SMs; see Chapter 2, Section 6).
  • register: 65,536 32-bit registers per SM, with a cap of 255 per thread. Hardware allocates registers in chunks of 256 per warp, which means each thread's register count gets rounded up to a multiple of 8.

Now let's plug gemv v1 (<<<2304, 128>>>) from Primer 3 into these four pools and see how many CTAs each one allows:

  • warp slot: Each CTA has 128 threads, or 4 warps, which gives 64÷4=1664 \div 4 = 1664÷4=16 CTAs.
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32 CTAs.
  • SMEM (shared memory): smem[128] takes 512 B, plus the reserved 1 KiB for 1.5 KiB in total, which fits ⌊228÷1.5⌋=152\lfloor 228 \div 1.5 \rfloor = 152⌊228÷1.5⌋=152 CTAs.
  • register: The compiled kernel uses 22 registers per thread, which rounds up to 24 (the next multiple of 8). Each CTA takes 24×128=3,07224 \times 128 = 3{,}07224×128=3,072 registers, fitting ⌊65,536÷3,072⌋=21\lfloor 65{,}536 \div 3{,}072 \rfloor = 21⌊65,536÷3,072⌋=21 CTAs.

Take the minimum of those four numbers and you get 16 CTAs, or 16×4=6416 \times 4 = 6416×4=64 resident warps per SM—filling all 64 warp slots. That is where "16 CTAs per SM" in Chapter 2, Section 1 comes from. The number of resident warps on an SM divided by 64 is called occupancy. Calculating it from the resource pools like this gives the theoretical occupancy, which is 100% for v1. At runtime, actual occupancy fluctuates from cycle to cycle, which we did not measure.

Look closely at the cutoff for the register pool. As long as each thread uses at most 65,536÷(64×32)=3265{,}536 \div (64 \times 32) = 3265,536÷(64×32)=32 registers, all 64 warps fit on the SM. Once a thread goes past 32 registers, the register pool runs out before the warp slots do (drag the slider in Figure 3-1 to see this exact cutoff). What if a thread needs to keep more live variables on hand than the registers it gets? Then the compiler has to spill (register spilling) the extra variables into local memory—memory that is private to each thread, but physically lives in device memory and goes through L1 and L2 cache. Registers sit right next to the execution units and bypass the memory hierarchy completely. A spilled variable, on the other hand, has to travel through the memory hierarchy on every single access: about 54 clock cycles if it hits in L1, and about 600 clock cycles if it goes all the way to HBM.

At compile time, you can use __launch_bounds__ to tell the compiler the maximum number of threads per CTA and the minimum number of CTAs to keep on each SM. The compiler then caps how many registers each thread can use—trading per-thread register cap for higher occupancy. Suppose a 128-thread CTA needs to hold 40 live values per thread. At 40 registers per thread, each SM fits ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12\lfloor 65{,}536 \div (40 \times 128) \rfloor = 12⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs (48 warps). If you cap each thread at 32 registers, you fit 16 CTAs (64 warps) onto the SM, but now 8 values per thread spill to local memory and pay a memory round trip on every access.

So the four resource pools squeeze your kernel from both ends. If each CTA takes more registers or SMEM, fewer CTAs fit on each SM, and bytes in flight drop with them. Go the other way and force the register cap down to pack more CTAs, and you trigger register spilling (spill). Whether the extra warps make up for those spill round trips is something you have to measure. Chapter 8, Section 4 shows a real case where it backfires: at T=256T = 256T=256, forcing the register cap down to 72 spills 12 registers, and Stage 6 ends up running about 26 µs slower.

Since each SM can hold only a fixed number of CTAs at once, another common way to launch work is a persistent kernel. The grid launches just enough CTAs to fill a single wave, and each CTA stays on its SM, looping to take the next piece of work until the job is finished. For gemv, that loop is for (row = blockIdx.x; row < 2304; row += gridDim.x), where gridDim.x is the total CTA count of the launch. Each CTA therefore starts up once rather than waiting for new CTAs to schedule onto SMs for later rows (we did not measure how much time this saves). Resident CTAs can also hold intermediate state on the SM, or claim work from a counter to slice the job more finely.

Keep in mind, though, that making a kernel persistent does not make the tail wave disappear. If you spread 2,304 rows across 2,112 persistent CTAs, 192 CTAs still have to run a second pass for the last rows while the other 1,920 sit idle—the exact same tail-wave shape we saw in Chapter 2, Section 1. To shorten the tail wave, you still need to split the work more finely (Chapter 2, Section 5) or make the total work items an exact multiple of one wave's capacity.

The cost of a persistent kernel is one extra loop inside every CTA. When the total work cannot even fill a single wave, that loop is pure overhead. And when two back-to-back steps have an all-to-all dependency, a persistent kernel can synchronize across the whole GPU inside the kernel, but it still requires cooperative launch (Chapter 2, Section 6) and still has to wait for the slowest CTA every single time (Chapter 1, Section 3).

2How Many Sector Requests Does One Warp Load Instruction Generate?

Hardware requests memory in 32-byte sectors, sending one request for every sector a warp load instruction touches; the more contiguous the addresses and the wider each thread reads, the fewer requests go out and the more useful bytes come back.

First, let's separate two hardware sizes: a sector is 32 B, which is the smallest unit the memory system requests, while a cache line is 128 B, or 4 sectors. When a warp issues a load instruction, the LSU (Load/Store Unit) inside the SM collects all 32 thread addresses and merges any addresses that fall into the same 32 B sector into a single request. The tighter those addresses pack into sectors, the fewer requests go out—and that is coalesced access (coalescing).

Let's compare one load instruction for WWW across three versions of gemv (the three modes in Figure 3-2):

  • v0 and v1: As we saw in Primer 3, Section 6, one load instruction in v0 scatters across 32 sectors, while in v1 it lands in just 2. In the terms of this section, v0 sends 32 requests and v1 sends only 2 requests. What about the other 30 B in each sector that v0 does not use right away? Those happen to be the exact elements the same thread will read over the next 15 iterations, so they may stay in L1 and hit later—though we did not measure the L1 hit rate.
  • v5 (Section 8 of this chapter): Each thread switches to uint4 (a 16-byte vector load) to read 16 B (8 BF16 elements) in one go. Now a single warp instruction reads 32×16=51232 \times 16 = 51232×16=512 B—4 full cache lines, or 16 sectors—and uses 100% of the 512 B it fetches on the spot.

Put them side by side and the payoff is obvious: one instruction in v5 brings back 8× as many useful bytes as v1. So to keep the same number of bytes in flight, v5 needs only one-eighth as many load instructions for WWW as v1 (note that this is the count of load instructions for WWW, not the total instructions in the kernel).

Wide coalesced loads require contiguous data and 16 B address alignment. Watch what they do to your register budget, too: a 16 B load ties up its 4 destination 32-bit registers from the moment it issues until the data comes back. If a single thread keeps kkk such loads in flight at once, those pending loads alone take 4k4k4k registers (we will use this exact math in Chapter 4, Section 3).

What if the rows you need to read come from an index table and sit scattered across memory instead of next to each other? Then a warp cannot coalesce them across rows (that is exactly what happens with the KV cache in Chapter 7). In that case, the only way to keep enough bytes in flight is to keep more warps resident on the SM or have each thread issue multiple loads in flight at once (see Chapter 4, Section 3).

3How Does a Repeatedly Read Data Block Move into SMEM Without Passing Through Registers?

Hand regular rectangular tiles to TMA to move them into SMEM with a single instruction; use cp.async when gathering scattered rows by index.

When multiple tokens share the same block of weights WWW, many warps inside a CTA need to read that block over and over. Rather than having every warp fetch it from device memory on its own, we first stage it in SMEM as a tile so all warps can read it on chip (Chapter 5, Section 6 shows how Tensor Core consumes it). Let's do the math on one 16 KiB tile of WWW from qkv_gate, Wtile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{W_{tile}}{128,\;64}{BF16}Wtile​:[128,64]BF16: it has 128 rows of 64 BF16 elements (128 B) each. In device memory, those 128 row segments are each 128 B long, separated from one another by a full row stride of 16,384 B.

To move this 16 KiB tile into SMEM, the hardware gives us four paths (Figure 3-3; for Paths 1 and 2, we count a CTA of 128 threads, or 4 warps):

  • Path 1: Normal load into registers, then store to SMEM. Each thread issues 16,384÷(128×16)=816{,}384 \div (128 \times 16) = 816,384÷(128×16)=8 loads of 16 B. Across the CTA, that takes 32 warp load instructions plus 32 warp store instructions, or 64 instructions in total. If you keep all 8 loads in flight at once, each thread ties up 8×4=328 \times 4 = 328×4=32 staging registers; if you issue them one at a time, you need only 4 registers, but you pay for 8 serial round trips. Take this path only when you have to reformat the data in registers before writing it to SMEM.
  • Path 2: Per-thread asynchronous copy (cp.async). Each thread still computes its own addresses and together the warps issue 32 instructions, but the bytes go straight from L2 into SMEM without passing through registers (0 staging registers). On Hopper, TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) cannot gather rows through an index table in one command, so when we gather scattered rows by index (see Chapter 7, Section 5), we either take this path or issue one Path 3 1D bulk copy per row.
  • Path 3: TMA 1D bulk copy (cp.async.bulk). Give a start address and a byte count, and TMA copies one contiguous span of bytes; a single thread issues the instruction using 0 data registers. Because our tile of WWW is not one contiguous span in memory but 128 separate row segments, taking Path 3 means issuing one copy per row, or 128 instructions in total.
  • Path 4: TMA multidimensional tensor bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.tensor). We typically build a tensor descriptor on the CPU ahead of time that records the full tensor's dimensions, row stride, tile box size, swizzle mode, and out-of-bounds fill mode. Inside the kernel, a single thread passes the tile coordinates and issues 1 instruction. TMA computes all 128 segment addresses in hardware, fills out-of-bounds elements with 0 automatically, and can even reorder the bytes as they land in SMEM using the XOR rule from Section 7—all while using 0 data registers.

First, a concept from the memory model: the GPU memory model refers to different memory-access paths as distinct proxies (proxy), a distinction that extends beyond SMEM. Normal thread reads and writes go through the generic proxy. TMA reads and writes—as well as the Tensor Core instructions in Chapter 5 that read matrices from SMEM—go through the async proxy. When two proxies access the same address, nothing orders them automatically. To hand data off from one proxy to the other, you first have to cross a cross-proxy fence (fence.proxy.async).

So how does the handoff work when TMA reads data into SMEM? A hardware counter in SMEM tracks how many bytes still need to be written. Each time TMA finishes writing a batch of bytes, it subtracts them from that count. When the byte count hits 0, that satisfies one of the two conditions that let waiting warps move on (Section 5 covers the other). By the specification, a completed TMA read carries a built-in cross-proxy fence, so as soon as consumers see the completion signal, they can read SMEM directly and get the new data.

Picking one path over another does not change the HBM bandwidth ceiling: once enough bytes are in flight, both normal loads and TMA reach about 4.5 TB/s (see Chapter 2, Figure 2-3, and the chart in Section 4 of this chapter). Where Path 4 pays off is instruction and register overhead: 1 instruction takes the place of 32 to 64 instructions, consumes 0 data registers, and hands address calculation and bounds checking over to hardware.

What does Path 4 cost? First, each TMA transfer pays a fixed startup overhead. Second, the descriptor usually has to be built on the CPU ahead of time (you can also patch one from a template on the GPU, but that needs an extra fence), and the tile shape has a cap: at most 256 elements along each dimension. On Hopper, TMA also cannot gather several rows through an index table in one command (issuing one 1D bulk copy per row still works; Appendix A, Section 4 covers the next-generation change). Finally, when a tile is very small, the fixed startup overhead outweighs the instructions you save, though we did not measure the exact size where that flips.

4How Many Slots Does a Ring Buffer Need to Overlap Data Movement and Compute?

Cut SMEM into a ring of buffer slots so consumers compute on the slot that has arrived while the remaining slots stay in flight; once in-flight slots total about 48 KiB per SM, read bandwidth reaches the plateau.

If SMEM has only 1 slot, moving data and computing on it have to take turns, so every tile waits out a full memory round trip. To overlap the two, we cut SMEM into NNN buffer slots and cycle through them in order—0,1,…,N−1,0,1,…0, 1, \dots, N-1, 0, 1, \dots0,1,…,N−1,0,1,…—forming a ring buffer. To match, we split the warps in the CTA into two roles: one producer warp does nothing but issue TMA loads to fill empty slots with upcoming tiles, while the remaining consumer warps do nothing but read arrived slots and compute. Splitting warps by role like this is called warp specialization.

How many bytes do we need to keep in flight? That still comes straight from Little's Law in Chapter 2, Section 3: bytes in flight = bandwidth ×\times× round-trip latency. With TMA loads, our measurements hit the bandwidth plateau once each SM keeps about 48 KiB in flight (see the first chart below).

You might wonder why this 48 KiB differs from the 64 KiB we saw in Chapter 2, Section 3. There is no contradiction—both numbers are measured knee points, except Chapter 2 used normal 16 B loads and here we are using TMA. Compare the two through Little's Law at the same bytes in flight: with 16 KiB in flight per SM, a TMA round trip takes about 0.76 µs, while normal loads take about 0.94 µs; near the plateau, the two round trips are nearly identical (see the chart note above for the 48 KiB point). Because normal loads have a longer round trip at the same bytes in flight, they need 64 KiB in flight to reach the knee. Where that latency difference comes from, we did not measure.

When counting slots, remember that the 1 slot consumers are actively computing on has already landed in SMEM, so it does not count as in flight. That means the minimum number of slots you need in the ring is:

N=⌈bytes in flight needed per SMbytes per slot⌉+1N = \left\lceil \frac{\text{bytes in flight needed per SM}}{\text{bytes per slot}} \right\rceil + 1N=⌈bytes per slotbytes in flight needed per SM​⌉+1

Plug in 16 KiB per slot and you get N=⌈48÷16⌉+1=4N = \lceil 48 \div 16 \rceil + 1 = 4N=⌈48÷16⌉+1=4: 3 slots in flight plus 1 slot being computed on, taking 64 KiB of SMEM in total. This formula assumes consumers finish computing one slot no slower than memory bandwidth can deliver one slot (at ~34 GB/s per SM, delivering 16 KiB takes ~0.48 µs). When that holds, consumers still wait on data, but they are waiting on the bandwidth ceiling rather than round-trip latency. If consumers take longer than that to compute a slot, the bottleneck is on the consumer side: adding more slots will never reach the bandwidth plateau, and you have to size the ring by measuring at the consumers' actual speed.

What if the grid is too small to fill all 132 SMs? Then fewer active SMs have to pull the whole chip's bandwidth, so the bytes in flight needed on each active SM scale up in proportion. If only half the SMs are running, for instance, each active SM has to keep roughly twice as many bytes in flight.

The upside of a ring buffer is clear: data movement overlaps with compute, and keeping N−1N - 1N−1 slots in flight pushes read bandwidth onto the plateau (first chart). The price you pay is 16 KiB of SMEM for each extra slot, plus one dedicated producer warp for the ring. Do the capacity math: 4 slots plus the reserved 1 KiB take 65 KiB, so by the SMEM pool in Section 1, each SM fits at most ⌊228÷65⌋=3\lfloor 228 \div 65 \rfloor = 3⌊228÷65⌋=3 CTAs. Furthermore, the deeper you make the ring, the longer each step's data takes from issue until it is ready to read (see the second chart below). That follows directly from Little's Law in Chapter 2, Section 3: round-trip latency = bytes in flight ÷ bandwidth, so once bytes in flight grow faster than bandwidth, each round trip takes longer. Still, that longer round trip makes consumers wait extra time only when the ring is first filling up or when the next step's address becomes known late (we did not measure this effect separately).

As the chart shows, with only 1 slot in flight, read bandwidth reaches just 60%–70% of the plateau. Going from 3 in-flight slots to 4, however, gains less than 1% in bandwidth while costing another 16 KiB of SMEM. In practice, the sweet spot has to be measured on the real kernel: the expert kernel in Chapter 8 slows down when cut to 2 slots (Chapter 8, Section 9), whereas expanding the T=32T = 32T=32 projection kernel in Chapter 9 from 6 slots to 7 speeds it up by about 0.55 µs (Chapter 9, Section 2).

5How Do Producers and Consumers Hand Off a Slot Without Overwriting Data Before It Is Read?

Pair each buffer slot with two mbarrier objects—one for full, one for empty; consumers must not signal empty until the data read from the slot has returned to registers.

If you hand off buffer slots with __syncthreads(), the entire CTA has to stop together at every step: the producer warp cannot run ahead on its own, and consumers have to wait on each other. An mbarrier (a hardware-counted barrier) makes only the two sides using a given slot wait on each other, leaving every other warp free to keep running. Physically, an mbarrier is an 8-byte hardware object in SMEM that tracks two counts: how many threads still need to arrive (arrive), and how many bytes still need to be written (transaction bytes). Only when both counts hit zero does the current round finish and the barrier's phase flip. Hardware uses a single parity bit that alternates between 0 and 1 to tell adjacent rounds apart, so the same barrier object can be reused round after round.

We pair each slot sss with two barriers: full[s] (ready to read) and empty[s] (ready to write). Figure 3-5 walks through the handoff across round rrr and round r+1r+1r+1 in time order:

  • producer: First waits for the phase of empty[s] to flip, confirming the slot is free. Next, it arrives on full[s], registers the 16,384 bytes expected for this transfer, and issues the TMA load. Each time TMA finishes writing a batch of bytes, it subtracts them from full[s]; once both the arrival count and the byte count hit zero, full[s] flips phase.
  • consumer: Waits on full[s] until its phase flips, at which point the bytes written by TMA are already visible to it (Section 3). It then issues shared-memory loads from the slot, uses the loaded values in multiply-adds, and finally arrives on empty[s] to hand the empty slot back.

Here is a trap that is easy to fall into: issuing a shared-memory load only hands off a request to hardware; the actual bytes do not land in the destination register until tens of cycles later. That gives us one iron rule: Consumers must not arrive on empty[s] before the shared-memory loads from slot sss have returned to registers. If a consumer arrives too early, the producer sees empty[s] flip, assumes the slot is free, and kicks off the next round's TMA into that same slot. If the new TMA bytes overwrite the slot before those earlier shared-memory loads finish reading, the consumer ends up loading data from the next tile. Breaking read-before-write order like this is a write-after-read hazard (WAR). Worst of all, it raises no error—the output just comes out silently wrong. Chapter 8's expert kernel ran into this very issue, and stress testing (repeatedly replaying the kernel and checking its outputs) caught the overwrite.

You might ask: arriving on empty[s] carries a CTA-scope release by default (Chapter 2, Section 6), so why didn't it stop this overwrite? Two separate things are going on here:

  • First, the specification itself makes no such promise. That default release orders earlier shared-memory loads before the arrival only inside the generic proxy. The next round's TMA write into this slot goes through the async proxy, and PTX requires a cross-proxy fence whenever two proxies access the same address (Section 3).
  • Second, the compiled arrival instruction did not actually wait for those loads. When the arrival went out, the earlier shared-memory loads had not yet returned to registers. Adding an intra-CTA fence (fence.acq_rel.cta) before the arrival made it wait for the loads; the reason is not determined (see Chapter 8, Section 11).

In practice, there are two common ways to handle this. Both aim for the same thing: making sure the loads from slot sss are already back in registers by the time the arrival goes out. That closes the second issue; the first issue still has no guarantee in the specification, so both patterns rely on the loads having already finished before the arrival:

  • The first pattern is to use the loaded values in compute instructions before arriving. Because the compiler can still move those compute instructions past the arrival, you also put the intra-CTA fence from above right before the arrival so it waits for the shared-memory loads to return (Chapter 8, Section 11). Once the data is sitting in registers, no later write to SMEM through either proxy can touch it.
  • The second pattern is to issue the loads from slot sss, hold off on arriving, and wait on another signal first (in Chapter 8, that signal is the same step's full barrier on the activation ring buffer), then arrive on slot sss afterward. That intervening wait gives the loads from slot sss time to return to registers, though the specification does not guarantee it is long enough. You have to check the compiled instructions to verify that no load is still pending when the arrival goes out.

The final expert kernel in Chapter 8 uses the second pattern. After issuing the weight loads from slot sss, it waits on the same step's full barrier of the activation ring buffer, arrives on empty[s], and only then computes with those weights. Only on compiler versions whose compiled output we have checked does it omit the intra-CTA fence; every other compiler version retains the fence. In the earlier version that only deferred the arrival—before the fence was added—stress testing already brought overwrites down to 0, at a cost of about 0.4–1.6 µs (Chapter 8, Section 11).

The upside of paired mbarrier handoffs is that only the producer and consumers touching that slot wait on each other, while other warps keep moving. Even though a single thread's unloaded arrive-plus-wait round trip takes about 200 cycles, in the steady state of a warp-specialized loop each step's handshake adds only about 27 cycles. The cost is two 8 B counters per slot—and whenever consumers arrive a little later, the producer refills that slot a little later, which makes the ring slightly shallower in practice.

6What If Data-Movement Warps Have Excess Registers While Compute Warps Do Not Have Enough?

Reallocate registers per warpgroup at kernel entry using setmaxnreg: the producer warpgroup lowers its quota and returns registers to the CTA pool, and the consumer warpgroups raise their quota to claim them, keeping the CTA's total registers within the amount allocated at launch.

Four consecutive warps whose starting warp index is a multiple of 4 (128 threads in all) form a warpgroup. The setmaxnreg instruction (per-warpgroup register reallocation) operates on whole warpgroups, and all 128 threads in a warpgroup must execute it together.

Picture a CTA with 1 producer warpgroup and 2 consumer warpgroups. Because setmaxnreg works at warpgroup granularity, even though a single thread can issue TMA loads (Section 3), the producer role still has to occupy a full warpgroup of 128 threads, bringing the CTA to 384 threads in all. On the consumer side, threads must accumulate results across many tokens simultaneously. Say each consumer warpgroup computes a 64-token-row × 256-column FP32 output tile; every thread has to hold 128 partial sums in registers at the same time, on top of addresses and temporaries. In one version of our single-layer prefill and decode kernels, consumers are set to 232 registers, while the producer—which only issues copy and arrival instructions—is set to 40 registers.

If every thread in the CTA had to take the same number of registers, the math would never work: giving 232 registers to all 384 threads requires 384×232=89,088384 \times 232 = 89{,}088384×232=89,088 registers—23,552 more than the SM's 65,536 limit—so the CTA could not even launch on one SM. To fit 384 threads into an SM at launch, each thread can take at most ⌊65,536÷384⌋\lfloor 65{,}536 \div 384 \rfloor⌊65,536÷384⌋ rounded down to a multiple of 8, which is 168 registers. That leaves consumers with only 168 registers instead of the 232 set in the code (whether 168 registers would be enough or spill to local memory, we did not measure).

Reallocating registers by warpgroup right at kernel entry untangles this in four steps (Figure 3-6):

  • At kernel launch: All 384 threads start with 168 registers each, the largest multiple of 8 that fits in one SM (384×168=64,512≤65,536384 \times 168 = 64{,}512 \le 65{,}536384×168=64,512≤65,536; the next step up, 176, would take 67,584).
  • Producer releases registers: The 1 producer warpgroup runs setmaxnreg to drop its quota to 40, returning 128×(168−40)=16,384128 \times (168 - 40) = 16{,}384128×(168−40)=16,384 registers to the CTA pool.
  • Consumer claims registers: The 2 consumer warpgroups run setmaxnreg to raise their quota to 232, claiming those exact 256×(232−168)=16,384256 \times (232 - 168) = 16{,}384256×(232−168)=16,384 registers.
  • Result: The CTA uses 128×40+256×232=5,120+59,392=64,512128 \times 40 + 256 \times 232 = 5{,}120 + 59{,}392 = 64{,}512128×40+256×232=5,120+59,392=64,512 registers, matching the exact total allocated at launch.

With this handoff, consumers get all 232 registers they need to hold their 128 accumulators in registers. The tradeoff is that all 128 threads in each warpgroup have to execute the instruction together, and the producer warpgroup is left with just 40 registers per thread, so it cannot take on other work. Because 64,512 registers nearly fills the SM's register pool, each SM can hold only 1 such CTA at a time. Writing that CTA as a persistent kernel (Section 1) means it initializes just once and overlaps fetching the next tile with the current tile's epilogue (we did not measure those two savings separately). Even so, a persistent kernel is not an automatic win: Chapter 9, Section 6 shows a measured case where the exact same load work runs slower as a persistent kernel than with a normal launch (for reasons not determined).

When does reallocating registers fail to help? Lowering the producer's register quota alone does not automatically save time: one step in the multi-token GEMM of Chapter 6, Section 8 tried this and measured no runtime change (for reasons we did not measure). Going the other way and adding two more consumer warpgroups does not work either: 4 consumer warpgroups would need 4×128×232=118,7844 \times 128 \times 232 = 118{,}7844×128×232=118,784 registers, which is far beyond the SM's pool even after borrowing from the producer (Chapter 8, Section 9).

7Why Does One Warp Reading an SMEM Column Queue Up, and How Can We Stagger It with Zero Space Overhead?

Hardware organizes SMEM into 32 parallel 4-byte-wide banks, so requests in the same load that target different 4 B words within one bank must be served in serial order; bitwise-XORing the column chunk index with the row index spreads same-column data across distinct banks at zero extra byte cost.

Under the hood, SMEM is divided into 32 parallel shared-memory banks, each 4 B wide and able to serve one 4 B word per cycle. Consecutive 4 B words map to banks 0, 1, …, 31 in order, so every 128 B spans all 32 banks and SMEM as a whole can deliver at most 32×4=12832 \times 4 = 12832×4=128 B per cycle. Serving all requests of a load instruction in one pass is called 1 wavefront. At peak hardware rate, 1 wavefront takes 1 cycle; in the microbenchmark below, each extra wavefront adds about 2 cycles, and we did not measure why it is 2 rather than 1.

If threads in the same load request different 4 B words from the same bank, hardware cannot deliver them all in one pass; it splits the instruction into multiple wavefronts and serves them sequentially, which is a bank conflict. When multiple threads read the same 4 B word, hardware instead performs a broadcast of that word to all requesting threads at once with no conflict. Having DDD requests target distinct 4 B words in one bank produces a DDD-way bank conflict.

In our measurements, conflicts start slowing down back-to-back issue from 4-way onward: under an 8-way conflict, a single warp's SMEM read throughput drops to about a quarter (see the first chart below). For 16-byte loads, hardware breaks the warp into 4 groups of 8 threads and evaluates conflicts one 8-thread group at a time (see the second chart below).

Now let's return to the WWW tile from Section 3: each row is 128 B, divided into 8 chunks of 16 B indexed by c=0..7c = 0..7c=0..7. When consumers read this tile column-wise, each phase has 8 threads read the same column chunk ccc across 8 consecutive rows (8 threads ×\times× 16 B = 128 B, matching one 8-thread group). Without swizzling, row rrr, column chunk ccc sits at byte offset offset(r,c)=128r+16c\mathrm{offset}(r, c) = 128r + 16coffset(r,c)=128r+16c. Because the 8 rows sit 128 B apart, all 8 threads land on the exact same 4 banks—banks 4c..4c+34c..4c+34c..4c+3—causing an 8-way bank conflict. Each load is forced into 8 wavefronts, and reading all 8 chunk columns takes 64 wavefronts in total (Figure 3-7 Mode 1).

To fix this, we turn on XOR swizzle and change the on-chip byte offset to:

offset(r,c)=128r+16 (c⊕(r mod 8))\mathrm{offset}(r, c) = 128r + 16\,(c \oplus (r \bmod 8))offset(r,c)=128r+16(c⊕(rmod8))

Watch what happens now when you fix the column chunk index ccc and step rrr across 8 consecutive rows: c⊕(r mod 8)c \oplus (r \bmod 8)c⊕(rmod8) visits every number from 000 to 777 exactly once. Those 8 chunks of 16 B now land on 8 distinct groups of 4 banks, spreading cleanly across all 32 banks. The 8-way conflict drops to 0, each load finishes in 1 wavefront, reading all 8 columns takes just 8 wavefronts in total, and it costs zero extra bytes of SMEM (Figure 3-7 Mode 2).

What XOR swizzle requires in return is that both the SMEM writer and the SMEM reader use the same address formula. With TMA transfers, enabling 128 B swizzle in the host-side tensor descriptor makes the TMA hardware permute bytes by this formula automatically as it writes into SMEM (Section 3, Path 4). Watch one alignment rule: TMA hardware only requires a 128 B-aligned SMEM base address, but because the 128 B swizzle pattern repeats every 1,024 B (8 rows), the formula above anchors row 0 cleanly only when the buffer base is 1,024 B-aligned—otherwise the pattern shifts by (address÷128) mod 8(\text{address} \div 128) \bmod 8(address÷128)mod8 rows. Every kernel in this book aligns to 1,024 B.

There is another classic way to stagger banks: row-stride padding. It fits small tables where 32 threads read the same column of 4 B words across 32 rows. When the row width is 32 words (128 B), the same column across all 32 rows lands on a single bank, causing a 32-way conflict. Pad each row with 1 extra word so the width becomes 33 words, and the same column shifts by 1 bank on each row, spreading all 32 rows across all 32 banks at the cost of 4 extra bytes per row.

Each method is built for its own access pattern. Because the 128 B XOR swizzle pattern repeats every 8 rows, if you use it when reading a column of 4 B words across 32 rows, rows rrr, r+8r+8r+8, r+16r+16r+16, and r+24r+24r+24 still land on the same bank and leave a 4-way conflict—so that pattern needs row-stride padding instead. We will see XOR swizzle in action when reading the KV cache in Chapter 7, Section 5.

8gemv v3 → v5: Loading 16 Bytes per Thread Raises Bytes in Flight by 8×

v3 → v5 makes two changes: each thread switches to 16 B wide loads, and the kernel carries over the two residency hints from Chapter 2, Section 4; together they make the kernel about 2.5× faster.

Our starting point is v3 from Chapter 2, Section 8, with inputs W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 and x :  [8192]  BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}x:[8192]BF16 and output [2304][2304][2304]. That kernel launches 2,496 CTAs of 128 threads each, and because each thread reads just one 2 B element of WWW per iteration, each SM keeps only about 16×128×2 B=416 \times 128 \times 2\ \text{B} = 416×128×2 B=4 KiB in flight.

In v5, we switch both WWW and xxx to uint4 loads so each thread reads 16 B at a time (8 consecutive BF16 elements, matching Mode v5 in Figure 3-2). That requires each row to start on a 16 B boundary, which rows of 8,192×28{,}192 \times 28,192×2 B naturally satisfy. On each iteration, the thread converts those 8 BF16 elements to FP32 and accumulates their products:

acc+=∑i=07FP32(W[row,8k+i])⋅FP32(x[8k+i])\mathit{acc} \mathrel{+}= \sum_{i=0}^{7} \mathrm{FP32}(W[\mathit{row}, 8k+i]) \cdot \mathrm{FP32}(x[8k+i])acc+=i=0∑7​FP32(W[row,8k+i])⋅FP32(x[8k+i])

The three lines of C++ below sketch how one iteration issues the 16 B loads and converts the first two BF16 elements. uint4 is a 16-byte vector of four 32-bit integers whose .x/.y/.z/.w fields each pack 2 BF16 values, and __bfloat1622float2 converts a pair of BF16 values (__nv_bfloat162) into a pair of FP32 values (float2) in one call. The full kernel converts all four fields of w_vec—8 BF16 values in all—to FP32 for multiply-add:

// v5 sketch: each uint4 load reads 16 bytes of W and x (8 consecutive BF16)
uint4 w_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(&W[row * K])[k];
uint4 x_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(x)[k];
float2 wf0 = __bfloat1622float2(*reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat162*>(&w_vec.x));

Let's first work out residency using Section 1's rules (Figure 3-1): each thread in v5 takes 30 registers (up from 23 in v3). Rounded up to a multiple of 8, that lands at 32 registers—right on the 32-register cutoff from Section 1—so each SM still holds all 16 CTAs and 64 warps. If each thread used just 3 more registers (33 registers) and stepped past that cutoff, rounding up to a multiple of 8 would allocate 40 registers per thread and drop residency to ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12\lfloor 65{,}536 \div (40 \times 128) \rfloor = 12⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs per SM (we did not measure that variant).

Next, let's check bytes in flight using Section 2: the number of load instructions for WWW drops to one-eighth, while 64 resident warps ×\times× 512 B per warp load gives about 32 KiB/SM in flight—a full 8× jump over v3.

Still, 32 KiB in flight per SM reaches only about 83% of the bandwidth plateau (Chapter 2, Figure 2-3). Even when we estimate runtime from that 83% bandwidth plus fixed overhead, the estimate comes out noticeably faster than v5's measured time (see the chart note below), and we did not measure where that remaining gap comes from. On top of that, v5 still runs about 1.18 waves: after the 2,112 CTAs of the first wave finish, 384 half-row CTAs have to run a second wave.

9v5 → v6: Why Does Eliminating the Tail Wave Make Execution Slower?

v6 shrinks each CTA to a single warp; although all 2,304 CTAs now fit in a single wave, each SM gets only about 17 resident warps on average, dropping bytes in flight to ~8.7 KiB and pulling bandwidth down with it.

To get rid of v5's remaining tail wave, v6 shrinks each CTA from 128 threads down to 32 so that a single warp computes one full row:

gemv_v6<<<2304, 32, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);

Each thread still issues 16 B loads per iteration just as in v5, and a row's 32 partial sums still reduce through 128 B of SMEM (in Chapter 4, Section 5, we will replace that SMEM reduction by exchanging values directly across registers within the warp).

First let's check the pool limits from Section 1 (preset v6 in Figure 3-1): per-thread registers match v5, and each CTA uses 128 B of SMEM plus the 1 KiB reserved by the driver. Because each CTA now has only 1 warp, warp slots would allow 64 CTAs, but CTA slots cap each SM at 32 CTAs, giving the full GPU a single-wave capacity of 132×32=4,224≥2,304132 \times 32 = 4{,}224 \ge 2{,}304132×32=4,224≥2,304. All 2,304 CTAs fit in a single wave, so we no longer need v3's KKK-halves split or L2 merge.

Here is the catch: how many CTAs a resource pool allows is not how many CTAs your grid actually puts on the SM. The entire grid has only 2,304 CTAs. Spread across 132 SMs, each SM gets an average of just 2,304÷132≈17.452{,}304 \div 132 \approx 17.452,304÷132≈17.45 CTAs—or about 17 warps, down from 64 in v5—leaving nearly three-quarters of the warp slots empty. With 1 in-flight 16 B load of WWW per thread, each SM keeps only 17.45×512 B≈8.717.45 \times 512\ \text{B} \approx 8.717.45×512 B≈8.7 KiB/SM of WWW in flight, roughly a quarter of what v5 had.

The chart below shows the measured result: v6 runs slower than v5, moving in the exact direction predicted by the drop in bytes in flight. In v6, each thread issues only one 16 B load of WWW before using the result (about 8.7 KiB/SM in flight). After subtracting fixed overhead, achieved bandwidth is about 2.2 TB/s, which is higher than what you get by extrapolating from the round-trip latency in Chapter 2, Figure 2-3 (see the chart note). One possibility is that round-trip latency itself is shorter when fewer bytes are in flight, though we did not measure the cause separately.

So v6 gives us a clear measured counterexample: shrinking CTAs to eliminate a tail wave pays off only if it does not gut your bytes in flight, and when you do residency math, you have to count the warps actually placed on each SM, not just the ceiling allowed by the resource pools. Even so, the structure of v6 is well worth keeping: one warp computes one row, and the whole grid fits in a single wave. That gets rid of the tail-wave split and cross-CTA merge, and because all 32 partial sums for a row now live inside the same warp, we will soon be able to sum them directly in registers without touching SMEM at all (Chapter 4, Section 5).

As for the shared-memory half of this chapter—TMA, ring buffers, mbarrier, XOR swizzle, and setmaxnreg—we will see their measured payoff on the TTT-token qkv_gate matrix multiplication in Chapter 6, Section 8.

Takeaway: How quickly and safely an SM gets its data comes down to three things: how many contiguous useful bytes each load instruction brings back, how many bytes the warps actually resident on the SM keep in flight at once, and whether each SMEM buffer slot is handed back only after the data read from it has returned to registers.

Next chapter's question: In v6, each SM has only about 17 warps and 8.7 KiB in flight; how does each sub-partition inside the SM pick a warp to issue an instruction each cycle, and how can we make a single thread keep multiple loads in flight at once to push bytes in flight back above 64 KiB?

Chapter 4Level 4

Single SMSP — When Each Cycle Can Issue Only 1 Instruction, How Do We Keep Waiting from Stretching Total Runtime?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]: Single SMSP
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10
  • Appendices

At the end of Chapter 3, we shrank each CTA in gemv's v6 down to a single warp computing 1 row, and it actually ran slower than v5—because concurrent in-flight reads per SM dropped to just ~8.7 KiB (Chapter 3, Section 9). How do we push bytes in flight back up? To see that, we need to look one level deeper inside the SM: the SMSP (SM sub-partition, 4 per SM).

Chapter 3, Section 1 worked out that one SM holds at most 64 resident warps. Split them evenly across the 4 SMSPs, and each SMSP gets 1 warp scheduler and holds at most 16 resident warps. An SMSP scheduler can issue only 1 instruction per cycle, while a memory load waits tens to thousands of cycles—how do we keep that wait from turning straight into total runtime?

In this chapter we follow a single warp through one full pass: what it does while waiting for data, who waits for whom when its 32 threads split across branch paths, and why reducing 32 per-thread partial sums into one number leaves only 1 thread doing the work.

1Only 1 Issue Slot per Cycle: Which Waits Actually Count Toward Total Runtime?

An issue slot sits idle only on cycles when the SMSP has not a single eligible warp; whether those idle cycles add to total runtime depends on whether issue slots are the first resource to saturate.

On every clock cycle (Chapter 2, Section 2), the SMSP's warp scheduler scans the warps resident in its sub-partition (Figure 4-1). As soon as a warp has all the operands for its next instruction ready and the target execution unit is free, that warp is eligible.

Each SMSP has only 1 issue slot per cycle. The scheduler picks 1 eligible warp, issues 1 instruction from it, and marks that warp selected. Switching between warps takes zero time: every resident warp keeps its registers on-chip the whole time (Chapter 3, Section 1), so picking warp A on this cycle and warp B on the next never saves or restores any state. That part works just like hardware multithreading on a CPU. The difference is scale: CPU SMT (simultaneous multithreading) can issue instructions from several threads in the same cycle, but holds only a few thread contexts per core. An SMSP holds up to 16 warp contexts, yet issues only 1 instruction from 1 warp per cycle (fine-grained multithreading).

What about the other resident warps that don't issue on that cycle? They fall into two buckets. Some are not selected—ready to go, just not the warp chosen on this cycle. The rest are stalled, still waiting on data or a busy execution unit. Only when the entire SMSP has zero eligible warps does the cycle count as no eligible, leaving the issue slot idle. Even if 15 warps sit not selected on a cycle, as long as 1 warp issues an instruction, that cycle's issue slot is full.

When a 4-warp CTA lands on an SM, we assume its 4 warps go to the 4 SMSPs, 1 warp per SMSP. (NVIDIA documents only that a warp stays on one SMSP from launch to completion; it doesn't disclose the assignment rule.) You can see this in Mode 1 of Figure 4-1, which is v1 from Primer 3: each 128-thread CTA computes 1 row, and each thread loads one BF16 element (2 B) at a time. One SM holds 16 such CTAs, so each SMSP holds 16 warps—one from each CTA, each reading a different row of WWW. On every iteration, each warp sends 2 loads to the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3), one BF16 of WWW and one of xxx, and then quickly stalls waiting for the data to come back (the bytes-in-flight numbers below count only WWW). Once all 16 warps are stuck waiting, most cycles end up no eligible.

2Scoreboards and In-Order Issue: How Does a Warp Keep Moving After Firing a Load?

The scoreboard marks only the pending destination register as not ready, so the warp keeps going until the first instruction that uses it; the more independent instructions you pack in between, the fewer warps you need to keep the issue slot full.

Every GPU warp issues instructions strictly in program order (in-order issue), so it cannot jump ahead of a stalled instruction out of order. So how does it keep moving right after firing a load? With a scoreboard (Figure 4-2). When the warp issues a load, the hardware logs an entry on the scoreboard, and the warp keeps issuing the independent instructions that follow as long as they don't touch the pending result. Only when the warp hits the first instruction that actually uses that result does it wait for the scoreboard to clear, at which point the scheduler switches to another eligible warp. According to public reverse-engineering analyses, the compiler encodes ahead of time in the machine instruction which scoreboard to wait on and before which instruction to stall (NVIDIA's official documentation doesn't disclose this encoding; see Chapter 6, Section 5). When the data arrives and the scoreboard clears is tracked by the hardware at runtime. Global memory loads and shared memory (SMEM) loads use this exact same mechanism; only the number of wait cycles differs.

Now apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to a single SMSP, where the resource we want to keep fed is the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot. (Here we count instructions in flight; Section 3 will count bytes in flight.) Suppose a load takes DDD cycles to return, and a warp can issue nnn instructions—including the load itself—between firing the load and first using its result. Since the issue slot wants 1 instruction every cycle, keeping it full takes about D/nD / nD/n warps taking turns:

required resident warps≈⌈Dn⌉\mathrm{required\ resident\ warps} \approx \left\lceil \frac{D}{n} \right\rceilrequired resident warps≈⌈nD​⌉

Take a short-latency load first. A conflict-free SMEM load takes ~23 cycles (Chapter 3, Section 7). If each load is followed by 3 independent instructions (n=4n = 4n=4), then ⌈23/4⌉=6\lceil 23 / 4 \rceil = 6⌈23/4⌉=6 warps taking turns are enough to reach 0 no eligible cycles (Figure 4-2, Mode 4). With only 4 resident warps, they can't cover the whole wait window, and idle cycles show up on the timeline (Mode 3).

Now flip it around: what if the next load's address depends on the value returned by the previous load? Say three tables sit in SMEM and we chain lookups: idx = len[i]; p = table[idx]; v = data[p];. Right after each load issues, the very next instruction needs its result, pinning n=1n = 1n=1 at every step. At ~23 cycles per load, 3 chained loads wait ~69 cycles in total, stalling a single warp on the scoreboard three times in a row (Figure 4-2, Mode 1). A single serial chain can't be split apart on its own. If an outer loop wraps it, though, len[i + 1] in iteration i+1i + 1i+1 doesn't depend on iteration iii. While iteration iii is still waiting on data, the warp can fire off the next iteration's load early and stretch nnn larger (Chapter 7, Section 6). The catch is register pressure: every extra pending load ties up another set of destination registers, and using more registers may cut the number of resident warps (Chapter 3, Section 1). We check that trade-off in the next section when we run the numbers for v7.

3When Memory-Bound, Do You Feed the Issue Slot or HBM? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v6 → v7)

A memory-bandwidth-bound kernel needs to saturate SM-wide bytes in flight, not issue slots—and the way to do it is to have each thread fire several independent wide loads before using the first result.

Let's plug HBM into the issue-slot formula from Section 2. In Chapter 2, Section 2 we measured an unloaded HBM round-trip latency of ~600 clock cycles (~0.33 µs at ~1.8 GHz). With 1 pending load per warp and n=4n = 4n=4, filling the issue slot would take 600÷4=150600 \div 4 = 150600÷4=150 warps—way past the hard limit of 16 warps per SMSP. Under full load, the round-trip latency stretches to ~1.9 µs (Chapter 2, Section 3), which would demand even more warps. That math simply doesn't close: in gemv, the issue slots have to sit idle most of the time.

The good news is that it doesn't need to close. Two resources are racing to saturate first: the issue slot at 1 instruction per cycle, and HBM, which hits its bandwidth plateau at ~64 KiB of in-flight reads per SM (Chapter 2, Section 3). Whichever resource saturates first sets total runtime through its own Little's Law equation. Because gemv reads 37.75 MB of weights and uses each weight only once for a single multiply-add, HBM hits its ceiling long before the issue slots do.

Look back at Figure 4-1: both modes spend over 80% of their cycles in no eligible, yet one crawls and the other flies. The difference is how many bytes they keep in flight. In Mode 1 (v1 from Primer 3), each thread loads only 1 BF16 of WWW per iteration, so 16 warps on an SMSP keep just 1 KiB in flight at once, or 4 KiB across the whole SM. In v6, each thread keeps only one 16 B load of WWW in flight, which still comes to only ~8.7 KiB across the SM. Mode 2 puts just 4 warps on each SMSP, but has each thread keep eight 16 B loads of WWW in flight—16 KiB on that SMSP, and right at 64 KiB across the whole SM. Mode 1 and v6 are slow because they have too few bytes in flight, not because their issue slots sit empty. Under full load (~1.9 µs round trip), Mode 2 will have even more idle issue cycles than Figure 4-1 shows.

That is how v6 → v7 pushes bytes in flight back up: by firing wide loads back to back. Since a warp stalls as soon as it reaches the first instruction that uses a loaded result, peak in-flight reads per SM equal resident warps × 32 threads per warp × loads each thread issues before first use × bytes per load. In Chapter 3, Section 9 we worked out that v6 averages ~17.45 resident warps per SM and issues only one 16 B load of WWW per step before starting its multiply-adds. In v7, each thread first fires 8 independent 16 B (uint4) loads of WWW (along with as many loads of xxx) into 8 register groups, and only then starts the multiply-adds. Look at the compiled machine instructions (SASS; Chapter 6, Section 2 shows how source compiles to SASS), and 8 loads of WWW plus 7 loads of xxx sit ahead of the very first multiply-add. Counting only WWW, peak bytes in flight climb from ~8.7 KiB/SM to ~69.8 KiB/SM, crossing the 64 KiB/SM knee for the first time:

17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 8 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 69.8\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB

Keep in mind that 69.8 KiB/SM is a peak, not a time average. Only the opening 8 loads of WWW go out back to back; the later loads sit between multiply-add instructions and issue one by one only after the earlier multiply-adds have issued, so time-averaged bytes in flight stay below this peak (not measured; see Section 6).

What does v7 pay for those extra loads? Holding all those 128-bit loads in registers (8 groups of WWW plus the in-flight xxx loads) pushes per-thread register usage from 30 up to 83, which rounds up to 88 under the 8-register allocation granularity (Chapter 3, Section 1). Because the register file is split evenly across the 4 SMSPs and allocated per SMSP (⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5\lfloor 16{,}384 / (32 \times 88) \rfloor = 5⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5 warps per SMSP), each SM can still hold up to 20 single-warp CTAs—still above the 17.45 CTAs per SM assigned by the grid. So we don't lose a single resident warp, and peak bytes in flight scale by the full 8× (see the chart in Section 6 for the measured speedup). If register pressure pushed the residency cap below the 17.45 warps assigned by the grid, resident warps would drop and bytes in flight would no longer scale by 8× (we did not measure such a counterexample on gemv).

4When a Warp Issues One Branch Path at a Time, Who Waits for Whom?

Short conditionals use predication to mask writeback at almost no cost; long divergent branches inside a warp have to run one path after the other, while branches split along whole-warp boundaries never hold each other up.

Inside a warp, the 32 threads are called 32 lanes. Starting with compute capability 7.0 (NVIDIA's version number for a GPU architecture; H200 is 9.0), GPUs use Independent Thread Scheduling: each lane keeps its own program counter, which tracks the next instruction that lane will run. Yet on any given cycle, the warp scheduler still issues only 1 instruction from this warp, and the active lanes sitting at that instruction run it together. This execution model is called SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads; see Figure 4-3).

Every thread has a few 1-bit predicate registers, such as P0. On a short conditional like if (tid == 0) y[row] = sum;, the compiler doesn't emit a branch jump at all. Instead, it attaches a predicate (such as @!P0) to the instruction, issues it across all 32 lanes as usual, and lets the lanes where the condition is false suppress their writeback.

Once a branch body is long enough to need a jump, you get branch divergence. The hardware tracks which lanes take part in the current instruction with a 32-bit active mask. Lanes can split into sub-warp groups and reconverge later, but the warp issues instructions for only one path at a time while lanes on the other path sit idle. In the SASS we inspect, the compiler places a BSSY before a divergent branch to set the reconvergence point (Chapter 10, Section 9), and a BSYNC at the reconvergence point where lanes that finish first wait for the other path. Past BSYNC, the lanes that were active at BSSY run together again—all 32 of them if all 32 were active before the split, while any lanes that have already exited don't come back. If the warp finishes one path before starting the other, you pay the sum of both paths' runtimes, not the longer of the two (see Variant 3 below). Independent Thread Scheduling also means the 32 lanes of a warp are no longer guaranteed to stay in lockstep by default. When code needs them aligned at a specific point, it calls __syncwarp(mask): the lanes in the mask wait for each other there, and their earlier memory writes become visible to one another (we did not measure its standalone cost; Chapter 8, Section 11 uses it so each warp aligns before lane 0 issues a single release).

Figure 4-3 puts three branching variants side by side for warp 0's epilogue right after the CTA barrier (machine instruction counts are in the figure readout):

  • Variant 1 (predicated store): This does no additions and shows predication on its own. Only the lanes where the condition holds write out the value already in their registers; with a predicate attached, the store issues in a single pass with no jump.
  • Variant 2 (one-sided branch if (tid == 0) { 128 additions }, v1 epilogue): The other 31 lanes exit right at the branch entry (no other work follows, so the compiler ends them there), yet the warp can't leave the SMSP until lane 0 finishes summing smem[0..127]. We measure ~4 cycles before a floating-point multiply-add result is ready for the next instruction (Chapter 5, Section 1), and we estimate a floating-point addition at the same value. Running 128 serial additions therefore takes ~512 cycles, plus ~32 cycles for the first 16 B SMEM load (Chapter 3, Section 7). Throughout those ~544 cycles, just 1 of the 32 lanes is doing useful work (Figure 4-3 shows the case where the loop bound is hardcoded as the constant 128).
  • Variant 3 (two-sided branch, illustrative code if (lane < 16) {…} else {…}, 128 additions per branch): The two paths reconverge at BSYNC. If the warp finishes one path before starting the other, the 128 additions of the first 16 lanes and the 128 additions of the last 16 lanes add straight together (~2×5122 \times 5122×512 cycles; we did not measure whether the hardware interleaves the two paths to hide part of each wait), and all 32 lanes turn back on after BSYNC.

By contrast, if you split a branch along whole-warp boundaries—such as if (warp_id == 0)—all 32 lanes in a warp see the exact same condition, so the warp never diverges. That is how Chapter 3, Section 5 separates producer warps from consumer warps; the trade-off is that work can only be handed out in 32-thread chunks, and we did not measure the time cost of that coarser granularity separately. One more rule to keep in mind: __syncthreads() requires every thread in the CTA to reach the exact same barrier instruction, so you can't put it inside a branch taken by only some threads (Chapter 7, Section 7 shows how different branches can meet at a shared barrier).

In v1's SASS, every row uses Variant 2 to sum 128 partial sums (v2–v5 were not checked separately). By v6 and v7, each CTA is down to a single warp with just 32 partial sums, yet that same one-lane serial reduction still burns over a hundred cycles—as we'll price out and fix in the next section.

5Keeping the Reduction Inside One Warp: How Does Warp Shuffle Eliminate Shared Memory and CTA Barriers? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v7 → v8)

A reduction across at most 32 threads can read neighbor registers directly in 5 warp-shuffle steps, bypassing both shared memory and the CTA barrier.

Now replace v7's SMEM epilogue with a warp shuffle (Figure 4-4, Mode 2). In v8, the code calls __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, acc, o), which lets each thread read acc straight from the register of thread lane XOR o. The first argument is the lane mask: 0xffffffff means all 32 lanes take part, and the instruction itself reconverges those lanes at that point. Values move directly from register to register without ever touching memory. Compared with the SMEM version (Figure 4-4, Mode 1)—which retains a CTA barrier to wait until all 32 threads finish writing memory and make their stores visible to thread 0—a warp shuffle never writes to memory at all, so that barrier goes away too.

The reduction finishes in log⁡232=5\log_2 32 = 5log2​32=5 halving steps: stepping o = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 in turn, each step runs 1 warp shuffle followed by 1 addition; after 5 steps all 32 lanes hold the full sum, and lane 0 writes it out. Each warp shuffle still waits on the scoreboard mechanism from Section 2 before the following addition can use its result.

Put the two cycle budgets side by side for summing those 32 values:

  • v8 warp shuffle: Each warp shuffle takes ~24 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result, paired with one ~4-cycle addition; 5 steps plus the final store come to 5×(24+4)+1=1415 \times (24 + 4) + 1 = 1415×(24+4)+1=141 cycles in total, using 0 bytes of SMEM and 0 CTA barriers.
  • v7 SMEM epilogue: Having all 32 threads write to SMEM, cross the CTA barrier, and load back the first value takes 44.3 measured cycles in total; thread 0 then runs 32 serial additions in ~128 cycles, plus the final store, for ~173 cycles in total.

In wall-clock time, though, each row's epilogue saves only ~32 cycles, or ~18 ns at ~1.8 GHz. And because the entire grid fits in a single wave starting from v6 (Chapter 3, Section 9), all warps run their epilogues at the same time, so that 18 ns saving does not add up across rows.

Back in gemv, v8 drops v7's 128 B of SMEM and __syncthreads() and swaps in that 5-step warp shuffle. The immediate win is slightly fewer executed instructions and slightly fewer registers per thread than v7, while the grid still assigns 17.45 warps per SM on average (measured residency is ~16 warps per SM, or 24.8%).

What does it cost us? Two things. First, warp shuffle works only inside a single warp: a reduction across more than 32 threads (like v1) still has to shuffle within each warp first and then combine across warps through SMEM and a CTA barrier. Second, in v8 the compiler issues only 7 loads of WWW before starting the multiply-adds, tucking the 8th load into the middle of the first multiply-add group. That caps peak concurrent WWW loads in flight at 7 per thread (112 B), or ~17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 7 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 61.1\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB per SM—just shy of the 64 KiB knee; why the compiler chose this schedule was not determined.

6The gemv Evolution v6 → v7 → v8: Why Does One Step Save So Much and the Next Save So Little?

v7 shortens the memory wait across the whole loop; v8 saves at most ~18 ns by our cycle budget yet measures slightly faster still, with the extra gain not determined.

In the evolution chart below, we use PyTorch's matrix-vector multiplication function torch.mv as our baseline; under the hood, it calls NVIDIA's matrix library cuBLAS.

Look at v6 → v7 first: v7 runs ~1.43× faster than v6. Every step of the main loop across the 8,192 columns waits on HBM; once peak bytes in flight jump up (time-averaged bytes in flight were not measured; Section 3), that HBM wait shrinks right along with them. That speedup also puts v7 back ahead of torch.mv (v5 was already faster than it before v6 slipped behind).

Now look at v7 → v8. Going by our Section 5 cycle budget alone, v8 shouldn't run noticeably faster: its epilogue saves at most ~18 ns, issuing fewer instructions doesn't speed up a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel, and its peak bytes in flight are even slightly lower. So how do we tell whether a one-step change is a real speedup or just run-to-run variation (also called measurement noise)? We check two rules. First, across paired runs in the same round, the difference between the two versions must have the same sign every time. Second, that paired difference must exceed the largest gap between the medians of a single version within this set of runs—which we call its span below. Chapter 7, Section 1 gives the alternating paired ABBA setup and parameters, and Chapter 6, Section 8 gives the noise band for the full-graph replay chain.

Here we ran v7 then v8, and then reversed the order (v8 then v7), on each of two machines, for 4 paired runs in total (the chart shows the low and high of each version's 4 medians). Across those 4 runs, v7's own median span is 0.32 µs and v8's is 0.29 µs. Both spans are smaller than the 0.42–0.54 µs by which v8 beats v7 in each of the 4 paired runs, and all 4 runs have the same sign—so this step is a real speedup. Where that small extra gain comes from was not determined.

Even with v8's peak bytes in flight near the knee, its runtime still sits a fair bit above the bandwidth lower bound: inside the GPU kernel body, on top of the 8.3 µs needed to move the weights at steady-state bandwidth, ~3.6 µs remains (see the chart above). That extra 3.6 µs can come from three places. First are the memory round trips at the start and the end. Second, once the initial batch of loads has gone out, subsequent loads are interleaved with multiply-add instructions and can issue only after earlier multiply-adds issue, leaving time-averaged bytes in flight below the initial peak. Third, if the 2,304 rows are spread evenly across 132 SMs, some SMs get 18 rows and others get 17, so the SMs that finish 17 rows first sit idle (how hardware distributes CTAs across SMs is undocumented, and we did not measure the actual distribution). How much each of the three contributes was not measured separately.

One last piece of bookkeeping: why is the overhead ~2.8 µs here when Primer 3, Section 5 quoted 4.6 µs? Because they measure two different things: 4.6 µs is the full event-timed duration of an empty kernel (including the empty kernel's own execution on the GPU), whereas ~2.8 µs is the extra time outside a real kernel's GPU body (mostly launch and event-recording overhead; see Chapter 10, Section 1 for details).

Takeaway: An issue slot stays busy as long as at least 1 warp is eligible each cycle; a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel needs to saturate SM-wide bytes in flight by having each thread fire several independent wide loads back to back.

Next chapter's question: Once data lands in registers, we still have to unpack it and run multiply-add instructions; as the token count TTT grows from 1 to 8, which execution pipeline fills up first?
