By v8 in Chapter 4, peak bytes in flight are already close to the knee, yet the profiler measures an average bandwidth of only about 3.19 TB/s across the whole kernel (Section 8 chart), still short of the steady-state plateau from Chapter 2, Section 3. (Chapter 4, Section 6 listed three candidate reasons for that gap; we did not measure how much each one contributes.) Once the data lands in registers, we still have to unpack each BF16 pair and multiply-add it—so which execution pipeline do those instructions actually go to?

As the token count TTT grows from 1 to 256, how does arithmetic keep up with the weights we read in, and once we split KKK, how do we add the partial sums back into a single output correctly? We start at T=1T = 1T=1 to see why the arithmetic hides behind memory waits, and then see why the ordinary arithmetic pipelines bottleneck as soon as TTT hits 8—forcing us onto the Tensor Core.

1Which Pipeline Does an Issued Instruction Enter, and Which Bound Sets Loop Speed?

The minimum cycles per loop iteration is set by the largest of three lower bounds: issue slots, the busiest execution pipeline, and the dependency chain.

Look at Figure 5-1. Underneath each SMSP sit three baseline arithmetic pipelines. Because they have different lane widths, they take different numbers of cycles to accept 1 warp instruction (issue interval (initiation interval)):

  • FMA pipeline: 32 lanes wide, so it accepts 1 warp instruction every 1 cycle for single-precision multiply-add FFMA, addition FADD, and multiplication FMUL. It is built from two halves, and integer multiply-add IMAD can enter only one half, so IMAD is accepted at 1 instruction every 2 cycles.
  • ALU pipeline: 16 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 2 cycles. Integer addition and subtraction, three-input bitwise logic LOP3, shift SHF, and byte permute PRMT all run here.
  • SFU (Special Function Unit): 4 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 8 cycles. Exponential, reciprocal, and reciprocal square-root instructions run here.

Those cycle counts follow directly from each pipeline's lane width, and microbenchmark measurements match them. What people usually call a CUDA Core is one of the 32 FP32 lanes of the FMA pipeline. A program that uses only the standard pipelines (FMA, ALU, and SFU) and no Tensor Core is what we call a CUDA Core kernel. Each SMSP also has an LSU (Load/Store Unit, Chapter 3) for memory reads and writes, which we leave out of the arithmetic accounting below.

Put FMA, ALU, and SFU side by side, and their issue intervals stand in a 1:2:81 : 2 : 81:2:8 ratio. Combine those pipeline rates with the issue slot (Chapter 4, Section 1) and scoreboard dependencies (Chapter 4, Section 2), and the loop cycle lower bound (minimum cycles per iteration) is simply the maximum of three bounds. An out-of-order CPU can look past a stalled instruction and issue later independent instructions first, so only loop-carried dependency chains limit its speed. A GPU issues instructions in order (Chapter 4, Section 2), so even the longest dependency chain inside a single iteration stalls that warp; only other warps on the same SMSP can step in to fill those idle cycles, which is why we divide the third term by the number of resident warps:

min cycles per iteration=max⁡(Ninstr⏟issue slot, max⁡p Np⋅Ip, chain length×dependent-instruction latencyresident warps)\mathrm{min\ cycles\ per\ iteration} = \max\Big(\underbrace{N_{\mathrm{instr}}}_{\mathrm{issue\ slot}},\ \max_{p}\, N_p \cdot I_p,\ \frac{\mathrm{chain\ length} \times \mathrm{dependent\text{-}instruction\ latency}}{\mathrm{resident\ warps}}\Big)min cycles per iteration=max(issue slotNinstr​​​, pmax​Np​⋅Ip​, resident warpschain length×dependent-instruction latency​)

Here, "one iteration" means one warp executing the loop body once, and all three terms count SMSP cycles amortized per warp:

  • NpN_pNp​: the number of instructions routed to pipeline ppp;
  • IpI_pIp​: the issue interval of pipeline ppp;
  • dependent-instruction latency: the number of cycles from issuing an instruction until the next instruction that consumes its result can issue;
  • chain length: the number of instructions along the longest dependency chain in one iteration; other independent chains in the same warp advance in parallel and do not lengthen this term;
  • resident warps: the number of warps taking turns issuing instructions on the same SMSP.

Let's do the math for unpacking first. In Chapter 4, v8 calls a library helper to convert a 32-bit word holding 2 BF16 values into 2 FP32 values, which costs 3 instructions per word: 1 PRMT to extract the high half-word, followed by 2 left shifts by 16 bits. But BF16 is already the upper 16 bits of an FP32 number—converting it to FP32 just means sitting those 16 bits in the upper half of a 32-bit register and zeroing the lower 16 bits (see the bit layout diagram in Chapter 6, Section 1). Bitwise-AND the high half-word with 0xffff0000 (LOP3 on the ALU pipeline) and shift the low half-word left by 16 bits, and each word takes only 2 instructions. That is how v9 in Section 8 is written.

Now let's plug this 2-instruction-per-word unpacking loop into our three bounds. Splitting a row of 8,192 BF16 elements across 32 threads gives each thread 8,192÷32=2568{,}192 \div 32 = 2568,192÷32=256 BF16 elements, or 128 32-bit words. Both WWW and xxx need unpacking, so each thread issues (128+128)×2=512(128 + 128) \times 2 = 512(128+128)×2=512 unpacking instructions plus 256 FFMA instructions.

Average that per word pair (1 word of WWW paired with 1 word of xxx, or 4 BF16 elements in all): each word pair takes 4 unpacking instructions plus 2 FFMA instructions, or 6 instructions in total. Among the 4 unpacking instructions, 2 LOP3 instructions go to the ALU pipeline. For the 2 left shifts, the compiler emits some as SHF (on the ALU pipeline) and some as multiplication by 2162^{16}216 via IMAD (on half of the FMA pipeline). That averages about 3 ALU instructions per word pair, putting the ALU bound at about 6 cycles. Each 16 B uint4 holds 4 word pairs and costs about 24 ALU cycles. The FMA pipeline needs only about 12–16 cycles for it: 8 FFMA plus about 4 IMAD. It is a range because FFMA can go to either half of the FMA pipeline while IMAD uses only one half, and we did not measure how much the two overlap. Either way, the ALU pipeline hits its ceiling first.

Instruction ordering matters too (Figure 5-1, Modes 1 and 2). If ALU and FMA instructions alternate, each word pair finishes in 6 cycles with 0 idle cycles. If 3 ALU instructions issue back-to-back instead, the ALU accepts only 1 every 2 cycles and has no FMA instruction in between to interleave, so the scheduler has to wait—adding 2 idle cycles per word pair and stretching it to 8 cycles.

Here the compiler turns 122 of the 256 left shifts into IMAD, cutting the ALU unpacking instructions from 512 (if all used SHF) down to 390. That is a go-to move at this level: when one execution pipeline saturates while an adjacent one has headroom, rewrite with equivalent instructions to offload the work—moving left shifts onto the FMA pipeline is called left-shift FMA offloading. The trade-off: IMAD hands its result to the next LOP3 about 2 cycles later than an all-SHF sequence (measured in a microbenchmark; the cause was not determined), and if the adjacent pipeline is already full, offloading gains nothing. In Chapter 6, Section 3, we will apply this move by hand for 4-bit weight decoding.

Now check the third bound: the dependency chain. A single FFMA has a measured dependent-instruction latency of about 4.1 cycles, and we estimate FADD at the same value. One batch runs 8 independent chains of 8 multiply-adds each (one chain per uint4; see Section 8 for the v9 code), so the dependency-chain numerator is only 8×4.1≈338 \times 4.1 \approx 338×4.1≈33 cycles. Divided across about 17.45÷4≈4.417.45 \div 4 \approx 4.417.45÷4≈4.4 warps taking turns per SMSP (Chapter 4, Section 3), that comes to about 8 cycles per batch—nowhere near the issue-slot bound of about 192 cycles per batch.

Put all three together, and the issue-slot bound and the ALU bound tie as the tightest bound at about 24 cycles per uint4. At 512 B per warp (1 uint4 per thread) every 24 cycles, the full GPU can digest about 20 TB/s—more than 4× the 4.8 TB/s HBM peak. So at T=1T = 1T=1, arithmetic is nowhere near the bottleneck; it hides completely inside the time spent waiting on memory, as the v8 → v9 measurement in Section 8 will confirm.

Conversely, if a loop contains an exponential, the tightest bound shifts straight to the SFU: with 1 exponential per element and the SFU accepting only 1 instruction every 8 cycles, the loop is locked at a minimum of 8 cycles per element (Figure 5-1, Mode 3). Attention softmax runs straight into this wall (see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9).

2As T Grows Above 1: Where Does CUDA Core Lose to Tensor Core?

Paper peak throughput predicts a crossover at T≈14T \approx 14T≈14, but the measured crossover happens between T=4T = 4T=4 and 888: for every FMA pipeline instruction, about 2.2 instructions issue in total, pushing the issue slots to ~70% busy and the ALU pipeline to ~60% first.

In multi-request decode, speculative decoding verification, and prefill (Primer 1, Sections 5–7), one forward pass processes TTT tokens side by side: input x :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x:[T,8192]BF16 times weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 gives y=xWTy = x W^{\mathsf T}y=xWT. Throughout this chapter, we write NNN for the 2,304 rows of WWW (Primer 3 called it MMM). Counting all bytes read and written for WWW, xxx, and yyy, the arithmetic intensity (Primer 2, Section 4) is:

I(T)=2TNK2NK+2TK+2TN,N=2304, K=8192I(T) = \frac{2TNK}{2NK + 2TK + 2TN},\quad N = 2304,\ K = 8192I(T)=2NK+2TK+2TN2TNK​,N=2304, K=8192

When TTT is much smaller than N,KN, KN,K, I≈TI \approx TI≈T FLOP/B; as TTT grows, it crosses the 206 FLOP/B ridge point from Primer 2, Section 4 at T≈233T \approx 233T≈233. Let's estimate from paper peak throughput first. At the driver-reported maximum clock of 1.98 GHz, full-chip FP32 FMA peak throughput is 132×4×32×2×1.98 GHz≈67132 \times 4 \times 32 \times 2 \times 1.98\ \mathrm{GHz} \approx 67132×4×32×2×1.98 GHz≈67 TFLOP/s. Divide 67 TFLOP/s by 4.8 TB/s and you get ≈14\approx 14≈14 FLOP/B: if each weight per token needed only 1 FFMA instruction, you would not hit the CUDA Core ridge point until T≈14T \approx 14T≈14. One catch if you compare the two ridge points: the 989 TFLOP/s behind 206 FLOP/B is the datasheet rating, which works out to ~1.83 GHz, not the 1.98 GHz used here. At the same clock, Tensor Core throughput is 16× FP32 FMA (Section 3), so the two ridge points differ by 16×, not by 206÷14206 \div 14206÷14.

Now let's put both implementations on H200 and measure them head-to-head: (a) the CUDA Core version, which extends the hand-unpacked inner loop from Section 1 so one warp computes several tokens at once, reading each uint4 of WWW once and multiplying it across those tokens; and (b) the Tensor Core version, PyTorch's torch.matmul backed by cuBLAS (Chapter 4, Section 6), which runs on the Tensor Core at these TTT values. Figure 5-2 plots the data from the two latency charts below on log-log axes.

Look at the two latency charts above: at T=1,2,4T = 1, 2, 4T=1,2,4, (a) the CUDA Core version is still faster; starting at T=8T = 8T=8, (b) the Tensor Core version overtakes it and is already about 1.45× faster at T=8T = 8T=8.

Why does the CUDA Core version lose around 8 instead of 14? Because for every 1 FMA pipeline instruction (FFMA + IMAD), it has to issue about 2.2 instructions in total—the extra instructions go to the unpacking and address math we counted in Section 1. Divide by that 2.2× instruction overhead (14÷2.2≈614 \div 2.2 \approx 614÷2.2≈6), and the CUDA Core version hits its instruction-issue ceiling and leaves the memory-bandwidth-bound regime around T≈6T \approx 6T≈6. You can see it directly in the unit-utilization chart above: by T=8T = 8T=8, the issue slots and ALU pipeline are the busiest units at ~70% and ~60%, while the FMA pipeline sits at only ~30% and memory bandwidth drops to ~30% of peak. What the remaining ~30% idle issue-slot cycles stalled on was not measured separately. The measured crossover lands between T=4T = 4T=4 and 888 (T=5T = 5T=5–777 were not measured).

Does that ~2.2 ratio come down when one warp computes several tokens at once? Barely. Call twt_wtw​ the number of tokens one warp computes together (at T=8T = 8T=8, the fastest choice is tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4). When TTT is larger than twt_wtw​, the grid splits the tokens into groups and re-reads WWW for each group. The twt_wtw​ tokens do share the unpacking of WWW, but each token brings its own xxx, which still has to be loaded and unpacked separately. Count the compiled arithmetic instructions (unpacking plus multiply-add) per FMA pipeline instruction, and you get about 1.9 at tw=1t_w = 1tw​=1 and about 2.0 at tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4. Sharing the WWW unpacking does not bring it down: at tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4 the compiler emits only about 20% of the left shifts as IMAD (versus about half at tw=1t_w = 1tw​=1), so fewer unpacking instructions land on the FMA pipeline. The measured "total instructions ÷\div÷ FMA pipeline instructions" is 2.24 and 2.21, barely moving with twt_wtw​. The rest, ~0.3 (at tw=1t_w = 1tw​=1) and ~0.25 (at tw=4t_w = 4tw​=4), comes from load, address, final-reduction, and similar instructions, which we did not break down one by one.

Switching to the Tensor Core has a trade-off of its own: cuBLAS sits on a flat ~19 µs plateau all the way from T=1T = 1T=1 to 32. For T≤4T \le 4T≤4, the CUDA Core version finishes below that line, so calling cuBLAS is actually slower (see the latency chart). Between T=1T = 1T=1 and 128, every cuBLAS torch.matmul call launches 2 kernels: one using Split-K (Chapter 2, Section 5) to compute partial matrix products, and a second to sum those partial results—paying for an extra kernel launch and an inter-kernel handoff gap (Chapter 1, Section 1). How much of that ~19 µs plateau comes from the extra launch and gap, and what makes up the rest, was not profiled item by item.

By the token count TTT entering qkv_gate, single-layer execution splits into three regimes, whose names we will use throughout the chapters ahead:

  • Regime I: T<8T < 8T<8 (measured at T=1,2,4T = 1, 2, 4T=1,2,4). CUDA Cores are still faster here, so our T=1T = 1T=1 gemv kernel stays on CUDA Cores; the bottleneck is the weight bytes we have to read.
  • Regime II: 8≤T<2338 \le T < 2338≤T<233 (measured at T=8…128T = 8 \dots 128T=8…128), where arithmetic intensity is still below the 206 FLOP/B ridge point. Here we have to switch to the Tensor Core, even though the full GPU remains memory-bandwidth-bound.
  • Regime III: T≥233T \ge 233T≥233, where arithmetic intensity reaches 206 FLOP/B or higher. Our sweep here only measured up to T=256T = 256T=256; by the arithmetic-intensity formula, a chunked-prefill chunk of T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 (Primer 2, Section 5) also lands in this regime (see Chapters 7–9 for larger TTT).

3How Large a Tile Does One Tensor Core Instruction Compute, and Where Do Its Operands Come From?

Each SMSP is paired with a Tensor Core; across the whole SM, Tensor Core throughput is 16× that of the FP32 FMA pipeline and needs no unpacking, at the cost of a fixed instruction row height of 16 or 64.

A single Tensor Core does 1,024 FLOP per cycle (BF16 multiplication with FP32 accumulation; see Figure 5-3). With 4 per SM, a full SM delivers 4,096 FLOP per cycle, compared with 128×2=256128 \times 2 = 256128×2=256 FLOP per cycle across the SM's FP32 FMA pipelines—a full 16× jump. Better yet, because the hardware takes BF16 directly, all 512 per-thread unpacking instructions from Section 1 vanish, and the ALU pipeline is no longer a bottleneck.

The mMnNkK tag in the instruction name tells you the exact tile shape: one instruction multiplies an [m, k]×[k, n][m,\ k] \times [k,\ n][m, k]×[k, n] tile and accumulates the product into an [m, n][m,\ n][m, n] tile. Hopper gives us two families of Tensor Core instructions:

The first family is mma.sync (m16n8k16), issued by a single warp on its own with a minimum row height of 16. Before issuing it, threads must load both the left matrix AAA and the right matrix BBB from SMEM into registers. On H200, back-to-back issue takes 1 instruction every 6 cycles, reaching only about 67% of Tensor Core peak throughput. It fits cases where valid rows do not fill 64 rows, or where registers are too tight to spread across 128 threads (Chapter 8, Section 3 uses it when each expert gets only a few tokens).

The second family is wgmma (m64nNk16), which 1 warpgroup must issue together (Chapter 3, Section 6: 4 consecutive warps whose first warp index is a multiple of 4, or 128 threads). Why all 4 warps? Because the instruction specification says so: every thread in the warpgroup must execute the same wgmma. The result is split across the 4 warps too: under the specified accumulator layout, each warp's registers hold 16 rows, and the 4 pieces make up 64 rows. The common explanation is that the 4 warps sit on the 4 SMSPs and each SMSP's Tensor Core computes its own warp's 16 rows (Chapter 4, Section 1), but NVIDIA doesn't document this hardware detail. So all 4 warps must reach this instruction: it can only sit inside a branch whose condition comes out the same for the whole warpgroup (Chapter 4, Section 4). That scope is the warpgroup, narrower than the whole CTA that __syncthreads() needs, so the producer warp and the consumer warpgroup can take different branches (Section 5).

Its row height mmm is fixed at 64, while its column width nnn can be any multiple of 8 from 8 to 256. In BF16, k=16k = 16k=16, and once n≥64n \ge 64n≥64, the back-to-back issue interval comes right up to the ideal n/2n / 2n/2 cycles (m64n64k16 measures about 32 cycles, or about 99.8% of peak). Switch to FP8, and Tensor Core throughput doubles again: each instruction widens kkk from 16 to 32 while keeping the same issue interval.

Whenever the hardware reads a matrix operand directly out of SMEM, it uses a matrix descriptor: a 64-bit value encoding the starting address and layout of that matrix tile in SMEM. Depending on where the left operand AAA lives, wgmma runs in one of two modes:

  • SS mode: Both AAA and BBB sit in SMEM. The hardware reads both directly through two matrix descriptors, using zero operand registers and keeping only the FP32 accumulators in registers.
  • RS mode: AAA sits in registers across the 128 threads (4 32-bit registers holding 8 BF16 values per thread), while BBB stays in SMEM.

Look at the issue-interval chart above: SS mode is slightly faster when n≥64n \ge 64n≥64, while RS mode actually pulls ahead when n≤32n \le 32n≤32. Down at n=8n = 8n=8, SS takes ~18 cycles and RS takes ~17 cycles; the interval stops shrinking as n/2n / 2n/2 because we hit the per-instruction floor.

So when should you use RS mode? Only when the left matrix AAA is already sitting in registers:

  • Intermediate result of chained matrix multiplications: Once attention computes P=softmax(QKT)P = \mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\mathsf T})P=softmax(QKT), PPP is already in registers, so the second matrix multiplication reads it straight from registers in RS mode (Chapter 7, Sections 9–10). Forcing SS mode here would mean writing PPP out to SMEM first and adding the cross-proxy fence from Chapter 3, Section 3.
  • Compressed weights decoded to BF16 in registers and fed straight into the Tensor Core: This requires moving the weight matrix WWW to the left-operand AAA side (the next section shows how). It pays off only if decoding a weight tile takes less time than reading a 16-bit weight tile from HBM; otherwise it comes out slower (see Chapter 6, Sections 1–2 for the encoding and Chapter 6, Section 4 for measurements and counterexamples).

For standard dense BF16 matrix multiplication (such as our qkv_gate tiles at T≥128T \ge 128T≥128), we use SS mode.

Here is the price of switching to Tensor Core instructions: row height is locked at 16 or 64, which wastes work whenever valid rows do not fill the tile (next section); wgmma requires 4 warps to issue together, driving up register usage across all 128 threads at once, and RS mode takes extra operand registers on top. As a result, it loses in two places: first in Regime I (Section 2 latency chart), and second in MoE when each expert gets only a few tokens, where the extra registers and SMEM demanded by wgmma push occupancy down (see the measurements in Chapter 8, Section 4).

4When T Is Only 8 to 32, How Do We Fill the 64-Row Left Matrix? (swap-AB: Swapping Operands A and B)

Using yT=WxTy^{\mathsf T} = W x^{\mathsf T}yT=WxT puts the thousands of rows of WWW on the fixed 64-row operand-A side and the TTT rows of xxx on the variable-nnn operand-B side so all 64 rows hold real data; at small batch sizes, the real saving is accumulator registers.

Look at the standard layout first: put the input x :  [T,  8192]  BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16}x:[T,8192]BF16 on the left (m=64m = 64m=64 rows) and the weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 on the right (n=64n = 64n=64). The fraction of those 64 rows that hold real data is the row fill ratio. At T=8T = 8T=8, only 8 of the 64 rows hold real tokens and the other 56 rows are padded with zeros, wasting 87.5% of compute; T=16T = 16T=16 and 323232 likewise waste 75% and 50% (Figure 5-4, Mode 1).

The fix is swap-AB (swapping operands A and B, Figure 5-4 Mode 2): flip the two sides so rows of WWW sit on the mmm side (filling all 64 rows at 100%) and xxx moves to the variable-nnn side with n=Tn = Tn=T. When TTT is not a multiple of 8 (such as T=5T = 5T=5), we pad nnn up to 8. Once T=128T = 128T=128, xxx already fills two 64-row tiles on its own, so swapping operands saves no cycles (Figure 5-4, Mode 3).

Both instructions do the exact same amount of useful work (8 tokens × 64 rows of WWW), and m64n8k16 runs about 1.76× faster per instruction than m64n64k16 (see the issue-interval chart in Section 3). Still, in the early part of Regime II (T=8–32T = 8\text{–}32T=8–32), the full GPU is memory-bandwidth-bound, so those instruction cycles are already hidden behind the time spent reading weights. What swap-AB really buys us here is registers: per-thread FP32 accumulators drop from 32 right down to n/2n / 2n/2, taking only 4 registers at n=8n = 8n=8. The price you pay is that the accumulators now hold the transposed yTy^{\mathsf T}yT, so you have to transpose the tile through SMEM once before writing it out to global memory—and once T≥64T \ge 64T≥64, swap-AB brings no gain at all. Neither the gain from saving registers nor the time spent on the SMEM transpose was measured on its own; in our multi-token GEMM evolution chain (Chapter 6, Section 8), swap-AB is measured together with another change in a single step.

5Asynchronous wgmma: How Do We Keep the Tensor Core Busy While Preparing the Next Input Group?

Using wait_group<1> keeps 1 commit group executing on the Tensor Core while waiting for the next buffer slot and issuing the next group, at the cost of releasing each SMEM slot one step later.

Issuing a group of wgmma instructions takes four steps: first issue wgmma.fence (so the accumulator registers are ready to hand over to the Tensor Core), then fire several wgmma instructions in a row, seal them into a commit group with commit_group, and finally call wait_group<N>—which waits until at most NNN commit groups remain unfinished.

Across Sections 5–7, we use our hand-written multi-token qkv_gate kernel as the running example (Chapter 6, Section 8 walks through its full evolution). Inside each CTA, 1 producer warp fills an SMEM ring buffer via TMA (Chapter 3, Sections 4–5), while 1 or 2 consumer warpgroups issue wgmma. Tiled matrix multiplication steps along the inner dimension KKK by a fixed column width each time (such as 64 columns); each step is a K-step. On every K-step, the consumer reads a tile of xxx and a tile of WWW from one slot of the ring and does four things in order: wait for the slot to fill (full barrier, Chapter 3, Section 5), issue SS-mode wgmma, wait on the commit group, and return the slot (empty barrier).

Compare the two wait strategies in Figure 5-5:

  • wait_group<0> (Mode 1: synchronous drain): Every step waits until the current group finishes completely and writes its results back to registers before waiting for the next slot and issuing the next group. As a result, every single step exposes an extra drain latency—measured at about 53 cycles in 64-column SS mode from issuing the last instruction until all results write back.
  • wait_group<1> (Mode 2: 1-group in-flight overlap): After issuing group iii, the consumer waits only for group i−1i - 1i−1 to finish and moves right on. While group iii is still running on the Tensor Core, the consumer is already waiting on slot i+1i + 1i+1 and getting the next group ready. Drain latency is exposed only once, on the very last step.

Watch the buffer-slot lifetime closely. In SS mode, both AAA and BBB sit in SMEM, so while group iii is in flight, the Tensor Core is still reading slot iii. Therefore, the consumer returns slot i−1i - 1i−1 to the producer only after wait_group<1> returns and confirms that group i−1i - 1i−1 is done. Slot iii stays held by the consumer until the next step, leaving the producer with "slots − 1" in-flight slots to rotate through. In RS mode, BBB is still read from SMEM, so the SMEM slot still goes back one step late. On top of that, the operand-AAA registers need protecting: until the in-flight group retires, you can't overwrite the AAA registers it reads—either wait for it to retire before overwriting them (as the cross-iteration overlap of P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V in Chapter 7, Section 10 does), or alternate between two register sets.

So the price of this overlap is 1 fewer rotatable ring-buffer slot (plus 1 extra set of operand-AAA registers in RS mode when alternating between two sets). And if preparing the next group takes longer than the matrix multiplication itself, overlap cannot hide that preparation time and the Tensor Core stalls anyway (Chapter 6, Section 4 shows a measured weight-decoding counterexample). How much time this step saves on qkv_gate on its own was not measured.

6The K Loop of One Tile: How Deep Must the Ring Be and How Much Must Each Slot Hold So the Tensor Core Never Waits for Data?

The number of in-flight buffer slots times the MMA time per slot must cover the buffer-slot round-trip time. That round trip includes a fixed intercept that does not shrink when a slot gets smaller, so widening the tile to double the compute per slot covers it more easily than adding more slots.

Let's start with the anatomy of a single K-step (Figure 5-6 Mode 1, our qkv_gate tile at T=128T = 128T=128). Tile height BM\mathrm{BM}BM runs along token count TTT, and tile width BN\mathrm{BN}BN runs along output columns NNN: each CTA computes a BM=128\mathrm{BM} = 128BM=128 row × BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 column output tile, stepping along KKK by BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64 each time, while KKK is partitioned three ways with Split-K = 3 (Chapter 2, Section 5). Inside each CTA, 1 producer warp and 1 consumer warpgroup share an 8-slot SMEM ring buffer.

Each slot in the ring holds an xxx tile xtile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}xtile​:[128,64]BF16 plus a WWW tile Wtile :  [64,  64]  BF16\shape{W_{\mathrm{tile}}}{64,\;64}{BF16}Wtile​:[64,64]BF16, or 24,576 B in total. The producer waits for an empty slot, sets the expected transaction bytes, and fires two TMA copies; once all 24,576 B land in SMEM, the full barrier flips phase (Chapter 3, Section 5). On the consumer side, BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64 is sliced into four k=16k = 16k=16 pieces; the upper and lower 64-row half-tiles each take 4 instructions, totaling 8 SS-mode m64n64k16 instructions (~256 cycles). The consumer then seals them into a commit group, calls wait_group<1> (Section 5), and returns the previous slot i−1i - 1i−1 to the producer. Throughout the loop, each thread holds 64 FP32 accumulators, each mapped to a fixed cell of the output tile (see the layout card in Figure 5-6 Mode 1).

Now let's time the buffer-slot round-trip time for a single slot: the clock starts when the consumer returns an empty slot at the empty barrier, runs while the producer fires TMA and the bytes land in SMEM, and stops once the full barrier flips phase so the consumer can use that slot again. Fitting measured main-loop runtimes under full load at T=256T = 256T=256 gives an estimate for the slot round-trip time: ≈1.12 µs+slot bytes÷172 GB/s\approx 1.12\ \text{µs} + \mathrm{slot\ bytes} \div 172\ \mathrm{GB/s}≈1.12 µs+slot bytes÷172 GB/s (the intercept was not measured separately). Next, we apply this formula to test whether 3 in-flight slots cover one slot round trip at BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 (see the chart in this section). Notice that the 1.12 µs intercept exceeds the unloaded round-trip latency; the extra time may come from queueing delay (see Chapter 2, Section 3; not measured separately). The 172 GB/s rate in the denominator is the arrival rate seen by a single CTA: because many CTAs share the xxx tile and mostly hit in L2, multiplying the single-CTA rate by the total CTA count comes out higher than HBM bandwidth.

Apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to this ring buffer: the in-flight slots held by the producer must cover the slots the consumer burns through during one round trip. For the Tensor Core not to wait for data, we need

(in-flight slots)×(per-slot MMA time)≥per-slot round trip(\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}) \times (\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time}) \ge \mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}(in-flight slots)×(per-slot MMA time)≥per-slot round trip

Here per-slot MMA time depends on the work per slot, and in-flight slots = slots − 1 (Section 5); the per-slot interval is whichever of the two terms is larger:

per-slot interval=max⁡(per-slot MMA time, per-slot round tripin-flight slots)\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ interval} = \max\Big(\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time},\ \frac{\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}}{\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}}\Big)per-slot interval=max(per-slot MMA time, in-flight slotsper-slot round trip​)

Compare two tile widths at T=256T = 256T=256 (BM=256\mathrm{BM} = 256BM=256, BK=64\mathrm{BK} = 64BK=64). Here the 8 warps of two consumer warpgroups share the SM's 4 SMSPs and 4 Tensor Cores (the cards in Figure 5-6 Modes 2 and 3 list the bytes and cycles per slot):

  • BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 (Figure 5-6 Mode 2): SMEM fits at most 5 slots, leaving 4 slots in flight, and the slot round-trip time is ~1.36 µs. Each slot runs 16 wgmma instructions in ~513 cycles (converting cycles to µs across this section at ~1.8 GHz gives ~0.285 µs). Those 4 in-flight slots cover only ~1.14 µs in total, which cannot hide the ~1.36 µs slot round-trip time.
  • BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 (Figure 5-6 Mode 3): Per-slot MMA compute (1,025 cycles) doubles to ~0.57 µs, while the formula above predicts that the slot round-trip time rises only slightly to ~1.41 µs. SMEM fits 4 slots, leaving 3 slots in flight that cover 3×0.57=1.71 µs≥1.41 µs3 \times 0.57 = 1.71\ \text{µs} \ge 1.41\ \text{µs}3×0.57=1.71 µs≥1.41 µs, which hides the round trip. We need 2.5 in-flight slots, so 3 in-flight slots are enough with about half a slot of headroom.

Widening the tile from BN=64\mathrm{BN} = 64BN=64 to BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128 halves the number of output-column tiles from 2,304÷64=362{,}304 \div 64 = 362,304÷64=36 to 18. To keep the total CTA count close to a full wave across the 132 SMs (Chapter 2, Section 1), we simultaneously raise Split-K from 3 (108 CTAs) to 7 (126 CTAs)—note that this adjustment is to keep a full wave on the GPU, not to hide the slot round trip.

The KKK dimension spans 8,192÷64=1288{,}192 \div 64 = 1288,192÷64=128 K-steps in all. Since 3 and 7 do not divide 128 evenly, the largest slice takes 43 steps and 19 steps respectively, and total duration tracks that heaviest slice (Chapter 2, Section 1). For BN=128\mathrm{BN} = 128BN=128, the measured 11.16 µs main-loop duration closely matches the 10.8 µs estimate converted at ~1.8 GHz.

Look at the chart above: widening the tile speeds up the main loop by about 1.28×, and Tensor active cycles on the busiest SM climb from 76% to 88% of main-loop cycles (see Chapter 6, Section 8 for where this step sits in the multi-token GEMM evolution chain). Roughly half of the time saved comes from the busiest CTA doing ~12% less work (19 steps × 128 columns vs. 43 steps × 64 columns, or 2,432 vs. 2,752), and the other half comes from finishing that same work faster. Between the two bars, all three parameters change together, and the full kernel saves less time than the main loop does (that gap may come from adding the extra partial sums under Split-K = 7; see Section 7). How much queueing adds to the intercept, how the savings split between the two halves, and how much each of the three changes contributes were not measured separately.

Here is the trade-off when you widen BN\mathrm{BN}BN: you double the MMA compute per slot and cut the total grid-wide bytes moved from L2 into SMEM by ~40%, in exchange for three costs:

  • Per-thread FP32 accumulators double from 64 to 128 (using 64 more registers per thread; Chapter 3, Section 1).
  • Each SMEM slot gets larger, so the ring shrinks from 5 slots to 4.
  • Split-K goes from 3 to 7, more than doubling the partial sums we have to add together at the end (Section 7; see Chapter 6, Section 8 for numerical accuracy).

Push the slot size too far, though, and SMEM cannot even hold enough slots to cover the round-trip latency, slowing the kernel down instead (Chapter 9, Section 2 and Chapter 9, Section 7 show measured counterexamples).

7After One Tile Finishes: How Do We Add the Partial Sums from Multiple Slices Back into One Output Tile?

Partial sums are converted to BF16 and written to SMEM, and a single TMA tile reduction adds them to the output in global memory; before the addition, each slice first confirms through a release/acquire chain that Slice 0 has zeroed the output.

Split-K cuts the inner dimension KKK into segments, handing each segment to one CTA; below we call one segment and its CTA a K-slice (split-K partition), with Slice 0 computing the first segment. Earlier versions in our multi-token evolution chain (Chapter 6, Section 8) use the parallel slice reduction from Chapter 2, Section 7. Here we compare against a more direct baseline: each consumer thread packs its accumulators in pairs (two adjacent BF16 values in one 32-bit word, BF16x2) and fires element-by-element global atomic adds at the output. Hopper hardware supports this instruction natively rather than spinning in the compare-and-swap retry loop of Chapter 2, yet 128 threads each firing 32 scattered atomic adds into L2 still drags out the epilogue and eats extra registers. And either way, because the reduction adds onto the existing contents of output yyy, we have to zero out this output tile (ytile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}ytile​:[128,64]BF16 at T=128T = 128T=128) before adding to it.

Our new writeback takes three steps (Figure 5-7):

  • This kernel writes BF16 output, so each consumer thread first rounds and packs its 64 in-register FP32 accumulators pairwise into 32 BF16x2 words;
  • Next, 8 stmatrix instructions (each writing several 8×88 \times 88×8 submatrices from warp registers into SMEM) write the ytile :  [128,  64]  BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16}ytile​:[128,64]BF16 tile (16,384 B) into Slot 0 of the ring buffer—all K-steps are finished by now, so the slot is free to reuse;
  • Finally, 1 thread issues 1 TMA tile reduction, which tells TMA to atomically add those 16,384 B element by element into the output in global memory. The instruction specification names only global memory as the target; we infer that the addition happens at L2. The tile as a whole is not one atomic operation, so additions from different slices can interleave. The thread waits until TMA finishes reading SMEM, then exits; no separate reduction kernel is needed.

How do we make sure the output tile has been zeroed before any slice adds to it? The main chain is "zero-init → release → acquire → cross-proxy fence → TMA tile reduction", built on the cross-scope cumulativity from Chapter 2, Section 6:

  • Prologue: The same kernel replays repeatedly inside a CUDA Graph (Chapter 1), so each output tile keeps a ticket counter and a "zeroing complete" flag that both only increase and are never reset to zero. On each call, exactly SSS slices (SSS is the Split-K count) each do a relaxed atomic add on the counter to claim a ticket ttt, giving the call index n=⌊t/S⌋n = \lfloor t / S \rfloorn=⌊t/S⌋. Once Slice 0 zeros the output tile, it adds 1 to the flag, and every slice (including Slice 0) waits until the flag is >n> n>n.
  • Slice 0 publishes zero-initialization:
    1. Before entering the main loop, the 128 consumer threads zero the output tile.
    2. Inside the main loop, before returning an empty slot each time, the 128 consumer threads first pass a named barrier. The named barrier gates only these 128 consumer threads without blocking the producer warp; once past it, all 128 threads have finished writing zeros. One elected thread from warp 0 alone then arrives on the empty barrier. Arriving on an mbarrier carries CTA-scope release semantics, while waiting on that barrier carries acquire semantics. That way the empty barrier still waits for only 1 arrival, and by the specification that single arrival carries the zero-initialization writes of all 128 threads. This chain was not verified in SASS.
    3. By the time the producer has issued all TMA loads for its slice, it has already waited on a slot return from the consumers (acquire). Right then, it issues a red.release.gpu on the global-memory "zeroing complete" flag: a non-fetching atomic add with device-wide (device scope, written .gpu in the instruction name; Chapter 2, Sections 6–7) release semantics. The end of this section explains why we pick this timing.
  • Every slice (including Slice 0) writes back:
    1. After finishing the main loop, the 128 consumer threads first pass a named barrier to confirm they are done with the ring-buffer slots.
    2. Thread 0 repeatedly reads the flag with acquire until the current call's zero-initialization is published.
    3. Thread 0 immediately issues a global cross-proxy fence fence.proxy.async.global, ordering the zero-initialization writes it just acquired before the upcoming TMA reduction.
    4. All consumer threads write their partial sums into SMEM with stmatrix, issue the shared-memory cross-proxy fence fence.proxy.async.shared::cta (Chapter 3, Section 3) so those normal stores are visible to TMA's subsequent SMEM read, and pass another 128-thread named barrier.
    5. Thread 0 issues the TMA tile reduction and waits until TMA finishes reading SMEM.
  • Validity conditions:
    1. Only consumers waiting on the flag spin-wait; Slice 0's producer never waits on another CTA. The grid has at most 132 CTAs (each CTA's ring takes 192–200 KiB of SMEM, so at most 1 CTA fits per SM; Chapter 3, Section 1), and no long-running kernel on another stream or in another process holds SMs. When both hold, Slice 0's CTA can get an SM and will not deadlock. This is an operating condition under single-layer deployment, not a specification guarantee like cooperative launch in Chapter 2, Section 6.
    2. Slice 0 must run more K-steps than there are slots in the ring buffer; otherwise the producer has not waited for a slot return, and the zero-initialization writes are not on the chain.
    3. The counter and flag use 32-bit signed integers that only increase, so a continuously running service must reset them before wrap-around; switching to 64-bit counters removes this requirement. Our kernel here stays on 32-bit.
    4. Each (T,S)(T, S)(T,S) configuration has its own counter and flag buffer, and a given buffer is used with only one SSS. If two SSS values shared a buffer, ⌊t/S⌋\lfloor t / S \rfloor⌊t/S⌋ would no longer be the call index; we do not use it that way. At any given moment, a buffer may also be used by only one call; replaying sequentially on a single stream satisfies this condition automatically.

Look at the epilogue chart above: at both TTT values, the epilogue shrinks to about one-third of what it took before.

Now let's weigh the trade-offs of this change. Compared with per-thread BF16x2 atomic adds, the epilogue shrinks to about one-third, and the only new cost is one extra 128-thread named barrier per K-step. Compared with launching a separate reduction kernel that adds slices in a fixed order, we save one kernel launch at two costs: first, each slice rounds its partial sum to BF16 before adding; second, the addition order depends on arrival order at L2, so the result is not guaranteed to be bitwise deterministic (see Chapter 2, Section 7 on floating-point non-associativity and Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured output error). Neither the gap between the epilogue time saved and the full-kernel time saved nor the standalone cost of adding one named barrier per K-step was measured separately.

Why pick that exact moment to issue the release? Two measured counterexamples show why. In the first counterexample, Slice 0 zeros the output and issues red.release.gpu right at kernel entry. Under memory-ordering semantics, a release only requires earlier reads and writes to be observed by other threads before the flag; by itself, it does not block later reads. Yet this release compiles down to a device-scope memory fence instruction (for its cost, see Chapter 2, Section 6). In measurement, that fence stalls waiting for the freshly issued zeroing stores, keeping consumer warpgroup 0 from issuing wgmma in the meantime and slowing this CTA down by 2–3 µs. In the second counterexample, holding the release until the whole main loop finishes makes the remaining slices wait longer during the epilogue; for that reason, the T=128T = 128T=128 kernel issues the release right after the producer has fired its final load. Moreover, if the consumers write this flag in the middle of the instruction sequence that issues wgmma, the compiler stops overlapping those wgmma instructions and slows down the main loop (measured in Chapter 6, Section 6).

8gemv Evolution v8 → v9: A Quarter Fewer Instructions, So Why No Time Saved?

At T=1T = 1T=1, runtime is set by the weight bytes read and the bytes in flight; both versions read the same bytes with the same WWW reads in flight, and the arithmetic cycles we save were already hidden inside the time spent waiting on memory.

Compare the inner loops of v8 and v9 (Figure 5-8), and v9 changes two things:

  • Unpacking implementation: It switches to the hand-written unpacking from Section 1, cutting each 32-bit word from 3 instructions down to 2.
  • Accumulation method: For every loaded uint4, v8 starts an 8-multiply-add chain from 0 and adds it into acc with 1 FADD. v9 instead keeps 8 accumulators running across batches and merges them only at the end of the loop, cutting the merge FADD count as well.

Both versions fully unroll the loop and issue the exact same number of WWW loads per batch; in the compiled SASS, both place 7 WWW loads before the first multiply-add and interleave the later loads among the multiply-adds (Chapter 4, Section 3).

Look at the two charts above: across 4 paired runs, two tie and two leave v9 slightly slower; the difference does not keep the same sign, so by the criterion in Chapter 4, Section 6 it does not count as a speedup. Instruction count drops by about a quarter, yet v9 reads the exact same bytes from HBM as v8, with the same occupancy and the same WWW reads in flight (Chapter 4, Section 5). Only the in-flight xxx loads drop, from 7 to 5, and xxx is just 16 KiB; HBM throughput is almost unchanged. At T=1T = 1T=1, all three arithmetic bounds from Section 1 sit below the limit set by the weight bytes read and bytes in flight (Chapter 4, Section 3), so lowering the arithmetic bound leaves runtime unchanged—making this step a direct measured example of saving arithmetic without saving time.

Where does v9 pay off? As soon as TTT grows: every token has to repeat unpacking and multiply-add, and v9's inner loop is the starting point for the CUDA Core curve in Figure 5-2. The cost is writing hand-crafted bitwise unpacking code; no extra hardware-resource cost was measured.

Since cutting arithmetic instructions inside a single kernel at T=1T = 1T=1 cannot save time, where do we push next? We shrink the bytes each weight takes up (Chapter 6, Section 7; see Chapter 9 for cross-kernel launch overhead).

Takeaway: At T=1T = 1T=1, the arithmetic hides inside the time spent waiting on memory; once TTT reaches 8, the issue slots and the ALU pipeline get busy first, so we must switch to the Tensor Core. Once on the Tensor Core, we need asynchronous overlap and enough work per slot to keep it from waiting on data, and after splitting KKK, we also have to add the partial sums back into a single output correctly.

Next chapter's question: When TTT is small, runtime comes right back down to the weight bytes read; how can we store each weight in fewer bits and reconstruct it in registers with a handful of integer instructions?

Single Instructions and Bits — How Can Weights Take Fewer Bits Without Decoding Instructions Eating Back the Saved Time?
