At the end of Chapter 5, v9 cut the instruction count by about one quarter, yet runtime did not budge — because at T=1T = 1T=1, execution time tracks the bytes you haul in from HBM (see Chapter 5, Section 8). Once your in-flight reads are already close to the 64 KiB/SM knee point, the most direct way to go faster — short of keeping even more reads in flight — is simply to read fewer bytes.

Level 6 zooms all the way in to a single machine instruction and the individual bits inside a 32-bit register. Here we work out three things: first, how many bits we can shave off each weight (either losslessly down to 12 bits, or using the model's native 4-bit format); second, how many integer instructions it takes inside 32-bit registers to unpack those weights back; and third, whether those extra decoding instructions eat back the time we saved on memory. To answer that third question properly, we also need to read the actual machine code emitted by ptxas and check whether it serialized instructions that should overlap — that is the other half of Level 6 (Sections 5 and 6). Section 8 then walks through the complete multi-token GEMM progression from g0 to g5, pointing each step back to the chapter that introduced its underlying mechanism.

1Which of the 16 Bits in BF16 Can We Skip Storing? (C12 Lossless Weight Format)

The low byte of BF16 must be kept intact; when the top 7 exponent bits fall within a window of 8 adjacent values, the high byte needs only 1 sign bit plus a 3-bit offset, compressing each weight to 12 bits.

Before we touch any bits, we need to know what the accuracy rules allow. Expert weights ship in a lossy 4-bit format from the start (Section 3; Chapter 8, Section 1), whereas dense projection weights have to enter the math at their exact published BF16 values. Our correctness test enforces this with two checks. The first leaves only one non-zero element in xxx, so the output pulls out a single column of WWW, and each column's relative error must stay within 0.001. Quantizing the weights down to 8 bits produces an error far above that limit, and the benchmark rules permit only lossless compression in any case. The second check feeds general inputs: the full output's relative L2 error against the exact FP64 product (the square root of the sum of squared errors divided by the square root of the sum of squared exact values) must not exceed 0.01, each row must stay within 0.05, and the output must contain no NaN or Inf—leaving room for the rounding differences of parallel accumulation (used in Section 8).

If we cannot lose precision, where can we save bits? Look at how the floating-point bit fields line up in Figure 6-1. An FP32 number has a 1-bit sign sss, an 8-bit exponent eee (with bias 127), and a 23-bit mantissa mmm. BF16 keeps only 7 mantissa bits — it is literally the top 16 bits of FP32, with the exact same exponent width and bias — so it represents

w=(−1)s 2e−127 (1+m/27)w = (-1)^s\,2^{e-127}\,(1 + m/2^7)w=(−1)s2e−127(1+m/27)

That bit-field alignment is why, back in Chapter 5, Section 1, shifting a BF16 value left by 16 bits gave us a valid FP32 number right away.

Now split a 16-bit BF16 weight right down the middle into two bytes:

  • high byte: the 1-bit sign sss plus the top 7 bits of the exponent (e≫1e \gg 1e≫1).
  • low byte: the lowest 1 bit of the exponent plus the 7-bit mantissa mmm.

Let's trace a concrete weight w=0.02w = 0.02w=0.02 from qkv_gate (the weight matrix WWW from our main gemv running example; see Primer 2, Section 1 for its tensor shape). Its BF16 encoding is 0x3CA4, or 0 01111001 0100100 in binary: the sign bit is s=0s = 0s=0, the 8-bit exponent is e=121e = 121e=121, and the top 7 exponent bits give e≫1=60e \gg 1 = 60e≫1=60. The low byte is 0xA4, where the top bit 1 is the lowest bit of the exponent and the other 7 bits are the mantissa.

Of those two bytes, the low byte is distributed randomly across weights, so there is no way to compress it losslessly. The regularity sits in the 7 bits of the high byte. Both the NyoomFloat12 paper (Together AI, 2026) and nf12 (an open-source 12-bit weight library following the same idea) rest on the same premise: in trained large-model weights, e≫1e \gg 1e≫1 concentrates in 8 adjacent integers [base, base+7][\text{base},\ \text{base}+7][base, base+7] (corresponding to the 16 adjacent BF16 exponents [2 base, 2 base+15][2\,\text{base},\ 2\,\text{base}+15][2base, 2base+15]). We call the smallest integer of this 8-bin window the exponent window base (base), and we pick one base per matrix offline so that the fewest weights fall outside the window.

We tested this distribution only on normal random weights with mean 0 and standard deviation 1/K1/\sqrt{K}1/K​ — all timings in this chapter use those same random weights, and real model weights were not measured. For these weights, the chosen window starts at base=54\text{base} = 54base=54, which covers magnitudes in [2−19, 2−3)[2^{-19},\ 2^{-3})[2−19, 2−3), or roughly 1.9×10−61.9\times10^{-6}1.9×10−6 to 0.1250.1250.125, so typical weights like 0.020.020.02 land squarely inside the window.

With that 8-bin window in place, we can define our own 12-bit weight format, C12 (12-bit lossless weight format):

  • For a weight that lands inside the window, the high byte keeps only the 1-bit sign plus the 3-bit window offset d=(e≫1)−based = (e \gg 1) - \text{base}d=(e≫1)−base (4 bits in total). Together with the 8-bit low byte kept as-is, each weight takes 12 bits. For w=0.02w = 0.02w=0.02 above, base=54\text{base} = 54base=54 gives d=60−54=6d = 60 - 54 = 6d=60−54=6, so its 4-bit code is 0 110.
  • For an escaped weight (outlier) whose e≫1e \gg 1e≫1 falls outside the window, open-source nf12 uses whole-group escape: as soon as 1 weight in a group of 8 escapes, it marks the entire group as escaped and reads back all 8 original BF16 values from a separate escape table, keeping the decoded weights bit-exact. C12 does not do this. An escaped weight still stores an in-window approximation in the main table (our gemv and the T=32T = 32T=32 Tensor Core kernel both set its offset ddd to 0, while some other kernels clamp ddd to 000 or 777), and its position and true value go into a separate side table. Where the exact value comes back depends on the kernel: gemv adds the difference back into the output (Section 2), while the T=32T = 32T=32 Tensor Core kernel XOR-patches the decoded value in registers before feeding it to the matrix multiplication.

Let's run the byte math for qkv_gate. Packing every 8 weights into 12 B instead of 16 B cuts the footprint to 75% of the original size: the main table for W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 drops from 37.75 MB to 28.31 MB, plus a side table of about 0.07 MB under the random weights above. At H200's 4.8 TB/s peak HBM bandwidth (see Primer 2, Section 4), the lower bound for reading WWW once from HBM drops from 7.86 µs to (28.31+0.07) MB÷4.8 TB/s≈5.91 µs(28.31 + 0.07)\ \text{MB} \div 4.8\ \text{TB/s} \approx 5.91\ \text{µs}(28.31+0.07) MB÷4.8 TB/s≈5.91 µs. Keep in mind that this ~1.95 µs difference is only the gap between two theoretical lower bounds, not a measured speedup; we will look at the measured numbers in Section 7.

In HBM, we pack every 8 C12 weights into three 32-bit words: two low-byte words la (the low bytes of weights 0–3) and lb (the low bytes of weights 4–7), plus one codeword (cd) holding the 4-bit codes for all 8 weights. We do this packing once offline before running the model. Of course, if a matrix had widely scattered exponents, more weights would escape and the side table would grow accordingly; we have not measured such matrices. Over the next three sections, we will count the extra instructions needed to unpack these weights at runtime and see where the trade-off flips as TTT grows.

2How Do 9 Integer Instructions Decode 8 C12 Weights into BF16?

Eight weights are reconstructed into four BF16x2 registers in 9 ALU instructions: shift to align, mask, add the exponent window base, and permute bytes.

In a 32-bit register, two BF16 values sit side by side as a single BF16x2 (as we saw in Chapter 5, Section 7, with one weight in the low 16 bits and one in the high 16 bits). Our job is to turn the three 32-bit words la, lb, and cd back into four BF16x2 registers. The trick is how we lay out the bits inside cd offline: in byte iii of cd (i=0..3i = 0..3i=0..3), bits 2..02..02..0 hold the 3-bit offset of weight iii, and bit 7 holds the sign of weight iii. That leaves the middle bits free, so we pack the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i4+i4+i (from the second half of the 8-weight group) into bits 6..46..46..4, and we tuck the sign of weight 4+i4+i4+i into bit 3 of the next byte (with byte 3 wrapping around to byte 0).

Once cd is packed in this layout, walking through the four steps in Figure 6-2 (9 instructions in total) reconstructs all 8 BF16 weights. We write those 9 instructions directly in the C++ source using PTX (Parallel Thread Execution ISA), NVIDIA's virtual instruction set — a style known as inline PTX (asm). When CUDA C++ compiles, it first lowers to PTX, and the backend assembler ptxas (PTX optimizing assembler) then compiles that PTX into SASS (Streaming Assembler machine code), the actual machine instructions executed by the GPU. We count pipeline cycles on the compiled SASS (Section 5):

  1. 1 funnel right shift (SHF) (rotating cd right by 4 bits to get rt): SHF concatenates two 32-bit inputs into a 64-bit value and slices out 32 bits, so passing cd as both inputs gives us a 32-bit rotate. Rotating right by 4 bits drops the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i4+i4+i right into bits 2..02..02..0 of each byte in rt, while pulling its sign bit from bit 3 of the next byte down into bit 7 of the same byte — now aligned with the exact bit positions that weight iii occupies in cd.
  2. 2 three-input logic instructions (LOP3) bitwise-ANDed with 0x87878787 (one on cd, one on rt): the single-byte mask 0x87 = 1000 0111b keeps only the sign at bit 7 and the 3-bit offset in the low 3 bits, clearing the middle 4 bits to zero.
  3. 2 integer additions (VIADD or IADD3 in SASS) adding EXP_BASE: the constant EXP_BASE=base×0x01010101\texttt{EXP\_BASE} = \text{base} \times \texttt{0x01010101}EXP_BASE=base×0x01010101 packs one copy of the exponent window base base\text{base}base into each of the 4 bytes. After masking, each byte looks like s|0000|d; adding base\text{base}base turns it into s|(base + d), which is the exact high byte of BF16. Call the resulting word ha for the first 4 weights and hb for the last 4 weights. Because base+7≤127\text{base} + 7 \le 127base+7≤127, adding the low 7 bits never carries into the sign bit at bit 7, so a single 32-bit addition sums all 4 bytes in parallel without byte-to-byte interference.
  4. 4 byte permutes (PRMT): PRMT takes two 32-bit source registers (8 bytes total: source bytes 0..3 from the first register, 4..7 from the second) and picks 4 bytes using a 4-digit hexadecimal byte-permute selector mask to build a new 32-bit word, where the lowest hex digit (low 4 bits) selects byte 0 of the result. Reading from low byte to high byte, selector mask 0x5140 grabs source bytes 0, 4, 1, 5 — that is la byte 0, ha byte 0, la byte 1, and ha byte 1 — zipping low and high bytes together into the two BF16 values for weight 0 and weight 1; selector mask 0x7362 grabs bytes 2 and 3 to build weight 2 and weight 3. Running the same pair of PRMT instructions on lb and hb produces weights 4–7.

Follow w0=0.02w_0 = 0.02w0​=0.02 (0x3CA4) from Section 1 along red circle 1 in Figure 6-2 to see this in action: in byte 0 of cd, the low 3 bits are 110 and bit 7 is 0; bitwise-ANDing with 0x87878787 leaves byte 0 as 0x06; adding base=54\text{base} = 54base=54 (0x36) reconstructs the high byte 0x3C; and finally, the low 16 bits of PRMT(la, ha, 0x5140) stitch byte 0 of ha (0x3C) onto byte 0 of la (0xA4) to produce 0x3CA4, giving us back the exact BF16 weight.

How much does this 9-instruction sequence cost on the execution pipelines? All 9 SASS instructions (1 SHF, 2 LOP3, 2 integer additions VIADD / IADD3, and 4 PRMT) run on the ALU pipeline. At 2 cycles per ALU instruction (16 lanes; see Chapter 5, Section 1), unpacking 8 weights costs 18 ALU cycles. In terms of registers, the sequence reads 3 input registers and writes 4 output registers; although the C++ source declares 3 extra temporary registers, in the disassembled SASS the first decode group touches only 7 physical registers (see Figure 6-5).

How do we handle escaped weights that fall outside the window? In our gemv kernel, the 9-instruction sequence above has zero branches. It blindly decodes the d=0d = 0d=0 placeholder stored in the main table and feeds the resulting wrong weight w^\hat{w}w^ straight into the FFMA multiply-add (Chapter 5, Section 1). (The T=32T = 32T=32 Tensor Core kernel instead XOR-patches the decoded register from the side table before the matrix multiplication.) gemv fixes the result afterward by adding an escaped-weight correction term to the output:

yr=∑kw^rk xk+∑k∈Er(wrk−w^rk) xky_r = \sum_k \hat{w}_{rk}\,x_k + \sum_{k \in E_r} (w_{rk} - \hat{w}_{rk})\,x_kyr​=k∑​w^rk​xk​+k∈Er​∑​(wrk​−w^rk​)xk​

Here ErE_rEr​ is the set of escaped column indices in row rrr. In our C12 gemv kernel (where each warp computes 1 row; see Section 7), each warp checks the side table before entering the main K-loop, reads xkx_kxk​ at the escaped indices for its row, and accumulates the correction sum; once the main loop finishes, it adds that correction into the output yry_ryr​. That way, every weight inside the window is decoded bitwise-exact, and every escaped weight has its exact difference added back at the end. Mathematically, the result equals direct BF16 multiplication, though the lowest bits can differ slightly because the floating-point additions happen in a different rounding order (this error was not measured separately). On top of the 18 ALU cycles and temporary registers we counted above, the price you pay is reading and summing that side table before the main loop.

3How Do We Decode 4-Bit Weights (NVFP4) into BF16 in Registers?

Shifting the 4-bit code's sign to BF16 bit 15 and its magnitude to bits 8..68..68..6 yields the exact value times 2−1262^{-126}2−126; after offline nibble permutation, decoding 8 weights takes only 8 instructions.

In Chapter 8, Section 1, the model's expert weights ship in the 4-bit NVFP4 format, where every 16 weights share 1 scale factor (see Primer 2, Section 1). Here is how those bits are laid out:

  • Each 4-bit weight uses E2M1 bit fields: a 1-bit sign sss, a 2-bit exponent eee (exponent bias 1), and a 1-bit mantissa mmm. Across the 8 possible values of the 3-bit magnitude code ccc, the non-negative numbers v[c]v[c]v[c] are {0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}\{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6\}{0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}.
  • The block scale sblocks_{\text{block}}sblock​ shared by every 16 weights uses FP8 E4M3 bit fields (1-bit sign, 4-bit exponent with bias 7, and 3-bit mantissa), and the entire tensor then multiplies by one FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}stensor​. Put together, a weight's numerical value is

w=± v[c]⋅sblock⋅stensorw = \pm\,v[c]\cdot s_{\text{block}}\cdot s_{\text{tensor}}w=±v[c]⋅sblock​⋅stensor​

Inside each byte, the low 4 bits hold the even-indexed weight w2iw_{2i}w2i​ and the high 4 bits hold the odd-indexed weight w2i+1w_{2i+1}w2i+1​ — get those two nibbles backward and your matrix columns will be scrambled.

Hopper has no hardware instruction that converts 4-bit values straight into BF16, so we have to do it with bitwise ops in registers. Look at the bit alignment in Step 0 of Figure 6-3: if we drop the E2M1 sign bit into BF16 bit 15, the 2 exponent bits into bits 8..78..78..7, and the 1 mantissa bit into bit 6, and fill every other bit with 0, what BF16 number did we just build? By the formula from Section 1, that BF16 bit pattern evaluates to 2e−127(1+m/2)2^{e-127}(1 + m/2)2e−127(1+m/2), while the true E2M1 value is 2e−1(1+m/2)2^{e-1}(1 + m/2)2e−1(1+m/2). The two differ by the exact constant factor 2−1262^{-126}2−126.

Wait — does that still hold when the exponent bits are 0? A BF16 number whose 8 exponent bits are all 0 is a subnormal number, where values sit at uniform steps around 0 with magnitude 2−126⋅m/272^{-126}\cdot m/2^72−126⋅m/27. When you take the E2M1 code for 0.50.50.5 (0 00 1, so e=0e = 0e=0 and m=1m = 1m=1) and shift it into those same bit positions, you get 0x0040. That lands right in the BF16 subnormal range with value 2−126⋅0.52^{-126}\cdot 0.52−126⋅0.5 — the exact same 2−1262^{-126}2−126 factor (you can check the remaining magnitude codes in the Step 0 readout of Figure 6-3). That means we need zero special cases when the exponent is 0: for every weight, each BF16 halfword just keeps the 4 bits selected by mask 0x81C0 (bit 15 plus bits 8..68..68..6).

If we unpack weights directly from the published raw layout (where the low 4 bits of each byte hold the even index), the low nibble of byte jjj (j=0..3j = 0..3j=0..3) goes into the low halfword of BF16x2 and the high nibble goes into the high halfword. Each nibble's sign and 3-bit magnitude need their own shift-and-mask step:

uint32_t b  = x >> (8 * j);
uint32_t lo = ((b & 0x7u) << 6)  | ((b & 0x8u) << 12);   // w[2j]
uint32_t hi = ((b & 0x70u) << 18) | ((b & 0x80u) << 24); // w[2j+1]
D[j] = lo | hi;                                           // = BF16x2 × 2^-126

Why is that so instruction-heavy? Each BF16x2 has 4 separate fields — the sign and magnitude of both the low and high halfwords — and in the raw byte layout, all 4 fields sit at different bit distances from where they need to go, forcing a separate shift per field. When you compile that loop to SASS (Section 5), unpacking 8 weights (j=0..3j = 0..3j=0..3) balloons to 31 integer instructions: 16 three-input logic instructions (LOP3), 9 integer multiply-add left shifts (IMAD.SHL), and 6 funnel right shifts (SHF), or about 8 instructions per BF16x2.

We can cut that down dramatically by rearranging the nibbles offline when we pack the weights. In the expert kernels of Chapter 8, offline weight permutation places nibbles so that a single shift lines up multiple fields at the same time, shrinking the SASS sequence to 8 instructions per 8 weights: 4 shifts plus 4 three-input logic instructions (LOP3), where each LOP3 emits a finished BF16x2 (we skip the bit-by-bit permutation layout here; the bottom of Figure 6-3 shows a schematic view). The chart below compares the instruction counts before and after offline permutation.

Inside those 8 instructions, we write 2 left shifts as IMAD.SHL to move them onto the FMA pipeline (bottom timeline of Figure 6-3). That is the same left-shift offloading we saw in Chapter 5, Section 1: it cuts the ALU cost per 8 weights from 8×2=168 \times 2 = 168×2=16 cycles down to (2+4)×2=12(2 + 4) \times 2 = 12(2+4)×2=12 cycles. Chapter 8, Section 3 covers the measured gains and counterexamples across the expert kernel sizes.

Once we have the four decoded BF16x2 registers, we multiply them by the block scale using paired BF16 multiplies (HMUL2 on the FMA pipeline), which produces this thread's register slice of the left matrix AAA for warp-level mma.sync — its operand-A register fragment (see Chapter 5, Section 3). There is one catch: we still have to cancel the 2−1262^{-126}2−126 factor from our bit alignment, and multiplying the block scale by 21262^{126}2126 all at once would overflow the BF16 maximum (~21282^{128}2128). So we split that compensation across two steps:

  1. pre-multiplying the block scale by 2642^{64}264: when we unpack the FP8 block scale into BF16, we add an offset to its exponent that multiplies the block scale by 2642^{64}264. Because HMUL2 handles subnormal numbers normally without flushing them to 0, multiplying by 2642^{64}264 lifts the subnormal BF16 values for code ±0.5\pm 0.5±0.5 back into the normal BF16 range, leaving each scaled weight at "exact value ⋅sblock×2−62\cdot s_{\text{block}} \times 2^{-62}⋅sblock​×2−62".
  2. multiplying by 2622^{62}262 in the epilogue: after the matrix multiplication accumulates in FP32, the epilogue already has to multiply by the per-tensor FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}stensor​, so we fold an extra 2622^{62}262 into that FP32 multiply to cancel the remaining 2−622^{-62}2−62.

4When Does Compressing Weights Pay Off, and When Does It Lose?

12-bit weights pay off only when per-step decoding takes less time than reading 16-bit weights from HBM; on qkv_gate, C12 is used only for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, falling back to 16-bit BF16 for T≥128T \ge 128T≥128.

To see when weight compression helps and when it hurts, break a single K-step into three times (Figure 6-4): the time HHH to read one weight tile from HBM (which depends only on the byte count, not on TTT), the time DDD that the decoding threads spend, and the matrix multiplication time MMM (which grows with TTT). When those three stages run on separate hardware units with buffering in between, the step time is simply the maximum of the three; when the same group of threads runs two stages back-to-back, their times add together (Mode B of Figure 6-4). Now, the number of pure decoding instructions depends only on the number of weights and is independent of TTT. But in an RS mode kernel that feeds wgmma directly from registers, the same consumer threads have to both decode the weights and issue the wgmma instructions one by one, so DDD changes with both the number of consumer warpgroups and TTT.

That gives us a clean comparison. A 16-bit kernel does zero decoding, so one K-step takes max⁡(H16,M)\max(H_{16}, M)max(H16​,M); a 12-bit kernel takes max⁡(H12,D,M)\max(H_{12}, D, M)max(H12​,D,M). For T≤128T \le 128T≤128, both MMM and H12H_{12}H12​ are smaller than H16H_{16}H16​, which means the 12-bit kernel wins only when D<H16D < H_{16}D<H16​.

Let's put cycle numbers on H16H_{16}H16​ for a 64-row × 128-column tile of qkv_gate (8,192 weights; the unpooler kernel measured below also uses a 64 × 128 weight tile per K-step). In 16-bit BF16, that tile is 16,384 B; in 12-bit C12, it drops to 12,288 B. Across all 132 SMs on the GPU (see Primer 3, Section 1) running at ~1.8 GHz, the 16-bit MMA loop hits a measured ~4.15 TB/s (~17.5 B per SM per cycle), so reading one 16-bit weight tile takes H16≈936H_{16} \approx 936H16​≈936 cycles per step.

How fast can the ALU pipelines decode those 8,192 weights? If we look at raw ALU peak throughput, the 4 ALU pipelines on one SM can unpack at most 4×32×8=1,0244 \times 32 \times 8 = 1{,}0244×32×8=1,024 C12 weights (1,536 B) every 18 cycles, so 8,192 weights would take only 144 cycles at peak. What happens in a real 12-bit RS wgmma kernel is very different: in every K-step, each consumer thread has to decode its 64 assigned weights and issue 8 RS-mode MMA instructions one by one, while only 1 to 2 consumer warps per SMSP take turns issuing instructions. As we saw from the formula in Chapter 4, Section 2, 1 to 2 warps cannot hide dependent-instruction latency, so decoding becomes latency-bound and runs nowhere near the ALU pipeline peak.

When T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, the operator sits in the first half of Regime II (Chapter 5, Section 2), where cutting 25% of the weight bytes can save at most 25% of H16H_{16}H16​. Our 12-bit Tensor Core kernel for T=32T = 32T=32 uses 2 consumer warpgroups that take turns on adjacent K-steps. Each warpgroup handles every other step: from the start of one of its steps to the start of its next step takes ~1,730 cycles (including the time spent waiting for the other warpgroup), so alternating between the two warpgroups averages ~865 cycles per K-step. That cuts the per-step time by only ~8% (1−865/9361 - 865/9361−865/936) — well short of the 25% ceiling. At T=1T = 1T=1, gemv also sees only a ~7% measured speedup, though for a different reason that we will unpack in Section 7.

At T=128T = 128T=128, the operator is still in Regime II (arithmetic intensity ~120120120 FLOP/B, below the 206206206 FLOP/B ridge point), yet the 12-bit kernel actually runs slower. Why? Not because we ran out of Tensor Core FLOPS, but because the longest bar in each K-step shifts from HBM reads to the decoding threads. When decoded weights feed wgmma directly from registers (RS mode; see Chapter 5, Section 3), the same thread group has to decode weights first and then issue 8 wider (n=128n = 128n=128) RS-mode MMA instructions one after another (Mode B of Figure 6-4). Those 128 decoding threads need about 1,393 cycles per K-step (measured on the unpooler kernel at T=128T = 128T=128 with 1 consumer warpgroup). With 2 alternating warpgroups, the average drops only to about 1,260 cycles per K-step: nearly half the time stalls on barrier synchronization, and the two warpgroups almost never overlap (how these two cycle counts were measured was not verified). Since 1,393>9361{,}393 > 9361,393>936, each K-step of the 12-bit kernel takes ~1.5× as long as in the 16-bit kernel. We did not build a 12-bit RS version of qkv_gate for T=128T = 128T=128, but we ran paired measurements on unpooler and o in the same layer: the full unpooler kernel ran ~40% slower (see the chart below). On pooler and unpooler at T=128T = 128T=128, the final submission installs a different 12-bit RS kernel: 2 consumer warpgroups each own their own 64 rows of WWW and share the same xxx tile. Whenever a small block of WWW has more escaped weights than the side table can hold during packing, that case falls back to the 16-bit kernel (this book does not list paired timings comparing this version against the 16-bit version).

Once T≥233T \ge 233T≥233 and the operator crosses into Regime III, the 16-bit kernel's matrix multiplication time MMM already exceeds H16H_{16}H16​. At that point the kernel is compute-bound, so reading fewer bytes saves zero time and decoding only adds work. For larger TTT, the 12-bit format never wins again.

Our practical fix is dispatching the kernel by (operator, TTT): on the host side, we index a lookup table by operator and TTT to pick which kernel to launch, adding zero runtime branching. On qkv_gate, we launch the 12-bit weight kernel for T≤32T \le 32T≤32. At T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, we switch to the 16-bit weight SS mode kernel, which reads both operands straight from shared memory (Mode C of Figure 6-4) and runs 0 decoding instructions. The other dense projections follow the same rule, using 12-bit weights only at the TTT values where 12-bit wins in measurement (o likewise falls back to 16-bit at T≥128T \ge 128T≥128; for the pooler and unpooler exception at T=128T = 128T=128, see above).

5How Does Our Code Become 128-Bit Machine Instructions, and Why Do We Need to Read SASS?

ptxas allocates physical registers and reorders instructions to emit 16 B SASS words; according to public reverse-engineering studies, hardware mainly waits on prior results using the stall counts and scoreboard wait masks that the compiler encodes into SASS (NVIDIA does not publicly document this encoding), which is why we must inspect SASS.

All the instruction counts we used in Sections 2 and 3 — 9, 31, and 8 instructions — are compiled SASS counts, not lines of C++ or PTX. As we saw in Section 2, CUDA C++ compiles to PTX first and then ptxas assembles that PTX into SASS; let's look at what ptxas actually does under the hood and what sits inside a single SASS instruction word.

At the PTX level, your code is still written against an unlimited supply of virtual registers (%r1, %r2, …), with no physical register numbers and no final instruction order. When ptxas takes over, it does three jobs (Figure 6-5):

  1. register allocation: it maps virtual registers onto physical registers, which sets how many registers each thread uses and, in turn, how many warps can stay resident on each SM at the same time (see Chapter 3, Section 1).
  2. instruction scheduling: it reorders instructions to hide latency.
  3. SASS code generation: it lowers each PTX instruction into 0, 1, or several SASS machine instructions.

Sometimes that lowering is one-to-one. Our 9 lines of inline PTX for C12 decoding in Section 2 compile through ptxas into 9 SASS instructions (main panel of Figure 6-5).

Other instructions, however, do not map one-to-one (see the side panel of Figure 6-5). The first is cvt.f32.bf16, which converts BF16 to FP32. In SASS it turns into a PRMT or a shift instruction. This ties back to Section 1: BF16 is the top 16 bits of FP32, so converting the type is just moving bytes. The second is wgmma. For BF16 / FP16, its SASS mnemonic is HGMMA (for FP8 it is QGMMA), and wgmma.commit_group, which commits a group of matrix multiplications, has no SASS instruction of its own at all. It is only a group tag on the last HGMMA of the group, so that a later wait_group can wait by group (Section 6).

Every SASS instruction that comes out of ptxas is 128 bits (16 B) wide (this holds from compute capability 7.0, Volta, onward, including our Hopper GPU). According to public reverse-engineering studies, those 16 bytes carry a control word (stall count and scoreboard wait mask) written by ptxas, right next to the opcode and physical register numbers: it specifies which earlier results must finish before this instruction may issue, and how many cycles at minimum must pass after it issues before the next instruction can go. NVIDIA does not publicly document the bit encoding of this control word.

Back in Chapter 4, Section 2, we noted that the compiler decides ahead of time which scoreboard to wait on, and before which instruction, and writes that into the machine instructions. This 16 B control word is where it goes. In this reverse-engineered model, the warp scheduler (Chapter 4, Section 1) mainly reads the scoreboard mask and stall count from the control word at runtime to decide when the instruction can issue (public documentation does not state whether the hardware also runs other internal dependency checks). If ptxas stamps a wait onto an instruction, the execution pipeline stalls right there (ptxas will even reshuffle the instruction order you wrote by hand if it thinks that saves registers; see Chapter 8, Section 8). So to check that your machine code really overlaps the way you intended, you have to run disassembly (turning the compiled binary back into readable SASS text) and check the SASS yourself.

6Why Does One Extra Normal Instruction Inside an Async MMA Region Slow the Main Loop by More Than 2×?

When predicated normal instructions are mixed into an async wgmma region, ptxas inserts a drain barrier after every HGMMA, slowing the main loop by 2.35×.

Let's call the instruction bracket from Chapter 5, Section 5 the async wgmma region: you open with wgmma.fence, fire off several wgmma.mma_async instructions back to back, and close with commit_group and wait_group. Inside this async wgmma region, the accumulator registers belong to the Tensor Core, and multiple HGMMA instructions can overlap in flight.

What happens if you slip a normal instruction into the middle of that region? Look at a real bug we hit in Figure 6-6. In our T=128T = 128T=128 GEMM kernel for qkv_gate (one of the kernels on the multi-token GEMM evolution chain in Section 8; see Chapter 5, Section 6 for its tiling), each K-step issues 8 HGMMA.64x64x16 instructions. In an early version of the cross-slice readiness flag from Chapter 5, Section 7, we put the release-ordered global store st.release (Chapter 2, Section 6) right inside the async wgmma region. Only consumer thread 0 ran that store on one specific iteration (in the final version, we moved the release flag write outside the region to the producer warp).

When we compiled that early version, ptxas printed a serialization hint, saying that a non-wgmma instruction defined an accumulator register inside the async region. This is a performance hint (printed at the ptxas info level), not a compile error; we saw it with verbose ptxas output enabled (-Xptxas -v). Now, a global store does not write to registers at all. Yet dropping that conditional-branch flag write into the async wgmma region tripped ptxas's conservative serialization rule, and the wgmma instructions stopped overlapping (NVIDIA does not publicly document the internal heuristic ptxas uses for this check).

Look at what changes in the SASS. In the normal case (Mode 1 of Figure 6-6), each K-step contains only 1 WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x1 (the wait instruction compiled from wait_group<1> in Chapter 5, Section 5). Reverse-engineering analysis identifies gsb0 as the scoreboard that tracks unfinished wgmma groups; 0x1 allows the newest 1 wgmma group to keep running, so the pipeline does not drain. Once serialized (Mode 2 of Figure 6-6), every HGMMA is followed by 1 drain barrier WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (corresponding to wait_group<0>). Each one waits until no group is running and costs about 53 cycles (Chapter 5, Section 5). We saw this in a 4-HGMMA reproducer of this pattern and extrapolate it to the 8-HGMMA kernel. The chart below shows the main-loop runtime.

The takeaway is simple: put only the matrix multiplication instructions themselves inside the async wgmma region. Move any flag stores and branches outside the region and hand them to the producer warp (Chapter 3, Section 5) — that out-of-region pattern is what we showed in Chapter 5, Section 7, and it corresponds to the step in Section 8 of this chapter that switches to TMA tile reduction. Watch out for thread divergence too: any branch that diverges across threads inside the same warpgroup will also make ptxas serialize HGMMA instructions one by one (see Chapter 8, Section 9).

Our routine check comes down to two steps: turn on verbose ptxas output to see whether the serialization hint appears, and count how many DEPBAR instructions show up per K-step in the disassembled SASS.

7The Final gemv Step v9 → v10: Why Do 25% Fewer Bytes Yield Only a 7% Speedup?

Measured latency includes ~2.8 µs of launch and event-recording overhead, and reshaping the grid in v10 reduces in-flight reads and HBM throughput, leaving a net speedup of only ~7%.

In v9, peak in-flight WWW reads per SM reach ~61.1 KiB, right up near the 64 KiB/SM knee point from Chapter 2, Section 3 (see Chapter 4, Section 5 and Chapter 5, Section 8). For v10 (Figure 6-2 in Section 2), we launch 576 CTAs with 4 warps per CTA, reading the three words la, lb, and cd for every 8 weights and unpacking them in 9 instructions. Each thread keeps at most three 16 B WWW loads in flight (loads of xxx are not counted), so in-flight WWW bytes peak at ~26.2 KiB per SM. We took this grid and CTA shape from the final qkv_gate kernel of the Chapter 9 decode layer (the standalone dense-projection problem uses a different 12-bit gemv kernel: 1,152 CTAs of 288 threads each).

Because v10 changes both the CTA shape and the weight format at the same time, we build a control variant v10c to separate the two effects: it uses v10's CTA shape while keeping BF16 weights. Strictly speaking, even v10c changes two things at once: the CTA shape changes, and the in-flight reads get shallower (at most four 16 B WWW loads in flight per thread, for a peak of 34.9 KiB/SM). Also note one output difference: from Primer 3 through Chapter 5, v0 → v9 wrote FP32 outputs, whereas all three versions in the first chart below write BF16 outputs, which we mark by adding an n suffix to their names.

Before looking at the measured bars, let's work out the best-case speedup we could hope for. If we subtract the ~2.8 µs of launch and event-recording overhead from v9n's latency in the chart below and scale all of the remaining time down to 75% in proportion to the bytes read, we save at most ~20%. And because part of that remaining time does not scale with bytes read (Chapter 4, Section 6), the real saving has to be smaller than 20%.

Our paper ceiling says ~20%, yet the measured speedup is only ~7% (see the chart above). Where did the rest of the speedup go? Look at the HBM throughput reported by the profiler in the chart below: both v10cn and v10n drop to the same lower bandwidth plateau, well below v9n. When you compare v10n against v10cn at that same bandwidth, v10n reads ~25% fewer bytes and its kernel body runs ~25% faster (see the chart note below), so it cleanly beats the control variant; when you compare v10n against v9n, however, losing HBM throughput from the shallower in-flight reads eats back most of the byte-saving win.

There is also an instruction-count cost: unpacking C12 weights makes v10n execute ~40% more dynamic instructions than v9n. Meanwhile, the grid supplies an average of 17.45 warps per SM, and the profiler measures ~16 resident warps per SM on both kernels (25.6% on v9n and 25.1% on v10n, about one quarter of the 64-warp hardware limit, capped by grid size). In short, three candidate factors eat into the 25% byte reduction: shallower in-flight reads (a peak of 26.2 KiB/SM is less than half of the 64 KiB/SM knee point; see Chapter 2, Section 3), a higher dynamic instruction count, and the 4-warp CTA shape. We did not measure separately how much each of these three factors contributes, or what the time-averaged bytes in flight look like.

One more detail stands out in the control variant v10cn: of the ~4.5 µs by which v10cn trails v9n, roughly half (~2 µs) happens outside the kernel body. Its CUDA event time exceeds its kernel-body time by ~4.9 µs, whereas v9n exceeds its kernel body by only ~2.6 µs (what causes that extra ~2 µs was not measured). If we look strictly at the kernel body, switching to the new CTA shape costs ~2.2 µs, and switching to 12-bit weights wins back ~3.5 µs, leaving a net kernel-body saving of ~1.3 µs (applying 12-bit weights directly to v9's single-warp CTA shape was not measured).

Stepping back to look at the entire gemv progression: from v0 → v9 (with FP32 output), we sped the kernel up by ~45× across the evolution charts in Primer 3 through Chapter 5; v10n switches to BF16 output and adds the final step against v9n, which also writes BF16 output.

8Multi-Token GEMM g0 → g5 (T = 8..256): How Do the Mechanisms from Five of Levels 1–6 Stack Up Step by Step?

From g0 to g5, mechanisms from Levels 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 combine to beat cuBLAS across all four TTT values: ~1.41× faster at T=8T = 8T=8 and ~1.07× faster at T=256T = 256T=256.

This progression was measured only on qkv_gate across four settings: T=8,32,128,256T = 8, 32, 128, 256T=8,32,128,256 (T=16T = 16T=16 was not measured; see Chapter 5, Section 2 for the tensor shapes). Each reading in the first four charts below averages the medians of 4 full CUDA Graph replay runs and includes about 4.964.964.96 µs of empty-graph replay overhead. Several steps along the chain modify only some TTT values while leaving the remaining TTT values unchanged, and those unchanged pairs differ by at most 0.160.160.16 µs between versions, whereas a single version's own 4 medians span up to 0.540.540.54 µs. Between those two bounds, this section sets the noise band at 0.350.350.35 µs and labels any delta inside the band as noise.

The step names below keep our original experiment version IDs rather than mapping one-to-one to hardware levels. You will notice g3 is missing — that is because the Level 4 mechanisms from Chapter 4 are already superseded here by TMA and Tensor Core instructions rather than forming a separate step:

  1. g0: cuBLAS baseline (see Chapter 4, Section 6). At T=8/32/128T = 8 / 32 / 128T=8/32/128, cuBLAS uses Split-K (see Chapter 2, Section 5) and launches two back-to-back kernels — a main kernel that writes partial sums, followed by a second reduction kernel that adds them up — while at T=256T = 256T=256, cuBLAS runs a single kernel.
  2. g1a (fusing two kernels into one): launches only a single kernel where the last arriving CTA of each output tile sums that tile's partial sums in its epilogue (Chapter 1, Section 3 and Chapter 2, Section 6):
    • T=8/32T = 8 / 32T=8/32: uses wgmma with swap-AB (putting WWW on the 64-row operand-A side; see Chapter 5, Section 4) and launches 288 CTAs. This step both saves one launch and changes the MMA shape, so it runs faster (how much each change contributed was not measured).
    • T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256: launches only 72 CTAs (36 output tiles × Split-K 2), which runs 0.25 µs slower than g0 at T=128T = 128T=128 (within the noise band) and ~46% slower at T=256T = 256T=256. Two reasons explain the slowdown: first, 72 CTAs leave 60 SMs sitting idle (Chapter 2, Section 1); second, the single last-arriving CTA of each of the 36 output tiles has to read back and sum the FP32 partial sums of both split-K slices on its own, reading back 64 KiB per output tile at T=128T = 128T=128 and 128 KiB per output tile at T=256T = 256T=256 (Chapter 2, Section 7).
  3. g1 (Chapter 2 + Chapter 3): at T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256, raises Split-K to 3 and expands the grid to 108 CTAs, cutting idle SMs from 60 down to 24. We also switch the epilogue to parallel slice reduction (Chapter 2, Section 7) so each CTA claims 1/31/31/3 of the tile rows to sum in parallel, and upgrade data movement to a dedicated TMA producer warp, an mbarrier ring buffer (8 buffer slots at T=128T = 128T=128 and 5 buffer slots at T=256T = 256T=256; see Chapter 3, Sections 4–5), and 128 B XOR swizzle (Chapter 3, Section 7). All three changes went in together in the same version and were not measured separately. With g1, T=128T = 128T=128 beats cuBLAS for the first time, while T=256T = 256T=256 still trails cuBLAS (the cause was not measured). Here is a counterexample: Why not have each split-K slice atomically add its partial sum directly into the BF16 output? Under how this kernel is written, the compiler lowers scalar BF16 atomic adds into the compare-and-swap retry loop from Chapter 2, Section 7: because two adjacent BF16 columns share one 32-bit word, atomic adds to neighboring columns fight over the same 32-bit word, and the more threads contend, the more retries pile up. On the 12-bit weight qkv_gate kernel (T=16/32T = 16 / 32T=16/32), a scalar BF16 atomic-add epilogue makes the entire kernel about 2–3× slower than a tile-reduction epilogue (see the final chart in this section). To avoid that contention trap, split-K reduction has to use either parallel slice reduction, paired BF16x2 atomic adds, or TMA tile reduction (see Chapter 5, Section 7).
  4. g2 (Chapter 3, Section 6, setmaxnreg): a controlled experiment that drops the register cap of the producer warpgroup to 24 registers per thread (setmaxnreg applies at warpgroup granularity). That change yielded no speedup (landing inside the noise band), so we did not adopt it; we collected no profiler counters on this version, and why it yielded no gain was not measured.
  5. g4a (waves from Chapter 2, Section 1 + ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 4): mainly changes T=32T = 32T=32 (relative to g2, at T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256 it only removes g2's register cap and returns to g1's code). At T=32T = 32T=32, it replaces the 3-slot cp.async ring buffer (Chapter 3, Section 3) with 1 TMA producer warp plus a 9-slot ring buffer, dials Split-K down from 8 to 3, and shrinks the grid from 288 CTAs to 108. By the source code's SMEM footprint, the old kernel fits up to 2 CTAs per SM, so 288 CTAs come to ~1.1 waves: one full wave of 264 plus a 24-CTA tail (actual resident CTAs per SM were not measured). The new kernel's SMEM ring buffer fits only 1 CTA per SM, so all 108 CTAs run in a single wave. (Swap-AB was already in place back in g1a; this step did not add it.)
  6. g4b (Chapter 5, Section 7 + Section 6 of this chapter): at T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256, replaces the reduction with TMA tile reduction (Chapter 5, Section 7), which adds element-wise and atomically in place in global memory. Following the rule from Section 6, we hand the readiness flag writes to the producer warp outside the async wgmma region. That shaves ~1.3 µs off T=128T = 128T=128 and ~1.5 µs off T=256T = 256T=256 (see the charts below). Because the baseline here is g4a's parallel slice reduction rather than the BF16x2 atomic add from Chapter 5, Section 7, the savings differ from Chapter 5. Against the exact FP64 product, the relative L2 error of the full output creeps up from 1.6e-3 to 2.7e-3, still well under the 1e-2 limit of our second correctness check in Section 1. That bump matches what we expect from rounding each split-K slice to BF16 before accumulation (Chapter 5, Section 7), though we did not verify that this rounding is the sole cause.
  7. g4 (Chapter 5, Section 6): at T=256T = 256T=256, widens the tile column width BN from 64 to 128 (with Split-K = 7, a 4-slot ring buffer, and 126 CTAs), doubling how much Tensor Core work each buffer slot feeds (when Chapter 5, Section 6 measured this same change, the full kernel saved about 1.35 µs; because the two measurement methods differ, the time saved need not match). With g4, all four TTT values now beat cuBLAS. The output relative L2 error rises to 3.65e-3 (for the same reason as g4b; not determined separately).
  8. g5 (this chapter): brings in three changes together:
    • kernel rewrite: g1a through g4 were written in two high-level Python GPU kernel languages (Triton and Gluon) whose compilers emitted the descriptors and barrier code; g5 rewrites the kernels straight in CUDA C++ with inline PTX (Section 5), building the matrix descriptors, TMA tensor descriptors, and barrier phases explicitly in source code.
    • switching to 12-bit weights (C12) for T=8/32T = 8 / 32T=8/32: switches to the 12-bit weight kernel (with one offline weight permutation pass before execution), reading 25% fewer bytes and sharing the unpacked weights on chip across all 8 or 32 tokens. At T=8T = 8T=8, if we run the same upper-bound estimate from Section 7 on g4 → g5 (subtracting the 4.96 µs empty-graph replay overhead and scaling the rest of the time to 75% in proportion to bytes read), it predicts a ~2.7 µs saving, and we measure 2.95 µs (see the chart below). The ~0.2 µs gap between those two numbers sits inside our 0.35 µs noise band, so it does not count as an extra saving; on top of that, this step also rewrote the kernel in CUDA C++ (see the bullet above), and the two changes were not measured separately. Here at T=8T = 8T=8, the 16-bit baseline g4 is still g1a's 3-slot cp.async ring (288 CTAs) rather than the 16-bit loop of Section 4, so the ~8% estimate from Section 4 does not carry over.
    • keeping 16-bit weights (BF16) for T=128/256T = 128 / 256T=128/256: following the crossover boundary from Section 4, T=128T = 128T=128 stays on 16-bit weights and matches g4's latency; T=256T = 256T=256 also stays on 16-bit weights while switching to a BM = 128, BN = 192, 5-slot ring-buffer tiling with Split-K = 5 and 120 CTAs total. Those 120 CTAs fit into a single wave across the 132 SMs (leaving 12 SMs idle) and shave off a bit more time. The tiling change and the CUDA C++ kernel rewrite were not measured separately.

Takeaway: Compressing weights by a few bits saves HBM bytes at the cost of integer instructions in registers; the trade pays off only when decoding outruns HBM delivery without stalling the Tensor Core. How those instructions are actually scheduled in the end can only be seen by reading the SASS.

Next chapter's question: Part I dissected a single matrix multiplication all the way from the full GPU down to individual bits. In the next chapter, we zoom back out to a single layer of the model: how much historical KV cache does Stage 2 attention have to read at each step, and which of our six hardware levels bottlenecks it first?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → [Stage 2: Paged Attention] → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → Stage 6 routed experts → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

In Part I, we followed a single operator — gemv (qkv_gate in Stage 1 at T=1T = 1T=1) — down through all 6 hardware levels, and at the end of Chapter 6 we scaled that same projection up to T=256T = 256T=256 with multi-token GEMM (g0 → g5). Now Part II puts those same hardware mechanisms to work across the rest of the layer. Stage 1 hands off the qkv tensor (which packs query, key, value, and gate together) as the input to Stage 2. Where are the bottlenecks of Stage 2 paged attention under single-token decode, 8-token verification, and long-sequence prefill, and how does the kernel remove the slowest bottleneck step by step?

1What Does Stage 2 Compute, and What Quantity Governs Its Bottleneck?

Stage 2 turns qkv into the gated attention output; its bottleneck is governed by how many query rows share each key-value row.

Before we trace the math, let's get the basic numbers on the board. BBB is the number of concurrent requests, LLL is the number of new tokens per request in this forward pass, and T=B×LT = B \times LT=B×L is the total number of tokens in this forward pass (see Primer 2, Section 5). In token-by-token decode, L=1L = 1L=1; in verify, L=8L = 8L=8, where we stack 1 committed token and 7 draft tokens from the drafting mechanism into 8 rows and run them together (see Primer 1, Section 7); in prefill, LLL runs into the thousands. Each GPU holds 16 query heads and 2 KV heads (denoted g=0,1g = 0, 1g=0,1), with 64 dimensions per head. Because every 8 query heads share 1 KV head (GQA; see Primer 2, Section 1), each key-value row of a given KV head is shared across nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows.

Stage 2 takes qkv :  [T,  2304]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16}qkv:[T,2304]BF16 as input and slices it by column into q :  [T,  16,  64]  BF16\shape{q}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}q:[T,16,64]BF16, k :  [T,  2,  64]  BF16\shape{k}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}k:[T,2,64]BF16, v :  [T,  2,  64]  BF16\shape{v}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}v:[T,2,64]BF16, and gate :  [T,  16,  64]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{gate}}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}gate:[T,16,64]BF16, with column widths 1024+128+128+1024=23041024 + 128 + 128 + 1024 = 23041024+128+128+1024=2304.

Request lengths keep changing, and allocating contiguous device memory leaves fragments and forces data copies. So we store each request's historical keys and values in a paged KV cache, where each page can live anywhere in device memory. A page table page_table :  [B,  max_pages]  int32\shape{\mathrm{page\_table}}{B,\;max\_pages}{int32}page_table:[B,max_pages]int32 maps each request to its pages: each row corresponds to one request, and max_pages is the number of columns in the page table (no less than the page count of the longest request in the batch). Row b, column i records which physical page slot holds request b's page i; a new token can be appended to any free slot. Our workload sets each page to 1 token (page_size = 1), so reading every historical token takes a page-table lookup first. Section 6 deals with that wait.

In memory, the cache tensors have shape K_cache, V_cache :  [pages,  1,  2,  64]  FP8 E4M3\shape{K\_cache,\ V\_cache}{pages,\;1,\;2,\;64}{FP8\ E4M3}K_cache, V_cache:[pages,1,2,64]FP8 E4M3 (page slots, tokens per page, KV heads, head dimension), paired with sequence lengths seq_lens :  [B]  int32\shape{\mathrm{seq\_lens}}{B}{int32}seq_lens:[B]int32. Every historical token takes 2×2×64×1 B=256 B2 \times 2 \times 64 \times 1\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{B}2×2×64×1 B=256 B per layer on each GPU. A single token's K row packs 64 B from each of the two KV heads into 128 B total (and the same goes for the V row); a kernel that computes only one KV head reads only 64 B of that row, which we call a half-row (64 elements) below. Turning qkv into o_attn takes five steps:

  1. per-head RMSNorm (unweighted, computed in FP32; see Primer 1, Section 1 for the formula): q^=rmsnorm(q), k^=rmsnorm(k)\hat q = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(q),\ \hat k = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(k)q^​=rmsnorm(q), k^=rmsnorm(k); v is not normalized.
  2. RoPE (rotary position embedding): applied only in the 46 sliding-window layers and skipped in the 16 full-attention layers (for RoPE, see Primer 2, Section 2): rotate adjacent dimensions (2i,2i+1)(2i, 2i+1)(2i,2i+1) in FP32 by an angle determined by the token position.
  3. FP8 cast and KV cache write: cast q to E4M3; first divide new k and v by the cache's per-tensor scale factors (1 in scored cases), then cast them to E4M3 with saturation, clamped within the E4M3 maximum ±448\pm 448±448 (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout), and write them into the cache by page slot index.
  4. GQA attention: for a token at position ppp, a full-attention layer attends to all keys in 0..p0..p0..p, whereas a sliding-window layer attends only to the most recent 2,048 keys (max⁡(0,p−2047)..p\max(0, p-2047)..pmax(0,p−2047)..p); the LLL new tokens of the same request use a lower-triangular causal mask among themselves: oraw=softmax ⁣(5.4738 qfp8K⊤)Vo_{raw} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{5.473}{8}\, q_{fp8} K^{\top}\right) Voraw​=softmax(85.473​qfp8​K⊤)V Here the model also multiplies the dot product by 5.4735.4735.473 (an attention scaling factor fixed in the model configuration); combined with 1/64=1/81/\sqrt{64} = 1/81/64​=1/8, this folds into a single multiplier 0.6840.6840.684 applied to the dot product rather than to q.
  5. gated attention output: oattn=rmsnorm(oraw)⊙σ(gate)o_{attn} = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(o_{raw}) \odot \sigma(gate)oattn​=rmsnorm(oraw​)⊙σ(gate) producing o_attn :  [T,  1024]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{o\_attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16}o_attn:[T,1024]BF16 for Stage 3.

Read one KV head of one historical token (K 64 B + V 64 B = 128 B), and nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows use it; each query row does one 64-dimensional dot product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum, for 2×64+2×64=2562\times64 + 2\times64 = 2562×64+2×64=256 FLOPs in total. Divide that by the 128 B read, and you get the operations per byte read (arithmetic intensity; see Primer 2, Section 4): arithmetic intensity≈256nq128=2nq=16L FLOP/B\text{arithmetic intensity} \approx \frac{256 n_q}{128} = 2 n_q = 16L\ \mathrm{FLOP/B}arithmetic intensity≈128256nq​​=2nq​=16L FLOP/B In decode, L=1L = 1L=1 (nq=8n_q = 8nq​=8), so the arithmetic intensity is 16 FLOP/B. That 16 already sits above the ~14 FLOP/B ridge point of CUDA Cores (Chapter 5, Section 2), so CUDA Cores cannot keep up. On the Tensor Core, FP8 runs at twice the throughput of BF16 (Chapter 5, Section 3), which puts the ridge point at about 2×206=4122 \times 206 = 4122×206=412 FLOP/B (for 206, see Primer 2, Section 4), so the Tensor Core is still waiting on data. When we run decode on the Tensor Core, its lower bound is therefore the time to read KV. Move to 8-token verify (L=8L = 8L=8, nq=64n_q = 64nq​=64), and the arithmetic intensity rises to about 128 FLOP/B: CUDA Cores still cannot keep up, and on the Tensor Core the kernel remains bandwidth-bound. Move further to long-sequence prefill (LLL in the thousands), and the intensity shoots far past the ridge point into the compute-bound regime. As LLL grows, the bottleneck shifts the same way qkv_gate did with TTT in Chapter 5, except the horizontal axis here is nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L rather than TTT: the same T=32T = 32T=32 can be 32 decode requests (nq=8n_q = 8nq​=8) or 4 verify requests (nq=64n_q = 64nq​=64).

Two lower bounds anchor the two ends of this spectrum. Take decode first: for 1 request in a full-attention layer with 80,000 historical tokens, reading 20.5 MB of keys and values at 4.8 TB/s gives a bandwidth lower bound of about 4.3 µs. Decode has only 8 query rows, so the Tensor Core spends most of its time waiting on three things: at CTA entry, reading seq_lens first and then the page table, after which each page waits only for the page-table load to return (Section 6); fixed prologue and epilogue work per CTA (Section 4); and merging after splitting across segments (Section 3). Even after we tune the split count, the profiler clocks the attention kernel at about 13.8 µs on this shape, more than 3× the bandwidth lower bound: decode is latency-bound and cannot reach the pure bandwidth lower bound.

Now look at the other end, prefill: on a full-attention layer that appends 16,384 new tokens after 65,536 cached tokens, under the causal mask each new token attends to an average of nˉkey≈65,536+16,384/2=73,728\bar n_{key} \approx 65{,}536 + 16{,}384/2 = 73{,}728nˉkey​≈65,536+16,384/2=73,728 keys. Each query-key pair performs 4×644\times644×64 FLOPs, which adds up to 16 heads×16,384×nˉkey×64×4 FLOP≈4,948 GFLOP16\ \text{heads} \times 16{,}384 \times \bar n_{key} \times 64 \times 4\ \text{FLOP} \approx 4{,}948\ \text{GFLOP}16 heads×16,384×nˉkey​×64×4 FLOP≈4,948 GFLOP. In the final version of this chapter, both QK⊤Q K^{\top}QK⊤ and PVP VPV run in FP8; the FP8 peak is twice the BF16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s, or about 1,979 TFLOP/s (see Chapter 5, Section 3), which puts the compute lower bound at about 2.50 ms. Reading the KV cache for those 65,536 tokens once from HBM takes only about 3.5 µs, but every query tile has to re-read the keys it attends to from L2; we will calculate that L2 traffic in Section 4 once we have the tile count.

We evaluate every version in this chapter across 12 shapes: decode and verify with 1, 16, and 32 requests each (single-request history is 80,000 tokens, while 16- and 32-request histories are distributed within 80,000±7.5%80{,}000 \pm 7.5\%80,000±7.5%), with each workload split between sliding-window layers and full-attention layers. Shape labels below follow the pattern "decode / verify + request count + full-attention / sliding-window"; for example, "verify 32-request full attention" means 32 requests with 8 new tokens each (T=256T = 256T=256) on the 16 full-attention layers. The latency of each workload equals 46×46 \times46× sliding-window layer latency +16×+ 16 \times+16× full-attention layer latency, giving the 62-layer attention total for one step; we then take the geometric mean (the 6th root of the product of the 6 numbers) across the 6 workloads as the representative latency for the entire suite.

Every single-shape latency in this chapter comes from a paired ABBA benchmarking comparison of the attention operator in isolation: within the same process, we capture each shape as a CUDA Graph and replay it in full, flushing L2 before each replay. The old and new versions alternate in symmetric A, B, B, A order for multiple rounds (round count not recorded), and we take the median of each before subtracting; alternating within the same process shares the exact same inputs and cancels slow thermal and clock-frequency drift during the run. The noise-band rules follow Chapter 4, Section 6. Running two identical copies of the code as A and B through the same paired harness produces variation within about 0.4 µs on small shapes (and up to 1–2 µs on large shapes lasting over a hundred microseconds); any change with a delta smaller than that shape's noise band is recorded as "within the noise band."

In production, we run this model on the open-source inference framework SGLang, and our baseline for this chapter is SGLang's stock attention implementation. It runs the five steps above as 7 separate kernels, one after another: per-head RMSNorm (on sliding-window layers, RoPE runs inside the same kernel); a cast of k to FP8, a cast of v to FP8, and a cache write (3 kernels); a cast of q to FP8; paged attention (which may launch an extra merge kernel when split); and the gated output. The evolution versions in this chapter launch them as a PDL chain instead, where each kernel reads the output of the preceding kernel only after the wait call (see Chapter 1, Section 4).

2a0 (Part 1): Why Stack the 8 Query Heads of the Same KV Head as Matrix Rows?

Each CTA handles one KV head and stacks all query rows sharing that head into operand A, so each key-value tile is loaded into the SM once to multiply against all query rows.

Suppose you launch one CTA for each query head: then 8 separate CTAs all have to read the exact same KV row. Because many of those 8 reads hit the 60 MiB L2 cache (see Chapter 2, Section 2), the bytes read from HBM are not necessarily 8× higher — what you definitely cut is the number of transfers into the SM and the number of load instructions, dropping from 8 copies down to 1.

So for a given KV head ggg, we stack all nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L query rows that share it into Qg :  [8L,  64]  FP8\shape{Q_g}{8L,\;64}{FP8}Qg​:[8L,64]FP8; in verify, each query head has 8 new tokens, giving 64 rows in total. Each time a 64-token KV tile is loaded (K takes 4 KiB, and K plus V takes 8 KiB in total), we multiply QgQ_gQg​ by the transpose of Ktile :  [64,  64]  FP8\shape{K_{tile}}{64,\;64}{FP8}Ktile​:[64,64]FP8 to compute the entire score tile S :  [8L,  64]  FP32\shape{S}{8L,\;64}{FP32}S:[8L,64]FP32 in one pass.

That row count nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L also decides which Tensor Core instruction family we use (see Chapter 5, Section 3 for the two instruction families). In token-by-token decode (L=1L = 1L=1), there are only 8 rows. The kernel for decode 1- and 16-request sliding window places them into the 16 rows of mma.sync (m16n8k32), so half the rows are padding. The split kernel for decode full attention and decode 32-request sliding window swaps operands A and B instead (see Chapter 5, Section 4) and computes S⊤=KQ⊤S^{\top} = K Q^{\top}S⊤=KQ⊤: 16 keys sit on m=16m = 16m=16 and the 8 query rows fill n=8n = 8n=8 exactly, with zero padding. In exchange, it first converts FP8 K to FP16 losslessly and issues FP16 mma.sync (m16n8k16). Decode on the Tensor Core is bottlenecked on reading the KV cache (Section 1: latency-bound), so the Tensor Core has plenty of idle cycles; neither the 8 padded rows nor the FP16 conversion sits on the critical path. In verify, 64 rows fill m=64m = 64m=64 of wgmma to the brim. Verify full attention adopts wgmma from the early versions onward, whereas verify 16- and 32-request sliding window initially process 16-row groups with mma.sync before moving to wgmma in Section 5 (a2).

While we are at it, we also run the first matrix multiplication Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ directly in FP8: K in the cache is already FP8 E4M3 (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout), so once q is cast to E4M3 as well, the multiplication can consume the bytes of K directly and skip unpacking K to 16-bit first (except in the decode split kernel above that losslessly converts K to FP16 for KQ⊤K Q^{\top}KQ⊤). The trade-off is that casting q to FP8 introduces rounding error (accounted for in Section 8); how many HBM bytes this saves, and on which shapes it is a net loss, were not measured separately.

3a0 (Part 2): Before All Keys and Values Are Read, How Is the Softmax Denominator Computed on the Fly, and How Are Split Segments Merged Exactly?

Online softmax tracks only the running maximum, denominator, and unnormalized output, rescaling prior values by the exponential difference as each new key tile arrives and merging split-KV segments via log-sum-exp weights.

First, let's switch the exponential base to 2: the hardware transcendental instruction ex2 computes 2x2^x2x directly on the SFU (the machine instruction is MUFU.EX2; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for the SFU pipeline). If we multiply the dot product by 0.684×log⁡2e0.684 \times \log_2 e0.684×log2​e (log⁡2e≈1.4427\log_2 e \approx 1.4427log2​e≈1.4427) before taking 2x2^x2x, we get the exact same math as base eee. Every score sss below already bakes in this factor.

The naive way to compute softmax makes two passes over memory: pass one finds the full-row maximum m=max⁡kskm = \max_k s_km=maxk​sk​ and the denominator l=∑k2sk−ml = \sum_k 2^{s_k-m}l=∑k​2sk​−m (subtracting mmm prevents exponent overflow), and pass two computes ∑k2sk−mvk/l\sum_k 2^{s_k-m} v_k / l∑k​2sk​−mvk​/l. Doing that forces us to read the keys and values twice. The single-pass method (online softmax) fuses both passes into one sweep: whenever a new key tile arrives, we find the tile maximum mtilem_{tile}mtile​ and update mnew=max⁡(mold,mtile)m_{new} = \max(m_{old}, m_{tile})mnew​=max(mold​,mtile​). Because our running lll and OOO were scaled against moldm_{old}mold​, multiplying both by the rescaling factor α=2mold−mnew\alpha = 2^{m_{old}-m_{new}}α=2mold​−mnew​ shifts them onto mnewm_{new}mnew​: l←α l+∑k∈tile2sk−mnew,O←α O+∑k∈tile2sk−mnew vkl \leftarrow \alpha\, l + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}},\qquad O \leftarrow \alpha\, O + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}}\, v_kl←αl+k∈tile∑​2sk​−mnew​,O←αO+k∈tile∑​2sk​−mnew​vk​ Once all tiles have streamed through, a final division gives o=O/lo = O / lo=O/l. Packing the 2sk−mnew2^{s_k-m_{new}}2sk​−mnew​ values within a tile into a matrix gives the attention score weight matrix P, which turns the two recurrences into l←αl+P1l \leftarrow \alpha l + P\mathbf{1}l←αl+P1 and O←αO+PVO \leftarrow \alpha O + P VO←αO+PV. Both "P · V" and "BF16 P" below refer to this matrix.

Let's trace a small example you can check by hand (and play tile by tile in Figure 7-3): take one query row, 3 key tiles with 2 keys per tile, and base-2 pre-scaled scores Tile 1 =[1,3]= [1, 3]=[1,3], Tile 2 =[2,5]= [2, 5]=[2,5], Tile 3 =[0,4]= [0, 4]=[0,4], where each key has a 1-dimensional value v: Tile 1 =[4,2]= [4, 2]=[4,2], Tile 2 =[0,8]= [0, 8]=[0,8], Tile 3 =[6,2]= [6, 2]=[6,2].

After Tile 1 arrives: m=3m = 3m=3, l=2−2+20=1.25l = 2^{-2} + 2^{0} = 1.25l=2−2+20=1.25, O=2−2⋅4+1⋅2=3O = 2^{-2}\cdot 4 + 1\cdot 2 = 3O=2−2⋅4+1⋅2=3.

When Tile 2 arrives: mtile=5m_{tile} = 5mtile​=5 updates mnew=5m_{new} = 5mnew​=5, giving α=23−5=0.25\alpha = 2^{3-5} = 0.25α=23−5=0.25; rescaling and adding the new tile yields l=1.25×0.25+2−3+20=1.4375l = 1.25 \times 0.25 + 2^{-3} + 2^{0} = 1.4375l=1.25×0.25+2−3+20=1.4375, and O=0.25×3+2−3⋅0+1⋅8=8.75O = 0.25 \times 3 + 2^{-3}\cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 8 = 8.75O=0.25×3+2−3⋅0+1⋅8=8.75.

When Tile 3 arrives: mtile=4<5m_{tile} = 4 < 5mtile​=4<5, so α=1\alpha = 1α=1 (no rescaling needed); we get l=1.4375+2−5+2−1=1.96875l = 1.4375 + 2^{-5} + 2^{-1} = 1.96875l=1.4375+2−5+2−1=1.96875, O=8.75+2−5⋅6+2−1⋅2=9.9375O = 8.75 + 2^{-5}\cdot 6 + 2^{-1}\cdot 2 = 9.9375O=8.75+2−5⋅6+2−1⋅2=9.9375, and finally o=9.9375/1.96875≈5.048o = 9.9375 / 1.96875 \approx 5.048o=9.9375/1.96875≈5.048. Compare that with the two-pass method: ∑2s−5=2−4+2−2+2−3+1+2−5+2−1=1.96875\sum 2^{s-5} = 2^{-4}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}+1+2^{-5}+2^{-1} = 1.96875∑2s−5=2−4+2−2+2−3+1+2−5+2−1=1.96875 and ∑2s−5v=9.9375\sum 2^{s-5} v = 9.9375∑2s−5v=9.9375, which lands on the exact same result.

With the intra-tile recurrence in place, we can add Split-KV (partitioning along the key dimension): slice the visible keys of a request into SSS segments assigned to SSS CTAs. Each segment writes its partial results into a global-memory region called the workspace buffer, which typically stays hot in L2 right after being written (for the general pattern of merging partial sums across CTAs, see Chapter 2, Sections 6–7). Segment iii runs the recurrence above on its own slice and outputs oi=Oi/lio_i = O_i / l_ioi​=Oi​/li​ along with the log-sum-exp (lse) lsei=mi+log⁡2li\mathrm{lse}_i = m_i + \log_2 l_ilsei​=mi​+log2​li​. Because 2lsei=2mili2^{\mathrm{lse}_i} = 2^{m_i} l_i2lsei​=2mi​li​ is segment iii's exact unshifted denominator relative to 0, the total log-denominator across all keys is lse=log⁡2∑i2lsei\mathrm{lse} = \log_2 \sum_i 2^{\mathrm{lse}_i}lse=log2​∑i​2lsei​, and the merge step accumulates o=∑i2lsei−lse  oio = \sum_i 2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}}\; o_io=i∑​2lsei​−lseoi​ Multiplying by 2lsei−lse2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}}2lsei​−lse swaps out segment iii's own denominator and replaces it with the denominator across all keys. Now split the example above into two segments (Figure 7-3 Mode 2). Segment A holds Tiles 1–2: mA=5m_A = 5mA​=5, lA=1.4375l_A = 1.4375lA​=1.4375, 2lseA=32×1.4375=462^{\mathrm{lse}_A} = 32 \times 1.4375 = 462lseA​=32×1.4375=46, oA=8.75/1.4375≈6.087o_A = 8.75/1.4375 \approx 6.087oA​=8.75/1.4375≈6.087. Segment B holds Tile 3: mB=4m_B = 4mB​=4, lB=1.0625l_B = 1.0625lB​=1.0625, 2lseB=16×1.0625=172^{\mathrm{lse}_B} = 16 \times 1.0625 = 172lseB​=16×1.0625=17, oB≈2.235o_B \approx 2.235oB​≈2.235. The total denominator is 46+17=63=25×1.9687546 + 17 = 63 = 2^5 \times 1.9687546+17=63=25×1.96875, the merge weights are 46/6346/6346/63 and 17/6317/6317/63, and the weighted sum is 4663oA+1763oB=280+3863≈5.048\tfrac{46}{63} o_A + \tfrac{17}{63} o_B = \tfrac{280 + 38}{63} \approx 5.0486346​oA​+6317​oB​=63280+38​≈5.048, which is mathematically identical to no splitting; when the floating-point summation order differs, the last bit of the result may differ, and this only becomes important in Section 12.

Together, online softmax and Split-KV let us read the keys and values only once while spreading work across multiple CTAs. In exchange, we pay two costs: each tile adds one maximum reduction, one ex2, and an elementwise multiplication on OOO (Section 8 removes most of this); and splitting across segments writes an extra (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) per segment and runs an extra merge step. Meanwhile, Steps 1–3 of Section 1 (per-head RMSNorm, RoPE, and FP8 cast plus KV cache write) run in a separate kernel launched before the main kernel, called the prologue kernel. Put all of these together and we get our starting point a0: separate prologue kernel + GQA query-row stacking + FP8 Q⋅K⊤Q\cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ + fixed-split Split-KV + separate merge kernel, where the split count in a0 is fixed — for example, decode 1-request full attention is fixed at 128 segments.

4a0 → a1: Into How Many Segments Should One Request's Keys Be Split, and How Should They Be Balanced?

Split more finely at low concurrency to keep enough reads in flight, and less finely at high concurrency to avoid multi-wave CTA launch/exit overhead, while balancing work by actual sequence lengths.

Every split segment launches one CTA. Fitting the profiler readings on the decode 16- and 32-request shapes (fitting method not recorded) shows that each CTA spends about 2.04 µs per 64-key tile, plus about 6.6 µs of entry/exit overhead to read the page-table start offset, load Q, and write back (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) (distinct from the kernel launch gap in Chapter 1). Because most of this 6.6 µs is spent waiting on memory rather than saturating issue slots, CTAs within the same wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1) wait in parallel across the chip, and critical-path launch/exit overhead is bounded by approximately "waves × 6.6 µs" rather than "CTAs × 6.6 µs". On top of that, the merge step reads back one partial result per segment, which we account for separately.

So whether to raise or lower the split count SSS comes down to whether all CTAs already fit inside 1 wave. When they fit, splitting further adds no wave entry/exit overhead; once they spill past 1 wave, each additional wave pays the fixed per-CTA entry/exit overhead (about 6.6 µs) one more time. At this stage, the split kernel for decode full attention computes both KV heads in each CTA. For each 64-key tile, it uses the page table to randomly read 16 KiB of K and V for the two heads, or 8 KiB per KV head; we call this gather below. It places 4 CTAs per SM, so 1 wave holds 132×4=528132 \times 4 = 528132×4=528 CTAs (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how residency is calculated). Until Section 5 switches it to full-row gather, it gathers only a 64 B half-row per head at a time; in the isolated gather-only microbenchmark in Section 5 below, such 64 B half-row gather reaches 2.6–3.1 TB/s. Below 1 full wave, there are not enough bytes in flight to saturate HBM (see Chapter 2, Section 3): at low concurrency (decode 1-request full attention), 128 segments launch 128 CTAs — just 0.24 waves — and measured gather bandwidth crawls at about 1.3 TB/s; splitting into 256 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) keeps all CTAs within 1 wave while doubling in-flight reads, which makes execution faster.

At high concurrency, the math flips and we must split into fewer segments instead. Take decode 16-request full attention: keeping 128 segments launches 2,048 CTAs, or 3.88 waves; consolidating to 32 segments (512 CTAs, 0.97 waves) pulls the grid inside 1 wave, saving about 3 waves of entry/exit overhead and cutting the partial results read by the merge step to 1/4. Multiplying 3 waves × 6.6 µs predicts a maximum saving of about 20 µs, and the measured saving is about 12 µs; the source of the difference was not measured separately. Decode 32-request full attention and verify 16- and 32-request full attention likewise consolidate their segment counts, running faster by executing fewer waves or reading half as many partial results in the merge step (the time saved on each shape is shown in the chart below).

Full-attention verify at this stage uses the single-KV-head split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head, likewise placing 4 CTAs per SM, or 528 CTAs per wave). Consolidating verify 16-request full attention from 32 segments (1,024 CTAs, 1.94 waves) to 16 segments (512 CTAs, 0.97 waves) pulls it inside 1 wave, with most of the saving in the merge step (see the note in the chart below). Conversely, cutting verify 16-request full attention further from 16 segments down to 8 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) makes it much slower (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): once all CTAs already fit within 1 wave, cutting further saves zero waves and only drops co-resident CTAs per SM from about 4 to about 2 — halving in-flight reads — while doubling the number of tiles each CTA processes serially.

Verify 1-request sliding window has a neat boundary quirk of its own: the latest of the 8 new tokens attends to 7 more keys than the earliest, so at most 2,048+7=2,0552{,}048 + 7 = 2{,}0552,048+7=2,055 keys are visible, requiring ⌈2,055/64⌉=33\lceil 2{,}055 / 64 \rceil = 33⌈2,055/64⌉=33 tiles of 64 keys — 1 more than 32. Originally, each KV head was split into 32 segments, forcing 17 CTAs to process 2 tiles serially each. We first switch to 64 segments per KV head: 33 segments process 1 tile each and the remaining 31 empty segments write only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\inftylsei​=−∞, eliminating the serial wait for a second tile and saving about 1.10 µs (see the chart below). Later steps drop the empty segments to launch 33 single-tile CTAs per KV head (66 in total) and shrink the ring buffer here (see Chapter 3, Section 4) to 1 stage; those two steps were measured separately. The cost is that the merge step reads 33 (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) pairs.

Requests in the same batch often have different lengths: in this workload suite, historical lengths lie within ±7.5%\pm 7.5\%±7.5% of the mean, so the longest request is about 16% longer than the shortest (1.075/0.925≈1.161.075 / 0.925 \approx 1.161.075/0.925≈1.16). When segments are divided equally per request, CTAs for the longest request run about 16% longer than those for the shortest, holding up the last SMs at the tail. To fix this, we concatenate the keys of all requests into a single logical strip and partition it evenly across all CTAs by actual key count; the trade-off is that one segment may span two requests, requiring extra work in the merge step (measured results on verify appear in Section 7).

Prefill also needs to balance its tail, using a different kernel: each CTA has 1 producer warpgroup and 3 consumer warpgroups (Chapter 3, Sections 4 and 6). Each consumer warpgroup computes 64 query rows, so one CTA handles 24 tokens × 8\times\ 8× 8 query heads =192= 192=192 query rows for one KV head; its register usage allows only 1 CTA per SM, making 1 wave equal to 132 CTAs. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, the grid launches ⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366\lceil 16{,}384 / 24 \rceil \times 2 = 683 \times 2 = 1{,}366⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366 query-tile CTAs in total.

Each of those 1,366 query-tile CTAs streams all KV entries visible to it from L2: 1,366 CTAs ×\times× an average of about 73,728 visible keys ×\times× 128 B per key per KV head, totaling about 12.9 GB. At the 7.33 TB/s L2 read bandwidth measured by a microbenchmark on the same GPU, streaming through once takes about 1.76 ms, or about 70% of the 2.50 ms FP8 compute lower bound from Section 1: because this is shorter than the compute lower bound, prefill remains compute-bound, though L2 bandwidth has only about 30% headroom left.

We launch the 683 CTAs of each KV head in descending order of work from heaviest to lightest. As explained in Chapter 2, Section 1, CTAs do not switch in lockstep waves — as soon as an SM frees a slot, the next CTA is dispatched; under the causal mask, earlier query tiles attend to fewer keys and do less work, so the last CTAs dispatched onto SMs are the lightest 40 query tiles (40 CTAs). Once the dispatch queue drains, SMs that finish early sit idle waiting for this last batch of CTAs to complete. Splitting each KV head's lightest 40 query tiles into 4 segments along the key dimension (40 and 4 were tuned empirically) expands the grid to (683−40+40×4)×2=1,606(683 - 40 + 40\times 4) \times 2 = 1{,}606(683−40+40×4)×2=1,606 CTAs. We pay the entry/exit and merge overhead of 240 extra CTAs, and in return the final batch of CTAs takes only 1/4 of the original time, letting the tail SMs finish earlier and saving 345 µs at 65K history (see the chart below).

What if we replace static key-count balancing with dynamic claiming, where each CTA claims its next tile from a global counter? In measured runs, that is actually slower (about 23 µs slower on verify 32-request full attention). One key tile takes only about 2 µs (the 2.04 µs fitted value from Section 4), so adding an intra-CTA barrier and handoff on every claim raises the per-tile cost by about 10% and breaks the pipeline that prefetches the next tile's page-table entries (see Section 6). At the same time, static imbalance is at most about 16% to begin with and is already tiny once we split evenly by key count, so dynamic claiming has very little ceiling left to recover.

With a fixed segment count, short requests or sliding-window boundaries can also produce empty segments (start ≥\ge≥ end). On shapes that enable empty-segment skipping, an empty segment writes only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\inftylsei​=−∞ and skips writing an all-zero output. Because 2−∞=02^{-\infty} = 02−∞=0, the formula in Section 3 still holds, and when the merge step sees −∞-\infty−∞, it skips that segment directly. We did not measure the time saved by skipping empty segments separately.

No single combination of kernel and split count wins across all shapes, so a1 looks up a per-shape table. At this stage, decode sliding window and verify sliding window both use the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head; register usage sets 3–4 CTAs per SM). Decode full attention uses the two-KV-head split kernel described earlier in this section. Per-shape table lookup cuts the 6-workload geometric mean defined in Section 1 by about 8%; because this version also switched several kernels at the same time, not all 8% comes from table lookup alone (the final kernel assignment for each shape appears at the end of Section 12).

5a1 → a2 (Part 1): When Two KV Heads Share the Same 128 B K Row, How Should the Two Halves Be Read?

Launching the two CTAs that read the two halves of the same row back-to-back saves ~12 µs on 32-request full-attention verification; having a single CTA gather the full 128 B row raises gather bandwidth by 30%–50%+ in an isolated gather microbenchmark.

Because the page table scatters each token into an arbitrary page slot, the kernel sees a stream of random addresses. TMA multidimensional tensor copies cannot follow a page table. That leaves two options: each thread issues 16 B cp.async instructions, or each row gets one 128 B 1D bulk copy, cp.async.bulk (see Chapter 3, Section 3 for the four paths). The decode and verify kernels in this chapter gather row by row with 16 B cp.async.
