Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → Stage 2 paged attention → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → [Stage 6: Routed Experts] → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

Stage 6's 32 local NVFP4 experts hold the largest share of weights in a single layer. Why is the starter implementation that dequantizes one expert at a time so slow? And as the total token count TTT grows from 1 to 16,384, why does Stage 6 ultimately split into three distinct kernels by TTT, and how does each generation evolve from the last?

1What Five Steps Does Stage 6 Compute for Each Hit Pair, and How Does MeM_eMe​ Split Stage 6 into Two Regimes?

When the token count MeM_eMe​ routed to an expert is less than about 58, reading weights is slower than matrix multiplication: decode, verify, and T=753T = 753T=753 prefill fall below this threshold, whereas T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 prefill lies above it.

Stage 6 takes p :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16}p:[T,4096]BF16 from Stage 5, along with the routing indices topk_ids :  [T,  8]  int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32}topk_ids:[T,8]int32 and routing weights topk_weights :  [T,  8]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32}topk_weights:[T,8]FP32 from Stage 4. In each row, the 8 routing weights sum to 1 (see Primer 2, Section 2). All 256 experts in the model are split across 8 GPUs, and this GPU's 32 local experts stay resident in HBM (see Primer 1, Section 2). Once Stage 6 finishes, it outputs m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 7. A token toktoktok has 8 slots slotslotslot, and only a slot that lands on a local expert eee on this GPU counts as a hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e); if all 8 slots miss this GPU, that token's output row is all zeros.

For the MeM_eMe​ tokens that hit local expert eee on this GPU (one row per hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e)), Stage 6 runs five steps in order:

  1. gate/up projection (W13): [ gugate∣guup ]=ptok dequant(W13[e])⊤[\,gu_{gate} \mid gu_{up}\,] = p_{tok}\, \mathrm{dequant}(W_{13}[e])^{\top}[gugate​∣guup​]=ptok​dequant(W13​[e])⊤, producing the gate and up halves gu :  [Me,  8192]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{gu}}{M_e,\;8192}{FP32}gu:[Me​,8192]FP32. The first 4096 columns are the gate gugategu_{gate}gugate​, and the last 4096 columns are the up projection guupgu_{up}guup​. These are the FP32 accumulator values of the matrix multiply; the kernels below usually keep them in registers and pass them straight to Step 2.
  2. SwiGLU: inter=silu(gugate)⊙guupinter = \mathrm{silu}(gu_{gate}) \odot gu_{up}inter=silu(gugate​)⊙guup​, producing inter :  [Me,  4096]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{inter}}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16}inter:[Me​,4096]BF16 (see Primer 2, Section 2).
  3. down projection (W2): y=inter dequant(W2[e])⊤y = inter\, \mathrm{dequant}(W_{2}[e])^{\top}y=interdequant(W2​[e])⊤, producing y :  [Me,  4096]  BF16\shape{y}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16}y:[Me​,4096]BF16.
  4. post-expert RMSNorm: ynorm=rmsnorm(y⊙(1+wpost))y_{norm} = \mathrm{rmsnorm}\big(y \odot (1 + w_{post})\big)ynorm​=rmsnorm(y⊙(1+wpost​)), producing ynorm :  [Me,  4096]  FP32\shape{y_{norm}}{M_e,\;4096}{FP32}ynorm​:[Me​,4096]FP32. Here wpost :  [4096]  BF16\shape{w_{post}}{4096}{BF16}wpost​:[4096]BF16 (written as wpost_expertw_{post\_expert}wpost_expert​ in Primer 2, Section 2) is the post-expert RMSNorm weight shared across all experts, and a tiny constant ϵ\epsilonϵ sits inside the root mean square to prevent division by zero.
  5. weighted accumulation by routing weights: mtok+=topk_weights[tok,slot]⋅ynormm_{tok} \mathrel{+}= \texttt{topk\_weights}[tok, slot] \cdot y_{norm}mtok​+=topk_weights[tok,slot]⋅ynorm​, writing out m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16.

H200 Tensor Cores do not accept 4-bit floating-point (E2M1) inputs. After NVFP4 codewords are loaded onto the chip, the kernel must decode them to BF16 before feeding them into the matrix multiply. Each weight is w=c⋅sblock⋅stensorw = c \cdot s_{block} \cdot s_{tensor}w=c⋅sblock​⋅stensor​: a 4-bit codeword ccc multiplied by a block scale and then by a tensor scale (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout and decoding instructions). Counting the bytes, each codeword takes 0.5 B0.5\text{ B}0.5 B, every 16 weights share a 1 B1\text{ B}1 B block scale (0.0625 B0.0625\text{ B}0.0625 B per weight), and each projection matrix (W13W_{13}W13​, W2W_2W2​) of each expert carries one FP32 tensor scale, totaling 0.5625 B0.5625\text{ B}0.5625 B per weight. Within each expert, the gate half and the up-projection half share a single FP32 tensor scale (Section 13 explains why storing one scale is enough).

When we report Stage 6 latency below, we are measuring Stage 6 in isolation: within the same benchmark run, we alternate A/B paired comparisons before and after a change (see Chapter 7, Section 1 for the paired protocol and Chapter 4, Section 6 for the variation criterion). Single-layer latency, by contrast, covers all eight stages of a full layer in Chapter 9. Take the geometric mean of Stage 6 latency across the 6 decode (T=1,16,32T = 1, 16, 32T=1,16,32, with 1 new token per request) and verify (T=8,128,256T = 8, 128, 256T=8,128,256, with 8 new tokens per request) workloads and multiply by 60 (the middle 60 layers use 4-bit experts; see Primer 1, Section 2): that gives the 60-layer total. We compare that total against the baseline SGLang implementation, which invokes a 4-bit grouped-GEMM library routine once per projection (see the first chart at the end of the chapter); the prefill workloads at T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384 are treated separately in Sections 14–16.

Along the evolution chain, decode and verify start out sharing two kernel generations (m1 and m2), before the final deployment splits into three branches by TTT: m3 for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, m4 for T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256, and m5 for prefill.

Why split by TTT at all? Because the row count of an expert's matrix multiplication is simply the number of tokens MeM_eMe​ routed to that expert. At 3.56 FLOP/B3.56\text{ FLOP/B}3.56 FLOP/B per token against the H200 ridge point of 206 FLOP/B206\text{ FLOP/B}206 FLOP/B, an expert needs Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 tokens before matrix-multiply compute time catches up with the time to read its weights once from HBM (Primer 2, Section 5). Which 8 experts each token picks is the routing distribution: spreading tokens evenly across experts is uniform routing, clustering them onto a few experts is skewed routing, and our single-operator benchmarks generate multiple random routing distributions. That Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 line splits the workload into two regimes:

  • decode and verify (T=1..256T = 1..256T=1..256): Under uniform routing at T=256T = 256T=256, almost all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit, leaving each expert with an average of only 8 tokens. Under skewed routing, tokens pile onto fewer experts, so fewer experts get hit than under uniform routing. In this chapter's single-operator benchmark, at T=256T = 256T=256 the busiest GPU receives about 390 hit pairs and hits about 24 local experts on average, leaving each hit expert with an average of about 16 tokens—still far below 58. Only a few hot experts at T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 receive several dozen to over a hundred tokens, which we handle in Section 9. Throughout this regime, weight reads set the physical lower bound: the starter implementation m0 is slowed down by its per-expert loop (Section 2), while the first four kernel generations (m1 → m4) strip away on-chip decoding instructions, tail waves, and synchronization overhead step by step to approach that weight-read lower bound.
  • prefill (T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384): Under uniform routing, each local expert receives an average of 8T/256=T/328T / 256 = T / 328T/256=T/32 tokens—about 24, 94, and 512 tokens across the three points. T=753T = 753T=753 still sits below the ridge point, but T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 crosses 58, shifting the bottleneck of our fifth-generation kernel (m5) onto the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines.

Put the two physical lower bounds side by side, and this crossover is obvious. During prefill, all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit (906 MB906\text{ MB}906 MB in total), so reading their weights once at 4.8 TB/s4.8\text{ TB/s}4.8 TB/s takes at least 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, even if we count only the per-GPU mean of roughly TTT hit pairs, the math totals 16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP16{,}384 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4096^2 \approx 1{,}649\text{ GFLOP}16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP. Divided by the 989 TFLOP/s989\text{ TFLOP/s}989 TFLOP/s BF16 peak (since 4-bit weights unpack to BF16 on chip before the multiply), that puts the compute lower bound at no less than 1,668 μs1{,}668\ \mu\text{s}1,668 μs—nearly 9× the weight-read lower bound. In decode and verify, by contrast, we read only the hit experts, so the weight-read lower bound stays much smaller than 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs. At T=256T = 256T=256, the single-operator benchmark sets its lower bound at 108.9 μs108.9\ \mu\text{s}108.9 μs, whereas the compute lower bound is only about 29.7 μs29.7\ \mu\text{s}29.7 μs. A full 8-GPU deployment also has to wait for the slowest GPU and run a cross-GPU reduction; this chapter measures single-GPU latency under the routing load of the busiest GPU, excluding that cross-GPU reduction.

2Why Does the Starter m0 Take Tens of Milliseconds, and Why Is the First Grouped-GEMM Step m1a ~80× Faster?

m0 loops over experts one by one, launching small kernels and decompressing weights to FP32 in HBM; m1 switches to a single grouped-GEMM launch per projection with on-the-fly in-register decompression.

m0 is the plain-PyTorch starter implementation, not the kernel that baseline SGLang runs in production. On every call, it steps through all 32 local experts one by one in a Python loop—whether hit or not, running every token through each expert with routing weight 0 where not routed: for each expert, it decompresses that expert's entire weight set into a 201.3 MB201.3\text{ MB}201.3 MB FP32 dense matrix in HBM, converts it to BF16, and runs the matrix multiplies. Look at the HBM byte accounting for a single expert: the useful weights are only 28.3 MB28.3\text{ MB}28.3 MB, yet even counting only reading the 4-bit weights, writing out the dense FP32 matrix, and reading it back moves at least 28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB28.3 + 201.3 + 201.3 = 431.0\text{ MB}28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB—about 15× the useful bytes.

Across the 6 benchmark cases, the measured geometric-mean Stage 6 latency is about 37.8 ms37.8\text{ ms}37.8 ms. Across all 32 local experts, that HBM round trip alone costs at least about 2.9 ms2.9\text{ ms}2.9 ms even at full HBM bandwidth; its actual share was not measured separately (see the chart below). Beyond that round trip, each expert in the per-expert loop also runs two dequantizations (producing temporary FP32 and BF16 tensors), two BF16 matrix multiplications, SwiGLU, normalization, and a small launch that adds the weighted result across all output rows. The share of each item was not measured. m1a drops the HBM round trip, the per-expert loop, the temporary tensors, and the repeated small launches all at once, running about 80× faster than m0.

m1 removes that extra round trip in two steps. First (m1a in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we run token bucketing (grouping tokens that hit the same expert together) and then launch a single grouped GEMM grid per projection instead of launching once per expert. A grouped GEMM is a single launch where each CTA processes one token tile for one expert. Stage 6 now runs in four parts: "token bucketing → gate/up grouped GEMM (with SwiGLU) → down-projection grouped GEMM → post-expert RMSNorm and weighted accumulation." Once an expert's 4-bit codewords and block scales arrive on chip, we decode them to BF16 right in registers and feed them straight into the matrix multiply without writing back any dense weights; HBM reads the 4-bit weights only once. This step is faster on all 6 benchmark cases (see the first chart at the end of the chapter).

Second (m1 in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we interleave the gate and up projections in 32+3232 + 3232+32 rows so the gate and up outputs for the same row land in the same tile and can run SwiGLU directly. At the same time, we switch weight decoding to branchless bitwise unpacking (see Chapter 6, Section 3) and turn on Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL; see Chapter 1, Section 4) so the next kernel launches early to prefetch static weights. Even with those improvements, m1 still takes about 1.6× the latency of baseline SGLang, and only overtakes the baseline with m2 in the next section. What we pay for m1 is maintaining a fixed-shape token-bucketing index table ahead of the matrix multiplications; the overhead of that table and the individual shares of the three items in Step 2 were not measured separately.

3When MeM_eMe​ Is Only a Handful to a Dozen Tokens, How Do We Pipeline Weight Loads?

m2 switches to a pipelined wgmma tiled kernel, splitting along K at small batch sizes to fill SMs and using a multi-slot weight ring buffer to hide weight loads behind compute.

Step 1 replaces the kernel: m2 switches to Hopper's asynchronous wgmma instruction, placing the in-register decoded weights in operand A and the tokens on the operand-B side (swap-AB; see Chapter 5, Sections 3–5). m2 selects the matrix-multiply instruction according to tile height: 8-row tiles use warp-level mma.sync (for reasons explained in Section 4), while taller tiles use wgmma. Running wgmma with operand A in registers (RS mode; Chapter 5, Section 3) comes with a catch: weight decoding consumes ALU cycles and registers. If ALU decoding cycles exceed Tensor Core cycles, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 for a counterexample). In the Me<58M_e < 58Me​<58 regime, once we compress the decoding instructions tightly enough, the ALU is no longer the bottleneck.

Step 2 raises the tile count. The down projection has only 4096 output columns, half of the 8192 columns of the gate/up projection, so at T≤32T \le 32T≤32 there are not enough tiles to fill all 132 SMs. Following Split-K from Chapter 2, Section 5, at small TTT the down projection is sliced 2-way or 4-way along K, storing partial sums into a temporary BF16 matrix that the subsequent post-expert RMSNorm kernel reduces; at T=1T = 1T=1, even the gate/up projection lacks enough tiles and is sliced along K too. What Split-K costs us is writing and reading an extra buffer of partial sums and running the reduction additions, plus the lower precision of BF16 partial sums compared to FP32. Splitting too finely loses performance—cutting the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection into 4 slices makes it slower (see the second chart below).

Step 3 keeps weight loads continuously in flight. Prior to this step, weight unpacking had already moved to paired 4-bit nibble decoding (where each instruction unpacks two 4-bit codes into a packed BF16x2 pair at once; see Chapter 6, Section 3). Applying the multi-slot ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 4 (Figure 3-4), we then set up 3 shared-memory weight slots to keep enough bytes in flight to saturate HBM (Chapter 2, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 6). Taking out that 3-slot ring buffer alone slows Stage 6 down by 5–6 µs at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32.

At T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256, we likewise introduce a weight-only 2-slot ring buffer, which cuts Stage 6 latency by about 19 μs19\ \mu\text{s}19 μs at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). Opening too many ring slots consumes extra shared memory and drops occupancy (see Section 4; for the counterexample where too few slots leave insufficient bytes in flight, see Section 9). We also tried refilling ring slots early inside the loop, where the compiler inserted a CTA barrier between refilling and dequantization and made the kernel slower (see the second chart below).

Step 4 offloads the decoding left shift onto the FMA pipeline (left-shift FMA offloading; see Chapter 5, Section 1). Five of the six benchmark workloads speed up—saving up to about 9.4 μs9.4\ \mu\text{s}9.4 μs in Stage 6 at T=128T = 128T=128—with only T=8T = 8T=8 coming out slightly slower.

4Why Does the Same Occupancy Change Turn from Faster to Slower Under a Different Routing Distribution?

As the number of active experts varies with routing, the total tile count varies too; changing per-SM occupancy alters the wave count only for routing distributions that cross a full-wave capacity step.

Back in Chapter 2, Section 1, we calculated wave counts: when each SM holds kkk resident CTAs at once, a single wave fits 132k132k132k CTAs, and total runtime is approximately ⌈Ac/(132k)⌉×\lceil A c / (132 k) \rceil \times⌈Ac/(132k)⌉× the duration of one wave. The expert kernel adds a moving variable: the number of active experts AAA is not constant, because different routing distributions hit different numbers of local experts, so the device-wide tile count AcA cAc (where ccc is the CTAs per expert) fluctuates with the routing distribution. Any change that alters kkk shifts the capacity step 132k132k132k. Routing distributions whose tile counts land between the old and new steps run one wave more or one wave fewer, shifting latency by several to over ten microseconds; distributions that do not cross a step see only the small intrinsic cost or benefit of the change itself.

We have a direct measured example at T=8T = 8T=8. We replace mma.sync with wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 3); each expert launches c=128c = 128c=128 CTAs (gate/up projection 8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA8{,}192\text{ columns} \div 64\text{ columns/CTA}8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA), per-SM occupancy drops from k=9k = 9k=9 to k=8k = 8k=8, and a single wave shrinks from 1,1881{,}1881,188 CTAs to 1,0561{,}0561,056. The two routing distributions with A=9A = 9A=9 have 9×128=1,1529 \times 128 = 1{,}1529×128=1,152 CTAs, so they drop right across the boundary from 1 wave into 2 waves and slow Stage 6 down by over 10 μs10\ \mu\text{s}10 μs. The other three routing distributions (A=8A = 8A=8, still within 1 wave) run slightly faster instead (see the chart below). The same thing happens at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 when we expand the weight ring buffer from the previous section from 3 slots to 4 slots and per-SM occupancy drops from 8 to 7: across multiple routing distributions it averages about 1.9 μs1.9\ \mu\text{s}1.9 μs faster, yet under each of the two workloads one routing distribution regresses.

That directly sets a rule: every occupancy or register change to an expert kernel must be benchmarked across multiple routing distributions simultaneously; a change that wins on only one distribution is rejected. To stop a change from moving the wave step 132k132k132k, we pin each CTA's register and shared-memory usage to the exact quota that fits kkk CTAs per SM (Chapter 3, Section 1), isolating the change's own gain or loss. For instance, pinning the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection at 7 CTAs per SM turns its new weight-only 2-slot ring buffer from a loss of about 2.1 μs2.1\ \mu\text{s}2.1 μs into a gain of about 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.8 μs.

The cost of pinning occupancy is a tighter per-thread register cap. Push the compiler attribute __maxnreg__(N) too low and the compiler spills excess values to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1). Switching to wgmma at T=8T = 8T=8 and capping registers at 56 spills 8 registers per thread and slows Stage 6 by about 62 μs62\ \mu\text{s}62 μs; capping at 80 or 72 registers at T=256T = 256T=256 also causes slowdowns from register spilling (see the chart below).

Adding warps per CTA does not necessarily pay off either. Expanding each CTA from 8 warps to 16 warps at T=32T = 32T=32 (from 2 to 4 warps per SMSP) saves only about 0.85 μs0.85\ \mu\text{s}0.85 μs, which sits right around the run-to-run variation of the same configuration (about 0.78 μs0.78\ \mu\text{s}0.78 μs) and shows no clear gain, while costing an extra 8 warps of registers per CTA.

5How Do Blank Padding Rows in the Tail Tiles of Light Experts Stop Burning Tensor Core Cycles?

Check the valid row count at tile entry and step the MMA row height down through 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8 for partially filled tail tiles.

Because token bucketing in Section 2 requires all tokens in a tile to belong to the same expert, we have to pad each expert's token count up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM (BMBMBM is the number of tokens per tile, which maps to nnn of wgmma after swap-AB). Under skewed routing, many light experts receive only a few tokens, and the last tile of a heavy expert (its tail tile, a partially filled M-tile) often holds only a few valid rows as well; the extra rows padded at the bottom are called padding rows. If we do nothing, every matrix multiplication issues at the full tile height.

Tail-tile M-dimension trimming checks the valid row count at tile entry and picks a narrower MMA instruction shape whenever a tail tile has fewer than 32 valid rows. Because swap-AB puts tokens on the nnn side of wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 4), and the instruction shape m64nNk16 fixes m=64m = 64m=64 while letting nnn take any multiple of 8 (see Chapter 5, Section 3), a tail tile can step down through three heights: 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8.

How much tail-tile trimming saves varies with MeM_eMe​. On verify workloads (MeM_eMe​ around a dozen), tail tiles make up a large share of all tiles: clipping tail tiles down to 16 rows at T=256T = 256T=256 cuts Stage 6 time by about 26 μs26\ \mu\text{s}26 μs in one step, and introducing the 8-row tier saves even more. As MeM_eMe​ grows larger, on the other hand, the tail tile is only a small fraction at the end of a long queue, so the gain from trimming shrinks (the prefill kernel applies the same trimming; see Section 15).

What you pay for tail-tile trimming is generating extra narrow-tile code branches in the kernel and running one valid-row check at tile entry; at what workload size it loses performance was not measured.

6At T = 1..32, How Are Multi-Launch Round Trips Folded into a Persistent Kernel?

Fold bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection into a persistent kernel with 132 resident CTAs; for T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, split back into two PDL-chained kernels to avoid the grid barrier.

In Stage 6, m2 launches token bucketing, the gate/up projection, the down projection, and post-expert RMSNorm one after another, paying a tail wave on every launch.

In the third generation (m3), Stage 6 moves to a persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1): 132 CTAs stay resident on the SMs. At entry, each CTA works out which tiles it owns; it then steps through them one after another without exiting between tiles. Inside the kernel, Phase 0 runs token bucketing, followed by the gate/up projection with SwiGLU and then the down projection, streaming weights through a TMA ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Sections 3 and 4). Matrix multiplication inside m3 uses warp-level mma.sync (see Chapter 5, Section 3) rather than wgmma. Because m3 keeps 132 CTAs resident, it has no wave capacity steps (the Section 4 example, where occupancy dropped from 9 to 8 and crossed a wave step, was measured on m2's non-persistent grid); why mma.sync was still chosen was not determined. One mma.sync tile holds at most 8 tokens; experts with more than 8 tokens are handled below.

Phase 0 token bucketing inside the kernel also makes one change: instead of one thread serially scanning 256 slots (for example, 32 tokens×8 slots32\text{ tokens} \times 8\text{ slots}32 tokens×8 slots at T=32T = 32T=32), 8 warps scan 32 slots each in parallel. __ballot_sync collects a yes/no predicate from each of a warp's 32 lanes into a 32-bit integer where bit iii holds lane iii's answer, and __popc counts the set bits in that integer to tell us how many lanes in this warp hit. Each warp writes its hit count n to shared memory; after an intra-CTA barrier, summing n across the preceding warps gives this warp's write offset base:

hit  = (topk_id[slot] == e);              // each lane tests whether its slot hits expert e
mask = __ballot_sync(FULL, hit);          // FULL = 0xffffffff (all 32 lanes participate)
n    = __popc(mask);                      // number of hits in this warp
pos  = base + __popc(mask & lanes_below); // lanes_below = (1u << lane) - 1 (mask of lower-numbered lanes)

Now consider hot experts where tokens pile up. Because a single mma.sync tile holds up to 8 tokens, an expert routed 9–16 tokens executes a 16-token segment that feeds two 8-token tiles from the same decoded weight registers, reading its weights just once; an expert routed 17–32 tokens is broken into two segments. Once T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, hot experts accumulate still more tokens, prompting the switch to a new kernel in Section 9.

Once the gate/up projection and the down projection are merged into a single persistent kernel, the down projection has to wait until the entire GPU finishes writing inter. Because CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the conditions required without cooperative launch), the T=1T = 1T=1 persistent kernel uses cooperative launch; synchronizing all 132 resident CTAs across the grid barrier once costs about 1.4 μs1.4\ \mu\text{s}1.4 μs in a microbenchmark, and T=1T = 1T=1 retains this single cooperatively launched persistent kernel.

For T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, however, splitting the gate/up projection and the down projection into two kernels chained back-to-back with PDL pays off. Because each kernel uses at least 115 KiB115\text{ KiB}115 KiB of shared memory (about 115 KiB115\text{ KiB}115 KiB at T=8T = 8T=8 and about 129 KiB129\text{ KiB}129 KiB at T=16,32T = 16, 32T=16,32), the two kernels do not fit together inside the 228 KiB228\text{ KiB}228 KiB per SM. Still, as soon as a gate/up CTA exits an SM, that SM immediately accepts a down-projection CTA, preloads its weight ring buffer into shared memory while the other SMs are finishing, and then pauses at the synchronization point. Splitting into two kernels costs one extra PDL edge of about 0.64 μs0.64\ \mu\text{s}0.64 μs (see Chapter 1, Section 4) and pays off only when tail-wave skew leaves time to preload before the wait, netting under 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs in Stage 6 (see the chart below).

Can we stay in a single kernel and avoid the grid barrier? We tested fine-grained tile counters (where each finished inter tile increments its own counter so the down projection waits only for the tiles it needs) and in-band payload readiness flags (encoding the readiness flag and the inter payload in the same word). Every fine-grained counter handoff requires a device-wide memory barrier—the device-scope acq_rel memory fence from Chapter 2, Section 6: the issuing warp stalls until all prior writes reach L2, while other warps and SMs keep running. That slowed down several benchmark cases, and in-band payload readiness flags also slowed T=1T = 1T=1 by about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs (the exact causes of the slowdown in both approaches were not measured separately).

The post-expert RMSNorm kernel reads back y, skips non-local slots, and completes Steps 4 and 5 of Section 1; it already overlaps with the main kernel via PDL, and fusing it into the tail of the main kernel ran slower in single-operator tests.

7At Persistent Kernel Startup, Why Does Activation p Wait in Line Behind Weights?

At kernel entry, all 132 SMs issuing 3 weight slots simultaneously flood the memory queue with ~14 MB of requests; issuing p and Slot 0 first while delaying Slots 1–2 by a few hundred nanoseconds prevents p from queueing behind weights.

At T=1T = 1T=1, activation p is only a few kilobytes, yet kernel-entry timestamps show that loading p takes about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs longer than loading p in isolation. Why? Because normal global loads (LDG) and TMA requests (see Chapter 3, Section 3) contend for the same queue along the memory path (whether the bottleneck sits in L2 or in the HBM controller was not measured). That is queueing delay (see Chapter 7, Section 6): a small request of a few kilobytes gets stuck in line behind roughly 14 MB14\text{ MB}14 MB of bulk weight requests.

To fix it, we flip the issue order: issue the load of p and Slot 0 weights first, spin-wait on the GPU nanosecond timer for a few hundred nanoseconds, and only then issue Slots 1 and 2. Using a fixed delay without checking whether data has arrived is called open-loop staggering. At T=1T = 1T=1 (a single cooperative kernel), the delay is 500 ns500\text{ ns}500 ns. After splitting T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32 into two PDL kernels, the gate/up kernel likewise issues p ahead of the weight slots: T=8T = 8T=8 waits 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns, while T=16T = 16T=16 and 323232 simply issue p first with the delay set to 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns.

Because this is an open-loop wait, we cannot stretch the delay too far—waiting too long just artificially delays the weights. Sweeping the delay at T=8T = 8T=8 (see the chart below) shows the tradeoff: 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns (only issuing p first) captures only about half the gain, the three settings across 300–800 ns300\text{–}800\text{ ns}300–800 ns perform similarly (with 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns chosen in the end), and by 1,200 ns1{,}200\text{ ns}1,200 ns the saving drops back again.

The catch with open-loop staggering is that the best delay shifts with TTT, so each TTT needs its own sweep; a closed-loop alternative ("wait until p arrives, then issue Slots 1 and 2") was not measured. On the T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 kernel (Section 9), delaying Weight Slots 1 and 2 moves the first MMA instruction earlier by only about 0.4 μs0.4\ \mu\text{s}0.4 μs, and the upper bound on remaining savings at kernel entry is less than 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs, so we stopped here.

8In the SASS of the Post-Expert RMSNorm Kernel, What Did the Compiler Schedule Poorly, and What Can Be Loaded Before Waiting?

An empty asm volatile statement blocks rematerialization, and issuing loads via asm volatile blocks instruction sinking; both are only effects observed with the current compiler, not guarantees of the specification.

The first compiler rewrite we run into is rematerialization: instead of keeping a value that has already been computed, the compiler throws it away and recomputes it every time it is needed. Take this 4-line example: outside the loop, the kernel unpacks 16 BF16 weights w[i] to FP32 (Chapter 6, Section 1), adds 1.0f, and stores them into nw[i], then reuses nw[i] repeatedly inside the loop:

float nw[16];
for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; ++step)
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) acc[i] += x[step][i] * nw[i];

To save those 16 registers, ptxas may throw nw[i] away and unpack the BF16 w[i] to FP32 and add 1.0f again on every loop iteration. The numerical result stays identical, but every iteration runs 16 extra unpacks and 16 extra additions.

To stop ptxas from doing that, we place an empty inline-assembly barrier (asm volatile) asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i])); right after the precomputation:

for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
    asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i]));
}

Because this empty assembly statement declares that it "reads and writes nw[i]," the compiler must treat nw[i] as the output of an opaque instruction that cannot be rematerialized from w[i]. At runtime it emits 0 instructions, at the cost of holding 16 FP32 registers (64 B per thread) live throughout the loop; when registers are already tight, occupancy may drop by one step (not measured).

The second compiler rewrite is instruction sinking (code sinking), where the compiler moves instructions to a later point in the schedule. In Chapter 1, Section 4, the call cudaGridDependencySynchronize() that waits for the predecessor kernel compiles to griddepcontrol.wait in PTX and ACQBULK in SASS. Before that wait, the kernel can issue loads for data that the predecessor kernel does not write (such as this kernel's own static weights), overlapping those loads with the wait:

uint4 w0 = w_ptr[idx];              // load issued early
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();    // PTX: griddepcontrol.wait / SASS: ACQBULK
use(w0);                            // consumed only after the wait

griddepcontrol.wait acts like an acquire barrier (Chapter 2, Section 6). The PTX specification promises only one thing: it waits until all prerequisite grids have completed and their memory operations are visible to the current grid. So accesses after the wait cannot move ahead of it. But nothing in the specification stops normal loads that sit before the wait from moving down past it. Once those loads sink past ACQBULK, the overlap between loading and waiting is gone. When we issue those loads with asm volatile, the SASS from our build shows that the loads stay ahead of the wait. Still, the PTX specification makes no such promise, so you need to inspect the SASS again after changing compiler versions.

There is a strict correctness boundary here: data written by the predecessor kernel (its output tensors and the routing results it computed) is guaranteed to be visible only after griddepcontrol.wait. Loading predecessor outputs early is valid only when both grids belong to the same memory synchronization domain (the CUDA grouping that determines which kernels share fence synchronization; all kernels share the default domain unless configured otherwise) and the predecessor kernel finishes writing and executes a GPU-scope release fence before triggering the successor (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for the complete rules and measured data-race violations). Instruction sinking itself affects only speed, not correctness.

Stage 6's post-expert RMSNorm kernel ran into both compiler rewrites at once. The first was instruction sinking. In the single-operator benchmark, the kernel entry originally issued 4 pre-wait 16 B16\text{ B}16 B loads (w_post and topk_weights, 2 each) with ld.global.nc, which routes loads through the SM's read-only cache path. ptxas sank them past ACQBULK. We made two changes: we issued normal global loads via asm volatile, and we replaced the post-wait local[] loads with pre-wait topk_ids loads (2 each; local[] is the per-slot local expert index written by the main kernel, with −1 for a slot that is not on this GPU). Now all 6 LDG.E.128 instructions stay ahead of ACQBULK, saving up to about 0.7 μs0.7\ \mu\text{s}0.7 μs in Stage 6 at T=16T = 16T=16 (see the chart below). This pays off only when the main kernel does not occupy all 132 SMs, leaving an overlap window for the post-expert RMSNorm kernel. At T=128T = 128T=128, the post-expert RMSNorm kernel enters only after the main kernel's CTAs exit. There is no overlap window, and topk_ids becomes a cold HBM read where local[] would have hit in L2, so execution gets slower. The final single-operator version therefore enables this only for T≤32T \le 32T≤32.

Keep one caveat in mind: issuing all 6 prefetches is safe only in the standalone operator benchmark, where none of the 3 inputs is produced by a preceding kernel. Inside Chapter 9's full-layer pipeline, the Stage 4 kernel writes both topk_weights and topk_ids; without a preceding release fence, reading them ahead of the wait triggers the data race explained under the correctness boundary above. Consequently, the standalone post-expert RMSNorm kernel in the final full-layer build issues no loads ahead of the wait, deferring w_post, topk_weights, and the per-slot local expert index (which the Stage 4 kernel also writes in the full layer) until after the wait returns (Chapter 9, Section 5 states the rule for what may be read before wait).

Second was rematerialization: the 16 values nwi=1+wpost,inw_i = 1 + w_{post,i}nwi​=1+wpost,i​ that the post-expert RMSNorm kernel precomputed outside the loop were pulled back into the inner loop and recomputed, adding 321 FADD instructions. Adding the empty inline-assembly barrier cut static SASS from 1,603 instructions down to 1,120; across T≤32T \le 32T≤32, the latency delta is at most about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs, falling within run-to-run variation and showing no certain gain (see the chart below).

9At T = 128..256, Why Switch to a Persistent wgmma Kernel?

A persistent wgmma kernel with 132 resident CTAs lets up to 64 tokens routed to a hot expert share a single tile so weights are read only once, while eliminating full-kernel handoff waits between bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection.

m3 suffices for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, but by T=128,256T = 128, 256T=128,256, hot experts receive several dozen tokens each. Continuing with 8 tokens per pass would re-read a hot expert's weights on every pass, while falling back to m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme would pay 4 tail waves and force the down projection to wait for the entire gate/up kernel to finish before reading inter.

The fourth generation (m4) switches to a single persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1), completing in-kernel bucketing, the gate/up projection with SwiGLU, and the down projection in one launch. All 132 CTAs take work in the order of one shared subtask table: during in-kernel bucketing, each CTA builds an identical copy of that table in its own shared memory. At first, work is assigned statically across the CTAs; in the next section, CTAs claim it by atomic increments of one global counter. One subtask covers at most 64 token rows × 256 output columns of one expert. An expert with at most 64 tokens fits into a single tile, so its weights are read from HBM only once. A hot expert with more than 64 tokens splits into several 64-row token tiles; its first tile tags the weight loads with the L2 residency hint (evict_last; see Chapter 2, Section 4), so later tiles hit in L2 as much as possible. After SwiGLU, the output inter goes to a global intermediate matrix, and the down-projection phase reads it directly (Section 11 explains how the down projection knows that the inter tiles it needs are written). Meanwhile, the instruction family switches back from mma.sync in m3 to wgmma: once token counts reach several dozen rows, only wgmma, issued collectively by 4 warps, can keep the Tensor Cores fed (see Chapter 5, Sections 3 and 5). At T=256T = 256T=256, replacing the 4-kernel tiled scheme with this persistent wgmma kernel for the first time cuts Stage 6 latency by about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs. Its costs are three: only 96 registers per thread, 2 extra producer warps per CTA, and building that subtask table redundantly in every CTA.

In the initial version, each CTA has 18 warps (576 threads). During the kernel entry phase, 4 consumer warpgroups (512 threads) gather the activations of tokens hitting this GPU and write them into a global buffer; once the main loop begins, they dedicate themselves to matrix multiplication, while the other 2 warps serve exclusively as producers. Warp 16 uses TMA to feed the 3-slot shared-memory weight ring buffer. Warp 17 uses TMA to feed activations from the global buffer into the shared-memory activation ring buffer: the gate/up projection reads the gathered p, and the down projection reads the inter written by the gate/up projection. Slots in both ring buffers synchronize via full and empty mbarrier signals (see Chapter 3, Sections 3–5).

Only 96 registers per thread: in the Chapter 3, Section 6 example (1 CTA per SM, 2 consumer warpgroups), each consumer thread got 232 registers; here we have 4 consumer warpgroups, and 4×128×232=118,784>65,5364 \times 128 \times 232 = 118{,}784 > 65{,}5364×128×232=118,784>65,536 does not fit. When the compiler computes the register cap from __launch_bounds__, it rounds the thread count up to a multiple of 128: 576 threads are billed as 640, giving 65,536/640=102.465{,}536 / 640 = 102.465,536/640=102.4, which rounds down to a multiple of 8 to land on 96. That differs from the per-warp allocation formula in Chapter 3, Section 1, which would give 112 registers for 576 threads.

Profiling the initial build of this kernel turned up two problems. First, a runtime branch inside the wgmma pipeline region caused ptxas to serialize wgmma (placing a wait after every HGMMA; see Chapter 6, Section 6 for the mechanism), which we fixed by hoisting that branch out of the region. Second, the entry activation gather originally used scalar writes before we switched it to 16 B16\text{ B}16 B coalesced wide stores (see Chapter 3, Section 2). Prior to those two fixes, the kernel lagged behind the 4-kernel tiled scheme.

Now look at the byte budget of the weight ring buffer. Each slot holds 256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements256\text{ columns} \times \text{inner dimension } 256\text{ elements}256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements: 32 KiB32\text{ KiB}32 KiB of codewords plus 3 KiB3\text{ KiB}3 KiB of block scales packed to 6 bits, for 35 KiB35\text{ KiB}35 KiB in total. By the rule in Chapter 3, Section 4, while 1 slot is being computed, the remaining N−1N - 1N−1 slots are in flight: a 3-slot ring keeps 2 slots (70 KiB70\text{ KiB}70 KiB) in flight, whereas shrinking to 2 slots leaves only 1 slot (35 KiB35\text{ KiB}35 KiB) in flight—below the roughly 48 KiB48\text{ KiB}48 KiB per SM needed to saturate HBM. Shrinking the ring to 2 slots alone therefore slows Stage 6 by about 1.2–1.3 μs1.2\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}1.2–1.3 μs at T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below).

10How Do All 132 Resident CTAs Finish Together?

All four optimizations target tail latency: longest-processing-time-first ordering, atomic producer work claiming, reverse-order down-projection assignment, and tail K-halves splitting.

The duration of a persistent kernel equals the duration of its last-exiting CTA. When full heavy subtasks and light 8-row tail tiles (which still read an entire weight tile, taking about 17 μs17\ \mu\text{s}17 μs) are mixed together, whichever CTA lands a heavy task near the end stalls the entire GPU. Each of the four changes below pays off only when there is a tail skew to trim:

First is LPT (Longest Processing Time first scheduling), which we already used in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 4: we sort subtasks in descending order of padded token count so heavy subtasks run first and short 8-row subtasks fill the remaining gaps across SMs at the end. The cost is that every CTA runs the sort at entry; by T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384, the speedup disappears (at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, nearly every tile is already a full tile, so there are no short tail tiles left to pack; see the fourth chart below).

Second is dynamic work claiming (atomic ticket). Take a T=128T = 128T=128 routing distribution from the full-layer benchmark: 16 token tiles, each with 32 gate/up subtasks and 16 down-projection subtasks, for 768 subtasks in total. With static assignment, 108 CTAs get 6 subtasks and 24 CTAs get 5. That one-subtask gap comes from integer division and cannot be eliminated. The real saving comes from uneven subtask durations: gate/up and down-projection subtasks take different amounts of time, and so do full tiles versus short 8-row tail tiles. Under static assignment, a CTA that happens to be assigned several slow subtasks in a row drags out the tail, while SMs assigned only 5 subtasks finish early and sit idle. Instead, while the current subtask is running, each CTA's weight-producer warp uses a single atomic add on a global counter to claim the next subtask from its own shared-memory LPT subtask table. Dynamic work claiming pays off only when single-subtask duration far exceeds claiming overhead and claiming introduces no extra intra-CTA barrier: here a single subtask runs for over ten microseconds, and the claimed subtask is handed to consumers through shared memory without adding a barrier. In Chapter 7, Section 4, by contrast, one attention key tile takes only about 2 μs2\ \mu\text{s}2 μs, and every claim would add an extra intra-CTA barrier and handoff, which loses performance.

Third is reverse load-rank assignment, used under static work assignment. In the earlier version, the gate/up projection and the down projection claimed subtasks in the same alternating sweep order, so the heaviest down-projection subtasks landed on the exact CTAs that had just finished the heaviest gate/up subtasks, stacking two heavy phases onto the same SMs. Recording each CTA's load rank during the gate/up phase lets the down projection assign work in reverse order: the CTAs with the lightest gate/up load claim the heaviest down-projection subtasks first. On the T=256T = 256T=256 sliding-window layer, this speeds up single-layer latency by about 4%4\%4% (see the third chart below; when reverse assignment would lose performance was not measured).

Fourth is tail K-halves splitting (see Chapter 2, Section 5 for the K-halves mechanism). Two conditions trigger it. First, the final wave of the subtask table has at most 66 subtasks left (no more than half of 132). Second, after sorting by row count in descending order, the fifth-from-last token tile has only 8 rows. Because each token tile produces 16 down-projection subtasks, the last 5 token tiles cover 80 subtasks, which guarantees that all 66 split subtasks at the end of the table are short 8-row tiles. When both conditions hold, we split each of the last 66 subtasks in the table in half along K, creating 2 × 66 half-K tasks that divide evenly across all 132 SMs. Chapter 2, Section 5 splits only the subtasks left over in the final wave; here we also split subtasks from the end of the second-to-last wave to fill out a full set of 66. The first half writes out an FP32 partial sum and sets a readiness flag (release), and the second half waits on that flag (acquire) and adds its half in (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for the ordering rules of cross-SM partial-sum merging). That wait always finishes, for three reasons: all 132 CTAs are resident at once (the single-operator version guarantees this with cooperative launch; see Section 6), every first half sits ahead of its second half in the table, and the CTAs claim subtasks in table order. So the earliest unfinished subtask in the table only ever waits on subtasks that have already finished, never on a later subtask. With the split, the other half of the SMs, which would otherwise sit idle, get work too. The cost is an extra partial-sum matrix and a set of flags. Routing distributions that do not trigger splitting still pay for the branch and flag check and slow down (see the second chart below), so we enable splitting only when both conditions above hold.

11Why Do Consumers Stall on Synchronization, and How Do We Move GPU-Scope Releases Off the Critical Path?

When every consumer thread pays its own GPU-scope release, Stage 6 is measured about 93 µs slower; the fix has only one thread per warp issue the release once, and then hands the GPU-scope release to a dedicated warp.

In the persistent wgmma kernel, every time the consumer warpgroups finish a gate/up subtask, they set a completion flag to tell the down-projection phase that this inter tile has been written. The first bottleneck comes from per-thread releases: when all 512 consumer threads fire red.release.gpu at the same L2 counter, the resulting atomic requests pile up at that single L2 address and drag Stage 6 down by about 93 μs93\ \mu\text{s}93 μs. Instead, we align each warp with __syncwarp (see Chapter 4, Section 4) and have lane 0 alone issue one red.release.gpu, cutting the atomic requests from 512 down to 16. Below, we show how a dedicated release thread takes the GPU-scope release off the consumer path completely.

The remaining problem is that every GPU-scope release runs a device-wide memory barrier between subtasks (fence.acq_rel.gpu compiles to a sequence of several SASS instructions including MEMBAR.ALL.GPU). L1 caches across SMs are not automatically coherent. On the writer side, each device-wide memory barrier has to wait for all prior global writes to drain to L2, measuring 0.6–1.3 μs0.6\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}0.6–1.3 μs per barrier under full load. On the reader side, once a thread reads the flag with acquire.gpu, subsequent normal loads from that same thread see all prior writes published by the release (Chapter 2, Section 6). To publish completion flags and activation readiness, m4 makes three changes:

Step 1: publishing activation-gather readiness at kernel entry switches to a cross-proxy fence. Normal thread loads and stores travel through the generic proxy, whereas asynchronous TMA and wgmma reads travel through the async proxy; bridging the two takes fence.proxy.async (see Chapter 3, Section 3). On the reader side, the thread issuing TMA executes fence.proxy.async.global after ld.acquire.gpu and before issuing TMA (both when the gate/up projection reads gathered activations and when the down projection reads inter). On the writer side, 16 consumer warps write gathered activations into the global buffer at kernel entry, where previously every thread executed fence.acq_rel.gpu (5 SASS instructions). Now each thread executes only a single-instruction fence.proxy.async.global, and after a CTA barrier, thread 0 issues a single red.release.gpu; by cumulativity (Chapter 2, Section 6), this suffices (see the chart below for the speedup). For safety, we placed this cross-proxy fence on both the writer and reader sides; what happens if the writer-side fence is removed was not measured.

Step 2: consumers perform only an on-chip CTA-scope release and delegate the GPU-scope release to a dedicated release thread. Each time a consumer thread finishes a subtask, it issues red.release.cta on its warpgroup's shared-memory counter. A dedicated thread waits with ld.acquire.cta until all 4 warpgroup counters reach the target, and then issues a single red.release.gpu on behalf of the CTA for each subtask that needs a flag, in subtask order. Every gate/up subtask needs this flag; among down-projection subtasks, only the first half of a K-halves split from Section 10 needs a readiness flag (which this dedicated thread also publishes), while the remaining down-projection subtasks publish none. When the dedicated thread observes the counters via acquire, it also observes all writes performed by the consumers before their release. When it then issues a GPU-scope release, it publishes all writes it has observed—cumulativity holds across scopes as well (see Chapter 2, Section 6). After warp 17 in the down projection observes the flag via ld.acquire.gpu, it likewise executes fence.proxy.async.global before issuing TMA (see Step 1). Because all gate/up subtasks precede all down-projection subtasks in the subtask table, by the ordering invariant of Section 10 this wait cannot deadlock either.

Step 3: give the dedicated release thread its own dedicated release warp. Initially, the release thread lived on lane 1 of weight-producer warp 16. Although lane 0 and lane 1 of warp 16 each have their own program counter, the warp issues instructions for only one of their paths at a time (see Chapter 4, Section 4). While lane 1 polls and issues releases, lane 0's path waits for the warp to switch back, so lane 0 cannot issue the next round of weight TMA loads on time (how long each switch takes was not measured separately). We therefore add 1 extra warp per CTA (warp 18, expanding the CTA from 576 to 608 threads) and move the release thread there. At T=256T = 256T=256, deleting MEMBAR in place without moving the thread to a separate warp saves much less time (see the chart below), showing that most of the gain comes from no longer blocking lane 0. The cost is 32 extra threads per CTA (608 threads are still billed as 640 threads at the same 96-register per-thread cap from Section 9). Conversely, having this dedicated thread also emit per-phase signals to wake the post-expert RMSNorm kernel early does not pay off: the upper bound of tail latency that could be hidden is only 1.06–2.21 μs1.06\text{–}2.21\ \mu\text{s}1.06–2.21 μs, while emitting the signal itself costs 2.2–3.2 μs2.2\text{–}3.2\ \mu\text{s}2.2–3.2 μs, so every signaling variant tested ran slower.

There is also a correctness fix. Consumers must not arrive on the weight ring's empty barrier before the shared-memory loads from the slot have returned to registers; otherwise the producer's next TMA transfer can overwrite a slot that is still being read (see Chapter 3, Section 5 for the arrival rule). In the code, mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta uses the default .release.cta semantics. By the PTX specification, that orders prior shared-memory reads before the arrival only within the generic proxy; it does not cover the next round's TMA write, which goes through the async proxy (Chapter 3, Section 5). On top of that, the compiled arrival instruction did not wait for the scoreboard of preceding shared-memory reads (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for scoreboards). In the single-operator version, moving the arrival after the wait on the activation ring's full barrier (Section 9) reduced data races from 551 occurrences across ~4.58 million calls to 0, at the cost of slowing Stage 6 by 0.4–1.6 μs0.4\text{–}1.6\ \mu\text{s}0.4–1.6 μs (this is a correctness requirement, not an optional optimization).

Waiting on the activation ring's full barrier, however, has no data dependency on the weight reads. In the compiled T=256T = 256T=256 full-layer version of Chapter 9, even when the source code placed the decoding instructions that consume the weight registers before the arrival instruction, the compiler still sank them past it. Reordering the source alone was not enough, so we added an explicit fence.acq_rel.cta before the arrival. In SASS, that fence lowers to an instruction that waits until pending shared-memory loads land in registers; together, deferring the arrival site and inserting the fence bring unreturned loads across all arrival points down from 24 to 0. Why the default release did not emit that wait instruction was not determined; this is only what the current compiler does (Section 8). The race count of the fence version was not measured separately.

12Before Each CUDA Graph Replay, Who Zeros the Completion Counters?

Maintain even and odd counter arrays alternated by launch index; once a launch gets its ledger index, idle producer threads zero the opposite array for the next launch.

The completion flags in Section 11 are an array of global counters; on every CUDA Graph replay (see Chapter 1, Section 2), the next launch has to see all zeros. Previously, before each launch finished, every CTA ran an exit sequence (one device-wide memory barrier, two CTA barriers, one atomic increment, and several zeroing stores) so the last-exiting CTA could zero the counters. That exit sequence sat right on the critical path of the last-exiting CTA.

To get that cleanup off the tail, we switch to an even-odd ledger (ping-pong counter array): the counter buffer in device memory is doubled and split into an even ledger and an odd ledger (see Figure 8-11 for indices and buffer sizes). At kernel entry, thread 0 of each CTA runs atom.inc on a global counter to claim a ticket ttt (see Chapter 2, Section 7 for atomic ticket numbers). Because that instruction carries the upper limit 2G−12G - 12G−1 (where GGG is the number of CTAs per launch), hardware wraps the counter back to 0 once it hits the limit, keeping every ticket ttt between 000 and 2G−12G - 12G−1. Taking ⌊t/G⌋\lfloor t / G \rfloor⌊t/G⌋ gives 0 or 1 to pick which ledger this launch uses: each launch claims GGG tickets that all land on the same ledger, and the next launch switches to the opposite ledger. Lanes 1–31 of the weight-producer warp are otherwise idle; once Phase 0 bucketing ends and the CTA barrier hands them this launch's ledger index, they zero the inactive ledger for the next launch. The K-halves readiness flags and dynamic work-claiming counter from Section 10 are zeroed together inside the same even-odd ledger.

Why do tickets from two consecutive launches not interleave, and why does zeroing the opposite ledger never collide with the previous or next launch? Two preconditions guarantee this. First, every launch uses the same GGG, and all launches execute in order on the same CUDA stream. Second, every expert kernel launch is followed by the post-expert RMSNorm kernel; when that kernel's griddepcontrol.wait returns (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Section 8 of this chapter), the expert kernel before it has finished. The single-operator final expert kernel launches without PDL, so it enters only after the preceding post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes. By the time it enters, claims tickets, and zeroes the idle ledger, the prior expert kernel launch has exited completely and will not claim another ticket or touch that ledger. Likewise, the next expert kernel launch enters only after the current launch's post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes, by which time the current launch (zeroing stores included) has already finished.

Deleting the exit sequence from the tail of the kernel removes one device-wide memory barrier and two CTA barriers on the tail path, saving about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). The cost of the even-odd ledger is 4 KiB4\text{ KiB}4 KiB of extra device memory while shifting the zeroing stores onto the idle threads of the producer warp; whether any workload loses performance was not measured.

13What Bottlenecks the Gap Between Subtasks, and Why Does Folding the Scale into the Exponent Save Instructions?

The gap between subtasks is spent in the gate/up epilogue's SwiGLU, which is issue-slot bound; folding the tensor scale into the exponent argument and denominator cuts instructions from 9 to 7 per element, and the final version switches to a tanh⁡\tanhtanh form to cut them to 6.

Every subtask switch in the gate/up and down projections (including the tile epilogue; see Chapter 1, Section 3) takes about 1.31.31.3 and 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.8 μs, adding up to about 12.7 μs12.7\ \mu\text{s}12.7 μs across all switches of a CTA (6.1%6.1\%6.1% of total kernel runtime). In m4's main loop, we alternate 2 register buffers for decoded weights (operand A) to get the inputs for the next wgmma group ready ahead of time. At first we suspected that this subtask gap was waiting on data, so we tried adding a third operand-A register buffer (wait_group<2>; see Chapter 5, Section 5) to keep one more wgmma group in flight and hide the gap. That gave zero gain, showing data supply was not the bottleneck. Counting the cycles of a single subtask epilogue tells us why: the 4 consumer warps on one SMSP take 932 issue cycles in total, more than the 768 cycles of the SFU (MUFU instructions). That means the epilogue is bottlenecked by the issue slot, which can issue at most one instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1), rather than by SFU throughput (see Chapter 5, Section 1).

Here we also answer the question left open in Section 1: why do the gate half and the up-projection half of each expert share a single tensor scale sss? In the original model, the two halves have separate tensor scales sgs_gsg​ and sus_usu​; let r=su/sgr = s_u / s_gr=su​/sg​. Because SwiGLU is linear in the up projection uuu, changing uuu's scale from sus_usu​ to the gate scale sgs_gsg​ only multiplies the down-projection output yyy by a positive constant 1/r=sg/su1/r = s_g / s_u1/r=sg​/su​. And in Step 4 of Section 1, each expert runs its own RMSNorm right after the down projection and before the weighted accumulation across experts. Because RMSNorm divides a vector by its own root mean square, any positive constant c>0c > 0c>0 cancels out between numerator and denominator: ignoring the tiny constant ϵ\epsilonϵ, rmsnorm(c z)=rmsnorm(z)\mathrm{rmsnorm}(c\,z) = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(z)rmsnorm(cz)=rmsnorm(z). Each expert's gate/up projection therefore stores only a single tensor scale s=sgs = s_gs=sg​.

Because instruction count is the bottleneck, we use that shared scale sss to fold instructions algebraically. Let dg,dud_g, d_udg​,du​ be the unscaled accumulator values in registers before multiplying by sss (g=s dgg = s\,d_gg=sdg​, u=s duu = s\,d_uu=sdu​), and substitute them into SwiGLU:

silu(g) u=s dg1+e−s dg s du=dg duk+k⋅2 dg⋅(−slog⁡2e),k=1/s2.\mathrm{silu}(g)\,u = \frac{s\,d_g}{1 + e^{-s\,d_g}}\, s\,d_u = \frac{d_g\, d_u}{k + k \cdot 2^{\,d_g \cdot (-s \log_2 e)}},\qquad k = 1/s^2 .silu(g)u=1+e−sdg​sdg​​sdu​=k+k⋅2dg​⋅(−slog2​e)dg​du​​,k=1/s2.

Here both −slog⁡2e-s \log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk are constants per expert: multiplying once when computing the exponent argument and evaluating the denominator with a single FFMA(e, k, k) absorbs both multiplications by sss. That cuts the epilogue from 9 instructions per element down to 7; the build introducing this fold saves about 0.6 μs0.6\ \mu\text{s}0.6 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). The final version goes one step further and rewrites SwiGLU as silu(g)=g2(1+tanh⁡(g/2))\mathrm{silu}(g) = \frac{g}{2}(1 + \tanh(g/2))silu(g)=2g​(1+tanh(g/2)). With K=s2/2K = s^2/2K=s2/2 and A=KdgA = K d_gA=Kdg​, each element computes A(1+tanh⁡(dg⋅s/2))⋅duA(1 + \tanh(d_g \cdot s/2)) \cdot d_uA(1+tanh(dg​⋅s/2))⋅du​. A single tanh.approx (MUFU.TANH) replaces ex2 plus the reciprocal, dropping the epilogue to 6 instructions, with only 1 of them on the SFU. This chapter does not list the standalone gain of this step.

What epilogue scale folding costs is computing two scale constants before each subtask's epilogue (−slog⁡2e-s\log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk, or s/2s/2s/2 and K=s2/2K = s^2/2K=s2/2 in the tanh⁡\tanhtanh form), and relying on the gate and up projections sharing a single scale. This folding pays off only when the epilogue is issue-slot bound: porting it to Chapter 9's full-layer expert kernels (m3 and m4) trims 22%–41%22\%\text{–}41\%22%–41% of the epilogue instructions, yet inside the full layer those kernels are not issue-slot bound, leaving single-layer latency unchanged (0.999×0.999\times0.999×).

14When All 32 Experts Are Busy in Prefill, How Large Should the Grid Be and Who Dispatches Tiles to SMs?

m5 caps the main grid at twice the per-GPU average hit-pair count (~TTT) plus alignment padding, leaving any excess tiles to the tail loops inside the main kernels, while launching 9,216 ordinary CTAs for the down projection under the hardware block distributor.

Across the workloads in the earlier sections, the mean token count per expert remains under 58; in prefill, T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384 step past 58 (while T=753T = 753T=753 stays below the threshold). The fifth generation (m5) is the grouped GEMM built for prefill, and every optimization below is measured in paired ABBA runs against the immediately preceding version of m5 itself (m4 and m5 were not benchmarked against each other on the same shape). Three names appear throughout this section. The route-alignment kernel reorders hit pairs by expert, pads each expert up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM, and outputs the reordered token table and per-tile expert IDs. gemm1 is the gate and up projection (Step 1 of Section 1, computing SwiGLU in its epilogue). gemm2 is the down projection (Step 3 of Section 1).

Step 1 keeps only tiles belonging to this GPU: the route-alignment kernel outputs tiles only for the 32 local experts on this GPU, filtering out non-local slots at the source. The cost is pre-allocating a fixed-size worst-case buffer in device memory that CUDA Graph reuses on every replay (Chapter 1, Section 2). How much extra memory that buffer takes and when it would lose performance were not measured separately.

Step 2 sets the grid size. Each CUDA Graph replay uses the grid size fixed at capture (or at the last graph update; see Chapter 1, Section 2), while the actual number of local hits is only computed on the GPU during that replay. Originally, the grid was sized for the worst case: all 8 slots of every token landing on this GPU, plus one padding tile for each of the 32 local experts (1,056 tiles in total at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384). Counted under the busiest-GPU benchmark workload at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, 77% of the CTAs find no work upon entry and exit immediately, implying that only about 1,056×0.23≈2431{,}056 \times 0.23 \approx 2431,056×0.23≈243 tiles have actual work (see Figure 8-13). Across 8 GPUs, each GPU receives an average of 8T/8=T8T / 8 = T8T/8=T hit pairs regardless of routing skew. m5 takes twice the average as routing-skew headroom, adds at most 127 padding rows per expert (truncation is enabled only for T>3,012T > 3{,}012T>3,012, where m5 uses 128-row tiles; see Section 15), and truncates the grid at ⌈(2T+32×127)/128⌉\lceil (2T + 32 \times 127) / 128 \rceil⌈(2T+32×127)/128⌉ tiles. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, that caps the grid at 288 tiles, about 20% above the estimated ~243 active tiles (Figure 8-13). This factor of 2 is a design choice and was not calibrated against measured worst-case skew.

Should the active tile count ever exceed that cap, the tail loops inside gemm1 and gemm2 pick up the remaining tiles; under the benchmark routing distributions, overflow never occurs, and the runtime when overflow actually happens was not measured.

Step 3 decides who dispatches down-projection tiles. Earlier, gemm2 was written as a 264-CTA (2×1322 \times 1322×132) persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1) that claimed tiles at a fixed stride. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, tile completion times vary widely, and fixed-stride claiming cannot shift work from slow SMs to fast SMs: the profiler recorded 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s}60.3 μs of intra-kernel SM idle time. Reverting to a non-persistent grid launches 288×32=9,216288 \times 32 = 9{,}216288×32=9,216 standard CTAs (288 row tiles × 32 column tiles) so the hardware block distributor (see Chapter 2, Section 1) dispatches the next tile to whichever SM frees up first, cutting intra-kernel SM idle time from 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s}60.3 μs down to 18.6 μs18.6\ \mu\text{s}18.6 μs. That wins at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, where tiles are numerous and completion times vary. It is the exact flip side of the rule in Section 10: when tasks are long and numerous, the hardware block distributor acts as zero-barrier dynamic work claiming.

15Why Does the Main Loop Split into Two Paths Between T = 753 and T ≥ 3,012?

At T=753T = 753T=753, m5 selects 64-row tiles, and per-SM occupancy rises from 2 to 3 CTAs; at T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012, it takes the 128-row tile path and sets aside 4 gather warps to gather activations.

What the two paths share is only the outer setup (dispatched in code between T≤1,024T \le 1{,}024T≤1,024 and T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024): 4-bit weights are decoded to BF16 in registers and fed directly as operand A of wgmma (RS mode; Section 3), while tokens sit on the operand-B side in shared memory. On full tiles, the two GEMM kernels for T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024 pair 4 rotating operand-A register buffers (whereas m4 in Section 13 uses 2) with wait_group<2> so that 2 wgmma commit groups stay in flight concurrently (see Chapter 5, Section 5); the single-grid fused kernel for T≤1,024T \le 1{,}024T≤1,024 and the partial tiles for T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024 use only 2 operand-A buffers and wait_group<1>.

At T=753T = 753T=753, the tile height is set to 64 (see Section 5 for how tile height relates to MeM_eMe​), and each CTA has 128 threads (1 consumer warpgroup). Instead of threads issuing cp.async to load weights, the consumer warpgroup issues TMA loads directly. Dropping the copy-address registers lowers registers per thread from 180 to 155, allocated as 160 (registers are allocated in multiples of 8; 3×128×160=61,440≤65,5363 \times 128 \times 160 = 61{,}440 \le 65{,}5363×128×160=61,440≤65,536), raising per-SM occupancy from 2 to 3 CTAs (see Chapter 3, Section 1). A single weight decode is shared across up to 64 hit pairs (any unfilled rows are padding rows from Section 5; see Figure 8-14), speeding up single-layer latency by about 4%4\%4%. The tradeoff is that consumers issue extra memory-transfer instructions: applying this scheme to 128-row tiles at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 makes execution slower, and conversely, using 128-row tiles with two consumer warpgroups at T=753T = 753T=753—where an expert averages only a few dozen tokens and leaves most of a 128-row tile empty—also runs slower.

Next, for T≤1,024T \le 1{,}024T≤1,024, we apply single-grid fusion: folding gemm1, SwiGLU, and gemm2 into the same 64-row-tiled grid eliminates the tail drain and launch boundary between the two kernels. Registers per thread are capped at 128, fitting 4 resident CTAs per SM (4×128×128=65,5364 \times 128 \times 128 = 65{,}5364×128×128=65,536). Work assignment uses ticket numbers: each CTA claims a ticket upon entry (see Chapter 2, Section 7), where lower-numbered tickets execute gemm1 tiles first and higher-numbered tickets execute gemm2 tiles. A gemm2 tile acquires the completion counters of the specific gemm1 tiles it needs and starts as soon as they arrive, without waiting for the entire gemm1 phase to finish (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for acquire). Because each CTA claims its ticket via atomic add only after being scheduled onto an SM (see Chapter 2, Sections 6–7), the lower-numbered gemm1 tiles are guaranteed to be running already, so higher-numbered gemm2 tiles waiting on those completion counters cannot deadlock.

At T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012, we step the tile height up to 128. Those 128 token rows are scattered across the original sequence: the reordered token table stores each hit pair's pairpairpair index (hit-pair index) pair=tok×8+slotpair = tok \times 8 + slotpair=tok×8+slot, which maps back to token index ⌊pair/8⌋\lfloor pair / 8 \rfloor⌊pair/8⌋. Because Hopper's TMA cannot gather rows through an index table (see Chapter 3, Section 3; a row-gather mode is introduced only in the next architecture generation, see Appendix A, Section 4), gemm1 carves out 4 gather warps (128 threads in total) to gather activations row by row with cp.async, while TMA streams contiguous weights into the 3-slot ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Section 4 for producer/consumer specialization). On this path, producers issue loads 2 steps ahead across all three 3-slot rings (activations, weight codewords, and block scales), paired with 4 rotating operand-A register buffers, speeding up single-layer latency by about 5%5\%5% at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384. What the gather warps cost us is 128 threads and their registers. Skipping the dedicated gather warps and gathering activations in-kernel across wider token tiles disrupts the register budget and ring pipeline, buying zero gain at T=753T = 753T=753 and slowing execution at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012.

A few other 1%–2% refinements—merging the per-K-step CTA barriers, making gemm1 a persistent kernel, and applying producer/consumer specialization to full gemm2 tiles—are left out here.

Both the 64-row and 128-row paths also apply the tail-tile trimming from Section 5. We measure waste as the average number of rows issued per valid hit pair, where 1.0 means zero wasted rows. The larger MeM_eMe​ gets, the smaller the gain: a single layer runs about 4%4\%4% faster at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012, but only about 1%1\%1% faster at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 (see the chart below). In the implementation, a single scalar load plus a uniform branch (a conditional jump where all 32 lanes of the warp take the same path) checks whether every row from row rrr onward is padding; that keeps the ring-slot counters in uniform registers (UR; see Chapter 7, Section 7). Switching to an intra-CTA reduction forces those counters back into per-thread general-purpose registers and adds 34 instructions per K-step.

16Why Is the Prefill gemm1 Epilogue Slowed Down by Type Conversion?

Scalar FP32-to-BF16 conversion (F2F) shares the SFU pipeline with MUFU.EX2; replacing it with paired packed rounding (F2FP) moves the conversion off the SFU and nearly halves kernel-wide SFU utilization.

For T>1,024T > 1{,}024T>1,024, SwiGLU in gemm1's epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3) computes exponentials (MUFU.EX2). Before SwiGLU, the gate and up accumulator values are rounded to BF16 and converted back to FP32. That intermediate rounding carries over the numerical convention of the preceding kernel version, whereas the reference implementation stays in FP32 throughout without rounding. Originally, each value took one scalar conversion (F2F). On Hopper, F2F and MUFU.EX2 queue on the same SFU pipeline (the SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for pipeline definitions), stretching out the epilogue window.

To fix this, we call cvt.rn.bf16x2.f32 to round two FP32 values at once into a packed BF16 pair; it compiles to F2FP (paired packed conversion), which does not use the SFU. Replacing most of the scalar conversions in the epilogue with paired packed conversions cuts the profiler's kernel-wide average SFU utilization from 5.74%5.74\%5.74% down to 3.08%3.08\%3.08%, and the build introducing this change speeds up single-layer latency by about 0.3%0.3\%0.3% (see the chart below). Kernel-wide average SFU utilization is only a few percent because the main matrix-multiplication loop does not use the SFU, so the SFU is busy only during the epilogue. The cost of paired packed conversion is running shift and bitwise-AND instructions to unpack the two BF16 halfwords in the same register back into two FP32 values before feeding them into SwiGLU (adding a few ALU instructions). When the SFU is not the bottleneck in the epilogue, this change buys no speedup (it was not measured on the decode and verify kernels).

Stage 6 Routed-Expert Evolution Chain (m0 → m5)

Section 1 laid out how we dispatch across the three kernel families by TTT; here is the complete evolution chain from start to finish (see the charts below for step-by-step latency):

  • m0: Per-expert loop that decompresses weights to FP32 in HBM and reads them back (Section 2; m0 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m1: Single grouped-GEMM launch per projection that decodes 4-bit weights in registers and reads them only once (m1a, ~80× faster), followed by gate/up row interleaving, branchless decoding, and PDL (Section 2; m1 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m2: Pipelined wgmma tiling, Split-K, multi-slot weight ring buffer, pinned occupancy, and tail-tile M-dimension trimming, running ~2.0× faster than the baseline SGLang implementation (Sections 3–5; m2 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m3 (for T≤32T \le 32T≤32): Combines the persistent kernel, 16-token segments, two PDL-chained kernels, and entry staggering (see Sections 6–7; the two compiler fixes in Section 8 were measured only on the standalone Stage 6 operator).
  • m4 (for T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256): Combines the persistent wgmma kernel (saving about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256), tail balancing, the even-odd ledger, and epilogue scale folding, making the 60-layer total of the m3 + m4 version ~2.5× faster than the baseline (see Sections 9–13; this factor excludes the dedicated release thread and exclusive release warp).
  • m5 (for prefill T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384): Grouped GEMM for prefill; at the grid-truncation step, the two GEMMs total 4,207 μs4{,}207\ \mu\text{s}4,207 μs (about 2.4%2.4\%2.4% faster than before truncation; see Sections 14–16 for the other changes).

Measured against their respective physical lower bounds, decode and verify in the m3 + m4 build run at about 1.75× the weight-read lower bound, whereas prefill at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 in the grid-truncation build runs at about 1.4× the compute lower bound. Both ratios come from those respective intermediate builds; the final version was not re-measured. In Chapter 10, we will see how to track down, level by level, where most of the remaining gap goes.

Takeaway: An expert kernel has to adapt to the number of tokens MeM_eMe​ routed to each expert: below about 58, strip away HBM round trips, synchronization waits, and launch overhead; above it, keep the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines fed.

Next chapter's question: Now that we have both attention and the routed experts in hand, how do we wire the remaining dense projections (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7) together with the normalizations and gated residuals into a single-layer pipeline—and how do we squeeze the critical path down to its minimum? → Chapter 9

Chapter 9

When Scheduling a Single Layer's Kernels Across 132 SMs, Where Does the Time Above the Lower Bound Go, and How Much Can Scheduling and Kernel Handoffs Recover?
