The previous chapter left us with one question: how do we connect dense projections, normalizations, and gated residuals with attention and experts into a single-layer pipeline? Back in Primer 2, we drew all eight stages on a single GPU as a directed acyclic graph (DAG; see Primer 2, Section 3 and Figure P2-3) and worked out the layer's lower bound (counting dense weights in BF16; see Primer 2, Sections 4 and 5). Here we call the task-specified single-layer lower bound for each scenario the reference bound: 40.0 µs for the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer, 44.2 µs for the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, and 62.3 µs and 66.4 µs for the T=8T = 8T=8 sliding-window and full-attention layers. Note that this reference bound is not a lower bound on the bytes that any variant actually reads. The first eight chapters already made each stage's kernel fast on its own; yet when we string those kernels together along the DAG and replay them as a CUDA Graph, the baseline l0 still takes 71.4 µs on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer. In this chapter we chase a single question: where does the time above the reference bound go, and how much of it can scheduling and handoffs win back?

1Baseline l0: How Does a Single Layer's DAG Map to a Sequence of Kernels and Two CUDA Streams, and Where Does the Time Go?

l0 runs the forked branches in parallel across two CUDA streams; after subtracting ~5.4 µs of CUDA Graph replay overhead, the ~26 µs excess above the 40.0 µs reference bound is lost entirely inside the layer—within the kernels themselves and the handoffs between them.

First, let's be clear about scope: when we say a single layer in this chapter, we mean the eight stages running on a single GPU. A real 8-GPU run also performs three cross-GPU collectives inside every layer: an all-reduce after Stage 3 o, an all-reduce after Stage 6, and—when T≤8T \le 8T≤8—an all-gather of columns across GPUs after Stage 7 (see Primer 2, Section 2). None of the single-layer measurements in this chapter include those cross-GPU collectives.

To see where a single layer spends its time, we first need the critical path: the longest chain of "must wait for the previous step to finish" dependency edges from layer entry to layer exit. Single-layer latency is just the length of that critical path plus one CUDA Graph replay overhead (~5.4 µs, as we will see shortly). As long as side-stream kernels use only the SMs and bandwidth left idle by the main chain and finish before the join point, they add nothing to single-layer latency. Keep in mind, though, that all 132 SMs and HBM bandwidth are shared across the entire GPU—the moment a side-stream kernel competes with the main chain for SMs or bandwidth, it stretches the critical path instead (see Section 7).

We measure l0 through l3 backward: we start from l3 and turn off the changes from Sections 4, 3, and 2 one section at a time. That way, each step's delta shows what that section adds while earlier sections are on and later ones are off. Section 5 then adds one visibility fix on top of l3 to give this chapter's final version (we measured that fix only on a patched copy; the submitted file is still l3).

On the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer, the baseline l0 already fuses adjacent small steps and turns on PDL across part of the chain (we complete the remaining edges in Section 4). Running the layer launches 12 kernels in total: 10 on the main CUDA stream and 2 on a second stream, in the order shown in Figure 9-1. Stage 3 and Stage 8 each end with a boundary kernel that updates the FP32 residual stream stream and runs the next stage's RMSNorm across all 8,192 columns (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). Stage 5 normalization also sits in its own standalone kernel in l0 (we split it away in Section 3). Also, attention merge remains a separate kernel in this chain rather than using the fused version from Chapter 7, Section 12.

Stage 3's output h forks into two branches here. We call the second CUDA stream the side stream, and use it to launch kernels that do not depend on the current step of the main CUDA stream. The two streams synchronize through CUDA event (inter-stream event) markers—an event recorded on one stream that the other stream waits for. After the Stage 3 boundary kernel finishes, the main stream records an event. Once the side stream sees that event, it runs router to score all 256 experts, then runs the Top-8 kernel: it picks the top 8 experts by their biased scores, normalizes their weights using those 8 experts' unbiased scores, writes out topk_ids and topk_weights, and records a second event. Back on the main stream, the experts kernel waits for that side-stream event before reading the routing results.

Why does this pay off at T=1T = 1T=1? At T=1T = 1T=1, pooler on the main stream launches only 64 CTAs, 1 resident CTA per SM, so 68 of the 132 SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1) sit idle. While pooler streams its weights (~50 MB in 12-bit format), router and Top-8 on the side stream can use those 68 idle SMs. We did not measure which SMs they actually land on.

Of course, the side stream has a price: each layer records two extra events, and kernels from both streams must be able to co-reside on the chip (see Chapter 3, Section 1); once the main kernel fills all 132 SMs, side-stream kernels can only steal SMs from it (see Section 7). Section 4 presents the measured timeline in which the side branch completes ahead of pooler; how much time we would lose by disabling the side stream was not measured.

Every step in this chapter's evolution chain is measured the same way (see Primer 3, Section 5): we record the single layer into a CUDA Graph, flush L2 before each replay, time a full-graph replay with CUDA events, and take the median. The sliding-window layer attends over 2,048 historical tokens and the full-attention layer over 80,000 historical tokens, matching the reference bounds in Primer 2, Section 5. Note that every measured number includes ~5.4 µs of CUDA Graph replay overhead—even a graph with just 1 empty kernel takes that long to replay. Production serving records all 62 layers into a single graph so the whole model amortizes that cost, whereas the reference bound leaves it out. By the way, the 4.96 µs figure cited in Chapter 6 came from a separate batch of empty-graph replay measurements of the same class of overhead; the two numbers come from different experiments, and the cause of the difference was not determined.

The noise band for the single-layer evolution chain is ~0.5 µs, and the paired ABBA noise band for multi-token and prefill runs is ~0.5%; whenever a delta is smaller than the noise band, we report it as "within the noise band" (defined in Chapter 4, Section 6 and Chapter 7, Section 1).

Trace the evolution chain and that extra ~26 µs leaks out in four places: first, projections that read too many bytes or launch grids too small to fill a wave (Section 2); second, a standalone kernel that exists only to sum across a full row, plus a device-wide memory barrier that waits for all of a thread's prior writes to reach L2 (see Chapter 8, Section 11 and Section 3 of this chapter); third, the handoffs between kernels (Sections 4–5); and fourth, each kernel's main body together with its slowest-CTA tail duration (Section 6). Let's start with the leaks inside the projections themselves.

2l0 → l1: Once Projection Kernels Are Placed Inside a Single Layer, How Can They Read the Fewest Bytes and Fill All 132 SMs?

Because projections are bandwidth-bound, latency equals bytes read divided by achieved bandwidth; l1 reduces bytes read and sizes small-batch grids to fill a full wave.

Let's start with the 12-bit weight layout and decoding at T=1T = 1T=1. To read fewer bytes, we use 12-bit weights, which take 3/43/43/4 the bytes of 16-bit weights (see Chapter 6, Section 1); to saturate bandwidth, we put enough SMs to work and keep enough bytes in flight on each SM (see Chapter 2, Section 3). At T=1T = 1T=1 in l0, qkv_gate and pooler already use 12-bit weights, whereas the unpooler slice stays at 16-bit. Although that saves 26.0 MB of reads compared with an all-16-bit layer, we keep 40.0 µs as the common reference bound across the chapter so all four versions sit on the same scale. In l0, those two 12-bit weight matrices still use the old weight layout and decoder, and l1 does three things to them: first, it switches to the 9-instruction decoder from Chapter 6, Section 2; second, it reorders the pooler weight layout so that at every KKK-step the whole GPU reads a contiguous address range, while tagging the weight loads with the evict_first L2 residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4); and third, it prepares the escaped-weight corrections ahead of the final KKK-step. The bytes read stay the same, and the time drops.

Now look at SM occupancy and 12-bit weights at T=8T = 8T=8. When T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each GPU computes only its own 1,024 output columns of unpooler, a [1024, 4096][1024,\ 4096][1024, 4096] weight slice that takes 8.4 MB in 16-bit format (see Primer 2, Section 1). At T=8T = 8T=8, l0 still leaves this unpooler slice in 16-bit format: it cuts the 1,024 rows into 16 tiles of 64 rows each and splits KKK into 4 segments, launching only 16×4=6416 \times 4 = 6416×4=64 CTAs in total (Figure 9-2). That leaves 68 SMs sitting idle and falls short of HBM bandwidth. In l1, we compress this weight slice to 12-bit format (shrinking it from 8.4 MB to 6.3 MB) and split KKK into 8 segments instead, so 128 CTAs fill 128 SMs; the Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the 8 FP32 partial sums for each output directly, without needing an extra reduction kernel launch (for Split-K, see Chapter 2, Section 5).

At T=8T = 8T=8, qkv_gate in l0 also uses 16-bit weights. Variant l1 compresses it to 12-bit format, slices the 2,304 output rows into 36 tiles of 64 rows each, and splits KKK into 3 segments to launch 36×3=10836 \times 3 = 10836×3=108 CTAs. The grid and register math is the same as in Chapter 6, Section 8: each SM holds 1 resident CTA, so 108 CTAs fit in a single wave, whereas splitting into 4 segments would launch 144>132144 > 132144>132 CTAs and spill into an extra tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1).

The T=8T = 8T=8 numbers also include a zero-column shortcut that only works in single-GPU benchmarks. In the Stage 8 boundary kernel, the residual stream update is stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn))\mathrm{stream\_out} = \alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid} + \beta_2 \odot \mathrm{RMSNorm}(f \odot (1 + w_{\mathrm{post\_ffn}}))stream_out=α2​⊙stream_mid+β2​⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn​)) (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). In a single-GPU benchmark, the 7,168 output columns of fff owned by the other 7 GPUs are identically 0, so on those columns stream_out\mathrm{stream\_out}stream_out is just α2⊙stream_mid\alpha_2 \odot \mathrm{stream\_mid}α2​⊙stream_mid and does not depend on the experts or unpooler. Because α2\alpha_2α2​ is a fixed vector, the Stage 3 boundary kernel can precompute the sum of squares for those columns on the spot while writing stream_mid\mathrm{stream\_mid}stream_mid; the Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the squares across only this GPU's 1,024 columns and adds the number saved at Stage 3 to finish the RMSNorm. In a real 8-GPU run, an all-gather after Stage 7 first assembles all 8 GPUs' columns into 8,192 non-zero columns, so you cannot take this shortcut.

We get the biggest saving at T=8T = 8T=8 (~3.5 µs), though part of that comes from the single-GPU-only zero-column shortcut. If you look at the sliced unpooler kernel on its own, switching to 12-bit weights and expanding the grid to 128 CTAs cuts ~1.7 µs off its runtime (see the two charts below).

What is the price of these changes? Unpacking every 8 weights costs each thread 9 integer instructions (~18 ALU cycles), plus a side-table lookup to patch escaped weights (see Chapter 6, Section 2). At T=8T = 8T=8, the 8-way Split-K writes and re-reads 8×8×1,024×4 B=262,144 B≈0.26 MB8 \times 8 \times 1{,}024 \times 4\text{ B} = 262{,}144\text{ B} \approx 0.26\text{ MB}8×8×1,024×4 B=262,144 B≈0.26 MB of FP32 partial sums. l0's 4-way split already wrote and re-read ~0.13 MB, so only ~0.13 MB is new—far less than the 2.1 MB of weights we save. Once T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, 12-bit weights decoded by 1 warpgroup start to lose. Every projection then falls back to 16-bit weights, except the 2-warpgroup 12-bit unpooler at T=128T = 128T=128 (see Chapter 6, Section 4). The 1,024-column slice is used only for T≤8T \le 8T≤8 (see Primer 2, Section 1).

One more projection scheduling change shows up at larger batch sizes, outside the four l0 → l1 scenarios. When the batch size grows to T=32T = 32T=32, pooler launches only 64 CTAs (1 per SM) and streams its weights through a TMA ring buffer. By Chapter 3, Section 4, when all 132 SMs read at once, each SM needs ~48 KiB in flight; when only 64 SMs read, each of them has to keep 48×132/64≈9948 \times 132 / 64 \approx 9948×132/64≈99 KiB in flight. Out of 6 slots, 1 is being read by the consumer and the other 5 are in flight, totaling 80 KiB; with 7 slots, 6 are in flight for 96 KiB, making the standalone kernel ~0.55 µs faster (see the chart below; why it still falls short of the byte lower bound was not measured). The cost is one extra slot of shared memory per CTA, while occupancy stays at 1 CTA per SM; for the counterexample where we cut the ring shallower, see Section 7.

Now that we have plugged the leaks inside the projections, the next piece of overhead sits right between two projections: every cross-CTA full-row reduction for RMSNorm.

3l1 → l2: How Can a Cross-CTA Full-Row Reduction Avoid Paying for an Extra Kernel or a Device-Wide Memory Barrier?

Cross-kernel normalization splits column-wise gain and row-wise scaling across the preceding and succeeding kernels, while intra-cluster reduction uses direct remote SMEM writes (st.async) and local mbarrier.

Pre-Expert RMSNorm: Cross-Kernel Full-Row Reduction

Setting aside the full-row normalizations in the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels, every other normalization in the layer has already been folded into a neighboring kernel—except Stage 5 pre-expert RMSNorm (pre_expert_norm) (see Primer 2, Section 2; for Q/K and gated-output normalizations see Chapter 7, Sections 11–12, and for intra-expert normalizations see Chapter 8, Section 1). At T=1T = 1T=1, it still sits in a standalone kernel in l0 and l1. At T=8T = 8T=8, all versions already use the split we are about to describe: the pooler epilogue multiplies by the column gain and accumulates the sum of squares, leaving the per-row scale factor to be multiplied later without launching a standalone kernel.

Let xpool=h Wpooler⊤x_{\mathrm{pool}} = h\,W_{\mathrm{pooler}}^{\top}xpool​=hWpooler⊤​ be the result before Stage 5 normalization, with shape xpool :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{pool}}}{T,\;4096}{BF16}xpool​:[T,4096]BF16; the reciprocal root mean square of row mmm is

rm=114096∑kxpool[m,k]2+10−5r_m = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4096}\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2 + 10^{-5}}}rm​=40961​∑k​xpool​[m,k]2+10−5​1​

and the normalized output is

p[m,k]=rm⋅xpool[m,k]⋅(1+wk)p[m,k] = r_m \cdot x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k] \cdot (1 + w_k)p[m,k]=rm​⋅xpool​[m,k]⋅(1+wk​)

The model stores normalization weights as offsets relative to 1, so the applied gain is 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​; the 10−510^{-5}10−5 term in the denominator prevents division by zero.

Why can't pooler finish computing p[m,k]p[m,k]p[m,k] directly inside its own epilogue? Because pooler partitions the 4,096 output columns across different CTAs: each CTA holds only its own column segment of row mmm, and no single CTA can see the full-row sum of squares ∑kxpool[m,k]2\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2∑k​xpool​[m,k]2 across all 4,096 columns.

The way out comes from the linearity of matrix multiplication under row scaling: (rm xm) W⊤=rm (xm W⊤)(r_m\, x_m)\,W^{\top} = r_m\,(x_m\, W^{\top})(rm​xm​)W⊤=rm​(xm​W⊤): scaling a row before matrix multiplication is equivalent to multiplying by the matrix first and scaling the resulting row afterward. Look at the two factors in p[m,k]p[m,k]p[m,k]. The gain 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​ depends only on the column index kkk, and each pooler CTA already has the finished values for the columns it computes, so pooler can multiply by 1+wk1 + w_k1+wk​ right in its output epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3). Meanwhile, rmr_mrm​ depends only on the row index mmm, so the experts kernel can run its entire KKK loop first and then multiply its full-row FP32 accumulators (see Chapter 5, Section 6) by rmr_mrm​.

We have to do this scaling before SwiGLU, because silu(r a)≠r silu(a)\mathrm{silu}(r\,a) \ne r\,\mathrm{silu}(a)silu(ra)=rsilu(a) (for SwiGLU, see Primer 2, Section 2). In exact arithmetic the two orders give the exact same result; in BF16 the rounding point moves from ppp to xpool⋅(1+wk)x_{\mathrm{pool}} \cdot (1 + w_k)xpool​⋅(1+wk​), and the single-layer output still passes verification.

At T=1T = 1T=1 (Figure 9-3 Mode 1), each pooler CTA writes out xpool⋅(1+w)x_{\mathrm{pool}} \cdot (1 + w)xpool​⋅(1+w) and at the same time uses one atomic add (see Chapter 2, Section 6) to add its column segment's partial sum of squares into a single shared FP32 slot in global memory; once the PDL wait call returns, the experts kernel reads that slot and multiplies by rmr_mrm​. We keep that slot in FP32 both because scalar BF16 atomic adds compile down to a slow compare-and-swap retry loop as written in Chapter 6, Section 8's kernel, and because summing squares in FP32 preserves more precision. We zero the slot after the wait call of the Stage 3 boundary kernel (by which time the previous round's experts has already finished), and we place the atomic add after the wait call of pooler, so the order is always: previous read complete → zero → current accumulation (see Chapter 1, Section 4). That takes one kernel and the handoff in front of it off the critical path, cutting single-layer kernel launches from 12 down to 11.

What this split saves changes with the token count TTT. At T=1T = 1T=1, it saves one kernel handoff. By T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 (Figure 9-3 Mode 2), what it saves is an HBM round trip: a standalone normalization kernel has to read 24.7 MB of xpoolx_{\mathrm{pool}}xpool​ and write it back out, taking ~14 µs (see the chart below) and showing that those bytes go to HBM. Once we split the normalization, pooler divides the 4,096 columns into 16 column segments and each segment writes one partial sum of squares per row—producing a small partial-sum table rs :  [T,  16]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{rs}}{T,\;16}{FP32}rs:[T,16]FP32 that totals just 0.39 MB across the write and the read.

At intermediate token counts, the benefit is tiny or even negative: the standalone kernel already runs in just ~3.7 µs at T=753T = 753T=753, while splitting at T=128T = 128T=128 and 256 runs 0.5%–1.0% slower, so both of those settings retain the standalone kernel.

The price of splitting is that the pooler epilogue does one extra atomic add (or writes a 0.19 MB partial-sum table), and the experts kernel does one extra load plus a full-row scaling step. And because atomic-add arrival order is not fixed, the least significant bits of the output may change from run to run (see Chapter 2, Section 7).

Boundary Kernels: Intra-Cluster Full-Row Reduction

Now look at the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels. For T≤8T \le 8T≤8, each boundary kernel splits the 8,192 columns of each row across the 8 CTAs of one thread block cluster, 1,024 columns per CTA (see Chapter 7, Section 12). Every CTA needs the partial sums of squares from the other 7. Variant l1 exchanges them with a release-semantics cluster barrier. The 8 CTAs sit in the same GPC but may land on different SMs (CUDA guarantees only the same GPC; see Chapter 7, Section 12). The L1 caches of different SMs are not coherent with each other, so global data becomes coherent only at L2. The cluster barrier therefore has to wait until prior writes reach L2 (see Chapter 2, Section 6), and on H200 it also includes a device-wide memory barrier (see the barrier.cluster row of Appendix B, Quick Reference 3). The profiler samples warps at fixed cycle intervals and records why they cannot issue an instruction: on the T=16T = 16T=16 boundary kernels (2-CTA clusters), 36%–46% of the non-issued samples stall on the wait that this barrier compiles to; we did not sample the 8-CTA cluster at T≤8T \le 8T≤8 separately (for stall sampling, see Chapter 10, Section 7).

Variant l2 (Figure 9-3 Mode 3) replaces that barrier with st.async. Each CTA writes its partial sum of squares straight into each peer CTA's shared memory, while each receiver waits on its own local mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 5) until the expected byte count arrives (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the mechanism). Now the exchange waits only for those 8 partial sums: 7 from peers and 1 that the CTA wrote to itself. Kernel entry still runs one cluster barrier without device-wide release, to confirm that the peers' mbarriers are initialized; that barrier does not compile to a device-wide memory barrier. In isolated boundary-kernel benchmarks, this change saves 0.86–0.99 µs per call. Because the CTAs exchange only partial sums in shared memory, and each CTA writes its own columns into stream without reading any peer CTA's global writes, we no longer need that device-wide memory barrier here; the next kernel sees stream through the inter-kernel handoff.

The catch with direct remote-SMEM exchange is that it is easier to get wrong: our first implementation reused the same shared-memory buffer across two row reductions, and the shared-memory read/write hazard checker (see Chapter 10, Section 4) caught 8 write-after-read hazards (WAR; see Chapter 3, Section 5), which we fixed by giving each reduction its own buffer. Where this approach would start to lose was not measured.

Putting both changes together gives l1 → l2, saving ~1.8 µs on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer (see the chart below for all four scenarios). At T=8T = 8T=8, pre-expert RMSNorm was already split (see the start of this section), and Stage 8 already takes the zero-column shortcut. Once we put the changes back into the single layer, only the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window delta clears the noise band. In the other three scenarios, the expected savings do not show up: the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer likewise drops one pre-expert RMSNorm kernel and the handoff in front of it, and switches both boundary kernels to direct writes; at T=8T = 8T=8, only the Stage 3 boundary kernel changes, saving ~0.9 µs per call when measured on its own. The cause was not determined.

4l2 → l3: How Can Every Inter-Kernel Handoff Be Hidden Inside the Preceding Kernel's Epilogue?

l3 completes the PDL edges along the main chain so successor kernels enter early to prefetch weights; using PDL safely requires two rules: pair predecessor and successor calls, and place the trigger point according to how many SMs are free.

PDL lets a successor kernel enter SMs early while the preceding kernel is wrapping up, and then pause at wait until the preceding kernel finishes and its writes become visible (see Chapter 1, Section 4). Inside a layer, dense projection weights are already fixed before the layer starts and do not depend on the previous step's activations, so the next dense projection kernel can start reading its own weights without waiting for the previous kernel to finish. Routed experts are the one exception: which expert weights to read depends on Top-8's output (see Section 5).

In l2, most edges on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer already use PDL: for example attention → o, Stage 3 boundary kernel → pooler, and experts → unpooler → Stage 8 boundary kernel. The edges that still lack PDL are qkv_gate → attention on both layer types (for the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, attention merges inside the split-KV kernel without a separate merge kernel; see below), the o projection at T=8T = 8T=8, and pooler → experts: across those boundaries, the successor still waits for the predecessor to exit completely before launching. In l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 1), we attach the PDL launch attribute to the rest of the main-chain successors (leaving o on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer and router on the side stream as ordinary launches) so they can land on SMs early; among them, the expert kernels load their opening batch of weights into the shared-memory ring buffer ahead of wait, whereas the o projection at T=8T = 8T=8 (up to 32) issues the hardware prefetch instruction prefetch.global.L2 before wait (see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2): it only tells the hardware to move that weight tile from HBM into L2, taking none of this thread's registers; once wait returns, the kernel uses TMA to read the tile from L2 into shared memory. As for o on the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer, it already loads its CTA's entire weight tile directly into registers before wait in l2.

To get PDL right across a full layer, we have to follow two rules.

Rule 1: PDL must be paired across predecessor and successor kernels. Along a multi-kernel chain, every middle kernel is both the successor of the previous step and the predecessor of the next step: the predecessor has to fire its trigger call on time, and the successor has to launch with the PDL attribute and call wait before reading dependent data. Leave out either half, and the successor waits until the predecessor exits completely before launching—so by the time it hits wait, there is nothing left to overlap. In an earlier baseline, attention on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer ran as a split-KV kernel plus a separate merge kernel, and both lacked the launch attribute and the trigger call, so neither edge overlapped; adding the missing halves makes the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer ~1.2 µs faster (paired ABBA measurement; see the chart below; the final version takes the second path of Chapter 7, Section 12 instead, merging via the last arriver inside the split-KV kernel). You can only see this cross-kernel overlap in a full-layer replay (see Chapter 10, Section 1).

Rule 2: Where to place the trigger call depends on how many SMs the predecessor kernel frees up. Back in Chapter 1, Section 4, we placed the trigger call after the main loop because early-entering successor CTAs take up SMs and hold onto registers and shared memory while they wait (see Chapter 3, Section 1). That only hurts, however, when all the SMs on the chip are already full. As we saw in Section 1, pooler at T=1T = 1T=1 uses only 64 of the 132 SMs and leaves 68 SMs idle. Variant l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 2) therefore sets the 132-CTA experts kernel as the PDL successor of pooler and has pooler fire its trigger call right at kernel entry. By design, experts is also supposed to wait for Top-8 on the side stream to join, yet on measured timelines experts enters ~2.65 µs before pooler finishes (see Section 5 for how this cross-stream join behaves). Its first 68 CTAs land on the idle SMs and start running prologue setup work right away: compacting local expert IDs, initializing barriers, and loading the first weight tile. The other 64 CTAs enter as pooler CTAs exit.

We measured the added PDL edges and early entry of the experts kernel together: l2 → l3 saves the most on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer (~3.6 µs), with all four scenarios shown in the chart below.

The price of this handoff optimization is that early-entering successor CTAs hold onto their registers and shared memory the whole time they wait. Even after every CTA of the preceding kernel exits, the hardware still has to confirm that all prior writes are visible to the successor before it lets the successor's wait call return; Section 6 measures how long that handoff gap takes. And if a successor enters too early and fights the predecessor kernel for SM resources, the whole pair runs slower instead—see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 7, Section 11 for counterexamples.

There is a catch, though: that prologue setup work reads topk_ids—written by Top-8 on the side stream—before wait, and that cross-stream read steps across a memory-visibility boundary.

5l3 → Fixed: What Can an Early-Entering Kernel Read Before wait?

Before wait, a kernel may in general read only data unmodified during the current graph replay (i.e., static weights); reading the predecessor's output before wait requires the predecessor to execute a gpu-scope release fence before issuing the trigger call.

A data race is when two threads (in the same kernel or in different kernels) access overlapping addresses, at least one of them writes, no causal order links them, and they are not both strong operations such as atomics. In PTX, the trigger call is written griddepcontrol.launch_dependents and the wait call griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 8).

By the PTX specification, the PDL mechanism itself gives two visibility paths that guarantee a predecessor kernel's writes are visible to its successor. Path 1: every writing thread in the predecessor first runs fence.release.gpu (a gpu-scope release fence; or the threads can pass an intra-CTA barrier and let one thread run the fence for the whole CTA, as in Chapter 2, Section 6), then calls launch_dependents in program order. If both grids sit in the same memory synchronization domain, the spec says this release fence synchronizes with the start of the successor grid, so the successor sees those writes the moment it launches. A memory synchronization domain is a tag CUDA attaches to each kernel launch; we use the default setting throughout, which puts all kernels in the same domain. Path 2: in every other case, writes are guaranteed visible only after the successor's griddepcontrol.wait returns (for release, acquire, and memory scope, see Chapter 2, Section 6). Every kernel along the chain finishes only after its own wait returns, so waiting for the previous kernel also waits for every earlier one. Under these two paths, unless you take Path 1, code before wait may read only data that nobody writes during the current replay—that is, static weights. Code before wait must also never write a buffer that any earlier kernel, the previous one included, might still be reading. That is why Section 3 zeroes the FP32 accumulation slot only after wait; otherwise the previous round's experts might still be reading it, and a release fence in the predecessor does not change that rule. (A third route is not part of PDL: polling a release/acquire flag under the memory model, as in Chapter 2, Section 6. This chapter's PDL chain does not use it; only the T=128T = 128T=128 merged launch in Section 7 does, so the side stream can wait for the router scores.)

Why did reading topk_ids before wait in l3 look safe at first? The main stream that carries experts first waits on the completion event recorded after Top-8 on the side stream, and an event join normally waits for the whole Top-8 grid to finish. In eager mode—where the CPU launches kernels one by one without capturing a graph—that is exactly what happens. Capture the chain into a CUDA Graph, though, and as soon as experts carries the PDL launch attribute, this cross-stream event-join edge behaves differently. It runs as a programmatic dependent edge: the successor may launch before the predecessor's writes are visible (even before the predecessor finishes, if it triggers early), and it waits only at wait. So experts can enter SMs before Top-8's writes are visible. Public CUDA documentation says only that, after stream capture, a kernel with the PDL launch attribute gets a programmatic dependent edge; it does not say whether a cross-stream event-join edge does the same. We found out by testing: in a control experiment, a predecessor kernel on the side stream triggers at kernel entry, and a PDL successor on the main stream reads its output before wait. Eager mode fails 0 of 50 runs; graph mode fails 50 of 50, with wrong outputs (the original report was not kept).

A CUDA Graph reuses the same topk_ids buffer on every replay. When Top-8 triggers at kernel entry (Figure 9-5 Mode ①), experts gets to the buffer first every time and reads the previous replay's expert IDs, which look completely valid. Our surviving records show the single-layer output completely wrong: the update this layer adds to the residual stream has a relative error of 0.7–1.09 against the reference implementation (the original report was not kept). Turn off Top-8's entry trigger so that it triggers implicitly at kernel exit (Figure 9-5 Mode ②, i.e., l3), and 240 standard replay tests show 0 errors (0 errors gives only an upper bound on the failure rate; see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). But 0 errors is not a guarantee. Top-8 in l3 never calls launch_dependents, so the trigger happens implicitly after all its CTAs exit. The CUDA Programming Guide states that the successor's CTAs may still launch before the predecessor's writes are visible. Only a returned wait guarantees that experts sees topk_ids. So l3 is still outside both guaranteed visibility paths; it just fails less often (see Chapter 2, Section 6).

Scale the replay count past 550,000 per shape and per version, spread across multiple H200 GPUs (see the chart below), and the race shows up. We call a single-layer output a severe numerical corruption when its relative L2 error exceeds 0.01 against a verified-correct output for the same input—one that the same version produced earlier and that passed the numerical-tolerance check. We re-checked 36 such outputs against the numerical tolerance (0.119–0.150; see Chapter 10, Section 4), and all 36 failed it. One GPU in our test pool failed far more often than the rest, so we left it out of the tally. Without that outlier, l3 on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer still hits 1 severe numerical corruption about every 11,000 replays; the chart below shows the other three scenarios. The failure rate stays flat during steady-state execution, so it is not a warm-up effect. We also had CTA 0 of experts log the expert IDs it read before wait (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the logging method). It repeatedly read IDs that did not match the current replay, and every mismatch we checked was exactly the previous replay's IDs.

As Section 4 noted, Top-8 decides which experts experts reads, so its whole prologue setup depends on topk_ids: compacting the local indices that land in this GPU's 32 local experts, initializing barriers, and loading the first weight tile. The two visibility paths at the start of this section give two fixes. Fix (a) moves the topk_ids read, and all prologue setup that depends on it, to after wait (Figure 9-5 Mode ③). Fix (b) has every Top-8 CTA pass an intra-CTA barrier after writing, let one thread run fence.release.gpu, and then call launch_dependents explicitly. Fix (b) is correct under both edge types. But whether it lets the prologue overlap with Top-8 depends on the graph-capture behavior that the docs do not spell out for cross-stream edges. This chapter's final single-layer version uses Fix (a). The submitted file is still l3, without this fix.

With Fix (a) in place, ~2.26 million total replays across all four shapes ran with 0 severe numerical corruptions. Aside from severe numerical corruptions, a separate class of small deviations (relative error ~0.003) that still pass single-layer verification shows up just as often before and after the fix, so it does not come from the topk_ids race (its cause was not determined). The fix in this chapter modifies the expert kernel used for T≤8T \le 8T≤8. At T=16T = 16T=16, the layer dispatches a separate early-entering expert kernel that likewise reads topk_ids ahead of wait. We did not modify that kernel; the same fix should apply there too, though neither the fix nor its failure rate was measured.

At T=8T = 8T=8, l3 originally failed only once every ~840,000 runs, so running ~560,000 error-free replays on the fixed version cannot prove the fix by count alone (see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). Instead, safety at T=8T = 8T=8 comes straight from the spec: whether that cross-stream edge runs as a regular event edge or as a programmatic dependent edge, Top-8 is done and its writes are visible once wait returns, so reading after wait is always safe.

Moving the 3.2 µs prologue setup after wait slows down the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer by only ~1.35 µs (see the chart below for all four scenarios). After this fix, when the experts kernel enters SMs early, it no longer runs its prologue setup ahead of time. Variant l2 and the fixed version were not timed in the same experiment, and how much the PDL edges vs. early expert entry each contributed—as well as how fast Fix (b) runs—was not measured.

Take the ~5.4 µs CUDA graph replay overhead off the fixed version's 67.8 µs, and the single layer still sits ~22 µs above the 40.0 µs reference bound. Is that remaining time sitting in the handoffs between kernels, or inside the kernels themselves?

6How Much Time Can Fusing a Single Layer into a Megakernel Recover?

Very little: replacing kernel boundaries with device-wide counter handoffs saves at most ~0.66 µs, and fusing multiple stages into a megakernel is ~10% slower on the weighted score; most of the excess time lies inside each kernel's main body and tail.

First, let's see where the time goes. Here we dissect a slightly earlier build of the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer with PDL enabled and the data race unfixed, which takes 68.2 µs without timestamp probes. Because this is a different build from l3 in Section 4, you cannot compare their total latencies directly. Every CTA records three timestamps: when it enters, when wait returns, and when it exits (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the method).

These timestamps split the waiting between kernels and the waiting inside each kernel into two numbers: the handoff gap, which is the time on the critical path from the last CTA exit of the preceding kernel to the first wait return in the next kernel; and the tail duration (CTA exit skew), which inside a single kernel is the time from the median CTA exit to the last CTA exit. Even if you fused multiple stages into a persistent full-chip megakernel, at most you could ever win back those two pieces—totaling ~12.5 µs.

Break that 68.2 µs total apart (see the chart below) and you see right away that the bulk of the time sits in the ~50 µs of kernel main bodies—roughly 1.25× the 40.0 µs reference bound. Handoff gaps and tail durations each take only ~6 µs, where each handoff gap includes acknowledging that every CTA of the previous grid has exited and flushing its writes. In this build, the experts stage (Chapter 8) has a byte lower bound of ~11.8 µs (reading 2 full local experts); its main body runs ~6.6 µs above that bound, and its tail duration alone makes up more than half of the entire layer's tail duration. The chart values already have the probe overhead factored out (Figure 9-6).

Now let's do the math on what fusing into a megakernel actually costs. Within a single layer, every output of y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx depends on the entire input vector xxx written in segments across all CTAs of the previous stage; thus every CTA of the next stage must wait for all CTAs of the previous stage to finish writing. If you marked individual tiles ready so the next stage could consume each tile as soon as it arrived, you could in theory hide part of the tail duration, at the price of per-tile acquire polling and finer-grained synchronization (this approach was not measured). When a megakernel hands off stages through a device-wide counter (working the same way as the grid barrier in Chapter 8, Section 6), the next stage still has to wait for the slowest producer CTA to finish writing xxx, so the tail duration does not go away; and the SMs that free up during the tail are already busy prefetching weights, so there is no extra work left to pack into them. To shrink each kernel's tail duration, you have to balance the load inside the heavy kernels themselves (see Chapter 7 for attention and Chapter 8 for experts).

To measure that, we built a synthetic memory-streaming chain: for each of the six weight-reading stages in a single layer, it reads one segment of that stage's byte count (qkv_gate and pooler at 12-bit, o and the unpooler slice at 16-bit, router at FP32, and experts at 4-bit), ~169 MB in total. Because this chain reads 2 full local experts instead of the ~1.87 local experts counted in the reference bound (75% of the mean distinct local experts touched on the busiest GPU; see Primer 2, Section 1), the chain's byte lower bound is higher than l0's byte lower bound in Section 2. On this chain, each device-wide counter handoff adds 1.08 µs. Out of the 8 handoff gaps in the layer, only the two entering attention merge and pooler are longer than that, and each one saves ~0.33 µs—at most 0.66 µs in total, or about 1% of the layer (see the chart below).

That same 6-stage synthetic memory-streaming chain also isolates the cost of the persistent kernel structure itself: when we write those exact same 6 stages as a persistent kernel that does zero waiting between stages (see Chapter 3, Section 1), it still runs 8.3 µs slower than a standard launch reading the same bytes (see the chart below). The cause was not determined, and the overhead when scaled up to the full single layer was not measured. Because this control kernel does no inter-stage synchronization, its numerical results are wrong—it is only there to measure the structural cost of persistence itself. On top of that, every stage fused into a single kernel has to share one compile-time register and shared-memory budget, which forces lightweight stages to run under the occupancy cap of the heaviest stage (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

We also tried actually fusing Stages 6 through 8 (from experts through the Stage 8 boundary kernel) and adjacent steps of Stages 2–3 into megakernels; weighted across the 6 decode and verify shapes (see Chapter 8, Section 1) using the model's 46 sliding-window to 16 full-attention layer ratio, the fused versions ran ~10% slower.

Packing a small kernel into the epilogue of the preceding kernel (see Chapter 1, Section 3) is also slower. With PDL, that small kernel has already entered early on other SMs; once you pack it into the epilogue, it gives up that early entry, and the entire merge step gets serialized onto the last CTA. On the T=256T = 256T=256 sliding-window layer (called verify 32-request sliding window in Chapter 7), folding the attention merge step into the last CTA of the split-KV kernel makes the single layer 6.75 µs slower. On this shape, our single layer keeps the split-KV kernel plus a separate PDL merge kernel (whereas the standalone operator in Chapter 7, Section 12 takes the third path, with CTAs in the same cluster writing partial results directly into one another's shared memory). Chapter 7's second path (last-arriver merge) is used for 1-, 16-, and 32-request full-attention decode and 32-request sliding-window decode: each row is wrapped up by that row's own last-arriving CTA, spreading the epilogue work across different CTAs.

At this point, the T=1T = 1T=1 layer is scheduled around its own shape. Once the batch size changes, the number of SMs occupied by pooler changes with it, and the trade-offs of the two earlier techniques flip as well.

7At Larger Batch Sizes: How Does the Number of Idle SMs Reshape the Schedule?

A side stream generally pays off only when the main kernel does not saturate HBM bandwidth and either leaves idle SMs or allows SM co-residency; the stream schedule must switch per TTT.

Once the main kernel saturates HBM bandwidth or fills all SMs, every extra byte read and every SM occupied by a side-stream kernel stretches the main kernel. As the token count TTT changes, both conditions shift together (Figure 9-7; for residency limits, see Chapter 3, Section 1).

At T=1T = 1T=1, pooler launches 64 CTAs and leaves 68 SMs idle, so router and Top-8 run on the side stream (Section 1) and the first 68 CTAs of experts enter SMs early (Section 4).

At T=128T = 128T=128, both router and pooler launch 128 CTAs: router's 4-slot ring buffer takes ~128 KiB of shared memory, and pooler's 8-slot ring buffer takes ~193 KiB of shared memory (for ring buffer slots, see Chapter 3, Section 4). Together they need 128+193>228 KiB128 + 193 > 228\text{ KiB}128+193>228 KiB, exceeding the per-SM shared-memory limit (see Chapter 3, Section 1), so the two kernels cannot co-reside on the same SM; pooler can only enter after router runs on its own and exits, and router's standalone run plus the handoff takes ~8.5 µs in total. Cutting pooler's and router's ring buffers shallower to squeeze both onto the same SM makes the sliding-window layer 8.4 µs (T=128T = 128T=128) and 5.0 µs (T=256T = 256T=256) slower instead.

What actually works here is a merged launch. router and pooler read the same input h, so we put the router projection and pooler into one kernel: each CTA first computes its slice of router scores through the same shared-memory ring buffer, then goes straight into the pooler main loop. The layer reads the same total bytes as before, with router's 8.4 MB of weights streaming through pooler's ring buffer. The side stream keeps only a 1-CTA wait kernel, which polls the completion counter written by the merged kernel and launches Top-8 once all 128 slices of router scores are in. The sliding-window single layer runs 1.30% faster (paired ABBA median; see the chart below). At T=256T = 256T=256, the change falls inside the ~0.5% paired noise band and shows no measurable gain, so we keep the two kernels separate there.

At T=753T = 753T=753, prefill pooler slices its output into 128×256128 \times 256128×256 tiles to launch 96 CTAs, leaving 36 SMs idle. Putting router, Top-8, and the route-alignment kernel—which sorts token indices by expert and pads each bucket to the tile size (see Chapter 8, Section 14)—on the side stream to run in parallel across those 36 idle SMs makes the single layer ~3.2% faster (see the chart below).

Step up to T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012, and pooler fills all 132 SMs. If we keep running pooler first with router on the side stream, the single layer runs 0.76% slower; launching router on the side stream right after the Stage 3 boundary kernel (without waiting for pooler) is also 1.01% slower. So at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012, we run router first on the main stream and pooler after it on the main stream, placing only the lightweight Top-8 and route-alignment kernels on the side stream to overlap with pooler.

At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, pooler has far more than 132 output tiles and keeps every SM busy from start to finish. If pooler went first, router could start only after it finished, so we keep the T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 schedule: router runs first on the main stream, and the lightweight Top-8 and route-alignment kernels overlap pooler on the side stream. This only partly fits this section's rule: pooler fills all 132 SMs and leaves none idle, and we did not measure separately how much Top-8 and the route-alignment kernel overlap pooler on the side stream, or whether that overlap helps or hurts.

Using idle SMs to take on the second-wave tiles of qkv_gate at T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 (see Chapter 2, Section 5) makes qkv_gate finish 8.7 µs earlier; across the whole layer, the sliding-window layer runs ~0.47% faster, whereas the full-attention layer runs 0.10% slower because its KV preparation kernel on the side stream competes for SMs—so the final version enables this split on sliding-window layers only.

8Placing This Layer Back into All 62 Layers: Which Part of One Decode Step Do This Book's Measurements Cover?

Summing the 62 final single-layer latencies at T=1T = 1T=1 gives 4,329.2 µs, which overcounts 62 single-layer graph replay overheads and omits 186 cross-GPU collectives, token embedding, lm_head, and sampling.

The solid bars in Figure 9-8 are the 62-layer single-GPU body that this book measures (46 sliding-window layers and 16 full-attention layers).

Add up all 62 single-layer reference bounds and you get ~2.55 ms, which is higher than the ~1.87 ms number from Primer 1. The 2.55 ms sum adds the expert weights counted in the reference bound plus the KV cache and activations, and leaves out lm_head (the chart below breaks out the three pieces).

How does the measured 4,329.2 µs sum (46×67.79+16×75.6846 \times 67.79 + 16 \times 75.6846×67.79+16×75.68) differ from a real one-step decode? On one hand, it counts the 5.4 µs single-layer graph replay overhead from Section 1 62 times, whereas real serving amortizes graph replay across one 62-layer graph (how much replay overhead remains after amortization was not measured). Layers 0 and 61 also store their experts in BF16 (see Primer 1, Section 2), while this sum treats every layer as 4-bit experts, biasing the total low (the difference was not measured separately).

On the other hand, the four light-gray segments in Figure 9-8 lie outside single-layer, single-GPU benchmarking, and we measured none of them. Before Layer 0, the vocabulary embedding table is split by rows across all 8 GPUs, so the token lookup is followed by an all-reduce across GPUs (see Primer 1, Section 1). Each layer has 3 cross-GPU collectives (see Section 1). At T=1T = 1T=1, the all-reduce after o moves a :  [1,  8192]  BF16\shape{a}{1,\;8192}{BF16}a:[1,8192]BF16 (16 KiB), the all-reduce after Stage 6 moves m :  [1,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{1,\;4096}{BF16}m:[1,4096]BF16 (8 KiB), and the all-gather after Stage 7 takes 1,024 BF16 elements from each GPU (2 KiB) to gather f :  [1,  8192]  BF16\shape{f}{1,\;8192}{BF16}f:[1,8192]BF16 (16 KiB). H200's inter-GPU NVLink runs at 900 GB/s bidirectional and 450 GB/s unidirectional, so one 16 KiB copy takes ~36 ns on the wire (16,384 B÷450 GB/s16{,}384\ \mathrm{B} \div 450\ \mathrm{GB/s}16,384 B÷450 GB/s). Even in the all-reduce, where each GPU sends its 16 KiB to each of the other 7 (112 KiB in total), the bytes take only ~255 ns. So bytes are not the cost: the cost is that all 186 collectives across the 62 layers sit on the critical path, and we did not measure their latency. After Layer 61 and the final RMSNorm, this GPU's slice of lm_head reads 413.8 MB (an 86.2 µs byte lower bound at 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Sections 3–4), followed by an all-gather of logits across GPUs and token sampling. If the serving engine uses speculative decoding, each step also adds the draft model plus a T=8T = 8T=8 verification pass (see Primer 1, Section 7; we did not measure the draft model's latency).

Chapter Evolution Chain (l0 → l1 → l2 → l3 → Fixed)

  • l0 (Section 1): baseline obtained by turning off the changes from Sections 2–4 in l3, with the main chain on one CUDA stream and router plus Top-8 on the side stream.
  • l0 → l1 (Section 2): projections switch to the 9-instruction decoder from Chapter 6; we reorder the pooler weight layout, add the evict_first L2 residency hint, and prepare escaped-weight corrections before the final KKK-step. For 8-token verify, both qkv_gate and unpooler switch to 12-bit weights with launch grids sized to fit in a single wave. At T=1T = 1T=1, qkv_gate and pooler already use 12-bit weights in l0.
  • l1 → l2 (Section 3): we split pre-expert RMSNorm across the pooler epilogue and expert accumulators, and boundary kernels exchange partial sums via direct remote-SMEM exchange.
  • l2 → l3 (Section 4): we complete the PDL edges along the main chain, and the first 68 CTAs of the experts kernel enter early on the SMs left idle by pooler (containing the data race analyzed in Section 5).
  • l3 → Fixed (Section 5): we move the topk_ids read in the T≤8T \le 8T≤8 experts kernel after wait, eliminating that cross-stream data race (measured on a patched copy; the submitted file is l3).

Takeaway: Most of a single layer's execution time sits inside the kernels themselves: scheduling and handoffs bring the T=1T = 1T=1 sliding-window layer down from 71.4 µs to 67.8 µs in the final version, and fusing the layer into a megakernel cannot recover the rest.

Chapter 10

Given a Slow Kernel, How Do We Measure It Accurately and Diagnose Its Bottleneck Level by Level?
