The previous chapter ended with a question: when you get a brand-new slow kernel, how do you pin down where it stalls level by level without guessing? Only two things can fool you on a slow kernel: measuring the time wrong, or looking at the wrong level. So this chapter starts with how to measure latency right, and then walks through the profiler level by level from the outside in. Before touching any code, we first bound how much time a fix could possibly save; at the end, we list the four hardware limits on H200 that software cannot change and can only work around. Throughout the chapter, we keep using single-request gemv to show the readings at each level, bringing in operators from Part II only when a phenomenon does not show up in gemv.

1Why Do CUDA Event Timing and the Profiler Report Two Different Latencies, and What Should Each Be Used to Read?

CUDA event timing includes launch and event-recording overhead, while the profiler times only the kernel itself. Use event timing to report microsecond savings, and use the profiler to see where the kernel is bottlenecked.

For kernel-level profiling in this book, we use Nsight Compute (NCU). It focuses on one kernel at a time and replays that kernel across multiple passes, collecting one set of hardware counters per pass. Because NCU flushes the caches between passes by default, those counters give you cold-cache readings. Its gpu__time_duration.sum metric is the gap between two timestamps written by the GPU front end—the hardware that processes the command stream before the grid goes out to the SMs. It records the start timestamp after launch setup, right before dispatching the grid to the SMs, and records the end timestamp after the GPU finishes waiting for all work to complete (WaitForIdle). So this number leaves out CPU-side launch and event-recording overhead, but it is longer than the pure execution span from the first CTA starting to the last CTA exiting; by how much, we did not measure.

Take gemv v8 from Chapter 4, Section 6 and measure it both ways: the CUDA event timing from Primer 3, Section 5 comes out ~2.8 µs longer than the gpu__time_duration.sum reported by NCU, as shown in the chart below.

Where does that extra ~2.8 µs in CUDA event timing go? Most of it is the launch command and event-recording overhead sitting between the two timing events, which NCU does not measure. Also, the two runs did not use the exact same machines and their SM clock frequencies may differ; we did not measure how much each of those two factors contributed. Do not compare this 2.8 µs directly with the 4.6 µs from Primer 3, Section 5: the two numbers do not measure the same thing, because 4.6 µs also includes the GPU execution of the empty kernel itself.

NCU 2025.1, the version used in this book, locks the SM and memory clocks to their lower base clock by default; newer NCU releases lock them to boost frequency instead, so check --clock-control before you profile. In this run, we turned clock locking off and the SM ran at ~1.96 GHz. We did not record the SM frequency during CUDA event timing, and we did not measure the effect of clock frequency on v8 latency separately.

So when you report how many microseconds an optimization saves, always use CUDA event timing, not NCU duration. To time a single kernel, wrap a single launch in CUDA events; to time a single layer, wrap one CUDA Graph replay in events. If you want to time one specific kernel inside a CUDA Graph replay, use the Activity API of NVIDIA's profiling interface CUPTI (CUDA Profiling Tools Interface): instead of replaying that kernel in isolation, it records the GPU start and end timestamps of every kernel during graph replay. Conversely, when you want to know why a kernel is slow, switch to NCU to read the bandwidth share, stall sampling share, and instruction counts.

2Why Must We Read 512 MiB to Flush L2 Before Every Timed Run—and Why Only Read, Not Write?

A single operator's weights fit inside the 60 MiB L2 cache, so without a flush you measure warm-cache latency; if you flush L2 with writes, you can even invert the speed ranking of two versions.

Before every timed run, do a 512 MiB read flush outside the start and end timing events: read a buffer much larger than L2 once so all the old data in L2 gets replaced with clean cache lines.

Why flush L2 at all? Compare Mode 1 and Mode 3 in Figure 10-1. The weights W :  [2304,  8192]  BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}W:[2304,8192]BF16 of qkv_gate take up only 37.75 MB, which easily fits inside the H200's 60 MiB L2 cache. If you run the same kernel back-to-back in a loop without flushing, most of WWW is already sitting in L2 from the second iteration onward; in production, though, 62 layers take turns running and L2 is cold whenever a layer reads its weights (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

Warm L2 and cold L2 give wildly different numbers. Take gemv v1 from Primer 3, Section 6: on the same H200 GPU and in the same process, timing without an L2 flush comes out ~30% shorter than timing after a 512 MiB read flush, as shown in the chart below. If you choose a kernel design from warm-cache timings, the winning variant may not hold up in production.

And why must the L2 flush only read, never write? If you flush L2 by writing a 512 MiB buffer (Figure 10-1 Mode 2), you leave the 60 MiB L2 cache packed with modified dirty cache lines that have not been written back to HBM yet. When the tested kernel then goes to read WWW, L2 probably has to write each evicted dirty line back to HBM before pulling in a new line, stealing a chunk of HBM bandwidth.

Worse yet, a write flush can flip the measured speed ranking of two versions. That is why we withdrew v4 from the gemv evolution chain. Starting from v3 (Chapter 2, Section 8), v4 added cache hints to the loads of WWW and xxx: the L2 residency policies from Chapter 2, Section 4, plus matching L1 eviction hints—evict_first on WWW and evict_last on xxx (see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Item 24 for the code). With a 512 MiB write flush, v4 looked ~10% faster than v3 (see the first chart below). Once we switched to a 512 MiB read flush and tested in both forward and reverse orders across two H200 GPUs, all 4 medians of v4 came out above v3, averaging ~1 µs slower (see the second chart below). Those two charts come from two runs on different machines; put them side by side and you see that after switching to a read flush, v3 got ~5 µs faster while v4 barely moved. Because we did not run a same-machine control that changed only the flush method, blaming the whole ~5 µs on the write flush is an inference; our guess is that tagging WWW with evict_first in v4 changed the order in which dirty cache lines got evicted.

So we do not count v4 as a step, and the evolution chain jumps straight from v3 to v5; for why v4 saves no time under a read flush, see Chapter 2, Section 4.

After a read flush, L2 is just as cold as when 62 layers rotate in production, and the interference from dirty cache line writebacks is gone. The cost is an extra 512 MiB read outside the timing events on every iteration, which stretches the total wall-clock time of the experiment (by how much, we did not measure). Keep in mind, though, that if an input is naturally warm in production—like the activations just written by the preceding kernel inside the same layer—cold-flushing an isolated single kernel will make it look artificially slow. When you time a single layer, wrap the whole layer in one CUDA Graph replay so warm intra-layer data stays in cache naturally (see Chapter 9, Section 1).

3How Much Must Two Versions Differ Before One Is Truly Faster?

Run the two versions alternately in A, B, B, A order inside the same process to cancel linear drift; then run an A/A null-hypothesis control to measure the operator's noise band, and count a delta only when it clears that band.

First, see why you cannot time two versions on different machines and subtract the numbers directly, as shown in the chart below. Take the exact same version of gemv and run it on two different H200 GPUs with the same cold-L2 CUDA event timing: setting aside v0 (which takes nearly 700 µs), the medians on the two machines differ by up to 0.32 µs. Now look at v8 → v9 in Chapter 5, Section 8: across 4 paired comparison rounds, two rounds tied and two rounds came out slightly slower for v9, with every delta smaller than the span of v8's own 4-round medians. That puts the change in v9 squarely inside measurement noise (see Chapter 4, Section 6 for the criterion).

Why does the alternating A, B, B, A order from Chapter 7, Section 1 cancel drift? Even on a single machine, back-to-back runs experience slow latency drift driven by temperature, clock frequency, and other factors (whose individual contributions we did not measure). If you run NNN back-to-back iterations of A followed by NNN back-to-back iterations of B as in Figure 10-2 Mode 1, the later B runs execute in a consistently slower state, mixing that drift straight into the difference. Switch to the A, B, B, A order in Figure 10-2 Mode 2 and label the four runs in a group as timestamps 1,2,3,41, 2, 3, 41,2,3,4: the mean timestamp of A is (1+4)/2=2.5(1+4)/2 = 2.5(1+4)/2=2.5, and the mean timestamp of B is (2+3)/2=2.5(2+3)/2 = 2.5(2+3)/2=2.5. As long as drift across those four runs is roughly linear, A and B see the exact same average drift, which cancels out when you subtract them. Run multiple groups in a row and take the median of the per-group deltas, and you also iron out random jitter within individual groups.

Once linear drift is canceled, we run the A/A null-hypothesis control from Chapter 7, Section 1—feeding two identical copies of the code as A and B into the same paired ABBA harness. On the dense projection kernels, the largest observed difference is 0.13 µs, so we set the winning threshold at 0.15 µs; note that this threshold is simply the maximum observed A/A delta, not a statistical confidence interval.

You have to calibrate the noise band separately for each operator rather than applying one constant across the whole book; the chart below shows the noise band for each operator.

What is the catch with paired ABBA benchmarking? Each group takes 4 runs, and both A and B have to stay loaded in the same process at the same time (see Section 5 for how to keep their device memory allocations from crowding each other and skewing the numbers). Also, if a non-linear jump like a sudden clock drop hits mid-run, the symmetric order cannot cancel it out (we did not measure behavior under such sudden jumps). And if one side computes wrong outputs, paired ABBA timing cannot make the delta meaningful either—so always check outputs before timing (see Section 4).

4Before Timing, How Do We Verify That a Version's Output Is Correct—and Stays Correct Every Time?

A version that computes wrong outputs can look faster because it skips work or changes power draw, so always check outputs before timing. Intermittent data races take large replay counts: seeing 0 errors in NNN runs shows only, with ~95% confidence, that the failure rate is below 3/N3/N3/N.

Always feed your tests non-zero random inputs rather than all-zero tensors: all-zero inputs can give you artificially fast readings (we did not measure the exact cause separately).

Timing a version that produces wrong outputs is pointless. In one full-layer comparison, we ran A several times in a row and then B several times in a row, and B came out ~8.55% faster than A—only for us to check the outputs and find that B was wrong. Two things were tangled up in that gap: B computed corrupted values (which can change chip power draw), and running A then B mixed in drift (see Section 3); we did not measure how much each contributed. Once we fixed the bug and re-tested with 20 groups of paired ABBA benchmarking, the speedup vanished completely.

Even after a single-run output check passes, you still have to watch out for intermittent concurrency data races. You can catch shared-memory read/write hazards and CTA barrier misuse with racecheck and synccheck in NVIDIA's runtime checking tool compute-sanitizer—but neither tool can see cross-kernel global-memory data races.

To catch an intermittent cross-kernel data race, your only option is counting errors across a huge number of replays. Take the topk_ids data race from Chapter 9, Section 5: on a T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer, it showed up only about once every 11,000 CUDA Graph replays, and at T=8T = 8T=8 it took about 840,000 replays to trigger once.

So how many error-free replays does it take before you can say a data race is fixed? That comes down to the rule of three. If the true per-run failure rate is ppp, the probability of seeing zero errors across NNN consecutive runs is:

(1−p)N≈e−pN(1 - p)^N \approx e^{-pN}(1−p)N≈e−pN

Set that probability to 5%5\%5% and take the natural log: since ln⁡0.05≈−3\ln 0.05 \approx -3ln0.05≈−3, you get pN≈3pN \approx 3pN≈3. In other words, seeing 0 errors across NNN consecutive replays does not prove the bug is gone—it only tells you with ~95%95\%95% confidence that the true failure rate ppp sits below 3/N3/N3/N. This bound assumes independent replays and an equal failure rate across GPUs; in Chapter 9, Section 5 one GPU failed far more often than the others, so the bound constrains the average failure rate across those GPUs.

Let's plug the numbers from Chapter 9, Section 5 into that formula. After the fix, 567,200 consecutive replays on the T=1T = 1T=1 full-attention layer (including the outlier GPU) produced 0 severe numerical corruptions. By the rule of three, that pushes the upper bound on the severe numerical corruption rate down to 3/567,200≈5.3×10−63 / 567{,}200 \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-6}3/567,200≈5.3×10−6. Before the fix, the failure rate was ~9.2×10−59.2 \times 10^{-5}9.2×10−5: if the data race were still there, 567,200 replays should have hit it ~52 times, so seeing 0 proves the fix worked. Now look at T=8T = 8T=8: the original race triggered only about once every 840,000 runs. After the fix, we ran 556,000 replays and saw 0 errors—but even if the bug were completely unfixed, 556,000 runs would be expected to hit it only ~0.7 times, so that 0 proves nothing.

The catch with this check is that replay counting takes a lot of time: bounding the failure rate below ppp takes at least ~3/p3/p3/p runs, and turning on compute-sanitizer slows the kernel down heavily too (we did not measure the slowdown factor). When an intermittent race has an ultra-low trigger rate like the T=8T = 8T=8 case above, the replay count NNN you can practically run is too small to push 3/N3/N3/N below the original failure rate. At that point, only a proof from the memory-model specification itself can settle it (see Chapter 9, Section 5).

5How Do We Keep the Measurement Harness from Altering the Tested Kernel?

When probing timestamps inside a kernel, hold readings in registers and write them out at exit; when comparing two versions, keep the device memory allocation layout unchanged.

CUDA event timing gives you only the end-to-end duration of the whole kernel. If you want to know how long one slice inside a kernel takes—say, the prologue or the reduction tail step—you have to drop a timestamp probe into the kernel: a snippet of code that reads the clock and logs stage-by-stage elapsed time. That probe reads %globaltimer, a 64-bit global nanosecond timer register predefined by the PTX specification. The specification notes that this register is meant for NVIDIA tools and behaves in a target-specific way, without promising that readings across different SMs are strictly synchronized. On H200, we measured its smallest non-zero step at 32 ns, only 1/25 of the ~0.8 µs gaps in Chapter 9, Section 6. We did not measure whether readings skew across SMs, so whenever a sub-1 µs gap comes from subtracting timestamps across CTAs, this book treats it as an estimate only.

Write the probe the wrong way and it will directly stretch the code you are trying to measure. Recorded timestamps eventually have to go out to a global memory buffer; if every probe point first loads that buffer's output address from global memory, each probe adds a global memory load, and the store has to wait for that load to come back. We measured the elapsed time from function entry to the first useful compute instruction on a dense projection kernel, with the result shown in the chart below: a probe that loads the output pointer from global memory at every timestamp takes 0.576 µs longer than a probe that holds timestamps in registers and writes them out at exit—as large as the entire prologue the experiment was trying to measure (~0.1–0.6 µs), and larger than the reorderable portion inside it (0.06–0.4 µs). Holding timestamps in registers and writing them out at the end adds only a few register moves inside the measured interval.

Next, look at how device memory allocation affects neighboring operators. When we allocated an extra 84.9 MB buffer for new weights during setup, subsequent neighboring operators whose code we had not touched at all shifted in latency by ±0.5%–1%—for instance, unpooler at T=32T = 32T=32 slowed down by ~0.5%, enough to drown out small real wins. We infer that allocating an extra buffer alters the virtual and physical addresses the device memory allocator assigns to subsequent tensors, shifting which HBM partitions they map to (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

So when you compare two versions, do not change the order or total byte count of device memory allocations. You can keep the layout fixed in two ways: either build the new-format weights in place inside an old buffer that is no longer used, or use a fixed device memory pool where all tensors are carved at fixed offsets out of one pre-allocated block of device memory. Also, a CUDA Graph saves each kernel's parameters—every address included—at capture time, and every replay reuses those exact addresses. To change an address, you first update the graph with Graph Update (for example cudaGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams) and only then replay it (see Chapter 1, Section 2). So any temporary workspace buffer used for timing must also be allocated and warmed up before you capture the graph.

These precautions have their own costs. Each 64-bit timestamp takes up two 32-bit registers, which in a kernel already near its register cap can lower occupancy or trigger register spilling (we did not measure the actual impact; see Chapter 3, Section 1). A fixed device memory layout is also more tedious to maintain, and it only keeps neighboring operators steady rather than making anything faster. Finally, when a single execution of the candidate code is shorter than 32 ns, in-kernel timestamp probing cannot resolve it; as long as that code runs enough times for its total cost to clear the noise band, you can measure it from the outside with the perturbation test in Section 8.

6The Outer Three Levels (Levels 1–3): Which Metric Do We Check on the Timeline, the Full Chip, and a Single SM, and What Fix Does Each Point To?

Diagnose from the outside in: check first whether the timeline has gaps, then how many bytes the full chip reads and whether it has a tail wave, and finally whether a single SM spills registers or falls short on bytes in flight.

Until you rule out outer-level bottlenecks, do not rush to tune inner-level code—the code you optimize may not even sit on the critical path (see Section 8).

Start at Level 1: Timeline (see Chapter 1, Section 1). Open the system-wide timeline profiler Nsight Systems: it plots CPU launches and the start and end of every GPU kernel on the same timeline, so you can see at a glance whether idle gaps sit between adjacent kernels. If tensor shapes are fixed and CPU launch gaps show up on the timeline, capture the chain into a CUDA Graph (see Chapter 1, Section 2). If hardware handoff gaps from the predecessor's tail still remain between adjacent graph nodes after capture, turn on PDL so the dependent kernel enters early (see Chapter 1, Section 4). Only small kernels whose gaps even PDL cannot hide are worth fusing.

Chapter 9, Section 6 showed what happens when you ignore that rule: fusing kernels that were already hidden—or merging stages into a megakernel—made execution slower instead. On the gemv chain, the step at this level is v2 (see Chapter 1, Section 5).

Once the timeline is packed tight, zoom in to Level 2: Full Chip (see Chapter 2, Sections 1–3). First put your measured latency next to the theoretical lower bound: for gemv, reading WWW once has a bandwidth lower bound of 7.86 µs (see Primer 2, Section 4). Next check two numbers in NCU: achieved HBM bandwidth as a percentage of peak in the Speed Of Light (SOL) panel, and measured HBM bytes read (dram__bytes_read.sum) in the Memory Workload Analysis panel (or collected directly as a metric). Those two numbers put you in one of three cases:

  • measured bytes read significantly exceed algorithmically required bytes: either your global loads are not coalesced, or the cache is getting flushed and reading the same bytes twice. Drop down to Level 3 to check coalescing and cache behavior.
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes, but achieved bandwidth is a low share of peak: you are not reading extra bytes—the bytes are simply not arriving fast enough. gemv v9 lands right here: NCU measures 37.78 MB read, almost identical to the 37.75 MB of WWW, yet achieved bandwidth reaches only ~66% of peak. Its per-SM bytes in flight are already near the 64 KiB saturation line (see Chapter 2, Section 3 and Chapter 4, Section 3; note that this 66% is averaged across the whole kernel including ramp-up and tail, while steady-state bandwidth was not measured separately).
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes and achieved bandwidth is near peak: you have hit the physical ceiling of HBM. Tweaking the schedule will not squeeze out any more time; the only way forward is reading fewer bytes—for example, by compressing weight bit-width as in Chapter 6, Section 4.

While you are at the full-chip level, also check whether all 132 SMs finish together. Probe %globaltimer and %smid (the current SM ID) at kernel entry and exit using the pattern from Section 5. If you see the final batch of CTAs dragging on across only a few SMs, you have a tail wave. In gemv v1, for example, launching one CTA per row fills 2,112 CTA slots in the first wave and leaves the remaining 192 CTAs as a tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1); v3 splits each of those 192 rows into two half-row CTAs to flatten that tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 8).

Once you rule out the full-chip lower bound and tail waves, step into Level 3: Single SM (see Chapter 3) and check four readings in order:

  1. ptxas -v prints each kernel's register count and register-spill byte counts (spill stores / loads). Check first that spilling is 0; the moment it is non-zero, register accesses degrade into round trips to local memory in device memory (see Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 6).
  2. Next, check whether each SM keeps enough bytes in flight. By Little's Law from Chapter 2, Section 3, when all 132 SMs read concurrently, ld.global needs ~64 KiB / SM and TMA needs ~48 KiB / SM (see Chapter 3, Section 4); if only half the SMs are reading, the bytes in flight each SM must keep outstanding double. Both numbers are bandwidth knee points measured at full load; because round-trip latency is shorter under lighter load, falling slightly short of the threshold gives up very little bandwidth. In Chapter 3, Section 9, however, v6 shrank each CTA to 1 warp, dropping bytes in flight all the way to 8.7 KiB / SM and slowing the kernel right down.
  3. Third, open NCU's Memory Workload Analysis panel to check what fraction of bytes in each global memory request is actually used (see Chapter 3, Section 2), and whether shared memory hits bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 7).
  4. Fourth, in the Launch Statistics and Occupancy panels, check the resident CTAs per SM and the achieved occupancy (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

7The Inner Three Levels (Levels 4–6): Which Metric Do We Check on the Scheduler, Execution Pipelines, and SASS?

Check first whether the scheduler has an eligible warp every cycle and what stall reasons dominate; then check which execution pipeline or issue slot is saturated; finally, read the SASS machine code to see whether the compiler inserted drain waits or reordered instructions.

Follow the lower half of Figure 10-3 into Level 4: SMSP Scheduler (see Chapter 4). At a fixed cycle interval, the profiler samples a warp and logs whether it issued an instruction on that cycle or why it could not issue. The share of non-issuing samples attributed to a given reason is its stall sampling share (note that the profiler counts not selected as one of the reasons). In the Scheduler Statistics panel, check the active issue-slot share and the share of cycles with no eligible warp; for the breakdown of stall reasons, check the Warp State panel; and to map stalls back to exact source lines, compile with -lineinfo and open the Source Counters page.

If issue slots are busy and the top warp state is not selected, your warps are already eligible and simply yielded that cycle's issue slot to another warp on the same scheduler (see Chapter 4, Section 1). In that case, skip straight to Level 5. If the no eligible share is high instead, match the top stall reason against the list below:

  • long_scoreboard: warps are waiting for global memory loads to come back, either because per-thread in-flight reads are too shallow or because address math has serial dependencies (see Chapter 4, Section 2). On gemv, the number to watch is average stall cycles per issued instruction: v6 stalls for 12.9 cycles, and v7 drops to 8.1 once we expand per-thread in-flight WWW loads to 8.
  • mio_throttle / short_scoreboard: MIO is the SM's memory input/output instruction queue. It carries shared-memory instructions, special math instructions such as MUFU, and dynamic branches; once it fills up, later instructions have to wait. short_scoreboard means a warp is waiting for the result of an MIO operation—most often a shared-memory load sitting too close to the instruction that uses it, though frequent MUFU or dynamic branches can cause it too. The fix is to separate the producer and consumer instructions (see Chapter 4, Section 2). mio_throttle means the MIO queue itself is full; the fix is to send fewer instructions into that queue or offload work to another pipeline.
  • barrier: warps arrive at the CTA barrier __syncthreads at uneven times (see Primer 3, Section 4). Fix it by balancing the work across warps or switching to a named barrier that waits on only a subset of threads (see Chapter 5, Section 7).
  • wait: NCU defines this as a warp waiting on a fixed-latency execution dependency. Based on public reverse-engineering analyses, the compiler encodes this stall count directly in the instruction's control bits—a format NVIDIA does not document (see Chapter 6, Section 5). The fix is more instruction-level parallelism or a better instruction order. For waits on the asynchronous matrix multiply wgmma.wait_group, see Chapter 5, Section 5. The NCU documentation files stalls on warpgroup wait instructions under warpgroup_arrive; whether WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE is the wait instruction it means was not verified by measurement.

Once you confirm that the scheduler is issuing instructions every cycle, step into Level 5: Execution Pipelines (see Chapter 5). Open NCU's Compute Workload Analysis panel and read the utilization of each physical execution pipeline along with the total executed instruction count:

  • one execution pipeline is near saturation while neighboring pipelines sit idle: rewrite the math on the crowded pipeline into equivalent instructions that run on an idle neighbor (see Chapter 5, Section 1). In the prefill loop of Chapter 7, for example, online softmax pushed the 4-lane SFU to 77.3%, so we offloaded row sums and exponentials onto other pipelines (see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9).
  • no single execution pipeline is saturated, yet issue slots are already busy: now the bottleneck is the issue slots themselves, because each SMSP can issue at most 1 instruction per cycle. Shuffling work between pipelines will not help; you have to cut the total instruction count directly through algebraic folding and packed instructions—which is how we caught the expert epilogue bottleneck in Chapter 8, Section 13.

The classic cautionary tale at this level is gemv v9 from Chapter 5, Section 8: v9 applied a textbook Level 5 fix—breaking the accumulator dependency chain and cutting total executed instructions by ~24%—yet latency did not budge. The Level 2 reading from Section 6 tells you why: v9 was still bottlenecked on memory. Level 5 fixes pay off only after you have cleared Levels 2–4.

Finally, drop down to Level 6: SASS (see Chapter 6, Section 5). Run cuobjdump --dump-sass to read the generated machine code directly, and check three things in particular:

  • Check whether the compiler inserted WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (a drain wait) after every HGMMA. If it did, your async region has collapsed into one-by-one synchronous execution; see Chapter 6, Section 6 for the cause and the ptxas performance warning.
  • Check whether the compiler sank your early read-only prefetch ld.global.nc instructions past the PDL wait instruction from Chapter 1, Section 4, or repeatedly recomputed loop invariants inside the inner loop. Reading SASS is how we caught both rematerialization and instruction sinking in Chapter 8, Section 8.
  • Check whether the consumer of an on-chip ring buffer still has shared-memory loads in flight when it arrives on empty[s]: if so, you have the write-after-read hazard (WAR) from Chapter 3, Section 5. After fixing it, scan the machine code to confirm that every shared-memory load (LDS in SASS) has returned before each arrival.

On the gemv chain, the Level 6 step is v10's in-register 12-bit weight decoding in Chapter 6, Section 7 (see Chapter 6, Section 2 for the decoding instruction sequence).

8Is a Code Segment Truly on the Critical Path, and How Much Can Optimizing It Save at Most?

Skip the candidate code at runtime while keeping the machine code unchanged, and measure the latency delta with paired ABBA benchmarking: if latency stays flat, the main track hides that code; if latency drops, the drop is the maximum speedup you can get from fixing it.

On a GPU, HBM / TMA transfers, Tensor Cores, and ordinary arithmetic pipelines run in parallel along separate tracks (see Chapter 5, Section 1). Whenever a shorter arithmetic or synchronization branch sits completely hidden behind a slower main track, reducing that branch to 0 cycles leaves total runtime completely unchanged (see Chapter 4, Section 1).

How do you test whether a branch is hidden before you spend time rewriting it? Run the perturbation test (ablation test) shown in Figure 10-4: keep the non-zero random inputs unchanged, skip the candidate code behind a runtime parameter switch that compile-time dead-code elimination cannot see through (set to run in the baseline and to skip in the test arm), and measure the CUDA event timing delta with paired ABBA benchmarking. Despite the "ablation" name, it is strictly a runtime skip: the skipped instructions stay right where they are in the machine code, and you do not delete a single line of source.

Why not just delete the code in the source file? Because the moment you delete source lines, ptxas sees a different control-flow graph (see Chapter 6, Section 5) and re-decides loop unrolling and register allocation across the whole kernel—so the compiled binary is no longer the same kernel. Take the expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9: we wanted to know the maximum possible savings from the entry step where consumers gather activations xxx. Deleting that code in source bloated the machine code by ~12% and made the kernel run 23–26 µs slower instead (see Figure 10-4 Mode 3). Once we switched to a runtime skip, the machine-code size stayed identical. At T=256T = 256T=256, even though we derived that the first HGMMA started 5–7 µs earlier, the whole kernel sped up by only a measured 3.11 µs—and that is the speedup upper bound for optimizing this section (see the chart below for each TTT).

A perturbation test gives you one of two outcomes:

The first outcome is total latency unchanged: the candidate branch is completely hidden behind a slower main track, so optimizing it buys you nothing. This book has no example of a runtime skip leaving latency unchanged; the MUFU.TANH experiment below modifies source code and serves only as corroborating evidence. In one version of the Stage 6 expert kernel (Figure 10-4 Mode 1), the activation epilogue used the hardware hyperbolic tangent instruction MUFU.TANH to compute sigmoid(x)=0.5 (1+tanh⁡(x/2))\mathrm{sigmoid}(x) = 0.5\,(1 + \tanh(x / 2))sigmoid(x)=0.5(1+tanh(x/2)). Deleting MUFU.TANH in source code changed total latency by 0.0%, whereas replacing it with a multi-instruction polynomial approximation slowed execution by 0.4%—corroborating indirectly that a single MUFU.TANH likely did not block the critical path. Chapter 8, Section 13 walks through the cycle accounting that shows the epilogue is actually limited by issue-slot instruction count.

The second outcome is total latency decreases, as shown in Figure 10-4 Mode 2 and the chart below. For Stage 5 pooler at T=256T = 256T=256, skipping the final cross-CTA reduction tail step cut latency by ~4.9 µs, setting the speedup upper bound for optimizing that step. Only after confirming that upper bound did we rewrite the tail step as a TMA tile reduction following Chapter 5, Section 7; paired benchmarking measured a 2.66 µs net saving, well within the upper bound.

Here are the trade-offs of a perturbation test:

  • What you gain: you find out whether a code segment is worth optimizing before you spend time rewriting it.
  • What it costs: each suspect code segment requires compiling a separate binary with a runtime conditional switch and running a round of paired ABBA benchmarking; the runtime branch itself adds a few instructions, which sit in both the baseline and test arms and cancel out.
  • When it can mislead: if the skipped code produces data that later steps consume, the resulting corrupted values may steer subsequent code down a different control-flow path or alter power draw and clock frequency (see Section 4). Then the measured delta reflects more than just omitting that segment, and the upper bound is only a rough estimate.

9What Does It Take for a Change to Count as a Real Win?

For a change to count as a real win, it must clear three bars: exceed the noise band under paired ABBA timing, keep the same sign on re-runs, and cause no regressions across all input shapes inside the full layer.

The first rule is: fewer static instructions do not guarantee a speedup; the delta must clear the operator's A/A noise band and keep the same sign on re-runs. In the Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel of Chapter 8, Section 9, rewriting the second-stage writeback to use predicated execution cut the compiler-inserted branch reconvergence instruction BSSY (see Chapter 4, Section 4) from 123 instructions down to 58—more than a 50% reduction. Now look at paired ABBA benchmarking (chart below). At T=256T = 256T=256, the change moved latency by −0.29 µs, while the A/A control arm of two identical copies in the same job differed by +0.25 µs on its own; at T=128T = 128T=128, the change moved latency by +0.05 µs, against +0.14 µs on the control arm. Across both shapes, the measured deltas fall within this kernel's ~±0.4 µs noise band, so we record zero speedup for the change. If you look only at static instruction counts or run only a single pass, you will mistake random jitter for a real speedup.

The second rule is: after winning in an isolated kernel benchmark, a change must be re-tested inside the full layer across all input shapes. A change that wins when you benchmark the kernel in isolation does not necessarily win inside the full layer: SMs that sat idle in isolation may be busy running other kernels on parallel branches, occupancy can shift, and cross-kernel handoffs can slip out of alignment. Chapter 9, Section 7 gives two examples. Offloading the second-wave tiles of qkv_gate made qkv_gate finish earlier; across the whole layer, though, it won only on sliding-window layers and ran slightly slower on full-attention layers where the side-stream kernel competed for SMs, so the final version turns it on for sliding-window layers only. Likewise, whether concurrent stream scheduling wins or loses flips across token counts.

Whenever you report a speedup, state the measurement baseline explicitly: whether it is the isolated single-kernel cold benchmark from Section 2 of this chapter, or the single-layer CUDA Graph replay from Chapter 9, Section 1. Never mix numbers from the two measurement baselines in the same evolution chain.

What does enforcing these two rules cost? Verification time: every change takes at least two rounds of paired ABBA benchmarking plus a full-layer re-run across all input shapes. Small changes whose true gain is smaller than the noise band get filtered out by these rules; whether stacking multiple rejected small changes would clear the noise band was not measured.

10At the End of the Diagnostic Tree: Which Bottlenecks Cannot Be Fixed in Software?

After you walk all six levels of the diagnostic tree, four hardware limits on H200 remain that software can only work around, never eliminate.

  1. Hardware Limit 1: Register file capacity (Level 3). Large-tile matrix-multiplication accumulators sit directly in the vector registers of the 4 warps, sharing each SM's pool of 65,536 32-bit registers with ordinary thread variables (see Chapter 3, Section 1). In Chapter 3, Section 6, we used setmaxnreg to squeeze the producer warpgroup down to 40 registers per thread and give the consumer warpgroups 232 registers per thread just to fit 2 consumer warpgroups. In Chapter 8, Section 9, with 4 consumer warpgroups, no register reallocation could give each consumer thread 232 registers; the compiled kernel ends up with 96 registers per thread.
  2. Hardware Limit 2: 4-warp warpgroup issue (Levels 4–5). Asynchronous matrix multiplication wgmma carries .sync.aligned: all 4 warps in the same warpgroup must execute the same instruction, or behavior is undefined (see Chapter 5, Section 3 and Appendix A, Section 2). In the Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel of Chapter 8, Section 9, 84%–94% of the measured non-issuing stall samples at each HGMMA land on warpgroup_arrive. NCU defines this as a warp stalled on WARPGROUP.ARRIVE or on a warpgroup wait instruction: because a warpgroup MMA acts like a barrier across the 4 schedulers, one late-arriving warp makes the other warps wait. That reading alone cannot tell you whether a warp is waiting for the other warps in its warpgroup or waiting for data.
  3. Hardware Limit 3: 4-bit weight conversion (Level 6). Hopper has no hardware instruction to convert 4-bit floating-point NVFP4 directly into BF16. Unpacking every 8 four-bit weights takes 8 integer instructions, and you still have to multiply the unpacked values by the block scale before feeding them to a Tensor Core instruction (mma.sync in the small-batch kernel, or left operand AAA of RS-mode wgmma in the large-batch persistent kernel; see Chapter 6, Section 3). Of those 8 unpacking instructions, 6 run on the ALU pipeline and 2 run on the FMA pipeline. Whenever decoding takes longer than loading weights and multiplying matrices, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 3).
  4. Hardware Limit 4: Non-contiguous row gather (Level 3). On Hopper, TMA tensor copies come in two modes only: rectangular tiles (tile) and im2col for convolutions, plus cp.async.bulk for 1D contiguous byte copies (see Chapter 3, Section 3 and Appendix B, Item 33). None of them can gather scattered rows by arbitrary row indices in one command. So when Chapter 7, Sections 5–6 read non-contiguous KV rows through a page table, tensor TMA is off the table, and each row has to move on its own: either every thread issues 16 B cp.async copies, or one 1D cp.async.bulk goes out per row. This book's decode and verify kernels do the former (see Chapter 7, Section 5).

Those four limits are the exact four lines inside the endpoint box at the bottom of the diagnostic tree in Figure 10-3 (Readings point to hardware itself → Appendix A).

Takeaway: Get the timing right first, walk the profiler level by level from the outside in, and bound the maximum speedup with a perturbation test before rewriting any code; only a change that clears the noise band and causes no regression inside the full layer counts as a real win.

Next question: Which of these four limits does the next-generation Blackwell (B200) architecture change in hardware, and how? → Appendix A.

Appendix A

Four H200 Hardware Limits That Software Cannot Change: How Does Blackwell (B200) Change Them in Hardware?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10
  • Appendix A: From H200 to B200

Chapter 10, Section 10 left us with four hardware limits on H200 that software cannot change. Below we walk through how the next-generation Blackwell architecture (B200, target architecture sm_100a) changes the hardware at each one, compared against H200 (target architecture sm_90a).

First, let's be clear about one thing: B200 speeds up single-request decode through wider HBM, not through the four on-chip changes below. Dividing the public 8-GPU node spec by 8 gives a single B200 about 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. Counting only the fixed ~9.0 GB of dense and lm_head weights that each GPU reads on every forward pass (see Primer 1, Section 4), the weight-read lower bound drops from ~1.87 ms on H200 to ~1.12 ms. Note that this ratio compares weight-read lower bounds, not full decode latency (the lower bound leaves out the busiest GPU's expert weights and the KV cache; for handoff gaps and tail duration, see Chapter 9, Section 6; for CUDA Graph replay and the 186 cross-GPU collectives, see Chapter 9, Section 8).

All four changes below live on-chip; where they really help is prefill, large-batch verify, large-batch expert computation, and attention loads of non-contiguous KV rows. Every measurement in this book was taken on H200; we did not measure any latencies on B200, so the trade-offs in each section below are derived directly from the PTX specification.

1Can Accumulators Avoid Occupying Vector Registers?

Blackwell adds a dedicated 256 KiB Tensor Memory (TMEM) separate from vector registers, where fifth-generation Tensor Core instructions write their accumulators directly.

Recall the H200 register file capacity limit from Chapter 10, Section 10: with the wgmma tile shape from Chapter 5, Section 3, splitting a 64×25664 \times 25664×256 FP32 accumulator (m64n256k16) evenly across 128 threads takes 64×256/128=64 \times 256 / 128 =64×256/128= 128 registers per thread—eating roughly half of the 255-register per-thread cap for the accumulator alone (Figure A-1, Mode 1, left).

Blackwell solves this by adding a dedicated on-chip TMEM (Tensor Memory), separate from the vector register file (see Figure A-1, Mode 1, right). In the PTX specification, each CTA on sm_100a sees a TMEM of 128 rows × 512 columns of 32-bit cells, so its capacity is:

128×512×4 B=256 KiB128 \times 512 \times 4\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{KiB}128×512×4 B=256 KiB

At runtime, a CTA asks the hardware for TMEM columns with tcgen05.alloc (which blocks if not enough columns are free) and returns them with tcgen05.dealloc when done. The fifth-generation Tensor Core MMA instruction tcgen05.mma places accumulator DDD directly in TMEM: left matrix AAA can come from SMEM or TMEM, and right matrix BBB comes from SMEM. Accumulator DDD no longer occupies the vector register file from Chapter 3, Section 1. This change helps the large-batch persistent wgmma expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9 and the large-tile matrix multiplications in prefill, both of which hit the register quota on H200.

Once the accumulator moves into TMEM, you can spend the freed vector registers on address calculation, prefetching, or higher occupancy. In return, you pay three costs: first, the kernel must explicitly call tcgen05.alloc / tcgen05.dealloc to claim and release TMEM; second, before the epilogue runs, it must pull the results back into general-purpose registers via tcgen05.ld; third, hardware restricts each warp in a warpgroup to accessing only its own 32 rows of TMEM (128 rows split across 4 warps). At small shapes like T=8T = 8T=8, where the accumulator is already small and vector registers are plenty, that extra round trip between TMEM and registers adds overhead for zero gain.

2Can Matrix Multiplication Avoid Requiring 4 Warps to Issue Together?

wgmma requires 4 warps to issue together; tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread.

Chapter 10, Section 10 showed the 4-warp warpgroup issue limit on H200: on Hopper, the accumulator is spread across the registers of all 4 warps (128 threads) in one warpgroup (Figure A-1, Mode 2, left). The wgmma.mma_async instruction carries the .sync.aligned suffix; under the PTX ISA specification, .aligned defines a thread group for each instruction and requires every thread in that group to execute the same instruction—for wgmma.mma_async, all 4 warps in the warpgroup—or behavior is undefined. Before issue, wgmma.fence orders register accesses; after issue, wgmma.wait_group waits for completion (see Chapter 5, Section 5).

Now that the accumulator lives in TMEM (Section 1), Blackwell's tcgen05.mma switches to single-thread issue just like TMA in Chapter 3, Section 3 (Figure A-1, Mode 2, right): launching a matrix multiplication takes only 1 thread in 1 warp issuing 1 instruction. That thread waits on an mbarrier until the data is ready (see Chapter 3, Section 5), while the remaining warps do not have to execute the MMA instruction and can go compute addresses, run activation functions, or move data on their own. This change targets the large-batch persistent wgmma expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9 and the multi-warpgroup matrix multiplications in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 7.

The trade-off is that the single issuing thread has to manage mbarrier waits and completion notifications itself, and you have to repartition work in your kernel code to keep the freed warps busy. Also remember that the warpgroup_arrive stall does not tell you whether warps are waiting for peer warps in the warpgroup or waiting for data; if they are mainly waiting for data, switching to single-thread issue will not remove that wait either. How much each cause contributes was not measured on either H200 or B200.

3Can 4-Bit Weights Avoid Unpacking in Registers?

Blackwell Tensor Cores provide block-scaled MMA instructions, but they require both input matrices to be low-bitwidth floating point; because this model's activations are BF16, using them requires quantizing the activations first.

We saw the 4-bit weight decompression limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: on Hopper, you have to unpack NVFP4 weights with integer instructions in general-purpose registers and multiply by their block scale factors before feeding them into left operand AAA of the Tensor Core instruction (mma.sync for small batches, or RS-mode wgmma in the large-batch persistent kernel; see Figure A-1, Mode 3, left, and Chapter 6, Section 3).

Blackwell's fifth-generation Tensor Core adds the block-scaled MMA instruction tcgen05.mma.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale (see Figure A-1, Mode 3, right). In the PTX specification, both operands AAA and BBB must be 4-bit E2M1 floats, and each carries one UE4M3 (unsigned E4M3) block scale factor per 16 elements. The Tensor Core applies the scales and multiply-accumulates directly in hardware, so no integer unpacking happens in general-purpose registers. That fits the Stage 6 expert computation in Chapter 8, with one catch: this model's expert activations are BF16 (see Primer 2, Section 2). To use this instruction, you must first quantize the activations to NVFP4. The other route is kind::mxf8f6f4 with activations quantized to FP8, but its block scale is one UE8M0 per 32 elements: an 8-bit, exponent-only factor that can only be a power of 2. Quantizing activations changes the numerical results, and this book did not measure that.

Hardware block-scaled MMA cuts out the in-register integer decoding instructions, so the ALU and FMA pipelines spend zero cycles decoding weights. Beyond the activation quantization above, you pay two costs: first, weights and block scale factors must follow the exact block size and memory layout the hardware expects, or else loading weights requires an extra layout permutation; second, this model's NVFP4 weights also carry one tensor scale per tensor (see Chapter 8, Section 1) that this instruction does not apply, so you still have to multiply by it separately in the epilogue. Whether this model's existing weight layout can feed this instruction directly was not measured.

In the T=1T = 1T=1 decode regime on H200, software decoding instructions already hide behind the wait for weight bytes returning from HBM (see Chapter 6, Section 4). Because B200's estimated HBM bandwidth is ~1.67× that of H200, that latency-hiding window shrinks; whether software decoding still stays hidden on B200 was not measured.

4Can TMA Gather Non-Contiguous Rows by Row Index?

Blackwell TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode: a single command specifies 4 row indices, and hardware gathers all 4 rows directly into one SMEM tile.

We saw the non-contiguous row gather limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: here, one row means a 128 B K row or V row. When each page holds only 1 token, those KV rows sit scattered across device memory, so Hopper has to move each row on its own (per-thread cp.async copies, or one 1D cp.async.bulk per row); this book's kernels use per-thread cp.async (see Figure A-1, Mode 4, left, and Chapter 7, Section 5).

On Blackwell, TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode (Figure A-1, Mode 4, right): one TMA command gives the hardware 4 non-contiguous row indices, and TMA gathers all 4 rows and packs them into the same SMEM tile, cutting out the per-thread address math and the string of cp.async instructions. This change targets Stage 2 attention in Chapter 7, Section 5, where decode and verify gather non-contiguous KV rows one row at a time.

With .tile::gather4, gathering non-contiguous rows by row index can also run through single-thread-issued TMA. The catch is that .tile::gather4 supports only 2D tensors, taking a fixed 4 row indices and 1 starting column index each time. Those 4 row indices still have to be read from the page table first: the three-hop pointer wait for page-table lookup in Chapter 7, Section 6 does not change, and gather4 saves only the per-thread issue after the row indices return. Also, each command moves only 4×128 B=512 B4 \times 128\ \mathrm{B} = 512\ \mathrm{B}4×128 B=512 B: by Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3), TMA on H200 needs ~48 KiB in flight per SM (Chapter 3, Section 4), which works out to ~96 commands. B200 has higher bandwidth and needs even more bytes in flight; whether 1 thread can issue commands that fast was not measured.

There are also cases where gather4 does not help: if the number of rows you need to gather is not a multiple of 4, the final request leaves some slots unused; and if each page holds multiple contiguous tokens, the rows within a page are already stored contiguously, so ordinary rectangular-tile TMA per page is all you need.

Takeaway: B200 addresses in hardware the four H200 limits that software can only work around, not remove. That mainly helps prefill, large batches, and non-contiguous row gather in attention; faster single-request decode still comes from wider HBM.

Appendix B

Where Does an Unfamiliar SASS Instruction Come From, Which Hardware Pipeline Does It Use, and Which Level Does It Belong To?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]

At the end of Appendix A, we asked: when you run into an unfamiliar SASS instruction, where does it come from, which hardware pipeline does it use, and which level does it belong to? This appendix covers only instructions whose PTX or source-code forms appear in the main text or figures, and the SASS column gives the mnemonics seen in the disassembly in this book. We group them by function into four quick-reference tables, followed by an alphabetical mnemonic index at the end.

We assign each entry to a level by the hardware it uses, and the "Where used in this book" column points to the section that explains or uses it:

  • Level 1: Grid launch and handoff, and grid-wide synchronization; see Chapter 1.
  • Level 2: Operations that act directly on the central L2 cache or across SMs, including L2 residency hints and prefetching, L2 atomics and reductions, device-wide memory barriers and release/acquire operations, and thread block clusters and DSMEM; see Chapter 2.
  • Level 3: Data paths and resources inside a single SM, including normal global loads and stores through the local SM L1 cache, SMEM, TMA, cp.async, mbarrier, setmaxnreg, and intra-CTA memory fences; see Chapter 3.
  • Level 4: SMSP scheduling, including CTA barriers and warp-level barriers, warp shuffles, warp votes, branches, scoreboard waits, and special-register reads such as clock counters and thread indices; see Chapter 4.
  • Level 5: Execution pipelines and Tensor Core, including FMA, ALU, and SFU arithmetic and transcendental instructions, as well as HMMA, HGMMA, and QGMMA; see Chapter 5.
  • Level 6: Bits and machine code, including bit permutation and packed type conversion, SASS encoding, and group flags encoded in the control bits; see Chapter 6.

1How Do We Dissect and Read a Single SASS Instruction?

A SASS mnemonic combines an opcode with modifier suffixes, followed by operands for the destination register, memory descriptor, and 64-bit address.

Getting from source code to machine code goes through three layers: CUDA C++ → PTX → the 128-bit (16 B) SASS instruction words emitted by ptxas (see Chapter 6, Section 5). Let's take Mode 1 in Figure B-1, LDG.E.EF.128 R8, desc[UR12][R8.64], and break it apart. This instruction is a 16 B-wide streaming global load with an L2 residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4 and Chapter 3, Section 8):

  • LDG: the opcode for a global memory load;
  • .E: an instruction modifier suffix that selects a 64-bit extended address;
  • .EF: a suffix carrying the evict_first eviction priority hint; NVIDIA does not document whether it acts on L1 or L2 (in this book's samples, the PTX specifies both L1::evict_first and an L2 residency policy, while the disassembly shows only one .EF suffix and one desc[URn] operand);
  • .128: each thread loads 128 bits (16 B) at once into four consecutive 32-bit vector registers R8..R11;
  • desc[UR12]: a 64-bit memory descriptor held in uniform register UR. We infer, but have not determined, that it encodes the L2 residency hint from Chapter 2, Section 4 (created with createpolicy in PTX). UR is shared across the entire warp (see Chapter 7, Section 7), and instructions whose mnemonics start with U read and write it;
  • [R8.64]: a 64-bit byte address formed by the register pair R8:R9.

2Why Does One PTX Instruction Not Always Become One SASS Instruction with the Same Name?

ptxas may compile a single PTX instruction into zero standalone instructions, expand it into a multi-instruction sequence, or map it to a different mnemonic and operands.

  • Category 1: No standalone SASS instruction. Take wgmma.commit_group (see Chapter 5, Section 5 and Chapter 6, Section 6): it takes up no separate instruction word in SASS, and is encoded directly as the group flag at the end of the last HGMMA in that batch (see Quick Reference 3, Item 45).
  • Category 2: Expanded into a multi-instruction SASS sequence. A single-warp FP8 matrix multiplication mma.sync … e4m3 on sm_90a first uses F2FP to unpack FP8 into FP16 and then issues 2 back-to-back HMMA instructions (see Quick Reference 3, Item 41). Likewise, the cluster barrier (barrier.cluster.arrive/wait) in Chapter 9, Section 3 compiles into UCGABAR_ARV / UCGABAR_WAIT, and its default form also prepends a device-wide memory barrier (MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR) before the arrival and appends CCTL.IVALL after the wait (see Quick Reference 3, Item 39).
  • Category 3: Renamed mnemonic or encoded as an operand/modifier. Cache modifiers on global loads become suffixes in SASS, and we infer that some go into a descriptor operand. For instance, the load with createpolicy in Chapter 2, Section 4 gets the .EF / .EL suffix in SASS, and we infer, but have not determined, that its L2 policy sits in the desc[URn] operand of LDG (plain loads without hints carry desc[URn] too); see Quick Reference 2, Item 24.

Why the mismatch? Because the PTX specification defines only semantics, not a fixed SASS instruction sequence. NVIDIA has not published hardware details for ERRBAR and CGAERRBAR inside the device-wide memory barrier; this book records only the sequence seen in sm_90a disassembly, so re-check the disassembly whenever you switch compiler versions.

3Quick Reference 1: Arithmetic, Transcendental Functions, and Type Conversions

When you look up an instruction in this group, check first which pipeline it runs on—FMA, ALU, or SFU (see Chapter 5, Section 1). Arithmetic and transcendental functions sit at Level 5, while bit permutation and packed type conversions sit at Level 6.

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes

2 add.f32; mul.f32 FADD, FMUL FMA pipeline · Level 5 Primer 3, Section 4; Chapter 5, Section 1 a+b, a*b, __fadd_rn, __fmul_rn; using __fadd_rn / __fmul_rn stops the compiler from contracting a*b+c into FFMA, at the cost of issuing 1 extra instruction

Both skip the Newton-Raphson iterations and branches of IEEE div.rn.f32, at the cost of lower precision than IEEE standard division

4Quick Reference 2: Global and On-Chip Memory Access and Asynchronous Copy

Here the first question to ask is which path the data takes: LDG / STG moving data in and out of registers through the Load/Store Unit (LSU), LDGSTS writing directly into SMEM while bypassing registers, or TMA initiated by a single thread (for the differences among the three paths, see Chapter 3, Section 3).

Accesses that act directly on L2 sit at Level 2: loads and stores that bypass L1, L2 residency policies, and L2 atomic reductions. Normal global loads and stores through the local SM's L1, along with SMEM, TMA, and cp.async, sit at Level 3.

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes

With PDL enabled, this book infers that the preceding and dependent kernels that overlap with this kernel count too (see Chapter 9, Section 5)

In the PTX specification, .cg is only a weak cache hint; polling a synchronization flag requires ld.relaxed.gpu or ld.acquire.gpu (see Chapter 2, Section 6)

24 createpolicy.fractional .L2::evict_first.b64; ld.global .L1::evict_first .L2::cache_hint LDG.E.EF, LDG.E LSU + L2 · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 2 Inline PTX; this book's samples set both an L1 hint and an L2 residency hint from createpolicy, and the disassembly shows the .EF / .EL suffix plus the desc[URn] operand (we infer, but have not determined, that the L2 policy is encoded in desc[URn]); if the retained data would not be evicted from L2 anyway, adding the hint saves no time (see Chapter 2, Section 4)

If the prefetch comes too early and streaming data evicts the line from L2 before use, the kernel reads HBM one extra time (see Chapter 7, Section 6)
26 ld.local; st.local Not recorded in this book's disassembly LSU → L1 → L2 (backed by global memory) · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 1; Chapter 3, Section 6; Chapter 10, Section 6 Register spilling (ptxas -v reports spill), dynamically indexed local arrays, or uninlined function stack frames; seeing local memory loads and stores means register accesses have degraded into global memory round trips
27 ld.param.*; ld.const LDC SM constant cache · Level 3 Chapter 4, Section 4 (Figure 4-3) Kernel parameters or __constant__ variables; can also load warp-uniform constants directly into uniform registers UR (see Chapter 7, Section 7)
28 ld.shared.b32; ld.shared.v4.b32; st.shared::cta.v4.b32 LDS, LDS.64, LDS.128, LDS.U8, LDS.U16, STS, STS.64, STS.128 LSU → SMEM · Level 3 Primer 3, Section 4; Chapter 3, Section 7 __shared__ array loads and stores; 1-to-1 with bit-width suffixes; when different lanes in the same wave hit the same 4 B bank, the accesses serialize (see Chapter 3, Section 7)
29 cp.async.cg.shared.global [dst],[src],16; cp.async.ca.shared.global LDGSTS.E.BYPASS.128, LDGSTS.E.BYPASS.128.ZFILL, LDGSTS.E, LDGSTS.E.64 LSU (L2 direct write to SMEM) · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 7, Sections 5–6 __pipeline_memcpy_async or inline cp.async; writes directly to SMEM without passing through private registers; .cg (16 B only) compiles into .BYPASS.128 to bypass L1, and zero-filling out-of-bounds elements generates .ZFILL; the cost is that every thread must still compute addresses and issue instructions
30 cp.async.bulk.tensor .2d.shared::cluster.global .mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes Not recorded in this book's disassembly Dedicated in-SM TMA unit · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 6 Inline PTX; 1 thread issues it using 0 data registers, at the cost of constructing a descriptor on the host first, restricted tile shapes, and no support for non-contiguous row gather on Hopper (see Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 10, Section 10)
31 cp.async.bulk.tensor .2d.global.shared::cta .bulk_group; cp.async.bulk.commit_group; cp.async.bulk.wait_group UTMASTG.2D, UTMACMDFLUSH, DEPBAR.LE TMA unit · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 7 Inline PTX; asynchronously writes an SMEM tile back to global memory: the store itself compiles into UTMASTG, commit_group compiles into UTMACMDFLUSH, and waiting for completion compiles into DEPBAR.LE SB0, N; before initiating the writeback, threads must execute fence.proxy.async.shared::cta and complete intra-CTA synchronization (see Chapter 5, Section 7)
32 cp.reduce.async.bulk .tensor.2d.global.shared::cta .add.bulk_group UTMAREDG.2D.ADD, UTMAREDG.3D.ADD TMA unit + global-memory atomic reduction (inferred at L2) · Level 2 Chapter 5, Section 7; Chapter 6, Section 8; Chapter 10, Section 8 Inline PTX; sends an SMEM tile straight to global memory, where hardware adds it in atomically, element by element, without reading the old value back into the SM (we infer this happens at L2; not determined); the cost is non-deterministic floating-point atomic accumulation order (see Chapter 5, Section 7)
33 cp.async.bulk .shared::cluster.global .mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes Not recorded in this book's disassembly TMA unit · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 3 Inline PTX; 1D contiguous byte-stream copy without a tensor descriptor; requires 16 B alignment for both address and byte count, and copying non-contiguous rows requires issuing 1 instruction per row (see Chapter 3, Section 3)

5Quick Reference 3: Barriers, Cluster Shared Memory, and Tensor Core

In this group, producers move data with TMA or st.async and signal arrival through mbarrier in the SM synchronization unit SYNCS, while consumers compute on the Tensor Core with HGMMA / QGMMA (see Chapter 3, Section 5 for mbarrier, Chapter 7, Section 12 for DSMEM, and Chapter 5, Section 5 for wgmma).

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes

35 mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta.b64; mbarrier.arrive.expect_tx .shared::cta.b64 state,[addr],txcount SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64, SYNCS.ARRIVE.TRANS64.A1T0 SYNCS unit · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 5; Chapter 5, Section 6 Inline PTX; a plain arrival carries .A1T0 (arrival count + 1, expected bytes 0), and registering TMA byte counts uses .TRANS64 with a register operand; if a consumer arrives on empty[s] before its shared memory load (LDS) returns, it triggers a write-after-read hazard (WAR) (see Chapter 3, Section 5)
36 mbarrier.try_wait.parity .shared::cta.b64 p,[addr],phase; mbarrier.test_wait SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT, SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64 SYNCS unit · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 5; Chapter 5, Section 6 Inline PTX; try_wait compiles into .TRYWAIT, waits in hardware until the phase bit flips or the wait times out; if the bit has not flipped, @!P BRA retries
37a fence.proxy.async .shared::cta FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S LSU / memory pipeline · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 7 After normal threads finish writing to SMEM, they must execute this async-proxy fence before the async proxy of TMA or wgmma can see the new data
37b fence.proxy.async .global FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G LSU / memory pipeline · Level 3 Chapter 5, Section 7; Chapter 8, Section 11 Bridges the generic proxy and the async proxy within the current thread when normal stores write global memory that TMA (the async proxy; for proxies, see Chapter 3, Section 3) later reads or reduces. On the read side, place it after ld.acquire.gpu and before issuing TMA; for the write-side usage, see Chapter 8, Section 11
38 st.async.shared::cluster .mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes .v4.f32 [ra],{..},[mbar] Not recorded in this book's disassembly Cluster interconnect + remote mbarrier · Level 2 Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 9, Section 3 Inline PTX; writes data into the SMEM of a remote CTA in the same cluster and automatically decrements the expected byte count on the remote mbarrier
39 barrier.cluster.arrive {.relaxed/.release}.aligned; barrier.cluster.wait {.acquire}.aligned MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, UCGABAR_ARV, UCGABAR_WAIT, CCTL.IVALL Cluster barrier unit · Level 2 Chapter 9, Section 3 cooperative_groups::this_cluster().sync() or inline PTX; default cluster.sync() compiles into MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + UCGABAR_ARV (release arrival) and UCGABAR_WAIT + CCTL.IVALL (acquire wait, waiting for prior writes to be acknowledged by L2 and invalidating the local SM L1). Use .relaxed only when data written before the barrier is not read after the barrier, or when data has a separate completion notification (such as st.async with mbarrier); otherwise the barrier no longer guarantees data ordering
40 mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16 .row.col.f32.bf16.bf16.f32 (or .f16) HMMA.16816.F32.BF16, HMMA.16816.F32 Local SMSP Tensor Core · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 3; Chapter 6, Section 3; Chapter 7, Section 2 Inline PTX; 1-to-1, with operands AAA and BBB and accumulator DDD all held in vector registers

42 wgmma.mma_async.sync.aligned .m64n64k16.f32.bf16.bf16 HGMMA.64x64x16.F32.BF16 All 4 Tensor Cores in the SM · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 5 Inline PTX; 1-to-1, with fixed m=64m = 64m=64 and nnn in 8..2568..2568..256 (in steps of 8), reading AAA and BBB from SMEM via uniform-register descriptors gdesc[URn]; the cost is that 4 warps must issue together and accumulators occupy vector registers (see Chapter 10, Section 10)
43 wgmma.mma_async.sync.aligned .m64n32k32.f32.e4m3.e4m3 QGMMA.64x32x32.F32.E4M3.E4M3 All 4 Tensor Cores in the SM · Level 5 Chapter 5, Section 3; Chapter 7, Section 10 Inline PTX; FP8 wgmma compiles into native QGMMA (k=32k = 32k=32; for throughput, see Chapter 5, Section 3), passing left matrix AAA from each warp's vector registers (RS mode; see Chapter 5, Section 3)
44 wgmma.fence.sync.aligned WARPGROUP.ARRIVE Executing unit not documented · Level 4 Chapter 5, Section 5; Chapter 10, Section 10; Appendix A, Section 2 Inline PTX; 1-to-1, executed before the first wgmma, or after normal instructions access accumulator registers (or the register fragments of AAA in RS mode), ordering only accesses to those registers; ordering prior writes to SMEM matrices before wgmma reads requires fence.proxy.async (Item 37a). Because it carries .aligned, all 4 warps of the warpgroup must execute the same instruction; .sync only makes the 32 threads of one warp wait for each other, and PTX does not state whether the 4 warps wait for each other (see Appendix A, Section 2)
45 wgmma.commit_group .sync.aligned HGMMA, QGMMA (with trailing gsb0 flag) Control bits on the last HGMMA / QGMMA · Level 6 Chapter 5, Section 5; Chapter 6, Section 6 Inline PTX; has no standalone SASS instruction and is encoded as the trailing gsb0 group flag on the last HGMMA / QGMMA instruction of that batch

48 stmatrix.sync.aligned .m8n8.x4{.trans}.shared.b16 STSM.16.M88.4, STSM.16.MT88.4, STSM.16.M88, STSM.16.MT88.2 LSU → SMEM · Level 3 Chapter 5, Section 7 Inline PTX; the inverse of ldmatrix, writing accumulator register fragments directly into SMEM in a swizzled layout for subsequent TMA writeback or TMA tile reduction
49 setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned .u32 N; setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned .u32 N USETMAXREG.TRY_ALLOC.CTAPOOL (inc), USETMAXREG.DEALLOC.CTAPOOL (dec) Intra-CTA register-pool allocator in the SM · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 7; Chapter 10, Section 10 Inline PTX; NNN is in 24..25624..25624..256 (a multiple of 8), where dec releases excess producer registers back to the CTA pool and inc claims registers for consumers (blocking when the pool lacks enough registers); requires the entire warpgroup to execute the same instruction (.sync.aligned; see Appendix A, Section 2)

6Quick Reference 4: Warp Operations, Memory Fences, Atomic Operations, Grid Handoff, and Control Flow

The intra-warp collectives SHFL and VOTE sit at Level 4: SHFL is issued by the LSU pipeline to the L1TEX unit (see Chapter 4, Section 5), and for VOTE see Chapter 7, Section 9 and Chapter 8, Section 6. Device-wide memory barriers, L2 atomics, and release/acquire handoffs sit at Level 2 (see Chapter 2, Section 6), while PDL grid handoffs and grid-wide synchronization sit at Level 1 (see Chapter 1, Section 4, Chapter 7, Section 12, and Chapter 8, Section 6).

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes
50 shfl.sync.idx.b32; shfl.sync.bfly.b32; shfl.sync.up.b32; shfl.sync.down.b32 SHFL.IDX, SHFL.BFLY, SHFL.UP LSU → L1TEX shuffle unit · Level 4 Chapter 4, Section 5 __shfl_sync(m,v,lane), __shfl_xor_sync, __shfl_up_sync, __shfl_down_sync; __shfl_xor_sync compiles into .BFLY (butterfly shuffle)
51 vote.sync.ballot.b32; vote.sync.any.pred; vote.sync.all.pred VOTE.ANY Warp vote unit · Level 4 Chapter 7, Section 9; Chapter 8, Section 6 __ballot_sync(m,p) (see Chapter 8, Section 6), __any_sync (see Chapter 7, Section 9), __all_sync; ballot compiles into VOTE.ANY Rd, PT, Ps (returning a 32-bit mask)
52 bar.warp.sync mask WARPSYNC.ALL, WARPSYNC, WARPSYNC.COLLECTIVE, BSSY, BSYNC Warp scheduler reconvergence unit · Level 4 Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9 __syncwarp(mask) or inline bar.warp.sync; a full mask compiles into WARPSYNC.ALL when a standalone instruction is needed (after a structured if already reconverged by BSSY / BSYNC, ptxas may elide WARPSYNC); the compiler automatically inserts the BSSY / BSYNC reconvergence instruction pair around divergent branches (see Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9)
53 bar.sync 0 (i.e., barrier.sync.aligned 0) BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING SM CTA barrier unit · Level 4 Primer 3, Section 4; Chapter 4, Section 4 __syncthreads(); 1-to-1; when warps arrive unevenly, the wait time equals the difference between the latest and earliest arrivals
54 bar.sync id, n; bar.arrive id, n BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING, BAR.ARV SM CTA barrier unit · Level 4 Chapter 5, Section 7; Chapter 7, Section 7 Inline bar.sync id, n, bar.arrive id, n (defaults to .aligned; how a barrier that involves only a subset of the CTA's warps squares with the literal .aligned wording in the specification is not determined in this book; see Appendix A, Section 2); the hardware barrier ID id (0..15) and thread count n are encoded as immediates (see Chapter 5, Section 7; Chapter 7, Section 7), and BAR.ARV arrives without waiting
55 fence.acq_rel.cta; fence.acq_rel.gpu; fence.sc.cta; fence.sc.gpu MEMBAR.ALL.CTA, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, MEMBAR.SC.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, CCTL.IVALL LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 (.cta belongs to Level 3) Chapter 8, Section 11 __threadfence_block() (fence.sc.cta), __threadfence() (same semantics as fence.sc.gpu; in this book's disassembly, inline fence.sc.gpu expands into 4 instructions, MEMBAR.SC.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + CCTL.IVALL; a separate nvrtc build of __threadfence() adds 1 MEMBAR.ALL.CTA in front, 5 in total, and we did not keep its PTX); when you need only acq_rel semantics, write inline fence.acq_rel.cta / fence.acq_rel.gpu. A device-wide memory barrier waits for prior writes to be acknowledged by L2 and invalidates the local SM L1. For one-way producer-consumer handoffs, acq_rel is sufficient; acq_rel does not prevent a store in this thread from reordering with a subsequent load from a different address, whereas when both sides first write their own flag and then read the other side's flag (the Dekker pattern), you need fence.sc to forbid that reordering
56 fence.release.gpu Not recorded in this book's disassembly LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 9, Section 5 Inline PTX; it defines ordering only: it orders this thread's prior reads and writes before subsequent strong writes or griddepcontrol.launch_dependents. A strong write is a store with a memory-ordering qualifier such as st.relaxed; a plain st is a weak write. Making prior writes visible to another thread requires pairing with one of two patterns: a subsequent strong write (such as st.relaxed to a flag paired with an acquire load on the receiving side; see Chapter 2, Section 6), or a griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ordered after it in program order (within the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting; see Chapter 9, Section 5). Supported starting from sm_90
57 atom.global.add.u32; atom.global.add.f32; atom.global.exch; atom.global.inc ATOMG.E.ADD.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.EXCH.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.INC.STRONG.GPU LSU → L2 atomic unit · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 6, Section 8 atomicAdd, atomicExch, atomicCAS, atomicInc, and fetch_add when you use the return value; performs a read-modify-write at L2 and waits for the old value to return, incurring one extra L2 round trip compared to fire-and-forget REDG; as written in Chapter 6, Section 8's kernel, scalar BF16 atomic add compiles down to a compare-and-swap retry loop (Chapter 5, Section 7 covers the paired .bf16x2 form)
58 red.global.add.f32; red.global.add.v4.f32; red.global.add.s32; red.global.min.u64 REDG.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU, REDG.E.ADD.F32.FTZ.RN.STRONG.GPU, REDG.E.ADD.F32x4.FTZ.RN.STRONG.GPU LSU → L2 reduction unit · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 7; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 9, Section 3 atomicAdd(p,v) when you ignore the return value, and vector atomicAdd(float2* / float4*); the compiler automatically lowers these into fire-and-forget REDG (at the cost of not returning the old value)
59 ld.acquire.gpu.global.u32 [a]; red.release.gpu.global.add.s32 [a],v; atom.acq_rel.gpu LDG.E.STRONG.GPU, CCTL.IVALL, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, REDG, ATOMG, ATOM LSU + L2 · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 11 cuda::atomic_ref<int, thread_scope_device> (store / load / fetch_add) or inline ld.acquire.gpu, red.release.gpu; PTX guarantees ordering only; invalidating L1 and waiting for L2 acknowledgment is how the local SM implements it (for coherence at L2 while L1 is non-coherent, see Chapter 2, Section 6): ld.acquire.gpu expands into LDG.E.STRONG.GPU + CCTL.IVALL, and red.release.gpu expands into MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + REDG; when the compiler cannot prove the address is in global space (as with cuda::atomic_ref on a generic pointer), acq_rel fetch_add emits generic-address ATOM.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU bracketed by MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR and CCTL.IVALL
60 griddepcontrol.wait; griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ACQBULK, PREEXIT Hardware grid distributor and SM · Level 1 Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 8, Section 8; Chapter 9, Section 5 cudaGridDependencySynchronize(), cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion(), or inline griddepcontrol (see Chapter 8, Section 8). wait → ACQBULK: blocks until the predecessor grid finishes and its writes are visible. launch_dependents → PREEXIT: once all CTAs issue it or exit, the hardware can schedule the dependent grid. Under the PTX specification, if a predecessor thread executes fence.release.gpu before launch_dependents (with both grids in the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting), its prior writes are visible from the start of the dependent grid; otherwise they are guaranteed to be visible only after the dependent grid executes griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 9, Section 5). Triggering too early makes the dependent grid occupy SMs while it waits idle (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 7, Section 11)
61 Standard library implementation (undocumented; inferred in this book: global atomic counter + device-wide memory barrier + polling + bar.sync) Not recorded in this book's disassembly L2 atomic unit + per-SM polling · Level 1 Chapter 8, Section 6 cooperative_groups::this_grid().sync() (used with cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel); this book infers that the standard library builds it from a CTA barrier, a device-wide memory barrier, and L2 counter polling (which load form the polling uses was not verified); all CTAs of the grid must be co-resident (see Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 6)
62 mov.u64 d, %clock64; mov.u64 d, %globaltimer CS2R Special-register read · Level 4 Chapter 2, Section 2; Chapter 10, Sections 5–6 clock64(), clock(), or inline read of %globaltimer and %clock64; in this book's disassembly, clock64() compiles into CS2R R2, SR_CLOCKLO and a %globaltimer read compiles into CS2R R4, SR_GLOBALTIMERLO, each reading 64 bits in 1 instruction; clock() reads only the 32-bit %clock and is not recorded in this book's disassembly (the minimum step size of %globaltimer is measured at 32 ns; see Chapter 10, Section 5)
63 bra; bra.uni; exit BRA, EXIT, BSSY, BSYNC Branch and issue unit · Level 4 Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9 if / for, return; warp-uniform branches carry .U, whereas divergent branches are bracketed by BSSY ... BSYNC (for the cost of branch divergence, see Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9)
64 mov.u32 %tid.x; mov.u32 %ctaid.x; mov.u32 %ntid.x; mov.u32 %nctaid.x S2R, R2UR Special registers and uniform register file · Level 4 Primer 3, Section 3; Chapter 7, Section 7 threadIdx.x, blockIdx.x, blockDim.x, gridDim.x; S2R reads into a per-thread vector register R, and R2UR copies a vector register value into a uniform register UR shared across the entire warp (see Chapter 7, Section 7)

Takeaway: When you spot an unfamiliar SASS instruction, look up its mnemonic in this appendix to see what source pattern produced it, which pipeline it runs on, which level it belongs to, and which section of this book uses it. To trace an instruction back to a specific source line, compile with -lineinfo and check the source view in NCU (see Chapter 10, Section 7).
